questions.stem: The compound in Portland cement chiefly responsible for the EARLY strength (up to 7 days) is:
options: Tricalcium silicate (C₃S)
Dicalcium silicate (C₂S)
Tricalcium aluminate (C₃A)
Tetracalcium alumino-ferrite (C₄AF)
questions.solution:
**Tricalcium silicate, C₃S (alite).**

**The four Bogue compounds and what each contributes:**

| Compound | Name | Typical % | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C₃S — tricalcium silicate** | **ALITE** | **45-55** | **EARLY strength, up to about 7 days; substantial heat** ← |
| **C₂S — dicalcium silicate** | **BELITE** | **20-30** | **LATER strength, from 7 days to a year and beyond; LOW heat** ← |
| **C₃A — tricalcium aluminate** | **CELITE** | **8-12** | **FLASH SET if uncontrolled; the HIGHEST heat; the most vulnerable to SULPHATE attack** ← |
| **C₄AF — tetracalcium alumino-ferrite** | **FELITE** | **6-10** | **Little strength; gives the GREY COLOUR** ← |

> **The two silicates together supply nearly all the strength, and the division between them is the essential fact: C₃S is FAST, C₂S is SLOW, and the balance between them determines how a cement develops.**

| Age | Strength contributed mainly by |
|---|---|
| **1 to 7 days** | **C₃S** ← |
| **7 to 28 days** | **C₃S, with C₂S beginning** |
| **28 days to 1 year and beyond** | **C₂S** ← |

> **The ultimate strengths of the two are comparable; they differ in the RATE at which they are reached.**

**How the proportions are varied to make the different cements:**

| Cement | C₃S | C₂S | C₃A | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ordinary Portland (OPC 33/43/53)** | **Normal** | Normal | Normal | General use |
| **RAPID HARDENING** | **RAISED, and ground FINER** ← | Reduced | — | **Early formwork striking; cold weather; precast** |
| **LOW HEAT** | **REDUCED** | **RAISED** ← | **REDUCED** ← | **MASS concrete — dams, thick rafts** |
| **SULPHATE RESISTING (SRC)** | — | — | **REDUCED below 5 %** ← | **Sulphate-bearing soils and groundwater** |
| **White cement** | — | — | — | **C₄AF minimised — it is what makes cement grey** ← |

> **The LOW HEAT and SULPHATE RESISTING rows show the same lever used for different ends, and both act on C₃A because it is the compound responsible for both the heat and the sulphate vulnerability.**

> **Reducing C₃A therefore cures two problems at once — and the cost is a slower early strength gain, since the same change reduces the early reaction generally.**

**Why C₃A must be controlled at all — the role of GYPSUM:**

> **C₃A reacts with water almost instantly. Left alone it would cause a FLASH SET: the cement would stiffen within minutes of mixing and be unusable.**

> **GYPSUM (calcium sulphate) is therefore interground with the clinker, at 3 to 5 per cent. It reacts with C₃A to form ETTRINGITE, a coating that armours the C₃A grains and delays their reaction until the silicates have begun.**

| Gypsum content | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **TOO LITTLE** | **FLASH SET — rapid, irreversible stiffening with heat evolved** ← |
| **CORRECT (3-5 %)** | **Normal setting: initial set not before 30 minutes, final set not after 600 minutes** ← |
| **TOO MUCH** | **Unsoundness — DELAYED expansion as ettringite forms later in the hardened paste** ← |

> **FLASH SET must be distinguished from FALSE SET, which is a different phenomenon with an opposite remedy:**

| | FLASH SET | FALSE SET |
|---|---|---|
| **Cause** | **Uncontrolled C₃A hydration** | **Dehydration of the gypsum during grinding, which then re-crystallises** ← |
| **Heat evolved** | **YES, considerable** ← | **NO** ← |
| **Reversible?** | **NO — the concrete is lost** ← | **YES — further mixing WITHOUT adding water restores workability** ← |

> **The practical rule follows directly: stiffening WITHOUT heat is a false set and is cured by continued mixing, and ADDING WATER at that moment is the error to avoid — it would raise the water-cement ratio permanently to fix a problem that mixing alone would have solved.**

**The HEAT OF HYDRATION, since it follows the same compounds:**

| Compound | Heat of hydration (J/g) |
|---|---|
| **C₃A** | **866 — by far the highest** ← |
| **C₃S** | **502** |
| **C₄AF** | **419** |
| **C₂S** | **260 — the lowest** ← |

> **In MASS concrete the heat cannot escape, so the interior rises in temperature while the surface cools — and the resulting differential produces THERMAL CRACKING.**

> **The controls follow from the table and from the mix: use low-heat cement, replace part of the cement with FLY ASH or SLAG, reduce the total cement content, pre-cool the aggregates or use ice as mixing water, place in shallow lifts, and embed cooling pipes in the largest pours.**

> **The temperature DIFFERENTIAL rather than the absolute temperature is what cracks the concrete, so insulating the surface to keep it warm is as effective as cooling the core — which is counter-intuitive and is standard practice.**

examTip.trick: **C₃S (alite) = EARLY strength; C₂S (belite) = LATER strength; C₃A = flash set, most HEAT, sulphate vulnerability; C₄AF = the grey COLOUR.** Their ultimate strengths are similar — they differ in RATE.
examTip.trap: **FLASH set (C₃A, WITH heat, irreversible) versus FALSE set (dehydrated gypsum, NO heat, reversible by mixing).** Adding water to a false set is the error — it permanently raises the w/c to fix what mixing alone would cure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Low-heat and sulphate-resisting cements both work by cutting C₃A** — one compound causing both problems. And in mass concrete it is the temperature DIFFERENTIAL that cracks, so insulating the surface works as well as cooling the core.

questions.stem: The FINENESS MODULUS of a fine aggregate is found to be 2.6. This sand would be classified as:
options: Very fine sand
Fine sand
Medium sand
Coarse sand
questions.solution:
**FINE sand.**

**The classification by fineness modulus:**

| Fineness modulus | Classification |
|---|---|
| **2.2 to 2.6** | **FINE sand** ← |
| **2.6 to 2.9** | **MEDIUM sand** |
| **2.9 to 3.2** | **COARSE sand** |
| **Below 2.2** | Very fine — generally unsuitable alone |
| **Above 3.2** | Too coarse for most concrete work |

> **A value of 2.6 sits at the boundary and is conventionally taken as fine sand — and the useful working range for concrete sand is 2.2 to 3.2, with 2.6 to 3.0 preferred for most mixes.**

**How the fineness modulus is computed, since the definition explains what it means:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Sieve the sample through the standard set: 80 mm, 40, 20, 10 mm, then 4.75, 2.36, 1.18 mm, 600, 300, 150 µm** ← |
| **2** | **Find the CUMULATIVE percentage RETAINED on each sieve** ← |
| **3** | **SUM those cumulative percentages** |
| **4** | **DIVIDE by 100** ← |

> **A worked example for a fine aggregate:**

| Sieve | % retained | CUMULATIVE % retained |
|---|---|---|
| **4.75 mm** | **2** | **2** |
| **2.36 mm** | **8** | **10** |
| **1.18 mm** | **20** | **30** |
| **600 µm** | **25** | **55** |
| **300 µm** | **30** | **85** |
| **150 µm** | **13** | **98** |
| **Pan** | 2 | — |
| **SUM of cumulative % retained** | — | **280** ← |
| **FINENESS MODULUS** | **280/100** | **2.80 — a MEDIUM sand** ← |

> **What the number means physically: a HIGHER fineness modulus indicates a COARSER aggregate, because more material is retained on the upper sieves and each retention is counted on every sieve below it.**

> **The relation being inverse to the name is the point most often inverted — "fineness modulus" rises as the material gets COARSER.**

**Why it matters — the effect on the concrete:**

| Sand too FINE (low FM) | Sand too COARSE (high FM) |
|---|---|
| **Very large SURFACE AREA, so MORE WATER is needed for the same workability** ← | Less water needed |
| **More cement needed to maintain the water-cement ratio** ← | Economical |
| **Higher SHRINKAGE and creep** | Lower |
| **A cohesive, sticky mix** | **HARSH, prone to SEGREGATION and BLEEDING** ← |
| **Good finishing surface** | **Poor finish; honeycombing** ← |
| **Uneconomical** | Difficult to place |

> **The SURFACE AREA argument in the first row is the mechanism behind nearly all of this and is worth grasping: water demand is governed by the total surface that must be wetted and lubricated.**

> **Halving the particle size DOUBLES the surface area for the same volume, so a fine sand demands markedly more water — and the extra water becomes capillary porosity, lowering strength and durability.**

> **That is why a sand's grading, not merely its cleanliness, is a strength issue.**

**GRADING ZONES, which are the more useful specification in practice:**

> **IS 383 classifies fine aggregate into four grading zones, Zone I (coarsest) to Zone IV (finest), by the percentage passing each sieve.**

| Zone | Character | Suitability |
|---|---|---|
| **Zone I** | **Coarsest** | Suitable; needs a richer mix or more fines |
| **Zone II** | **The reference grading** ← | **The most suitable for general concrete** |
| **Zone III** | Finer | Suitable, with adjustment |
| **Zone IV** | **Finest** | **NOT suitable for reinforced concrete unless tested and mix-designed specifically** ← |

> **The 600 µm sieve is the one that principally distinguishes the zones, and a sand's zone is checked against it first.**

> **The practical value of the zoning is that a mix design is quoted for Zone II and CORRECTED for the others — so a sand from a different zone is not rejected but adjusted for, by changing the fine-to-coarse proportion.**

**And the properties of aggregate that sit alongside grading:**

| Property | Requirement / typical value |
|---|---|
| **Silt and clay content (fine aggregate)** | **Maximum 3 % by weight; checked on site by the FIELD SILT TEST in a measuring jar** ← |
| **Deleterious materials — coal, lignite, shale, organic matter** | Limited; organic impurities test by sodium hydroxide colour |
| **Bulking of sand** | **Damp sand BULKS by 20-30 % in volume at 4-6 % moisture — critical for volume batching** ← |
| **Specific gravity** | 2.6 to 2.8 for normal aggregate |
| **Water absorption** | Below 2 % typically; must be allowed for in the mix water |
| **Flakiness and elongation index** | **Maximum 15 % (combined 40 %) — flaky particles reduce workability and strength** ← |
| **Impact / crushing value** | Maximum 30 % for wearing surfaces, 45 % otherwise |
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | Maximum 30 % for pavements |

> **THE BULKING OF SAND deserves the emphasis it is given because it silently ruins volume-batched concrete:**

> **Damp sand's particles are held apart by films of water, so the same weight occupies up to 30 per cent more volume. A box measured full of damp sand therefore contains far less sand than intended.**

> **The mix becomes deficient in fine aggregate and correspondingly over-rich in cement and water — a rich, harsh, expensive and often weaker concrete.**

> **The remedies are to measure the bulking (fill a container with damp sand, then saturate it and measure the drop) and to increase the sand volume accordingly, or to batch BY WEIGHT, in which case bulking is irrelevant entirely.**

> **Curiously, the bulking is greatest at moderate moisture and disappears when the sand is fully SATURATED — because the water films merge and the particles pack together again. So both dry and flooded sand measure correctly, and only damp sand misleads.**

examTip.trick: **FM = (sum of cumulative % retained)/100.** Fine 2.2-2.6, medium 2.6-2.9, coarse 2.9-3.2. A HIGHER fineness modulus means a COARSER sand — the relation is inverse to the name.
examTip.trap: **A finer sand needs MORE water** (greater surface area to wet), which becomes capillary porosity and lowers strength. Grading is a strength issue, not only a workability one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Damp sand BULKS 20-30 %, ruining volume batching** — greatest at moderate moisture and ZERO when fully saturated or fully dry. Batching by WEIGHT removes the problem entirely.

questions.stem: In a lime mortar, HYDRAULIC lime differs from FAT lime in that hydraulic lime:
options: Is obtained by burning pure limestone
Slakes vigorously with a large increase in volume
Contains clay impurities and can set under water
Is used only for whitewashing
questions.solution:
**It contains CLAY impurities and can SET UNDER WATER.**

**The classification of limes:**

| Lime | Clay content | Setting | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FAT lime (pure, rich, white, high-calcium)** | **Under 5 %** | **Sets by CARBONATION — absorbing CO₂ from the air; needs AIR, will not set under water** ← | **Plastering, whitewashing, mortar for ordinary masonry** |
| **HYDRAULIC lime — feebly, moderately or eminently** | **5-10 %, 11-20 %, 21-30 %** ← | **Sets by HYDRATION (like cement) as well as carbonation; SETS UNDER WATER** ← | **Masonry in damp conditions; foundations; thick walls** |
| **Poor lime (lean)** | **Above 30 %** | Sets poorly | Inferior work only |

> **The CLAY is what makes the difference: on burning, the clay's silica and alumina combine with the lime to form calcium silicates and aluminates — the same compounds as in Portland cement, in smaller quantity.**

> **Those compounds hydrate with water rather than needing atmospheric CO₂, which is precisely why hydraulic lime sets under water and fat lime cannot.**

> **The name follows from that property: HYDRAULIC means "setting in the presence of water", and it applies to hydraulic lime, to Portland cement and to pozzolanic mixtures for the same reason.**

**The properties compared, since they diverge in every respect:**

| Property | FAT lime | HYDRAULIC lime |
|---|---|---|
| **Colour** | **Pure WHITE** | Greyish, brownish |
| **SLAKING** | **VIOLENT, with much heat and a volume increase of 2 to 2.5 times** ← (option b) | **SLOW and sluggish; small volume increase** ← |
| **Setting** | **SLOW — carbonation may take months, and proceeds inward from the surface** ← | **Faster; hydraulic set within days** |
| **Strength** | **LOW** | **Higher, rising with the clay content** |
| **Plasticity and workability** | **EXCELLENT — very smooth and workable** ← | Less plastic |
| **Setting under water** | **NEVER** ← | **YES** ← |
| **Keeps in storage** | Poorly | Poorly — both absorb moisture |

> **Option (b) describes FAT lime's characteristic violent slaking, which makes it a well-made distractor — it is a real and distinctive property of the OTHER lime.**

**The lime cycle, which is one of the oldest processes in construction and is worth stating in full:**

| Step | Reaction | Name |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — CALCINATION (burning at 900-1000 °C)** | **CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂↑** | **Limestone becomes QUICKLIME** ← |
| **2 — SLAKING (adding water)** | **CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + HEAT** | **Quicklime becomes SLAKED (hydrated) lime** ← |
| **3 — CARBONATION (in the wall, over months)** | **Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O** | **Back to limestone** ← |

> **The cycle is CLOSED: the material ends as the same calcium carbonate it began as, having absorbed back exactly the carbon dioxide driven off in the kiln.**

> **That is a genuinely notable property and it is the basis of lime's revival in conservation and low-carbon construction — although the fuel burnt in calcination is not recovered, so the cycle is closed in chemistry and not in energy.**

> **QUICKLIME requires real care in handling: slaking is violently exothermic, the temperature can exceed 150 °C, and it can boil, spit and ignite adjacent combustible material. It burns skin and eyes severely, and it must be stored absolutely dry — quicklime that slakes in a store from atmospheric moisture has caused fires.**

**Why lime is still used at all, given that cement is stronger:**

| Advantage of lime | Note |
|---|---|
| **WORKABILITY and water retention** | **A lime mortar is far more plastic; masons prefer it** ← |
| **It is WEAKER than the units — as a mortar should be** | **Cracks run in the repairable joint, not through the brick or stone** ← |
| **AUTOGENOUS HEALING** | **Free lime dissolves and re-deposits, sealing fine cracks over time** ← |
| **It ACCOMMODATES MOVEMENT** | **Settlement and thermal movement are absorbed by many fine cracks rather than a few large ones** ← |
| **BREATHABILITY — high vapour permeability** | **Moisture escapes through the joint rather than being trapped in the units** ← |
| **Essential in CONSERVATION** | **Cement mortar in historic soft masonry destroys the units** ← |
| **Lower embodied carbon; and carbonation reabsorbs CO₂** | — |

> **The BREATHABILITY point is the one that decides conservation practice: a wall repointed in cement cannot release moisture through its joints, so the water is driven out through the FACE OF THE STONE instead.**

> **Salts crystallise there, the stone face spalls, and the repointing that was meant to protect the wall destroys it — slowly, over a decade or two, and irreversibly.**

> **That is why lime mortar is not a matter of authenticity or tradition in historic work but of physics, and why cement pointing on old masonry is regarded as damage rather than repair.**

**And the related material, SURKHI, since it appears with lime in this syllabus:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **Finely ground BURNT CLAY — powdered brick or specially burnt clay** ← |
| **What it does** | **A POZZOLANA: it reacts with the free lime, Ca(OH)₂, to form cementitious compounds** ← |
| **Effect** | **Gives HYDRAULIC properties to a FAT lime** ← |
| **Traditional use** | **Lime-surkhi mortar — the standard mortar of Mughal and colonial construction in the subcontinent** ← |

> **So surkhi achieves by ADDITION what hydraulic lime achieves by the limestone's own clay content — and the reaction is the same pozzolanic reaction met later in fly ash and silica fume.**

> **Lime-surkhi mortars in structures several centuries old are frequently found in excellent condition, which is a reasonable argument for the durability of the combination and a caution against assuming that stronger always means longer-lasting.**

examTip.trick: **Clay content is the whole distinction: fat lime under 5 % (sets by CARBONATION, needs air), hydraulic 5-30 % (sets by HYDRATION, works under water).** Option (b) is fat lime's violent slaking.
examTip.trap: **The lime cycle is CLOSED in chemistry — carbonation reabsorbs exactly the CO₂ driven off in the kiln** — but not in ENERGY, since the fuel burnt is not recovered.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cement pointing on historic masonry traps moisture, which then escapes through the STONE FACE and spalls it** — the repair destroys the wall. Lime's breathability is physics, not authenticity. And SURKHI (ground burnt clay) makes a fat lime hydraulic by pozzolanic reaction.

questions.stem: SEASONING of timber is carried out principally to:
options: Reduce the moisture content to a level in equilibrium with its service environment
Increase the timber's natural durability against insects
Darken the colour of the timber for appearance
Increase the timber's cross-sectional dimensions
questions.solution:
**To reduce the MOISTURE CONTENT to a level in equilibrium with the environment in which the timber will be used.**

**Why it matters — the moisture content figures:**

| Condition | Moisture content |
|---|---|
| **GREEN (freshly felled) timber** | **50 to 200 per cent of the dry weight — it can hold more water than wood** ← |
| **FIBRE SATURATION POINT** | **About 25 to 30 per cent — the cell WALLS are saturated but the cavities are empty** ← |
| **Air-dried timber** | **12 to 18 per cent** |
| **Kiln-dried for interior joinery** | **8 to 12 per cent** ← |
| **Timber in a heated interior** | **6 to 10 per cent** |

> **THE FIBRE SATURATION POINT IS THE CRITICAL THRESHOLD IN ALL TIMBER BEHAVIOUR, and it is worth being precise about:**

| Above the FSP | Below the FSP |
|---|---|
| **The water is FREE water in the cell cavities** | **The water is BOUND water in the cell walls** ← |
| **Losing it causes NO shrinkage** ← | **Losing it causes SHRINKAGE** ← |
| **Strength does NOT change** ← | **Strength INCREASES as it dries** ← |

> **So drying from 150 per cent to 30 per cent changes neither the dimensions nor the strength; drying from 30 per cent to 12 per cent shrinks the timber and roughly DOUBLES its strength.**

> **Everything that matters about seasoning happens below the fibre saturation point, which is why that number is the one to remember.**

**What seasoning achieves:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **DIMENSIONAL STABILITY** | **The shrinkage happens BEFORE the timber is worked and fixed, not after** ← |
| **Increased STRENGTH and stiffness** | **Roughly doubled from green to 12 per cent** ← |
| **Reduced weight** | Easier handling and transport |
| **Resistance to FUNGAL DECAY** | **Fungi need above about 20 per cent moisture; dry timber cannot rot** ← |
| **It takes PAINT, POLISH and GLUE** | **None of which adhere to wet timber** ← |
| **It can be treated with PRESERVATIVE** | **Preservative will not penetrate water-filled cells** ← |

> **The FOURTH row is the answer to option (b)'s suggestion: seasoning does not change the timber's natural durability, but it does remove the moisture that decay organisms require, and it enables the preservative treatment that provides real protection.**

> **So seasoning protects against decay INDIRECTLY, and the direct protection is a separate process.**

**The ANISOTROPIC shrinkage, which is why unseasoned timber distorts:**

| Direction | Shrinkage from green to oven-dry |
|---|---|
| **LONGITUDINAL (along the grain)** | **0.1 to 0.3 % — negligible** ← |
| **RADIAL (toward the pith)** | **2 to 6 %** |
| **TANGENTIAL (around the growth rings)** | **4 to 12 % — roughly TWICE the radial** ← |

> **THE TANGENTIAL-TO-RADIAL RATIO OF ABOUT 2:1 IS WHAT CAUSES EVERY DISTORTION DEFECT, and the reasoning is worth following because it explains all of them at once:**

> **Since a board shrinks about twice as much around the rings as across them, it cannot dry without changing shape — unless the rings happen to run straight across the section.**

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **CUPPING — the board curves across its width** | **The face nearer the bark shrinks tangentially more than the face nearer the pith; boards cup AWAY from the heart** ← |
| **BOWING — curvature along the length** | Uneven drying face to face |
| **SPRINGING — edgewise curvature** | Uneven drying edge to edge |
| **TWISTING / WARPING** | **Spiral or interlocked grain** ← |
| **CHECKS and SPLITS** | **The surface dries and shrinks while the interior is still wet — surface TENSION cracks** ← |
| **CASE HARDENING** | **The surface sets in tension while the core is still wet; the board later distorts violently when re-sawn** ← |
| **HONEYCOMBING** | **Internal splits from drying too fast — invisible from outside** ← |

> **The last two are DEFECTS OF SEASONING rather than of the timber, and both are caused by drying too quickly — which is why kiln schedules are gradual and controlled rather than simply hot.**

> **QUARTER-SAWN timber, cut so that the growth rings run roughly perpendicular to the face, exploits the ratio deliberately: the width then shrinks only radially, so the board stays flat.**

> **It is more expensive because it wastes more of the log, and it is used where stability matters most — flooring, joinery, musical instruments — which is a good illustration of a material property directly determining a manufacturing method.**

**The methods of seasoning:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **NATURAL / AIR seasoning** | **Stacked with SPACERS (stickers) under a roof with free air movement; 1 year per 25 mm of thickness is the rule of thumb** ← |
| **KILN seasoning** | **Controlled temperature, humidity and air flow; DAYS instead of years; reaches lower moisture contents than air drying can** ← |
| **Water seasoning** | Sap displaced by immersion, then air dried |
| **Boiling / steaming** | Rapid, but reduces strength somewhat |
| **Chemical (salt) seasoning** | Surface treated with a hygroscopic salt to slow surface drying |
| **Electrical / microwave** | Rapid, costly, small sections |

> **The ONE YEAR PER 25 MM rule for air seasoning is the figure worth carrying, and it explains why kilns exist: a 100 mm beam needs four years of air drying, which is an impossible constraint on a construction programme.**

> **And the essential detail of air seasoning is in the word STICKERS — the spacers between layers that allow air to circulate.**

> **Timber stacked in solid contact does not dry; it develops sticker marks, staining and fungal growth on the contact faces, and the pile may be ruined while appearing to be seasoning properly.**

examTip.trick: **Reduce moisture to equilibrium with service conditions** — green 50-200 %, air-dried 12-18 %, kiln-dried joinery 8-12 %.
examTip.trap: **The FIBRE SATURATION POINT (25-30 %) is the threshold for everything.** ABOVE it, drying changes neither dimensions nor strength; BELOW it, the timber shrinks and roughly DOUBLES in strength.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tangential shrinkage is about TWICE the radial** — which alone explains cupping, and why QUARTER-SAWN boards stay flat. Air seasoning takes about 1 YEAR PER 25 mm, which is why kilns exist. And always stack with STICKERS.

questions.stem: In brick masonry, the vertical joints in consecutive courses must NOT come one above the other. This requirement is met by:
options: Providing proper bond by lapping the bricks
Increasing the mortar strength
Using a thicker mortar joint
Soaking the bricks before laying
questions.solution:
**By providing proper BOND — lapping the bricks so that the vertical joints are staggered.**

**Why continuous vertical joints are unacceptable:**

| Consequence of an unbroken vertical joint | Note |
|---|---|
| **The wall becomes a set of INDEPENDENT COLUMNS rather than one wall** ← | **Each strip carries only its own load and buckles independently** |
| **No LATERAL DISTRIBUTION of a concentrated load** ← | **A point load spreads through a bonded wall at about 45°; through an unbonded one it does not spread at all** |
| **A CONTINUOUS PLANE OF WEAKNESS** | **A crack, once started, runs the full height with nothing to arrest it** ← |
| **Greatly reduced resistance to lateral load and to buckling** | Critical in seismic areas |

> **The SECOND row is the clearest way to see the purpose of bond: bonded masonry behaves as a single monolithic element because each brick ties the courses on either side of it together.**

> **The MINIMUM LAP is a QUARTER of a brick's length, and it is achieved by introducing a QUEEN CLOSER — a brick cut lengthwise in half along its width — next to the quoin (corner) header.**

**The principal bonds:**

| Bond | Arrangement | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **STRETCHER bond (running bond)** | **All stretchers; lap of half a brick** | **Only for HALF-BRICK (110 mm) walls — partitions, leaves of a cavity wall** ← |
| **HEADER bond** | **All headers; lap of half a header** | **For ONE-BRICK walls; also for curved work, where it follows a curve better** ← |
| **ENGLISH bond** | **Alternate courses of headers and stretchers** ← | **The STRONGEST bond; the standard for structural walls** ← |
| **FLEMISH bond** | **Headers and stretchers ALTERNATING in the SAME course** ← | **Better APPEARANCE; slightly weaker; more cut bricks (bats)** ← |
| **Double Flemish** | Flemish appearance on BOTH faces | More expensive |
| **Single Flemish** | **Flemish face, English backing — appearance outside, strength within** ← | A practical compromise |
| **Garden wall, raking, herringbone, zigzag, facing bonds** | Decorative or specialised | — |

> **ENGLISH against FLEMISH is the comparison that carries the point:**

| | ENGLISH | FLEMISH |
|---|---|---|
| **STRENGTH** | **GREATER — the preferred structural bond** ← | About 10 % less |
| **APPEARANCE** | Plainer | **More attractive** ← |
| **Cut bricks (bats) required** | **Fewer** ← | **More — hence more waste and labour** |
| **Economy** | **More economical** | Less |
| **Where used** | **Structural walls, engineering work** | **Exposed facework where appearance matters** |

> **The rule that follows is the one to remember: ENGLISH FOR STRENGTH, FLEMISH FOR APPEARANCE — and SINGLE FLEMISH gets both, with a Flemish face and an English backing.**

> **Flemish bond is weaker precisely because it contains more bats, and a bat contributes less to the bond than a whole brick — so the aesthetic advantage is bought with a structural cost.**

**The general rules of good bonding:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vertical joints in alternate courses must be in the SAME vertical line** | The pattern must repeat |
| **The LAP must be at least one QUARTER of a brick length** | Achieved by the queen closer |
| **Bricks must be of UNIFORM size** | **A bond depends on the modular relationship of length to width** ← |
| **The brick's LENGTH must equal twice its WIDTH plus one joint** | **190 = 2 × 90 + 10 — which is what makes bonding possible at all** ← |
| **Use whole bricks wherever possible; minimise bats** | Bats weaken and waste |
| **The wall must be raised UNIFORMLY; no part more than one metre above another** | **Uneven raising causes differential settlement and cracking** ← |
| **Where a break is unavoidable, use RAKING BACK, not toothing** | ← see below |

> **THE MODULAR RELATIONSHIP in the fourth row is the geometric fact on which the entire subject rests, and it is worth stating explicitly:**

> **A standard modular brick is 190 × 90 × 90 mm, and with a 10 mm joint it becomes 200 × 100 × 100 — so its nominal length is exactly TWICE its nominal width.**

> **That 2:1 relationship is what allows headers and stretchers to be combined in the same course and the courses to align — and a brick of arbitrary proportions could not be bonded at all.**

> **RAKING BACK against TOOTHING deserves the closing note: where work must be stopped and continued later, the wall should be stepped back gradually (raking back) rather than left with alternate bricks projecting (toothing).**

> **Toothed work is difficult to fill properly, the mortar in the vertical joints cannot be compacted, and a line of weakness results — so raking back is specified even though toothing looks like the tidier junction.**

examTip.trick: **Bond — lapping the bricks so vertical joints stagger, minimum lap a QUARTER brick, achieved with a QUEEN CLOSER at the quoin.** Without it the wall is a set of independent columns.
examTip.trap: **ENGLISH is the STRONGEST bond; FLEMISH looks better but is ~10 % weaker** because it contains more BATS. Single Flemish gets both: Flemish face, English backing.
examTip.mnemonic: **190 = 2 × 90 + 10 — a brick's length is exactly twice its width plus a joint**, and that 2:1 modular relationship is what makes bonding possible at all. And stop work by RAKING BACK, never toothing.

questions.stem: The purpose of providing a DAMP PROOF COURSE (DPC) at plinth level in a building is to prevent:
options: Rain water entering through the roof
Condensation on the internal wall surfaces
Rising damp from the ground moving up the walls by capillary action
Lateral seepage through the basement retaining wall
questions.solution:
**Rising DAMP — ground moisture drawn UP the walls by CAPILLARY ACTION.**

**The mechanism the DPC interrupts:**

> **Masonry is a network of fine pores, and fine pores draw water upward against gravity by capillarity — the finer the pore, the higher the rise.**

> **A wall standing in damp ground therefore acts as a wick, and moisture climbs until the rate of evaporation from the wall's face equals the rate at which it is drawn up.**

| Wall | Typical height of rise |
|---|---|
| **Dense engineering brick** | **0.3 to 0.6 m** |
| **Ordinary brickwork** | **0.5 to 1.2 m** ← |
| **Porous stone or soft brick** | **Up to 1.5 m and more** ← |
| **A wall whose face is sealed with cement render or a plastic paint** | **HIGHER still — the evaporation is blocked, so the water rises further to find a surface** ← |

> **The LAST ROW is the counter-intuitive and practically important one: SEALING THE FACE OF A DAMP WALL MAKES THE DAMP RISE HIGHER.**

> **The water has to leave somewhere. Blocking its escape at the bottom of the wall simply moves the problem up, and it often reappears above the render as a worse damp patch with salt crystallisation behind the seal, blowing the plaster off.**

> **So the standard homeowner's remedy — cement rendering the base of a damp wall — reliably makes the condition worse, and understanding capillarity is what predicts that.**

**The consequences of rising damp:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Damp patches, staining and a persistent musty smell** | The visible symptom |
| **EFFLORESCENCE and salt crystallisation** | **Ground water carries dissolved salts; the water evaporates and the salts remain, accumulating year after year** ← |
| **Plaster and paint failure** | Blistering, powdering, spalling |
| **Decay of embedded TIMBER — joist ends, wall plates, door frames** | **Above 20 % moisture, fungal decay begins** ← |
| **CORROSION of embedded metal** | — |
| **Reduced insulation, higher heating cost, cold surfaces** | **A wet wall conducts heat far better than a dry one** ← |
| **Health effects — mould, respiratory illness** | ← |

> **The SALT ACCUMULATION in the second row explains why rising damp gets progressively worse rather than reaching a steady state: the water evaporates and leaves its salts behind, so the concentration in the wall rises every year.**

> **Those salts are HYGROSCOPIC — they absorb moisture from the air — so eventually the wall stays damp even after the source is cut off, which is why a wall treated for rising damp must usually be replastered with a salt-resistant render as well.**

**The materials used for a DPC:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bitumen felt / bituminous sheet** | **Cheap, flexible, the traditional choice; can be squeezed out under heavy load** ← |
| **POLYTHENE / PVC sheet** | **Common, cheap, effective; must not be punctured** ← |
| **Mastic asphalt** | Excellent, jointless, also used for basement tanking |
| **Cement concrete (1:1.5:3) with a WATERPROOFING COMPOUND, 40-75 mm** | **The usual Nepali and Indian practice at plinth level** ← |
| **Engineering bricks or slate in cement mortar** | Traditional and durable |
| **Metal sheet — lead, copper** | Durable, expensive |

**The RULES for laying a DPC, which is where it usually fails:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **It must be CONTINUOUS and UNBROKEN over the full wall thickness** | **A single gap defeats the whole course** ← |
| **It must be at least 150 mm ABOVE the finished ground level** | **Otherwise splashing and ponding bypass it** ← |
| **It must be LAPPED at least 100 mm at joints, and sealed** | — |
| **It must LINK with the floor's damp proof membrane and with any basement tanking** | **A DPC and a DPM that do not connect leave a path around both** ← |
| **It must NOT be punctured by services, nails or fixings** | ← |
| **At door openings and steps, it must be STEPPED and continued, not stopped** | **A common omission** ← |
| **BRIDGING must be avoided — no render, plaster, earth or paving spanning across it** | **The commonest cause of failure** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS ARE WHERE DPCs ACTUALLY FAIL, and the point is worth making plainly: a DPC is almost never defective in itself — it is BYPASSED.**

| Bridging path | Note |
|---|---|
| **External render carried down over the DPC to the ground** | **The commonest of all** ← |
| **Ground or paving raised above the DPC level after construction** | **A path or a flower bed added later** ← |
| **Internal plaster carried down to the floor across the DPC** | ← |
| **Debris or mortar droppings left in a cavity, forming a bridge** | ← |
| **A porch, step or planter built against the wall above DPC level** | ← |

> **Every one of these is created AFTER the DPC was correctly laid, and mostly by later work rather than by the original builder — which is why a damp wall in an old building is usually a maintenance history problem rather than a construction defect.**

> **The diagnostic follows: before concluding that a DPC has failed, walk round the building and look for what is bridging it, because that is what will be found in most cases and it is far cheaper to remove than to install a new DPC.**

**And the other places a DPC is required, since plinth level is only the best known:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **At plinth level in every wall** | **Rising damp** ← |
| **Under and over WINDOW SILLS, and over openings** | Water penetrating the opening |
| **At the base of a PARAPET, and under the coping** | **Water entering the top of the wall — parapets are wetted on both faces and are a classic damp source** ← |
| **At the junction of a roof and a wall (flashing)** | Water running down the wall face |
| **In cavity walls, at the cavity tray over openings** | **Directs water in the cavity outward through weep holes** ← |
| **Basement walls and floors (tanking)** | **Lateral seepage under pressure — option (d)'s case, and a different system entirely** ← |

> **Option (d) names basement seepage, which is a real problem addressed by TANKING rather than by a plinth DPC: the difference is that tanking resists water under HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE over a whole surface, while a DPC merely interrupts capillary rise along a line.**

> **They are different problems needing different solutions, and confusing them leads to basements waterproofed with a material that would only ever have stopped a wick.**

examTip.trick: **DPC stops RISING DAMP — ground moisture drawn up by CAPILLARITY.** It must be continuous, at least 150 mm above finished ground level, and linked to the floor DPM.
examTip.trap: **Sealing the face of a damp wall makes the damp rise HIGHER** — the water must escape somewhere, so blocking evaporation moves the problem upward. The usual cement-render "cure" makes it worse.
examTip.mnemonic: **A DPC almost never fails — it gets BRIDGED:** render carried down over it, ground raised after construction, internal plaster crossing it, mortar droppings in the cavity. Look for the bridge before condemning the DPC.

questions.stem: The SLUMP test on fresh concrete measures:
options: The compressive strength at 28 days
The air content of the mix
The workability, or consistency, of the mix
The water absorption of the aggregate
questions.solution:
**The WORKABILITY (consistency) of the fresh mix.**

**The test and its values:**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Mould** | **A frustum of a cone: 200 mm bottom diameter, 100 mm top, 300 mm high** ← |
| **Filling** | **THREE layers, each tamped 25 times with a 16 mm rod** ← |
| **Measurement** | **The SUBSIDENCE of the concrete after the mould is lifted vertically** ← |

| Degree of workability | Slump (mm) | Suitable for |
|---|---|---|
| **VERY LOW** | **0-25** | **Road pavements, mass concrete with vibration** ← |
| **LOW** | **25-50** | **Foundations, mass concrete, canal linings** |
| **MEDIUM** | **50-100** | **Normal RCC — beams, slabs, columns** ← |
| **HIGH** | **100-150** | **Heavily reinforced sections, thin sections, difficult access** ← |
| **Very high / flowing** | **Above 150, measured by flow table** | **Self-compacting concrete, tremie work, pumped concrete** ← |

**The types of slump, since the SHAPE of the collapse is as informative as its height:**

| Slump type | Appearance | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **TRUE slump** | **The mass subsides evenly, keeping its shape** | **A satisfactory, cohesive mix — the only valid result** ← |
| **SHEAR slump** | **One half slides down an inclined plane** | **A LACK OF COHESION; the mix is harsh or lean. The test should be REPEATED, and a second shear slump indicates a deficient mix** ← |
| **COLLAPSE slump** | **The concrete collapses completely** | **Too WET, or a very high workability mix — the slump test is not applicable and the FLOW TABLE should be used instead** ← |

> **The SHEAR SLUMP entry carries the practically useful information: the number alone is not the result — the shape must be observed and recorded, and a shear slump means the mix is deficient in cohesion however acceptable its measured value.**

**What the slump test does and does not tell you:**

| It DOES indicate | It does NOT indicate |
|---|---|
| **CONSISTENCY, and hence a change in water content** ← | **STRENGTH — option (a)'s error** ← |
| **BATCH-TO-BATCH VARIATION — its most valuable use** ← | **Cohesion or segregation resistance directly** |
| **Whether more or less water than intended has been added** ← | Workability of very dry or very wet mixes |
| — | Air content, or aggregate absorption |

> **THE BATCH-TO-BATCH USE IS THE REAL VALUE OF THE TEST and is worth stating plainly: slump is a poor absolute measure of workability and an excellent RELATIVE one.**

> **If the mix design, materials and aggregate moisture are unchanged, then a change in slump means a change in WATER CONTENT — and that is the single most damaging uncontrolled variable on a concrete site.**

> **So a slump reading that has risen from 75 mm to 125 mm between batches is a warning that water has been added, and it is detectable in two minutes with a cone and a rod, on site, by anyone.**

> **That combination of sensitivity to the thing that matters most, and near-zero cost, is why the test has survived for a century despite being crude.**

**The other workability tests, and where each is appropriate:**

| Test | Suits | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **SLUMP** | **Medium workability, 25-150 mm** ← | Insensitive outside that range |
| **COMPACTING FACTOR** | **LOW workability mixes, where slump reads zero** ← | **The ratio of partially to fully compacted weight; 0.8-0.92 typical** |
| **VEE-BEE consistometer** | **VERY DRY mixes — pavement and precast** ← | **Measures the TIME in seconds to remould under vibration** |
| **FLOW TABLE** | **HIGH workability and self-compacting concrete** ← | Spread diameter after jolting |
| **Kelly ball penetration** | A quick site test on placed concrete | Rarely used now |
| **Slump FLOW and J-ring** | **Self-compacting concrete — flow AND passing ability** ← | The modern additions |

> **The pattern to notice: SLUMP is insensitive at both extremes, so a DRY mix needs the compacting factor or Vee-Bee, and a FLOWING mix needs the flow table.**

> **Reporting a slump of zero tells you only that the mix is drier than the test can measure — it does not distinguish a stiff but workable pavement mix from an unworkable one, and a compacting factor will.**

**And the factors that govern workability, since the test exists to monitor them:**

| Factor | Effect on workability |
|---|---|
| **WATER content** | **The dominant factor — and the one that must NOT be used to adjust it** ← |
| **Aggregate SHAPE** | **ROUNDED aggregate is far more workable than angular or flaky** ← |
| **Aggregate GRADING** | **Well-graded is more workable; gap-graded and single-sized are harsh** ← |
| **Maximum aggregate SIZE** | Larger size, less surface area, more workable |
| **Aggregate-cement ratio** | A leaner mix is harsher |
| **Fineness of the cement** | Finer cement, less workable at the same water |
| **ADMIXTURES — plasticisers** | **The correct way to increase workability** ← |
| **TIME and TEMPERATURE** | **Slump LOSS with time, accelerated by heat — 25-50 mm in the first 30 minutes is normal** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND SEVENTH ROWS TOGETHER STATE THE CENTRAL DISCIPLINE OF CONCRETE PRACTICE: when the concrete is too stiff to place, the answer is a PLASTICISER, a change of grading, or better compaction equipment — never more water.**

> **Adding water raises the water-cement ratio permanently and irreversibly, and the strength lost is never recovered. A bucket of water added at the pour to make placing easier can cost 15 per cent of the concrete's strength.**

> **The SLUMP LOSS in the last row is the honest complication: a mix that left the plant at 100 mm may arrive at 60 mm, and the temptation to "restore" it with water is exactly the error above.**

> **The correct response is to design for the slump required AT THE POINT OF PLACING rather than at the plant, and to use a retarding admixture where the haul is long or the weather hot — which is standard practice for ready-mixed concrete and is worth insisting on.**

examTip.trick: **Cone 200 bottom / 100 top / 300 high, three layers, 25 blows each.** Very low 0-25, low 25-50, medium 50-100 (normal RCC), high 100-150.
examTip.trap: **Record the SHAPE, not only the number: TRUE (valid), SHEAR (lacking cohesion — repeat, and a second shear slump condemns the mix), COLLAPSE (too wet — use the flow table).**
examTip.mnemonic: **Slump is a poor ABSOLUTE measure and an excellent RELATIVE one** — with everything else constant, a change in slump means a change in WATER. And when concrete is too stiff, the answer is a PLASTICISER, never a bucket of water.

questions.stem: The RADIUS OF GYRATION of a section about a given axis is defined as:
options: The distance from the axis to the section's centroid
√(I/A), where I is the moment of inertia about that axis and A the cross-sectional area
I/A, the moment of inertia divided by the area
The distance from the axis to the extreme fibre of the section
questions.solution:
**k = √(I / A)** — the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the area.

**What it means physically:**

> **The radius of gyration is the distance from the axis at which the WHOLE AREA could be concentrated, as a thin ring or a pair of points, WITHOUT changing the moment of inertia.**

> **From the definition I = A k², so k is the "effective distance" of the area from the axis in the sense that matters for bending and buckling.**

> **Option (c), I/A, has the wrong DIMENSIONS: I is a length to the fourth power and A a length squared, so I/A is a length SQUARED, not a length. The square root is what makes it a distance.**

> **That dimensional check alone eliminates option (c) without any recollection of the formula, and it is worth using — the radius of gyration must come out in millimetres.**

**Values for the standard sections, since they recur constantly:**

| Section | I about the centroidal axis | Area | k |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE b × d, about the axis parallel to b** | **bd³/12** | **bd** | **d/√12 = 0.289 d** ← |
| **CIRCLE of diameter D** | **πD⁴/64** | **πD²/4** | **D/4 = 0.25 D** ← |
| **Hollow circle, D and d** | **π(D⁴−d⁴)/64** | **π(D²−d²)/4** | **√(D²+d²)/4** ← |
| **Thin ring of mean radius R** | **≈ πR³t** | **2πRt** | **≈ R/√2 = 0.707 R** ← |
| **Triangle, base b, height h, about the centroidal axis** | **bh³/36** | **bh/2** | **h/√18 = 0.236 h** |

> **The CIRCLE's k = D/4 is worth memorising outright, and the RECTANGLE's k = d/√12 ≈ 0.289 d nearly so, because between them they cover most quick estimates.**

**Why the radius of gyration matters — COLUMN BUCKLING:**

> **The slenderness ratio, which governs every compression member, is λ = L_e / k.**

> **So the radius of gyration is not an abstract geometric property but the quantity that decides whether a strut is short and crushes or slender and buckles.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Buckling occurs about the axis of LEAST k** | **So k_min governs, always** ← |
| **A section with EQUAL k about both axes is the most efficient strut** | **Circular and square hollow sections** ← |
| **An I-section has a very small k about its MINOR axis** | **Typically a quarter of the major-axis value** ← |
| **A single ANGLE has its least k about the MINOR PRINCIPAL (v-v) axis** | **Smaller than about either geometric axis** ← |

> **THE EFFICIENCY POINT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL LESSON: for a given AREA of steel, the section that buckles at the highest load is the one that puts its material FURTHEST FROM THE CENTROID, equally in all directions.**

> **That is a hollow tube — which is why scaffold poles, bicycle frames, bracing members and lattice tower legs are tubular, and why nature builds bones and bamboo hollow.**

> **Bamboo is the striking case: a hollow tube with transverse diaphragms at the nodes, achieving a very high radius of gyration for its weight, which is exactly why it performs so well as a structural material in Nepali construction.**

**The PARALLEL AXIS THEOREM, which is how the values above are combined:**

> **I_axis = I_centroidal + A h²**

> **where h is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The moment of inertia is LEAST about the CENTROIDAL axis** | **The A h² term is always positive, so any parallel shift increases it** ← |
| **The theorem only works FROM the centroidal axis** | **Going between two non-centroidal axes requires passing through the centroid** ← |
| **The A h² term usually DOMINATES for a flange far from the axis** | **See below** ← |

> **For a built-up section the last point is the one that matters, and it is worth seeing in numbers.**

> **Consider an I-section flange, 200 mm × 20 mm, whose centre lies 240 mm from the neutral axis:**

| Term | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Own I_centroidal** | **200 × 20³/12** | **0.133 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **A h² term** | **(200 × 20) × 240²** | **230.4 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **Ratio** | — | **The A h² term is over 1,700 times the flange's own I** ← |

> **So a thin flange's OWN moment of inertia is almost negligible; nearly all of its contribution comes from its DISTANCE from the neutral axis.**

> **That single observation explains the shape of every efficient bending member: put the material as FAR from the neutral axis as possible, and use the web only to hold it there and carry the shear.**

> **It is why I-sections, box girders, trusses and hollow-core slabs all look as they do, and why increasing a beam's DEPTH is so much more effective than increasing its width — depth enters through h², width only linearly.**

**And the related section properties, to keep them apart:**

| Property | Symbol | Expression | Governs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Area** | **A** | — | **Direct stress, shear** |
| **First moment of area** | **Q or Ay** | **A × ȳ** | **Shear stress distribution, τ = VQ/Ib** ← |
| **Second moment of area (moment of inertia)** | **I** | ∫y² dA | **Bending stiffness and stress** ← |
| **SECTION MODULUS** | **Z = I / y_max** | — | **BENDING STRESS directly: σ = M/Z** ← |
| **RADIUS OF GYRATION** | **k = √(I/A)** | — | **BUCKLING, through λ = L_e/k** ← |
| **Polar moment of inertia** | **J = I_xx + I_yy** | — | **TORSION of circular sections** ← |

> **The distinction between Z and k is the one to hold: SECTION MODULUS is the property for BENDING STRENGTH, and RADIUS OF GYRATION is the property for BUCKLING.**

> **Both derive from I, and they answer different questions — which is why a deep slender I-section can have an excellent section modulus and a dangerously small minor-axis radius of gyration at the same time.**

examTip.trick: **k = √(I/A).** Option (c), I/A, has the wrong DIMENSIONS — it is a length squared. That check alone eliminates it. Circle k = D/4; rectangle k = d/√12 ≈ 0.289 d.
examTip.trap: **Buckling always occurs about the axis of LEAST k** — for an I-section the minor axis (about a quarter of the major value), for a single angle the v-v principal axis.
examTip.mnemonic: **In the parallel axis theorem the A h² term dominates:** a 200×20 flange 240 mm from the axis contributes 1,700 times its own I. Hence depth beats width (h² against linear), and hollow sections are the efficient struts. **Z for bending, k for buckling.**

questions.stem: In levelling, a BACK SIGHT is:
options: The last reading taken before shifting the instrument
Any reading taken on a point behind the instrument
A reading taken to check the collimation
The first reading taken after setting up the instrument, on a point of known elevation
questions.solution:
**The FIRST reading taken after setting up the instrument, on a point of KNOWN elevation** (a benchmark or a change point whose reduced level has already been established).

**The three kinds of staff reading:**

| Reading | Definition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **BACK SIGHT (BS)** | **The FIRST reading after each setup, on a point of KNOWN RL** ← | **ADDED to the RL to give the height of instrument** |
| **FORE SIGHT (FS)** | **The LAST reading before shifting the instrument, on the point that becomes the next known point** ← | **SUBTRACTED; taken on a CHANGE POINT** |
| **INTERMEDIATE SIGHT (IS)** | **Any reading between the BS and the FS at the same setup** | Subtracted; on points whose RL is wanted |

> **Option (a) defines the FORE SIGHT, which makes it the designed distractor — and the pairing is the standard confusion.**

> **The essential idea is that BS and FS are defined by their ROLE IN THE SEQUENCE, not by their direction: a back sight may be taken forward along the route and a fore sight backward.**

> **The names are historical and misleading, and remembering them by direction is the commonest error — which is exactly what option (b) invites.**

**The two methods of reducing levels:**

| Method | Procedure | Check |
|---|---|---|
| **HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT (collimation) method** | **HI = RL of known point + BS; RL of any point = HI − its staff reading** ← | **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** ← |
| **RISE AND FALL method** | **Compare each reading with the previous one: a SMALLER reading is a RISE, a LARGER one a FALL** ← | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** ← |

> **The comparison between them is worth knowing:**

| Aspect | HI method | Rise and fall |
|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | **FASTER — fewer computations** ← | Slower |
| **Suits** | **Many INTERMEDIATE sights — a longitudinal section, a contour grid** ← | **Few intermediates — a level circuit between benchmarks** |
| **Arithmetic check on INTERMEDIATE sights** | **NONE — an error in an IS is undetected** ← | **YES — every reading enters the rise/fall computation** ← |
| **Number of checks** | Two | Three |

> **The THIRD row is the substantive difference and the reason rise-and-fall survives despite being slower: in the HI method an intermediate sight enters only one subtraction, so a misbooked intermediate reading produces a wrong RL and NOTHING in the arithmetic reveals it.**

> **In rise and fall, every reading is compared with its neighbour and enters the totals, so an error shows up in the check.**

> **The practical rule follows: use the HI method for detail levelling where speed matters and the intermediate points are not critical, and rise-and-fall where the accuracy of every point must be verified — a benchmark transfer, or the levels for a structure.**

**The BALANCED SIGHTS rule, which is levelling's most important field practice:**

> **The back sight and fore sight distances at each setup should be kept EQUAL.**

| Error eliminated by balancing | Note |
|---|---|
| **COLLIMATION error — the line of sight not truly horizontal** | **The error is proportional to distance, so equal distances make equal errors that CANCEL in the difference** ← |
| **CURVATURE of the earth** | **Also proportional to distance² — cancels** ← |
| **Atmospheric REFRACTION** | **Largely cancels, though not perfectly since conditions may differ** ← |

> **This is the most valuable single technique in levelling, because it removes the instrument's principal systematic error WITHOUT the instrument being adjusted.**

> **A level with a significant collimation error will still give correct results if the sights are balanced — which is a striking and useful fact, and it is why precise levelling is always run with balanced sights and why the TWO-PEG TEST that measures the collimation error is run by exactly this arrangement.**

> **The corollary is also worth stating: an UNBALANCED sight, such as a long fore sight to a distant benchmark after a series of short back sights, imports the collimation error in full — so a single unbalanced setup can undo the care of a whole circuit.**

**The curvature and refraction correction, for when balancing is impossible:**

| Effect | Magnitude | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| **CURVATURE of the earth** | **0.0785 d² metres (d in km)** | **Makes the reading TOO LARGE** ← |
| **REFRACTION** | **About one seventh of the curvature, 0.0112 d²** | **Makes the reading TOO SMALL — it acts OPPOSITE to curvature** ← |
| **COMBINED correction** | **0.0673 d² metres, SUBTRACTED from the staff reading** ← | — |

| Sight distance | Combined correction |
|---|---|
| **100 m** | **0.7 mm — negligible** |
| **300 m** | **6 mm** ← |
| **1 km** | **67 mm** ← |
| **3 km** | **0.6 m** ← |

> **So for ordinary sights of 50 to 100 m the correction is negligible, which is why it is normally ignored — and for a reciprocal levelling across a wide river, where a sight of several hundred metres is unavoidable, it is substantial.**

> **RECIPROCAL LEVELLING is the technique for exactly that case: observations are taken from BOTH banks, and the mean of the two results eliminates curvature, refraction and collimation together — which is the balanced-sight principle applied where the sights cannot be balanced at a single setup.**

**And the sources of error in levelling, as a checklist:**

| Source | Control |
|---|---|
| **Collimation error** | **Balanced sights; two-peg test** ← |
| **Staff not VERTICAL** | **A circular bubble on the staff; or waving the staff and taking the MINIMUM reading** ← |
| **Staff SETTLEMENT at a change point** | **Use a firm change plate; a settling change point makes the errors ACCUMULATE in one direction** ← |
| **Instrument SETTLEMENT between BS and FS** | Set up on firm ground; do not touch the tripod |
| **Parallax** | Focus the crosshairs before the staff |
| **Refraction near the ground** | **Keep the line of sight at least 0.5 m above the ground on hot days** ← |
| **Booking and arithmetic errors** | The two checks above |

> **The MINIMUM READING rule for a non-vertical staff is worth a note because it is not obvious: a staff tilted in ANY direction gives a reading LARGER than the true vertical one, since the line of sight cuts a longer path across the tilted staff.**

> **So waving the staff slowly toward and away from the instrument and recording the SMALLEST reading gives the vertical value — a simple technique that needs no bubble and works in any direction of tilt.**

examTip.trick: **BS = FIRST reading after a setup, on a KNOWN point (added). FS = LAST reading before shifting, on a change point (subtracted).** Option (a) defines the fore sight.
examTip.trap: **BS and FS are defined by their ROLE IN THE SEQUENCE, not by DIRECTION** — a back sight may be taken forward along the route. Option (b) invites exactly that error.
examTip.mnemonic: **BALANCED SIGHTS eliminate collimation error, curvature and refraction together** — so a level with a real collimation error still gives correct results. And the HI method gives NO arithmetic check on intermediate sights; rise-and-fall does.

questions.stem: In the STRAIGHT LINE method of depreciation, the annual depreciation of an asset costing C, with scrap value S and useful life n years, is:
options: C/n
2C/n
(C − S)/n
questions.solution:
**(C − S)/n.**

**The methods of depreciation:**

| Method | Annual depreciation | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE (fixed instalment)** | **(C − S)/n — the SAME every year** ← | **Simple; the commonest** |
| **DECLINING BALANCE (constant percentage / diminishing value)** | **A fixed PERCENTAGE p of the current book value, where p = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n)** ← | **HIGH in early years, low later** |
| **SUM OF THE YEARS' DIGITS** | **(C − S) × (remaining life)/(sum of the digits)** ← | Also accelerated, less steeply |
| **SINKING FUND** | **An annual deposit earning interest, accumulating to (C − S) in n years** ← | **The depreciation charge is CONSTANT but includes interest** |
| **Production / service-unit method** | Proportional to output or hours used | Suits plant |

> **Option (b) is the declining balance RATE formula, offered as an annual amount — a well-made distractor, since it is the right expression for the wrong method and the wrong quantity.**

**Why the SCRAP VALUE is subtracted — the point of the question:**

> **Depreciation spreads the LOSS OF VALUE over the asset's life, and the asset does not lose ALL its value: at the end it is worth S.**

> **So the amount to be written off is (C − S), not C — and option (a)'s C/n over-depreciates by S/n each year, leaving the asset at a book value of zero when it is actually worth S.**

> **The scrap (salvage or residual) value may be a genuine resale value, a scrap metal value, or, for a building, essentially the value of the materials less the cost of demolition — which can be negative, in which case the depreciable amount EXCEEDS the cost.**

**A worked comparison, since the methods differ sharply in their early years:**

> **A plant item costs Rs 10,00,000, has a scrap value of Rs 1,00,000, and a life of 5 years.**

| Year | STRAIGHT LINE | DECLINING BALANCE (p = 1 − (0.1)^0.2 = 36.9 %) | SUM OF DIGITS (15) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **1,80,000** | **3,69,000** ← | **3,00,000 (5/15)** |
| **2** | **1,80,000** | **2,32,800** | **2,40,000 (4/15)** |
| **3** | **1,80,000** | **1,46,900** | **1,80,000 (3/15)** |
| **4** | **1,80,000** | **92,700** | **1,20,000 (2/15)** |
| **5** | **1,80,000** | **58,600** ← | **60,000 (1/15)** |
| **Total** | **9,00,000** | **9,00,000** | **9,00,000** |

> **All three write off the same total; they differ only in the TIMING.**

> **The declining balance charges more than twice as much as straight line in year 1 and a third as much in year 5.**

> **The argument for the ACCELERATED methods is that they match the actual pattern of value loss and of cost: a machine loses most of its market value in its first year, and its REPAIR costs RISE as it ages — so an accelerated depreciation charge plus rising repairs gives a more nearly CONSTANT total annual cost of ownership, which straight line does not.**

> **That is the substantive justification, and it is why plant is usually depreciated on a declining balance while buildings are depreciated straight line.**

**The SINKING FUND method, since it differs in kind rather than in timing:**

> **The other methods are ACCOUNTING allocations — they record a loss of value but set no money aside.**

> **A sinking fund actually DEPOSITS a sum each year in an interest-bearing account, so that the accumulated amount replaces the asset at the end of its life.**

> **Annual deposit = (C − S) × i/((1 + i)^n − 1)**

> **The factor i/((1+i)^n − 1) is the SINKING FUND FACTOR — which is what option (d) of the previous question named.**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The deposit is LESS than (C − S)/n** | **Because the interest does part of the work** ← |
| **At 8 % over 5 years, the factor is 0.1705** | **So Rs 9,00,000 needs 1,53,450 a year, against 1,80,000 straight line** ← |
| **The saving is the accumulated interest** | Rs 1,32,750 over the five years |

> **The sinking fund is the honest method for an asset that MUST be replaced — a bridge bearing, a pump, a roof — because it ensures the money exists when the time comes.**

> **Its practical weakness is that public bodies rarely maintain the fund: the deposits are diverted to current needs, the asset reaches the end of its life, and no money has been set aside.**

> **That is the ordinary mechanism by which infrastructure falls into disrepair, and it is an institutional failure rather than a technical one.**

**Why depreciation is calculated at all, since it is not a cash flow:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **To determine the true COST of using an asset** | **Essential in rate analysis for plant — a hired excavator's rate must recover its depreciation** ← |
| **To value the asset in the accounts** | Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation |
| **For TAXATION** | Depreciation is an allowable expense |
| **To decide WHEN TO REPLACE** | **See below** ← |
| **To provide for replacement** | Sinking fund |

> **The REPLACEMENT DECISION is the engineering application and it has a clean criterion:**

> **An asset's total annual cost is its depreciation (falling with age) plus its operating and maintenance cost (rising with age). The sum has a MINIMUM, and that year is the ECONOMIC LIFE — the optimum time to replace.**

> **Keeping an asset beyond its economic life is a real and common waste: the machine still works, so replacing it feels premature, while its rising repair bills and falling availability already exceed what a new machine would cost to own.**

> **And the reverse error — replacing too early — is equally real where an organisation's rules fix a replacement age regardless of condition.**

> **The correct answer is neither a fixed age nor "until it fails", but the year in which the equivalent annual cost is least — which requires the depreciation calculation this question is about.**

examTip.trick: **(C − S)/n — the SCRAP VALUE is subtracted.** Option (a)'s C/n over-depreciates by S/n a year and leaves a zero book value on an asset still worth S.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the declining-balance RATE formula p = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n)**, offered as an annual amount — the right expression for the wrong method and the wrong quantity.
examTip.mnemonic: **All methods write off the same total; they differ only in TIMING.** Accelerated methods are justified because repairs RISE as depreciation FALLS, giving a steadier total cost of ownership. And the ECONOMIC LIFE is the year where depreciation plus running cost is least.

questions.stem: On the plasticity chart used for soil classification, the A-LINE is given by:
options: PI = LL − 20
PI = 0.5 LL
questions.solution:
**PI = 0.73 (LL − 20).**

**What the A-line separates:**

| Position on the chart | Soil group |
|---|---|
| **ABOVE the A-line** | **CLAYS — symbol C (CL, CI, CH)** ← |
| **BELOW the A-line** | **SILTS and ORGANIC soils — symbols M and O (ML, MI, MH, OL, OH)** ← |

> **Option (a), PI = 0.9(LL − 8), is the U-LINE — the empirical UPPER BOUND above which no natural soil has been found to plot.**

> **A test result plotting above the U-line is therefore treated as a LABORATORY ERROR and the test is repeated, which makes the U-line a genuinely useful check rather than a classification boundary.**

> **So both (a) and (b) are real lines on the same chart, which is what makes this option set work.**

**The complete classification, since the chart has two axes:**

| Liquid limit | Compressibility | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| **LL < 35** | **LOW** | **L** ← |
| **35 ≤ LL < 50** | **INTERMEDIATE (medium)** | **I** ← |
| **LL ≥ 50** | **HIGH** | **H** ← |

> **So the classification is read off in two steps: the LL fixes the second letter (L, I or H) and the position relative to the A-line fixes the first (C, M or O).**

| Example | LL | PI | A-line value | Classification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Soil 1** | **42** | **22** | **0.73(42−20) = 16.1** | **PI above → CLAY; LL intermediate → CI** ← |
| **Soil 2** | **42** | **12** | **16.1** | **PI below → SILT → MI** ← |
| **Soil 3** | **60** | **35** | **0.73(60−20) = 29.2** | **Above → CH** ← |
| **Soil 4** | **28** | **9** | **0.73(28−20) = 5.8** | **Above → CL** |

> **Soils 1 and 2 have the SAME liquid limit and fall into entirely different groups — which is the point of the chart: LL alone does not classify a soil, and it is the COMBINATION of LL and PI that distinguishes a clay from a silt.**

> **Note that the Indian system uses the three-way L/I/H division, while the original Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) uses only L and H with the boundary at LL = 50 — so "CI" is an Indian designation with no USCS equivalent.**

**Why plasticity, rather than grain size, classifies fine soils:**

| Soil type | Classified by |
|---|---|
| **COARSE-grained (more than 50 % retained on 75 µm)** | **GRAIN SIZE and GRADING — the D₆₀/D₁₀ uniformity coefficient and the curvature coefficient** ← |
| **FINE-grained (more than 50 % passing 75 µm)** | **PLASTICITY — the Atterberg limits and the plasticity chart** ← |

> **THE REASON FOR THE SPLIT IS THE ESSENTIAL IDEA: for a coarse soil, the mechanical behaviour follows from the PARTICLE ARRANGEMENT — size, shape and packing — and grading captures it.**

> **For a fine soil, behaviour is governed by the MINERALOGY of the clay particles and their interaction with water, and grain size tells you almost nothing about that.**

> **Two soils of identical particle size distribution, one of kaolinite and one of montmorillonite, behave completely differently — and the Atterberg limits detect that difference where a sieve analysis cannot.**

| Clay mineral | Typical LL | Typical PI | Activity | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **KAOLINITE** | **35-100** | **20-40** | **0.3-0.5 — INACTIVE** ← | **Stable; little swelling** |
| **ILLITE** | **60-120** | **35-60** | **0.5-1.0 — normal** | Intermediate |
| **MONTMORILLONITE** | **100-900** | **50-600** | **1.0-7.0 — ACTIVE** ← | **Enormous swelling and shrinkage; the mineral in BLACK COTTON SOIL and bentonite** ← |

> **ACTIVITY = PI / (percentage of clay-size particles finer than 2 µm) — and it is the measure that isolates the mineral's contribution from the mere quantity of clay present.**

> **A soil with 20 per cent clay of montmorillonite is far more troublesome than one with 50 per cent kaolinite, and activity is what makes that comparison.**

**The Atterberg limits themselves, since they are what the chart plots:**

| Limit | Definition | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **LIQUID LIMIT (LL)** | **The water content at which soil begins to flow — the boundary between liquid and plastic states** | **Casagrande apparatus, 25 blows to close a 12.5 mm groove; or the cone penetrometer, 20 mm penetration** ← |
| **PLASTIC LIMIT (PL)** | **The water content at which a 3 mm thread just crumbles when rolled** ← | Thread rolling |
| **SHRINKAGE LIMIT (SL)** | **The water content below which further drying causes NO further volume reduction** ← | Mercury or wax displacement |
| **PLASTICITY INDEX** | **PI = LL − PL — the range of water content over which the soil is plastic** ← | Derived |

> **And the two derived indices that place a natural soil within that range:**

| Index | Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **LIQUIDITY INDEX** | **LI = (w − PL)/PI** | **Where the NATURAL water content sits: LI > 1 means the soil is effectively LIQUID and likely SENSITIVE; LI < 0 means it is drier than its plastic limit and stiff** ← |
| **CONSISTENCY INDEX** | **CI = (LL − w)/PI** | **The complement: CI = 1 − LI. A high CI means a stiff soil** ← |

> **THE LIQUIDITY INDEX IS THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE NUMBER OF THE SET, because the limits alone describe the soil's potential and LI describes its actual present condition.**

> **A clay with LL = 60 and PL = 25 could be a firm foundation material or a slurry, depending entirely on its natural water content — and LI is what tells you which.**

> **An LI approaching or exceeding 1 warns of a soil that will lose most of its strength if disturbed, which is the condition of the sensitive marine and lacustrine clays responsible for many flow slides.**

examTip.trick: **A-line: PI = 0.73(LL − 20).** ABOVE it clays (C), BELOW it silts and organics (M, O). Option (a) is the U-LINE, PI = 0.9(LL − 8) — the upper bound above which a result means a lab error.
examTip.trap: **LL alone does not classify** — two soils with LL = 42 and PI of 22 and 12 are CI and MI respectively. Coarse soils are classified by GRADING, fine soils by PLASTICITY, because a fine soil's behaviour is mineralogical.
examTip.mnemonic: **LL < 35 low (L), 35-50 intermediate (I), ≥ 50 high (H)** — the I band is Indian; USCS uses only L and H at LL = 50. And **ACTIVITY = PI ÷ % finer than 2 µm** isolates the mineral: montmorillonite 1.0-7.0, kaolinite 0.3-0.5.

questions.stem: A soil has a bulk unit weight of 19.6 kN/m³ at a water content of 12 per cent. Its DRY unit weight is:
options: 17.0 kN/m³
21.9 kN/m³
18.4 kN/m³
17.5 kN/m³
questions.solution:
**17.5 kN/m³.**

**The relation and the computation:**

> **γ_d = γ / (1 + w)**, with w as a DECIMAL fraction.

> **γ_d = 19.6 / (1 + 0.12) = 19.6 / 1.12 = 17.5 kN/m³** ←

| Distractor | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **21.9** | **γ × (1 + w) = 19.6 × 1.12 — MULTIPLYING instead of dividing** ← |
| **17.0** | γ − 0.12γ × ... an approximate subtraction of 12 per cent |
| **18.4** | γ − w in absolute terms, or another mis-step |

> **The 21.9 distractor is the important one, and the sense check that kills it is immediate: THE DRY UNIT WEIGHT MUST BE LESS THAN THE BULK UNIT WEIGHT, because drying removes water and therefore weight from the same volume.**

> **Any answer larger than the bulk value is wrong before any arithmetic is checked.**

**Where the relation comes from:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **Bulk unit weight** | **γ = W / V, the TOTAL weight over the total volume** ← |
| **Dry unit weight** | **γ_d = W_s / V — the weight of SOLIDS over the SAME total volume** ← |
| **Water content** | **w = W_w / W_s, so W = W_s(1 + w)** ← |
| **Therefore** | **γ = W_s(1+w)/V = γ_d(1+w)** ← |

> **The key point is that BOTH unit weights use the SAME TOTAL VOLUME V — the dry unit weight is not the unit weight of the solid particles, but the weight of solids in the soil's actual, unchanged volume.**

> **That is why γ_d is a measure of how densely the soil is PACKED, and it is why compaction is specified in terms of dry density rather than bulk density: adding water changes the bulk density without changing the packing at all.**

**The full family of three-phase relationships:**

| Relation | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Void ratio and porosity** | **e = n/(1−n); n = e/(1+e)** ← |
| **Dry unit weight from e** | **γ_d = G γ_w /(1 + e)** ← |
| **Bulk unit weight** | **γ = (G + Se) γ_w /(1 + e)** ← |
| **Saturated unit weight (S = 1)** | **γ_sat = (G + e) γ_w /(1 + e)** ← |
| **Submerged (buoyant) unit weight** | **γ' = γ_sat − γ_w = (G − 1) γ_w /(1 + e)** ← |
| **The basic identity** | **S e = w G** ← |
| **Degree of saturation** | S = V_w/V_v |

> **THE IDENTITY S e = w G IS THE MOST USEFUL OF THE SET, because it links the four quantities that are actually measured or wanted, and almost every three-phase problem reduces to it.**

> **For a SATURATED soil (S = 1) it becomes simply e = wG — so the void ratio of a saturated soil follows directly from its water content, with no other measurement needed.**

> **That is why a saturated sample's water content is such an informative measurement: it gives the void ratio, and from the void ratio every unit weight follows.**

**A worked continuation, to show the chain:**

> **Take the soil above (γ = 19.6 kN/m³, w = 12 %, γ_d = 17.5 kN/m³) with G = 2.68:**

| Quantity | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Void ratio** | **e = Gγ_w/γ_d − 1 = 2.68 × 9.81/17.5 − 1 = 1.502 − 1** | **0.502** ← |
| **Porosity** | **n = e/(1+e) = 0.502/1.502** | **0.334, i.e. 33.4 %** |
| **Degree of saturation** | **S = wG/e = 0.12 × 2.68/0.502** | **0.641, i.e. 64.1 %** ← |
| **Saturated unit weight** | **(2.68 + 0.502) × 9.81/1.502** | **20.8 kN/m³** |
| **Submerged unit weight** | **20.8 − 9.81** | **11.0 kN/m³** ← |
| **Air content** | **n(1 − S) = 0.334 × 0.359** | **12.0 %** |

> **Note the SUBMERGED unit weight in the fifth row: at 11.0 kN/m³ it is little over HALF the saturated value.**

> **That halving is why the position of the WATER TABLE matters so much in geotechnical work — raising the water table to the surface nearly halves the effective stress at every depth below it, and effective stress is what governs strength and settlement.**

> **A bearing capacity computed for dry conditions and a rising water table not allowed for is one of the standard ways a foundation design goes wrong, and the arithmetic above is why.**

**And the COMPACTION connection, since dry density is the compaction criterion:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Compaction is specified as a percentage of MAXIMUM DRY DENSITY** | **From the Proctor test — typically 95-98 % for a subgrade or an embankment** ← |
| **At the OPTIMUM MOISTURE CONTENT** | **The water content at which that maximum is reached** ← |
| **Adding water beyond the optimum REDUCES the dry density** | **Water occupies volume that particles could otherwise fill** ← |
| **The ZERO AIR VOIDS line** | **γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + wG) — the theoretical maximum, which compaction never reaches** ← |

> **The ZERO AIR VOIDS line in the last row is worth knowing because it is the check on a Proctor curve: no test point may plot to the RIGHT of it, since that would mean negative air content.**

> **A compaction curve whose points cross the line indicates an error in the specific gravity used or in the test itself — the same kind of impossibility check as the U-line on the plasticity chart.**

examTip.trick: **γ_d = γ/(1 + w) = 19.6/1.12 = 17.5 kN/m³.** Sense check: the DRY unit weight must be LESS than the bulk — so 21.9 (multiplying instead of dividing) is wrong on sight.
examTip.trap: **Both unit weights use the SAME total volume** — γ_d is the weight of solids in the soil's actual volume, not the unit weight of the particles. That is why compaction is specified in DRY density: adding water changes bulk density without changing the packing.
examTip.mnemonic: **S e = w G is the master identity** — and for saturated soil it becomes e = wG, so water content alone gives the void ratio. Note γ' ≈ half of γ_sat, which is why the water table position dominates effective stress.

questions.stem: In the approximate 2:1 method of estimating the vertical stress increase beneath a rectangular footing of size B × L, the stress at depth z is taken as:
options: Q / (B L)
questions.solution:
**Q / [(B + z)(L + z)].**

**Why the dimensions grow by z and not by 2z:**

> **The name "2:1 method" describes the SLOPE of the assumed spread: the load disperses at 2 VERTICAL to 1 HORIZONTAL.**

> **So at a depth z, the spread on EACH side is z/2 — and the total increase in each plan dimension is 2 × (z/2) = z.**

| Depth z | Spread each side | Increase in each dimension |
|---|---|---|
| **2 m** | **1 m** | **2 m** ← |
| **4 m** | **2 m** | **4 m** ← |

> **Option (b), (B + 2z), is the natural misreading of "2:1" and is the designed distractor — it would correspond to a 1:1 spread (45°), which disperses the load far too quickly and underestimates the stress.**

> **The safeguard is to remember the SLOPE rather than the formula: 2 down for 1 out, so z down gives z/2 out on each side.**

**A worked example:**

> **A footing 2 m × 3 m carries a total load of 900 kN. The stress increase at 3 m depth:**

| Quantity | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Contact pressure at the base** | **900/(2 × 3)** | **150 kPa** |
| **Spread dimensions at z = 3 m** | **(2 + 3) × (3 + 3)** | **5 m × 6 m** ← |
| **Stress increase** | **900/(5 × 6)** | **30 kPa** ← |
| **As a fraction of the contact pressure** | 30/150 | **20 per cent** ← |

> **So at a depth of 1.5 times the footing width, the stress has fallen to a fifth of its value at the base — which is the dispersion the method exists to capture.**

**How the method compares with the exact solution:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It assumes the stress is UNIFORM across the spread area** | **The true distribution is bell-shaped, greatest under the centre** ← |
| **It therefore UNDERESTIMATES the stress directly beneath the centre** | **By 20-30 % at shallow depths** ← |
| **It OVERESTIMATES near the edges of the spread area** | Where the true stress is small |
| **It improves with depth** | **Below about 2B the agreement with Boussinesq is good** ← |
| **It ignores the soil's layering and stiffness contrasts** | As Boussinesq does too |
