> **The method is therefore a QUICK ESTIMATE for settlement calculations and preliminary work, not a substitute for Boussinesq or Newmark where accuracy matters — and its systematic error near the surface is in the UNSAFE direction, which is worth knowing.**

**The PRESSURE BULB and the significant depth, which this leads to:**

| Contour | Depth below a square footing of width B |
|---|---|
| **0.5 q (50 % isobar)** | **About 0.5 B** |
| **0.2 q (20 % isobar)** | **About 1.5 B** ← |
| **0.1 q (10 % isobar)** | **About 2.0 B** ← |

> **THE SIGNIFICANT DEPTH — the depth below which the added stress is too small to cause appreciable settlement — is conventionally taken at the 20 PER CENT ISOBAR, that is about 1.5 B for a square footing and up to 3 B or more for a strip footing.**

> **That figure governs two practical decisions:**

| Decision | Note |
|---|---|
| **The DEPTH OF SOIL EXPLORATION** | **Boreholes must reach at least 1.5 B below the founding level, and deeper for a raft or a pile group** ← |
| **Which soil layers matter** | **A soft layer below the significant depth can be ignored; one within it cannot** ← |

> **And the STRIP footing's much deeper bulb is the fact most often overlooked: a long strip footing spreads its load in only ONE direction, so the stress decays far more slowly with depth than beneath a square footing of the same width.**

> **A 2 m square footing influences the soil to about 3 m; a 2 m wide strip footing influences it to 6 m or more.**

> **The consequence for a raft or a large footing group is dramatic: a 20 m raft influences the ground to 30 m and beyond, so a soft clay layer at 25 m depth — irrelevant to any individual footing — governs the settlement of the whole building.**

> **That is why the exploration depth for a raft is specified relative to the RAFT's width rather than to any column footing's, and it is a genuine and expensive error to investigate only to the depth an individual footing would require.**

examTip.trick: **Q/[(B+z)(L+z)].** The "2:1" is the SLOPE — 2 down to 1 out — so at depth z the spread is z/2 EACH SIDE, giving z added to each dimension. Option (b) is the natural misreading.
examTip.trap: **The method underestimates the centre-line stress by 20-30 % at shallow depth** — the unsafe direction — because it assumes a uniform spread where the true distribution is bell-shaped.
examTip.mnemonic: **Significant depth ≈ 1.5 B (the 20 % isobar) for a SQUARE footing, but 3 B or more for a STRIP** — a strip spreads in one direction only. Explore to 1.5 B below founding level, and for a RAFT that means 1.5 × the raft's width.

questions.stem: In the capillary zone above the water table in a fine-grained soil, the pore water pressure is:
options: Zero throughout
Positive and increasing upward
Negative, which increases the effective stress
Negative, which reduces the effective stress
questions.solution:
**NEGATIVE (below atmospheric), and it INCREASES the effective stress.**

**Why the pressure is negative, and why that strengthens the soil:**

> **Water is drawn up into the fine pores above the water table by surface tension, exactly as it rises in a capillary tube.**

> **The water in that zone is in TENSION — it is being held up against gravity — so its pressure is BELOW atmospheric, which is to say negative when measured as gauge pressure.**

> **Terzaghi's principle then gives the result directly:**

> **σ' = σ − u**

> **If u is NEGATIVE, then −u is POSITIVE, and the effective stress σ' EXCEEDS the total stress σ.**

| Zone | Pore pressure u | Effective stress |
|---|---|---|
| **Below the water table** | **POSITIVE, = γ_w × depth below** | **σ' = σ − u, REDUCED** ← |
| **At the water table** | **ZERO** | **σ' = σ** |
| **In the capillary zone above** | **NEGATIVE, = −γ_w × height above** ← | **σ' = σ + |u|, INCREASED** ← |
| **Above the capillary rise** | Effectively zero | σ' = σ |

> **So the capillary zone is STRONGER than it would be if dry — which is the opposite of the usual intuition that water weakens soil.**

**The everyday demonstration, which is worth carrying because it makes the principle memorable:**

| Sand | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **DRY sand** | **Will not hold a shape at all — it runs** ← |
| **DAMP sand** | **Holds a vertical face; sandcastles can be built** ← |
| **SATURATED sand** | **Collapses again — it flows** ← |

> **The damp sand's strength is entirely capillary: menisci between the grains pull them together, and that suction acts exactly like an effective confining stress.**

> **The strength it produces is called APPARENT COHESION, and the qualifier matters: it is not true cohesion at all, but friction mobilised by a negative pore pressure.**

> **It DISAPPEARS the moment the soil is saturated or fully dried — which is why it must never be relied upon in design.**

**Where the failure to appreciate that has practical consequences:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A temporary excavation stands vertically in damp silt or sand** | **And COLLAPSES WITHOUT WARNING when rain saturates it or when it dries out** ← |
| **A trench left open over a monsoon** | **The apparent cohesion that held it vanishes** ← |
| **Slope stability analysis** | **Using an apparent cohesion measured on a partly saturated sample OVERESTIMATES the factor of safety** ← |
| **Compaction** | **Capillary suction in a damp soil resists compaction — the reason for bulking** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW DESCRIBES A LEADING CAUSE OF FATAL ACCIDENTS IN CONSTRUCTION, and it is worth stating plainly: an unsupported trench in damp sandy soil looks perfectly stable, and gives no warning at all before it fails.**

> **A cubic metre of soil weighs about 1.8 tonnes, so a collapse burying a worker to the waist is frequently fatal from crushing alone.**

> **The rule is that excavations deeper than about 1.2 m must be SHORED, BATTERED or BENCHED regardless of how stable the face appears — and "it was standing fine yesterday" is precisely the reasoning that precedes these accidents, because yesterday the suction was there and today it is not.**

**The height of capillary rise:**

> **h_c = 4T cos α / (γ_w d)**, with T the surface tension (about 0.073 N/m at 20 °C) and d the pore diameter.

> **Since the pore size scales with the grain size, the practical form is h_c ≈ C/(e · D₁₀), with C an empirical constant.**

| Soil | Capillary rise |
|---|---|
| **Coarse gravel** | **A few centimetres — negligible** |
| **Coarse sand** | **0.1 to 0.15 m** |
| **Fine sand** | **0.3 to 1.0 m** ← |
| **SILT** | **1.5 to 10 m** ← |
| **CLAY** | **10 to 30 m and more** ← |

> **The INVERSE relation with grain size is the key: the FINER the soil, the HIGHER the rise, because the pores are narrower and the meniscus can support a taller column.**

> **SILT's position in this table makes it the most troublesome soil in several respects at once — high enough capillary rise to reach the surface from a deep water table, combined with enough permeability for water to move quickly.**

> **That combination is why silt is the classic FROST-SUSCEPTIBLE soil: capillary action feeds water continuously to a freezing front, ice lenses grow and heave the ground, and the thaw then leaves a saturated, weak layer.**

> **A clay draws water higher but too slowly to feed the ice lenses; a sand transmits water freely but cannot lift it far. Silt does both, which is exactly the wrong combination — and it is why silty subgrades are excavated and replaced in frost-prone regions.**

examTip.trick: **Capillary water is in TENSION, so u is NEGATIVE — and σ' = σ − u means a negative u INCREASES the effective stress.** The capillary zone is stronger than dry soil.
examTip.trap: **APPARENT cohesion is not cohesion** — it is friction mobilised by suction, and it vanishes on saturation OR on drying. Never rely on it: an unsupported trench in damp sand collapses without warning.
examTip.mnemonic: **Finer soil, HIGHER capillary rise: sand 0.1-1 m, SILT 1.5-10 m, clay 10-30 m.** Silt is the worst of both worlds — high rise AND enough permeability to feed a freezing front, which is why it is the classic frost-susceptible soil.

questions.stem: The triaxial test in which the sample is NOT allowed to consolidate and NO drainage is permitted during shear is designated:
options: Consolidated drained (CD)
Unconsolidated undrained (UU)
Consolidated undrained (CU)
Drained direct shear
questions.solution:
**UNCONSOLIDATED UNDRAINED (UU)** — also called the quick test.

**The three triaxial tests, distinguished by what is permitted at each of two stages:**

| Test | Consolidation under the cell pressure? | Drainage during shear? | Parameters obtained | Field situation it models |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **UU (quick)** | **NO** ← | **NO** ← | **c_u, φ_u = 0 for a saturated clay** ← | **END OF CONSTRUCTION — rapid loading of a saturated clay with no time to drain** ← |
| **CU (consolidated undrained)** | **YES** ← | **NO** ← | **c_cu, φ_cu; with pore pressure measured, also c′, φ′** ← | **Rapid CHANGE of loading on a soil already consolidated — sudden drawdown, a rapid excavation** ← |
| **CD (drained, slow)** | **YES** | **YES** ← | **c′, φ′ — effective stress parameters directly** ← | **LONG-TERM stability — the drained condition, and sands generally** ← |

> **The naming is systematic and needs no memorisation once seen: the FIRST word describes the consolidation stage and the SECOND the shearing stage.**

**Why φ_u = 0 for a saturated clay in a UU test — the result that most puzzles students:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **The sample is saturated and sealed — no drainage, so no volume change is possible** | **Water is incompressible and cannot leave** ← |
| **Raising the cell pressure therefore produces an EQUAL rise in PORE PRESSURE** | **Δu = Δσ₃, so the EFFECTIVE stress is UNCHANGED** ← |
| **Strength depends on EFFECTIVE stress** | **Which has not changed** ← |
| **So every specimen fails at the SAME deviator stress, whatever the cell pressure** ← | **The Mohr circles all have the same DIAMETER** ← |
| **The failure envelope is therefore HORIZONTAL** | **φ_u = 0, and c_u = half the deviator stress at failure** ← |

> **THE φ = 0 CONCEPT IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE CLAY — it is a property of the TEST CONDITION.**

> **The same clay tested drained will show a perfectly ordinary φ′ of 20 to 30 degrees. The zero appears only because the undrained condition prevents the effective stress from changing.**

> **That distinction is worth being firm about, because "clay has φ = 0" is a common and misleading shorthand.**

**Which test to use — the practical rule:**

| Question being asked | Analysis | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Will the embankment stand the day it is finished?** | **TOTAL stress (undrained)** | **UU, using c_u** ← |
| **Will it stand in twenty years?** | **EFFECTIVE stress (drained)** | **CD or CU with pore pressure, using c′, φ′** ← |
| **A rapid drawdown of a reservoir against a dam's upstream face** | Effective stress with the pore pressures existing at drawdown | **CU** ← |
| **Any problem in SAND** | **Drained — sand drains as fast as it is loaded** | **CD (or direct shear)** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS CONTAIN THE MOST IMPORTANT JUDGEMENT IN CLAY MECHANICS, and it is counter-intuitive:**

> **For an EMBANKMENT or a FOUNDATION on clay — a LOADING problem — the critical condition is at the END OF CONSTRUCTION.**

> **Loading generates POSITIVE pore pressures; as they dissipate, the effective stress rises and the soil gets STRONGER. So the worst moment is the beginning.**

> **For a CUTTING or an EXCAVATION in clay — an UNLOADING problem — the critical condition is in the LONG TERM.**

> **Unloading generates NEGATIVE pore pressures; as they dissipate, water is drawn in, the soil SWELLS and WEAKENS. So the worst moment is years later.**

> **The practical consequence is one of the well-attested observations in geotechnics: railway and road cuttings in stiff clay have failed DECADES after they were made, having stood perfectly well when new.**

> **An embankment that survives its construction is generally safe; a cutting that survives its construction may not be.**

**And the other shear strength tests, for completeness:**

| Test | Note |
|---|---|
| **TRIAXIAL** | **The most versatile: drainage controlled, pore pressure measurable, a known stress state, and any confining pressure** ← |
| **DIRECT SHEAR (shear box)** | **Simple and quick, but the failure plane is FORCED, drainage is uncontrolled and the stress distribution is non-uniform** ← |
| **UNCONFINED COMPRESSION** | **A triaxial test with σ₃ = 0; for saturated clays only; q_u = 2c_u** ← |
| **VANE SHEAR** | **In-situ, for SOFT sensitive clays that cannot be sampled undisturbed; gives c_u directly, and the sensitivity from a remoulded reading** ← |

> **The VANE SHEAR test earns its place for a specific reason: a soft sensitive clay is so disturbed by the act of sampling that a laboratory test on it measures the disturbance rather than the soil.**

> **Testing it in place avoids that entirely — and rotating the vane rapidly through several turns to remould the clay, then re-testing, gives the SENSITIVITY (undisturbed ÷ remoulded strength) in the same operation.**

> **That is an elegant piece of test design, and sensitivity values above about 8 mark the "quick" clays that can turn to liquid when disturbed.**
tags: end of construction versus long term

examTip.trick: **The FIRST word is the consolidation stage, the SECOND is the shear stage.** UU = neither; CU = consolidate, then shear undrained; CD = both drained.
examTip.trap: **φ_u = 0 is a property of the TEST, not of the clay** — undrained, Δu = Δσ₃ so the effective stress never changes and every Mohr circle has the same diameter. The same clay drained gives φ′ of 20-30°.
examTip.mnemonic: **LOADING (embankment, footing) is critical at END OF CONSTRUCTION — pore pressures dissipate and it gets STRONGER. UNLOADING (a cutting) is critical in the LONG TERM — it swells and WEAKENS.** Clay cuttings have failed decades after construction.

questions.stem: In a soil with an angle of internal friction φ, the failure plane is inclined to the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE at an angle of:
options: φ
questions.solution:
**45° + φ/2.**

**Where the result comes from:**

> **On the Mohr diagram, the failure point is where the Mohr circle TOUCHES the Mohr-Coulomb envelope.**

> **The angle subtended at the centre of the circle between the major principal stress direction and the failure point is 90° + φ.**

> **Since an angle at the centre is TWICE the corresponding angle on the physical plane, the failure plane makes (90° + φ)/2 = 45° + φ/2 with the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE.**

| φ | Failure plane inclination |
|---|---|
| **0° (a saturated clay, undrained)** | **45°** ← |
| **20°** | **55°** |
| **30°** | **60°** ← |
| **40°** | **65°** |

> **Option (a), 45°, is the correct value only for the special case φ = 0 — which makes it a well-made distractor, since it is right in the undrained-clay case that students meet first.**

> **Option (c), 45° − φ/2, is the angle the failure plane makes with the MINOR principal plane, and it is also the angle in the ACTIVE Rankine state — both real quantities in the same subject.**

> **The two are complementary: (45 + φ/2) + (45 − φ/2) = 90°, as they must be, since the principal planes are perpendicular.**

**Note carefully what the angle is measured FROM:**

| Measured from | Angle |
|---|---|
| **The MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE (which is HORIZONTAL when σ₁ is vertical)** | **45° + φ/2** ← |
| **The direction of the MAJOR PRINCIPAL STRESS (vertical)** | **45° − φ/2** ← |

> **A plane and its normal are 90° apart, so the same failure surface has two descriptions, and questions exploit the ambiguity relentlessly.**

> **The reliable habit: state what you are measuring from. In a triaxial specimen with σ₁ vertical, the major principal PLANE is HORIZONTAL, and the visible failure plane in a tested specimen makes 45° + φ/2 with the horizontal — which is why a sheared sand specimen shows a steep failure surface and a clay one shows a 45° surface.**

> **That is a genuinely useful check: look at the failed specimen, and its failure angle tells you roughly what φ was.**

**The associated relation between the principal stresses at failure:**

> **σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2)**

> **The quantity tan²(45° + φ/2) is the FLOW VALUE or coefficient of passive earth pressure N_φ:**

| φ | N_φ = tan²(45+φ/2) |
|---|---|
| **0°** | **1.0** |
| **20°** | **2.04** |
| **30°** | **3.00** ← |
| **40°** | **4.60** |

> **The value at φ = 30° is exactly 3, which is worth remembering as a check — and its reciprocal, 1/3, is K_a for the same friction angle.**

> **So the same function generates the active and passive earth pressure coefficients and the triaxial failure relation, which is why these appear together in the syllabus.**

| Coefficient | Expression | At φ = 30° |
|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE, K_a** | **tan²(45 − φ/2) = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ)** | **1/3** ← |
| **AT REST, K₀** | **1 − sin φ (Jaky, normally consolidated)** | **0.5** ← |
| **PASSIVE, K_p** | **tan²(45 + φ/2) = (1+sinφ)/(1−sinφ)** | **3** ← |
| **Relation** | **K_a × K_p = 1** ← | **and K_a < K₀ < K_p always** |

**Why the failure plane is NOT at 45° to the principal plane, as it would be for maximum shear stress:**

> **The plane of MAXIMUM SHEAR STRESS is always at 45° — that is a fact of stress geometry alone.**

> **But failure does not occur on the plane of maximum shear. It occurs on the plane where the shear stress first reaches the AVAILABLE STRENGTH, and the available strength itself depends on the NORMAL stress through τ_f = c + σ tan φ.**

| Plane | Shear stress on it | Normal stress on it | Available strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| **At 45°** | **MAXIMUM** | **Moderate** | Moderate |
| **At 45° + φ/2** | **Slightly less than maximum** | **LOWER** ← | **LOWER still — so it fails FIRST** ← |

> **So the failure plane is rotated away from the maximum-shear plane toward the plane of LOWER NORMAL STRESS, because reducing the normal stress reduces the frictional resistance faster than it reduces the driving shear.**

> **The rotation is exactly φ/2, and it vanishes when φ = 0 — which is why a saturated clay in undrained shear does fail at 45°, its strength being independent of normal stress.**

> **That reasoning is worth being able to reproduce, because it explains the formula rather than merely stating it, and it makes the φ = 0 special case obvious instead of exceptional.**

examTip.trick: **45° + φ/2 from the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE** (horizontal when σ₁ is vertical). Option (a) 45° is right only for φ = 0; option (c) 45° − φ/2 is the angle from the major principal STRESS direction, and also the active Rankine angle.
examTip.trap: **Always state what the angle is measured FROM** — a plane and its normal differ by 90°, and (45+φ/2) + (45−φ/2) = 90° exactly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Failure is NOT on the plane of maximum shear (45°)** — it rotates by φ/2 toward the plane of LOWER NORMAL STRESS, where friction falls faster than the driving shear. At φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3, K₀ = 0.5, K_p = 3, and K_a × K_p = 1.

questions.stem: For a normally consolidated soil with an angle of internal friction φ′, the coefficient of earth pressure AT REST is given by Jaky's expression:
options: K₀ = 1 − sin φ′
K₀ = (1 − sin φ′)/(1 + sin φ′)
K₀ = tan²(45° + φ′/2)
K₀ = 1 + sin φ′
questions.solution:
**K₀ = 1 − sin φ′.**

**The three coefficients, and why K₀ lies between the others:**

| State | Coefficient | At φ′ = 30° | Wall movement required |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45 − φ/2)** ← (option b) | **0.333** | **The wall moves AWAY from the soil** ← |
| **AT REST** | **K₀ = 1 − sin φ′** ← | **0.500** | **NO movement at all** ← |
| **PASSIVE** | **K_p = tan²(45 + φ/2)** ← (option c) | **3.000** | **The wall moves INTO the soil** ← |

> **Options (b) and (c) are the active and passive coefficients — real expressions from the same family, offered for the at-rest one.**

> **The ordering K_a < K₀ < K_p always holds, and it makes physical sense: releasing the soil laterally lets it push less, and compressing it laterally makes it push far more.**

**The MOVEMENT REQUIRED is the practical heart of this topic:**

| State | Wall movement needed to develop it |
|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **VERY SMALL — about 0.001 H for dense sand, 0.004 H for loose sand, 0.01-0.02 H for clay** ← |
| **PASSIVE** | **VERY LARGE — about 0.02 H for dense sand, up to 0.1 H or more for loose soil and clay** ← |

> **THE ASYMMETRY BETWEEN THESE TWO IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL FACT IN EARTH PRESSURE THEORY, and it has two consequences:**

> **First, the ACTIVE state is reached by almost any real wall. A retaining wall 6 m high needs to move only about 6 mm to mobilise active pressure fully — which any wall will do through its own flexure and foundation yielding. So designing for active pressure is realistic.**

> **Second, the PASSIVE state needs movements of 120 mm or more on the same wall — displacements far larger than a structure can tolerate. So the FULL passive resistance is usually NOT available at working conditions, and a large factor of safety (2 to 3) is applied to passive resistance for that reason, not merely for uncertainty in the soil.**

> **Treating passive resistance as freely available is one of the standard errors in retaining structure design.**

**Where the AT-REST condition actually governs:**

| Structure | Why K₀ applies |
|---|---|
| **BASEMENT walls, propped at floor levels** | **Restrained top and bottom — they cannot move enough to relieve to the active state** ← |
| **Bridge ABUTMENTS integral with the deck** | Restrained by the deck |
| **Rigid box culverts and shafts** | No movement possible |
| **Braced excavations** | **Struts prevent movement; pressures approach or exceed at-rest, and the distribution is quite different — see below** ← |
| **Massive gravity walls on rock** | Cannot yield |

> **The BASEMENT WALL is the case most often got wrong in ordinary building design: it is designed as a retaining wall using active pressure, when the floor slabs at its top and bottom prevent the movement that active pressure requires.**

> **Using K_a = 0.33 where K₀ = 0.50 applies understates the lateral load by a THIRD — and the resulting cracking of basement walls is a common defect.**

> **For OVERCONSOLIDATED soils K₀ is higher still, given approximately by K₀(OC) = (1 − sin φ′)·OCR^(sin φ′), and it can EXCEED 1 for heavily overconsolidated clays — meaning the horizontal stress is greater than the vertical.**

> **A basement in stiff overconsolidated London-type clay may face K₀ approaching or exceeding 1, which is three times the active value and a completely different design.**

**The BRACED EXCAVATION note deserves expansion, since its pressure distribution is genuinely different:**

| Aspect | Cantilever/yielding wall | BRACED excavation |
|---|---|---|
| **Pressure distribution** | **TRIANGULAR, increasing with depth** ← | **Roughly TRAPEZOIDAL or rectangular — the APPARENT PRESSURE diagram** ← |
| **Why** | **The wall rotates about its base, so the top yields most** | **The top is strutted FIRST and cannot yield; the excavation proceeds downward, so movement occurs at the BOTTOM** ← |
| **Design basis** | Rankine or Coulomb | **Terzaghi and Peck's empirical apparent pressure diagrams** ← |

> **The reason for the difference is entirely one of CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE, which is a good illustration of a general geotechnical principle: the pressure on a structure depends on how it MOVES, and how it moves depends on how it was BUILT.**

> **A braced excavation is strutted from the top down, so the top never gets the chance to yield into the active state, while the base does — inverting the usual pattern and producing the characteristic bulging pressure diagram.**

**And the DRAINAGE point that dominates all of these numbers in practice:**

| Condition | Lateral pressure |
|---|---|
| **Drained granular backfill, φ = 30°** | **K_a γ H = 0.33 × 18 × H = 6H kPa** ← |
| **The SAME backfill, fully SATURATED with no drainage** | **K_a γ′ H + γ_w H = 0.33 × 8.2 × H + 9.81H = 12.5H kPa** ← |

> **Water DOUBLES the lateral thrust — and it acts with a coefficient of 1.0, since water transmits pressure equally in all directions and has no friction angle to reduce it.**

> **That is why weep holes, a granular filter and a longitudinal drain behind a retaining wall are not optional details but the single most important provision in its design.**

> **More retaining walls fail from blocked drainage than from any error in the earth pressure coefficient — and the coefficient is what gets the attention.**

examTip.trick: **K₀ = 1 − sin φ′ (Jaky).** At φ = 30°: K_a = 0.33, K₀ = 0.50, K_p = 3.0. Options (b) and (c) are the active and passive expressions.
examTip.trap: **ACTIVE needs tiny movement (~0.001 H) and is always reached; PASSIVE needs ~0.02-0.1 H, far more than a structure tolerates** — so full passive resistance is usually NOT available, hence its large factor of safety.
examTip.mnemonic: **A propped BASEMENT wall cannot move, so K₀ governs, not K_a** — using 0.33 where 0.50 applies understates the load by a third. And WATER DOUBLES the thrust at a coefficient of 1.0: drainage beats any refinement of the coefficient.

questions.stem: A GRANULAR FILTER placed behind a retaining wall must satisfy the requirement that the filter material is:
options: Finer than the protected soil, so that no water can pass
Of exactly the same grading as the protected soil
Coarse enough to drain freely, yet fine enough to retain the particles of the protected soil
As uniform as possible, with a uniformity coefficient of 1
questions.solution:
**COARSE enough to drain freely, yet FINE enough to RETAIN the particles of the soil it protects.**

**The two requirements pull in opposite directions, and that is the whole design problem:**

| Requirement | Purpose | Criterion (Terzaghi) |
|---|---|---|
| **PERMEABILITY — the filter must pass water freely** | **So that pressure does not build up behind it** ← | **D₁₅(filter) ≥ 4 to 5 × D₁₅(soil)** ← |
| **RETENTION — the filter must not let the soil through** | **So that the soil is not washed away (piped) into the drain** ← | **D₁₅(filter) ≤ 4 to 5 × D₈₅(soil)** ← |

> **So the filter's D₁₅ is squeezed between two bounds — at least 4 times the soil's D₁₅ and at most 4 times the soil's D₈₅ — and a material satisfying both is the filter.**

> **A third criterion is usually added: D₅₀(filter) ≤ 25 × D₅₀(soil), and the filter should not be gap-graded.**

**A worked check:**

> **A silty sand backfill has D₁₅ = 0.06 mm and D₈₅ = 0.7 mm.**

| Criterion | Working | Bound on the filter's D₁₅ |
|---|---|---|
| **Permeability** | **≥ 4 × 0.06** | **≥ 0.24 mm** ← |
| **Retention** | **≤ 4 × 0.7** | **≤ 2.8 mm** ← |

> **So a filter sand with D₁₅ between about 0.24 and 2.8 mm satisfies both — a comfortable range, and a coarse concreting sand would do.**

> **Where the protected soil is a fine silt or clay the two bounds can close up or even cross, and a single-stage filter becomes impossible — which is why GRADED (multi-stage) filters are used, each layer filtering the one before it, progressing from fine to coarse.**

> **The alternative, now more usual, is a GEOTEXTILE filter, whose pore size can be specified directly and which needs no grading exercise at all.**

**Why option (d) is wrong, and why it matters:**

> **A uniformity coefficient of 1 means every particle is the same size — a single-sized material.**

> **That is undesirable in a filter: a well-graded filter is more stable, less liable to segregate during placing, and less prone to internal erosion of its own fines.**

> **A single-sized gravel also has very large voids relative to its D₁₅, so it may fail the retention criterion in practice even when the arithmetic passes.**

**What the drainage system behind a wall consists of:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **WEEP HOLES — 75 to 100 mm, at 1 to 1.5 m centres, sloping outward** | **Let the water OUT through the wall** ← |
| **A granular FILTER or a geotextile-wrapped drain behind the wall** | **Prevents the backfill washing out through the weep holes** ← |
| **A LONGITUDINAL perforated drain at the base** | **Collects the water and takes it to an outfall** ← |
| **A free-draining BACKFILL, or a drainage blanket** | Conducts water down to the drain |
| **An impermeable CAP or surface seal at the top** | **Keeps surface water OUT of the backfill in the first place** ← |
| **Provision for CLEANING and inspection** | Weep holes block |

> **THE WEEP HOLE WITHOUT A FILTER IS THE CLASSIC FAILURE, and it fails in a way that looks like success at first:**

> **The holes discharge freely and the wall appears to be draining. What is discharging is the backfill's fine fraction, washed out grain by grain.**

> **A void forms behind the wall, the ground surface above settles, and eventually either the wall is undermined or the holes block with the coarser residue — at which point the full water pressure develops against a wall never designed for it.**

> **So a weep hole must ALWAYS be backed by a filter, and the appearance of fines in the discharge is a warning that it is not.**

**The magnitude of what the drainage prevents:**

| Case, wall 6 m high, backfill γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30° | Thrust per metre |
|---|---|
| **DRAINED** | **½ × 0.33 × 18 × 6² = 107 kN/m** ← |
| **SATURATED, undrained (γ′ = 8.2 kN/m³, plus water)** | **½ × 0.33 × 8.2 × 6² + ½ × 9.81 × 6² = 49 + 177 = 226 kN/m** ← |
| **Ratio** | **More than DOUBLED** ← |

> **And the point of application also RISES, because the water pressure diagram is triangular from the top of the saturated zone — so the OVERTURNING MOMENT increases by even more than the thrust does.**

> **A wall designed for 107 kN/m and subjected to 226 kN/m at a higher lever arm has no factor of safety left at all, which is why drainage failure is the leading cause of retaining wall collapse.**

**And the same filter principle appears elsewhere, which is worth noting:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Behind retaining walls** | ← this question |
| **INVERTED FILTERS at the downstream toe of weirs and dams** | **Against piping — the same two criteria** ← |
| **Filter layers in an EARTH DAM's chimney and blanket drains** | **The most critical application; filter failure has destroyed dams** ← |
| **Around perforated subsoil drains** | Standard practice |
| **Under rip-rap and pitching on slopes** | **The stone armour is useless if the soil beneath washes out through it** ← |
| **Beneath a sub-base, as a separation layer** | Prevents subgrade fines pumping up |

> **The unifying idea across all of these is worth stating once: WHEREVER WATER LEAVES SOIL, IT WILL TRY TO TAKE THE SOIL WITH IT, and a filter is what lets the water go while keeping the soil.**

examTip.trick: **Two opposing criteria on the filter's D₁₅: ≥ 4-5 × D₁₅(soil) for PERMEABILITY, and ≤ 4-5 × D₈₅(soil) for RETENTION.** The filter's D₁₅ is squeezed between them.
examTip.trap: **A weep hole WITHOUT a filter looks like it is working** — it discharges freely, but what it discharges is the backfill's fines. A void forms, the surface settles, and the holes eventually block.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water more than DOUBLES the thrust (107 → 226 kN/m on a 6 m wall) and raises its point of application**, so the overturning moment grows even faster. Drainage failure is the leading cause of retaining wall collapse.

questions.stem: As per IS 2911, the minimum centre-to-centre SPACING of friction piles in a group is generally:
options: 1.5 times the pile diameter
3 times the pile diameter
2 times the pile diameter
6 times the pile diameter
questions.solution:
**3 times the pile diameter** for friction piles (with 2.5 d sometimes accepted as an absolute minimum, and 2.5 d permitted for end-bearing piles founded on rock).

**The spacing rules:**

| Pile type | Minimum centre-to-centre spacing |
|---|---|
| **FRICTION piles** | **3 d** ← |
| **END-BEARING piles (on rock or a hard stratum)** | **2.5 d** ← |
| **Piles through soft compressible clay** | **Wider — up to 4 d or more** ← |
| **Practical upper limit** | **4 d, beyond which the pile cap becomes uneconomically large** ← |

> **The reason FRICTION piles need MORE spacing than END-BEARING piles is the essential idea here:**

> **A friction pile transfers its load to the soil ALONG ITS SHAFT, into the surrounding ground. The stressed zones of neighbouring piles therefore OVERLAP, and the soil between them is loaded by both.**

> **An end-bearing pile delivers its load to a hard stratum at its TOE, where the stress is concentrated in a small zone and there is far less interaction.**

> **So the spacing rule is not arbitrary but a direct consequence of where each pile puts its load.**

**GROUP EFFICIENCY, which is what the spacing exists to protect:**

> **η = (capacity of the group) / (n × capacity of a single pile)**

| Soil | Typical group efficiency | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Piles in SAND, driven, closely spaced** | **η can EXCEED 1** ← | **DRIVING DENSIFIES the sand between the piles, so the group is stronger than the sum of its parts** ← |
| **Piles in sand, bored** | **η ≈ 0.7 to 1.0** | Boring loosens rather than densifies |
| **Piles in CLAY** | **η ≈ 0.6 to 0.9** ← | **Overlapping stressed zones; no densification** |
| **Widely spaced piles (above about 8 d)** | **η → 1** | No interaction |

> **THE SAND ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE RESULT WORTH KNOWING: driving piles into loose sand compacts it, so a driven pile group in sand may carry MORE than the individual piles would suggest.**

> **In clay there is no such benefit and the efficiency is always below one — so a clay group must be checked both pile-by-pile and as a BLOCK.**

**The BLOCK FAILURE check, which governs closely spaced groups in clay:**

| Mode | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **INDIVIDUAL pile failure** | **n × (single pile capacity)** |
| **BLOCK failure — the group and the soil between it fail as one large pier** | **Perimeter shear on the block + end bearing on its base area** ← |
| **The design capacity** | **The LESSER of the two** ← |

> **The block mode governs when the piles are close together, and it is a genuinely different mechanism: the soil trapped between the piles moves down with them, so the group behaves as a single deep foundation of the group's overall plan dimensions.**

> **Checking only the individual piles, as is often done, can therefore overestimate a closely spaced group's capacity substantially.**

**GROUP SETTLEMENT, which is the other and larger consequence:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A pile GROUP settles far MORE than a single pile at the same load per pile** ← | **Because the group's stressed zone extends far DEEPER** ← |
| **A single pile stresses the soil to about 1-2 pile diameters below its toe** | A shallow zone |
| **A group of width B stresses the soil to about 1.5 B below the equivalent raft level** ← | **Which for a large group is very deep indeed** ← |

> **THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT ABOUT PILE GROUPS, and it is regularly missed:**

> **A pile load test on a SINGLE pile shows a settlement of a few millimetres and is taken as proof that the foundation is satisfactory.**

> **But a group of 25 piles spanning 10 m stresses the ground to 15 m below its base — and a compressible layer at that depth, which the single pile never reached, will settle the whole group by an order of magnitude more.**

> **So a single-pile load test proves the capacity of a pile, and says almost nothing about the settlement of the group.**

> **The group settlement must be computed separately, treating the group as an EQUIVALENT RAFT — conventionally placed at two-thirds of the pile length for friction piles, or at the toe level for end-bearing piles — and the consolidation of every layer below that raft must be included.**

**And the associated design provisions:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **Minimum number of piles under a column** | **Usually 3, so the cap is stable against eccentricity; 2 requires a tie beam** ← |
| **PILE CAP overhang beyond the outer piles** | **100 to 150 mm** |
| **Cap embedded into the pile heads** | **50 to 75 mm, with the reinforcement anchored into the cap** ← |
| **TIE BEAMS between caps** | **Resist the moments from construction eccentricity, and are mandatory in seismic design** ← |
| **NEGATIVE SKIN FRICTION where fill or soft clay overlies** | **Adds load rather than resisting it — must be SUBTRACTED from capacity** ← |

> **The TIE BEAM requirement in the fourth row deserves the emphasis it is given in seismic areas: piles are slender and are poor at resisting lateral load and moment individually, and tying the caps together makes the foundation act as one unit rather than as a set of independent points.**

> **In the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, as in other events, foundation performance was rarely the primary failure — but where piles were used without adequate tying and without allowance for lateral load, the connection between pile and cap proved to be the weak link.**

examTip.trick: **3 d for FRICTION piles, 2.5 d for END-BEARING on rock.** Friction piles need more because they load the soil along the SHAFT, so their stressed zones overlap; an end-bearing pile delivers its load at the TOE.
examTip.trap: **Group efficiency can EXCEED 1 for DRIVEN piles in SAND** — driving densifies the soil between them. In clay it is always below 1, and the BLOCK failure mode must also be checked.
examTip.mnemonic: **A single-pile load test proves capacity and says nothing about GROUP SETTLEMENT** — a group of width B stresses the soil to 1.5 B below the equivalent raft, far deeper than one pile ever reaches. Compute the group as an EQUIVALENT RAFT at ⅔ the pile length.

questions.stem: The NET ULTIMATE bearing capacity of a foundation is obtained from the GROSS ultimate bearing capacity by:
options: Dividing by the factor of safety
Multiplying by the factor of safety
Adding the overburden pressure at founding level
Subtracting the overburden pressure at founding level
questions.solution:
**SUBTRACTING the overburden pressure at founding level:** q_nu = q_u − γD.

**The complete family of bearing capacity terms, which this question exists to separate:**

| Term | Definition | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **GROSS ULTIMATE, q_u** | **The TOTAL pressure at the base at which the soil fails in shear** | **From Terzaghi: cN_c + γDN_q + 0.5γBN_γ** ← |
| **NET ULTIMATE, q_nu** | **The NET INCREASE in pressure at failure, over what was already there** ← | **q_u − γD** ← |
| **NET SAFE, q_ns** | **Net ultimate divided by the factor of safety** ← | **q_nu / F** ← |
| **GROSS SAFE, q_s** | **Net safe plus the overburden restored** | **q_nu/F + γD** ← |
| **SAFE BEARING CAPACITY** | **The gross safe value — a SHEAR FAILURE criterion** ← | As above |
| **ALLOWABLE BEARING PRESSURE, q_a** | **The LESSER of the safe bearing capacity and the pressure that produces the permissible SETTLEMENT** ← | **The value actually used in design** ← |

> **Option (a), dividing by the factor of safety, takes NET ULTIMATE to NET SAFE — a real and adjacent step, offered for this one, which is what makes it the designed distractor.**

**Why the overburden is subtracted — the reasoning:**

> **Before the foundation is built, the soil at founding level already carries the weight of the soil above it, γD.**

> **Excavating removes that pressure; placing the foundation restores it and adds more.**

> **So the soil only experiences a NET INCREASE of (applied pressure − γD), and it is that net increase which causes settlement and which must be limited.**

> **The factor of safety is therefore applied to the NET value, not the gross — because applying it to the gross would penalise the designer for a pressure the soil was carrying quite happily beforehand.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The DEEPER the foundation, the greater γD, and the greater the gross safe capacity** | **Which is one reason deeper footings carry more** ← |
| **A FULLY COMPENSATED (floating) foundation has zero net pressure** | **The weight of soil excavated equals the weight of the structure — so in principle no settlement at all** ← |

> **THE FLOATING FOUNDATION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE LOGICAL LIMIT OF THIS IDEA and it is a real technique:**

> **A basement excavated deep enough that the soil removed weighs as much as the building imposed produces NO net increase in stress, so the soil is no more loaded than before and settlement is theoretically nil.**

> **It is used for heavy structures on soft clay where no other shallow solution exists — and the classic difficulty is the one met earlier: during construction, when the excavation is open and the building not yet built, the net pressure is strongly NEGATIVE and the basement will HEAVE, or float if the water table is high.**

> **So a compensated foundation is a settlement solution that creates a construction-stage problem, and both must be designed for.**

**The factor of safety, since it is applied at a specific point:**

| Aspect | Value |
|---|---|
| **Typical F against SHEAR failure** | **2.5 to 3.0** ← |
| **Applied to** | **The NET ultimate, not the gross** ← |
| **Why so high** | **Soil variability; limited sampling; the empirical nature of the bearing capacity factors; and the severity of a shear failure** ← |

> **Compare that with the factor of about 1.5 on the strength of concrete or steel: soil is a material the designer did not select, cannot specify and has sampled at a few points only — so a larger margin is warranted.**

**And the SETTLEMENT criterion, which usually governs in practice:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The allowable pressure is the LESSER of the shear and settlement criteria** | ← |
| **For most foundations on SAND, SETTLEMENT governs** ← | **Sands rarely fail in shear; they settle first** |
| **For soft CLAY, shear may govern** | Or settlement, depending on the layer |
| **For footings on rock or dense gravel** | Neither usually governs; the structure does |

> **The permissible settlements (IS 1904):**

| Structure and soil | Maximum TOTAL settlement | Maximum DIFFERENTIAL |
|---|---|---|
| **Isolated footings on SAND** | **40 mm** ← | **Angular distortion 1/300** ← |
| **Isolated footings on CLAY** | **65 mm** ← | 1/300 |
| **RAFT on sand** | **40 to 65 mm** | — |
| **Raft on clay** | **65 to 100 mm** ← | — |

> **THE DIFFERENTIAL SETTLEMENT IS WHAT DAMAGES A BUILDING, not the total — and that is the point worth carrying away.**

> **A structure that settles 100 mm UNIFORMLY suffers no structural distress at all; the doors still close and the frame is unstrained. Only its connections to external services and to adjoining ground are affected.**

> **A structure that settles 25 mm at one column and 5 mm at the next is DISTORTED, and the frame must accommodate that distortion through bending and shear it was not designed for.**

> **Hence the limit is expressed as ANGULAR DISTORTION — the differential settlement divided by the span between the points — with about 1/300 the threshold for cracking in a framed building and 1/150 the threshold for structural damage.**

> **The famous illustration is the Tower of Pisa, which has settled several metres in total without structural failure of the tower itself: it is the DIFFERENTIAL settlement — the tilt — that made it notable and that threatened it, not the magnitude.**

examTip.trick: **q_nu = q_u − γD.** The chain: gross ultimate → SUBTRACT γD → net ultimate → DIVIDE by F → net safe → ADD γD back → gross safe. Option (a) is the next step along, not this one.
examTip.trap: **The factor of safety applies to the NET value** — the soil was already carrying γD quite happily before the foundation existed, so penalising the designer for it would be wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **ALLOWABLE bearing pressure is the LESSER of the shear and settlement criteria — and on sand, SETTLEMENT almost always governs.** And it is DIFFERENTIAL settlement that damages buildings: 100 mm uniform is harmless, 20 mm differential is not. Limit angular distortion to ~1/300.

questions.stem: The excess pressure inside a spherical LIQUID DROPLET of diameter d, for a surface tension σ, is:
options: 4σ/d
2σ/d
8σ/d
σ/d
questions.solution:
**4σ/d.**

**The derivation, which also generates the other three cases:**

> **Consider a droplet cut in half. Two forces act on the hemisphere:**

| Force | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Pressure acting on the projected circular area** | **p × (πd²/4)** ← |
| **Surface tension acting round the circumference** | **σ × (πd)** ← |

> **Equating them: p × πd²/4 = σ × πd, so p = 4σ/d.**

**The related cases, which differ only in the NUMBER OF SURFACES:**

| Body | Excess pressure | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **LIQUID DROPLET** | **4σ/d** ← | **ONE surface, circumference πd** |
| **SOAP BUBBLE** | **8σ/d** ← (option c) | **TWO surfaces (inside and outside), so 2 × πd** ← |
| **LIQUID JET (cylindrical)** | **2σ/d** ← (option b) | **A cylinder of length L: p × dL = σ × 2L** ← |

> **Every distractor is therefore the correct answer to a NEIGHBOURING case, which is what makes the set demanding — the arithmetic is trivial and the discrimination is not.**

> **The mnemonic that keeps them straight: a BUBBLE has TWO films so it doubles the droplet's value (8σ/d); a JET is cylindrical rather than spherical, so it halves it (2σ/d).**

**The inverse dependence on size, which is the physically interesting part:**

| Droplet diameter | Excess pressure (water, σ = 0.073 N/m) |
|---|---|
| **1 mm** | **4 × 0.073/0.001 = 292 Pa** |
| **0.1 mm** | **2,920 Pa** |
| **0.01 mm (a fog droplet)** | **29,200 Pa ≈ 0.29 bar** ← |
| **1 µm** | **292,000 Pa ≈ 2.9 bar** ← |

> **So the SMALLER the droplet, the HIGHER its internal pressure — which has real consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Small droplets evaporate FASTER than large ones** | **Higher internal pressure raises the vapour pressure at the surface** ← |
| **In a mist, large droplets GROW at the expense of small ones** | **The small ones evaporate and the vapour condenses on the large — which is how rain forms** ← |
| **Very fine sprays require high pressure to produce** | **The nozzle must supply the surface energy** ← |
| **CAVITATION bubbles collapse violently** | **A shrinking bubble's internal pressure rises without limit** ← |

> **The RAIN FORMATION entry in the second row is a satisfying application: a cloud of uniform droplets is unstable, because any droplet that happens to be slightly larger has a slightly lower internal pressure and therefore grows while its neighbours shrink.**

> **That instability, driven purely by surface tension, is one of the mechanisms by which cloud droplets become raindrops.**

**SURFACE TENSION itself, since the formula depends on it:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Definition** | **Force per unit LENGTH along a line on the surface (N/m); equivalently, energy per unit AREA (J/m²)** ← |
| **Cause** | **A molecule in the bulk is pulled equally in all directions; one at the SURFACE has no neighbours above, so there is a net inward pull** ← |
| **Value for water at 20 °C** | **0.0728 N/m — high, because of hydrogen bonding** ← |
| **Effect of TEMPERATURE** | **DECREASES with rising temperature; becomes ZERO at the critical point** ← |
| **Effect of a SURFACTANT (detergent)** | **REDUCES it sharply — which is how detergents work** ← |

> **The DIMENSIONAL EQUIVALENCE in the first row is worth noticing: N/m and J/m² are the same units, and the two definitions are the same fact stated differently.**

> **Surface tension is the energy cost of creating new surface, and a liquid minimises its surface area for that reason — which is why a free droplet is spherical, the sphere having the least surface area for a given volume.**

**And where surface tension matters in civil engineering, since it is easily dismissed as a laboratory curiosity:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAPILLARY RISE in soils** | **The negative pore pressure and apparent cohesion discussed under soil mechanics** ← |
| **Capillary rise in masonry — rising damp** | **The reason a DPC is needed** ← |
| **Air entrainment in concrete** | **Air-entraining agents are surfactants; they stabilise fine bubbles** ← |
| **Flotation and froth processes** | Mineral processing |
| **Measurement errors in fine manometer tubes** | **A capillary correction is needed below about 6 mm bore** ← |
| **Formation of a meniscus in a piezometer** | Affects readings in fine tubes |
| **The behaviour of small-scale hydraulic MODELS** | **SCALE EFFECT — see below** ← |

> **The MODEL SCALE EFFECT in the last row is a genuine research difficulty: a hydraulic model scaled by Froude similarity does not reproduce surface tension correctly, because the Weber number is not matched.**

> **In a small model, surface tension is disproportionately strong relative to gravity, so thin sheets of flow — over a spillway crest or a weir at low head — behave differently from the prototype.**

> **The remedy is to keep model depths above a minimum (commonly 30 mm over a weir crest) so that surface tension effects stay negligible, which is a real constraint on how small a model may be built.**

examTip.trick: **Droplet 4σ/d, SOAP BUBBLE 8σ/d (two films), JET 2σ/d (cylindrical).** Every distractor is the correct answer to a neighbouring case.
examTip.trap: **Excess pressure varies INVERSELY with size** — a 1 µm droplet holds nearly 3 bar. That is why small droplets evaporate faster and large ones grow at their expense, which is one route to raindrop formation.
examTip.mnemonic: **N/m and J/m² are the same units** — surface tension is the energy cost of new surface, which is why a free droplet is spherical. And it does not scale in Froude models, so keep model heads above ~30 mm.

questions.stem: A NEWTONIAN fluid is one in which:
options: The viscosity is independent of temperature
The shear stress is zero at all rates of deformation
The shear stress is directly proportional to the rate of shear strain
A minimum shear stress must be exceeded before flow begins
questions.solution:
**The SHEAR STRESS is directly PROPORTIONAL to the rate of shear strain** — Newton's law of viscosity:

> **τ = μ (du/dy)**

> **where μ is the DYNAMIC (absolute) viscosity, and the relation is a straight line through the ORIGIN on a plot of τ against du/dy.**

**The classification of fluids by that plot:**

| Fluid | Behaviour | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **IDEAL fluid** | **τ = 0 always — zero viscosity; the horizontal axis** ← (option b) | **A theoretical construct only** |
| **NEWTONIAN** | **A straight line through the origin; μ constant** ← | **Water, air, kerosene, glycerine, most gases and thin oils** ← |
| **NON-NEWTONIAN, PSEUDOPLASTIC (shear-thinning)** | **Curve concave to the τ-axis; apparent viscosity FALLS as shearing increases** ← | **Blood, paint, polymer solutions, most slurries** ← |
| **NON-NEWTONIAN, DILATANT (shear-thickening)** | **Apparent viscosity RISES with shearing** ← | **Concentrated sand-water slurry, cornflour paste, quicksand** ← |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC (ideal plastic)** | **Needs a YIELD STRESS τ₀ before any flow; then linear** ← (option d) | **Toothpaste, drilling MUD, fresh CONCRETE, sewage sludge** ← |
| **Thixotropic** | **Apparent viscosity falls with TIME of shearing at a constant rate** ← | **Some paints, bentonite, sensitive clays** ← |
| **IDEAL SOLID** | The vertical axis — no deformation at all | — |

> **Options (b) and (d) describe the IDEAL FLUID and the BINGHAM PLASTIC respectively — both real categories from the same classification, offered for the Newtonian one.**

**Why the Bingham and thixotropic entries matter in civil engineering:**

| Material | Why the behaviour is exploited |
|---|---|
| **Fresh CONCRETE** | **It has a yield stress — which is exactly why it holds a SLUMP instead of flowing flat, and why the slump test works at all** ← |
| **BENTONITE slurry (in a diaphragm wall or a bored pile)** | **Thixotropic: it is PUMPABLE while being agitated and GELS when still, so it supports the trench wall and holds cuttings in suspension when circulation stops** ← |
| **Drilling mud** | The same property |
| **Sensitive CLAY** | **Thixotropy in reverse — remoulding destroys the structure and the strength; it partly recovers with time at rest** ← |

> **THE BENTONITE CASE IS THE MOST ELEGANT PIECE OF APPLIED RHEOLOGY IN CONSTRUCTION, and it is worth stating fully:**

> **A diaphragm wall trench is excavated under a bentonite slurry. While being pumped, the slurry is thin enough to circulate freely and carry the spoil out.**

> **When circulation stops, it GELS within minutes — so the excavated soil it is carrying stays in suspension instead of settling to the bottom of the trench, and the gel's yield strength plus its hydrostatic pressure holds the unsupported trench walls up.**

> **Restart the pump and it thins again. One material solving three problems — support, transport and suspension — purely through its non-Newtonian behaviour.**

**DYNAMIC against KINEMATIC viscosity, since both are called "viscosity":**

| Property | Symbol | Definition | SI unit | CGS unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DYNAMIC (absolute)** | **μ** | **τ / (du/dy)** | **Pa·s (= N·s/m²)** | **POISE; 1 Pa·s = 10 poise** ← |
| **KINEMATIC** | **ν** | **μ / ρ** ← | **m²/s** | **STOKES; 1 m²/s = 10⁴ stokes** ← |

> **The word KINEMATIC signals that the units contain only LENGTH and TIME — mass has cancelled out, because it is divided by density.**

> **That is why ν is the viscosity appearing in the Reynolds number (Re = VD/ν) and in most flow problems: what governs whether flow is laminar or turbulent is the ratio of viscous to inertial effects, and dividing by density performs exactly that comparison.**

> **Values for water at 20 °C: μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s, ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s — both worth carrying, and the second especially, since Re = VD/10⁻⁶ makes Reynolds numbers easy to estimate mentally.**

**And the opposite temperature behaviour of liquids and gases, which is the classic examination point:**

| Fluid | Viscosity with RISING temperature | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **LIQUIDS** | **DECREASES** ← | **Viscosity comes from intermolecular COHESION, which weakens as molecules gain energy and separate** ← |
| **GASES** | **INCREASES** ← | **Viscosity comes from MOLECULAR MOMENTUM EXCHANGE between layers, which intensifies as molecules move faster** ← |

> **The two mechanisms are entirely different, which is why the trends are opposite — and stating the mechanism is the reliable way to recall which way each goes.**

> **Everyday confirmation for the liquid case: engine oil and honey both thin markedly when warmed, and a cold engine is harder to turn over than a warm one.**

The constant being the dynamic viscosity.

examTip.trick: **τ = μ du/dy — a straight line through the ORIGIN.** Option (b) is the IDEAL fluid (τ = 0); option (d) is the BINGHAM PLASTIC (needs a yield stress first).
examTip.trap: **Liquids get LESS viscous when heated; gases get MORE.** Different mechanisms — cohesion for liquids, momentum exchange for gases — so state the mechanism to recall the direction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fresh concrete is a BINGHAM PLASTIC — a yield stress is exactly why it holds a slump.** And bentonite is THIXOTROPIC: thin while pumped, gelling when still, so it supports the trench and holds the spoil in suspension. ν = μ/ρ; for water ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s.

questions.stem: For a submerged CURVED surface, the VERTICAL component of the total hydrostatic force is equal to:
options: The weight of the liquid contained in the volume extending vertically from the surface to the free surface level
The force on the vertical projection of the curved surface
The pressure at the centroid multiplied by the curved surface area
Zero, because the vertical components cancel
questions.solution:
**The WEIGHT of the liquid in the volume extending vertically from the curved surface up to the free surface level** (real liquid, or the imaginary volume where none is physically present).

**The two components, which are found separately and then combined:**

| Component | How it is found |
|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL, F_H** | **The force on the VERTICAL PROJECTION of the curved surface — treated exactly as a plane surface** ← (option b) |
| **VERTICAL, F_V** | **The WEIGHT of the volume of liquid vertically above the surface up to the free surface** ← |
| **RESULTANT** | **F = √(F_H² + F_V²), at an angle θ = tan⁻¹(F_V/F_H) to the horizontal** ← |

> **Option (b) is the HORIZONTAL component, which makes it the designed distractor — both statements are true, of different components.**

**The "imaginary volume" qualification, which is where this becomes subtle:**

| Case | The volume | Direction of F_V |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid lies ABOVE the curved surface** | **The REAL liquid resting on it** | **DOWNWARD** ← |
| **Liquid lies BELOW the curved surface** | **The IMAGINARY volume that WOULD lie above it, up to the free surface level** ← | **UPWARD** ← |

> **The second case is the one that puzzles: a curved gate with water beneath it experiences an UPWARD vertical force equal to the weight of the water that is NOT there.**

> **The justification is straightforward once seen — the pressure at each point on the underside depends only on its depth below the free surface, and integrating those pressures over the surface gives exactly the weight of the column that would stand above it.**

> **So the imaginary volume is a computational device that gives the right answer, not a claim about where the water is.**

**Why this matters — the resultant passes through the centre of curvature:**

> **For a CIRCULAR arc surface, every element of pressure acts NORMAL to the surface, and a normal to a circular arc passes through its CENTRE.**

> **So the entire resultant force passes through the centre of curvature, whatever its magnitude and direction.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A radial (TAINTER / segmental) gate needs no gate-lifting force to overcome water pressure** ← | **The resultant passes through the pivot, so it exerts NO MOMENT about it** ← |
| **The hoisting effort is only that needed to lift the gate's own WEIGHT and to overcome friction** ← | **Which is why radial gates are used on large barrages** ← |
| **The trunnion (pivot) carries the whole thrust** | So it must be founded on massive piers |

> **THAT IS THE PRINCIPAL ENGINEERING APPLICATION OF THIS TOPIC, and it is a genuinely elegant one:**

> **A vertical lift gate on a barrage must be raised against enormous friction generated by the water thrust pressing it into its guides. A radial gate of the same size is turned about a pivot through which that thrust passes, so the water contributes nothing to the effort required.**

> **The hoisting machinery can therefore be a fraction of the size, the gate can be opened quickly during a flood, and the whole arrangement is more reliable — which is why the barrages on Nepali and Indian rivers use radial gates almost universally.**

**A worked example, to show the method:**

> **A quarter-circle gate of radius R = 2 m and width 3 m holds water to the level of its top, with the water on the concave side and the curved surface below the water.**

| Component | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Vertical projection** | **A rectangle 2 m deep × 3 m wide** | — |
| **F_H** | **ρg × h̄ × A = 9810 × 1.0 × (2 × 3)** | **58.9 kN** ← |
| **Volume above the surface** | **A quarter circle area × width = (πR²/4) × 3 = (π × 4/4) × 3** | **9.42 m³** ← |
| **F_V** | **ρg × volume = 9810 × 9.42** | **92.4 kN** ← |
| **Resultant** | **√(58.9² + 92.4²)** | **109.6 kN** ← |
| **Angle to horizontal** | **tan⁻¹(92.4/58.9)** | **57.5°** |

> **And that resultant of 109.6 kN acts along a line through the centre of the circle, which locates it completely without any centre-of-pressure calculation.**

> **That is the practical advantage of the curved-surface method: for a plane surface the centre of pressure must be computed separately, and for a circular surface the geometry supplies it free.**

**The plane-surface results, for contrast, since they are the companion:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Total force on a plane surface** | **F = ρg h̄ A, with h̄ the depth of the CENTROID** ← |
| **Depth of the CENTRE OF PRESSURE** | **h_p = h̄ + I_G sin²θ /(A h̄)** ← |
| **For a vertical rectangle with its top at the surface** | **h_p = 2H/3 from the surface — one third of the height above the base** ← |
| **Centre of pressure relative to the centroid** | **ALWAYS BELOW it, and it approaches the centroid as the depth increases** ← |

> **The last row is worth holding as a check: the centre of pressure can never be above the centroid, because the pressure always increases with depth — and for a deeply submerged surface the pressure is nearly uniform, so the two converge.**

examTip.trick: **F_V = weight of the liquid volume vertically above the surface up to the free surface; F_H = force on the VERTICAL PROJECTION.** Option (b) is the horizontal component — both statements are true, of different components.
examTip.trap: **Where the liquid is BELOW the surface, use the IMAGINARY volume that would lie above it, and F_V acts UPWARD.** The pressures depend only on depth, so the fictitious column gives the right answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a circular arc every pressure is normal, so the RESULTANT PASSES THROUGH THE CENTRE OF CURVATURE** — which is why a radial (Tainter) gate needs no force to overcome water thrust: the resultant exerts no moment about its pivot.

questions.stem: A pressure gauge on a pipeline reads 150 kPa where the local atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa. The ABSOLUTE pressure in the pipe is:
options: 49 kPa
150 kPa
251 kPa
101 kPa
questions.solution:
**251 kPa.**

> **Absolute pressure = GAUGE pressure + ATMOSPHERIC pressure = 150 + 101 = 251 kPa** ←

**The pressure scales, which this question exists to separate:**

| Term | Measured from | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **ABSOLUTE pressure** | **From a PERFECT VACUUM (absolute zero)** ← | **Can never be negative** ← |
| **GAUGE pressure** | **From LOCAL ATMOSPHERIC pressure** ← | **CAN be negative** ← |
| **VACUUM (negative gauge) pressure** | **How far BELOW atmospheric** ← | **Reported as a positive number of "vacuum"** |
| **Atmospheric pressure** | **101.325 kPa standard at sea level = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m of water = 1.013 bar** ← | **FALLS with altitude** |

> **The relations:**

> **p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge**

> **p_abs = p_atm − p_vacuum**

> **Option (a), 49 kPa, is the answer if the gauge reading is SUBTRACTED — which corresponds to a vacuum reading of 150 kPa, an impossible value since it exceeds atmospheric pressure.**

> **That impossibility is the sense check: THE GREATEST VACUUM OBTAINABLE IS ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE ITSELF, about 101 kPa, because absolute pressure cannot go below zero.**

**Why that limit has real engineering consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A SUCTION LIFT cannot exceed about 10.3 m of water in theory** ← | **And 6 to 7 m in practice, after friction, velocity head and vapour pressure** ← |
| **A pump cannot "pull" water up an unlimited height** | **Atmospheric pressure pushes it up; the pump only creates the low pressure** ← |
| **A SYPHON cannot lift water more than about 10 m over its crest** | **The same limit** ← |
| **CAVITATION occurs before the theoretical limit is reached** | **When the pressure falls to the VAPOUR PRESSURE, not to zero** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL LIMIT, and it is worth being precise about: water does not wait until absolute zero to misbehave. It BOILS when its pressure falls to the vapour pressure at the prevailing temperature.**

| Water temperature | Vapour pressure | Equivalent head |
|---|---|---|
| **10 °C** | **1.23 kPa** | **0.13 m** |
| **20 °C** | **2.34 kPa** | **0.24 m** ← |
| **40 °C** | **7.38 kPa** | **0.75 m** |
| **100 °C** | **101.3 kPa** | **10.33 m — it boils at atmospheric pressure, by definition** ← |

> **The last row states the definition of the boiling point in a way that makes the whole idea coherent: water boils when its vapour pressure EQUALS the surrounding pressure, and lowering the surrounding pressure therefore lowers the boiling point.**

> **Which is why water boils at about 85 °C in Kathmandu and around 71 °C at Everest Base Camp — and why cooking takes longer at altitude.**

**The ALTITUDE effect, since it is directly relevant here:**

| Elevation | Atmospheric pressure | Head of water |
|---|---|---|
| **Sea level** | **101.3 kPa** | **10.33 m** |
| **1,400 m (Kathmandu)** | **About 85 kPa** ← | **8.7 m** ← |
| **2,500 m** | **About 75 kPa** | **7.6 m** |
| **4,000 m** | **About 62 kPa** | **6.3 m** ← |

> **So a pump that will lift 6 m at sea level may manage only 4 m at 2,500 m elevation — and a pump selected from a sea-level catalogue and installed in the Nepali hills will cavitate.**

> **This is the same correction met in the turbine setting under Thoma's criterion, and it recurs wherever atmospheric pressure enters a calculation.**

> **The general rule: WHEREVER A CALCULATION USES ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE, USE THE LOCAL VALUE, NOT THE SEA-LEVEL ONE.**

**NPSH, which is how the pump case is formalised:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **NPSH AVAILABLE** | **What the installation offers: (p_atm − p_vapour)/γ − static suction lift − friction losses** ← |
| **NPSH REQUIRED** | **What the pump needs, from its manufacturer's curve** ← |
| **The requirement** | **NPSH available > NPSH required, with a margin** ← |

> **Every term in NPSH available except the pump's own characteristics is reduced by altitude, by warm water, by a high suction lift and by a long or narrow suction pipe.**

> **Which gives the practical rules for a pump installation: set the pump as LOW as possible relative to the water, keep the SUCTION pipe SHORT, LARGE and free of unnecessary fittings, and never throttle on the suction side.**

> **A pump that cavitates makes a characteristic sound like gravel passing through it, loses head and discharge, and pits its impeller — and the cure is almost always in the suction arrangement rather than in the pump.**

examTip.trick: **p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge = 101 + 150 = 251 kPa.** Option (a) subtracts, implying a 150 kPa vacuum — impossible, since the greatest vacuum available is atmospheric pressure itself.
examTip.trap: **Cavitation begins at the VAPOUR pressure, not at absolute zero** — 2.34 kPa at 20 °C. So the practical suction lift is 6-7 m, not the theoretical 10.3 m.
examTip.mnemonic: **Atmospheric pressure FALLS with altitude — about 85 kPa (8.7 m) in Kathmandu against 101 kPa (10.3 m) at sea level.** A pump chosen from a sea-level catalogue will cavitate in the hills. Always use the LOCAL atmospheric value.

questions.stem: Bernoulli's equation in its usual form is derived on the assumption that the flow is:
options: Unsteady, compressible and viscous
Steady, incompressible and NON-VISCOUS, along a streamline
Turbulent and rotational
Steady but compressible, with friction included
questions.solution:
**STEADY, INCOMPRESSIBLE and NON-VISCOUS (inviscid), applied along a STREAMLINE.**

**The equation and what each term represents:**

> **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant along a streamline**

| Term | Name | Physical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **p/γ** | **PRESSURE head** | **Flow work per unit weight** |
| **V²/2g** | **VELOCITY (kinetic) head** | Kinetic energy per unit weight |
| **z** | **DATUM (potential) head** | Potential energy per unit weight |
| **Sum** | **TOTAL head** | **Constant, for an ideal fluid** ← |

> **Every term has the dimension of LENGTH, which is why they are called "heads" and why the whole equation can be drawn as a diagram — the total energy line and the hydraulic gradient line.**

**The full list of assumptions:**

| Assumption | What fails if it is violated |
|---|---|
| **STEADY flow** | **An unsteady term must be added** ← |
| **INCOMPRESSIBLE fluid** | **For gases at high speed, a compressible form is needed** ← |
| **NON-VISCOUS (frictionless)** | **A head LOSS term h_f must be added — the most important departure in practice** ← |
| **Flow along a STREAMLINE** | **The constant differs from one streamline to another, unless the flow is also IRROTATIONAL** ← |
| **No energy ADDED or REMOVED** | **A pump adds head, a turbine removes it — both must appear explicitly** ← |
| **Flow along a single continuous path; no branching** | — |

> **THE STREAMLINE QUALIFICATION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OMITTED, and it matters: Bernoulli's constant is generally different for different streamlines.**

> **Only if the flow is also IRROTATIONAL does the same constant apply throughout the whole flow field — which is why irrotational flow is such a useful idealisation, and why potential flow theory is built on it.**

**The practical (engineering) form, which is what is actually used:**

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L**

| Added term | When |
|---|---|
| **h_L — total head loss** | **Always, in real flow: friction plus minor losses** ← |
| **h_pump** | Energy added by a pump |
| **h_turbine** | Energy extracted by a turbine |
| **α, the kinetic energy correction factor** | **Applied to V²/2g where the velocity is non-uniform: α = 2 for LAMINAR pipe flow, 1.03-1.1 for TURBULENT** ← |

> **The α = 2 for laminar flow in the last row is a substantial correction and is often forgotten: the parabolic velocity profile means the true kinetic energy is TWICE that computed from the mean velocity.**

> **For turbulent flow the profile is much flatter, so α is close to 1 and is normally ignored — which is why the correction is usually invisible in practice and then appears startlingly in a laminar problem.**

**The applications, since Bernoulli underlies most flow measurement:**

| Device | Principle |
|---|---|
| **VENTURIMETER** | **A contraction raises V and lowers p; the pressure difference gives the discharge** ← |
| **ORIFICE METER** | The same, with a sharp-edged plate; cheaper, greater loss |
| **PITOT TUBE** | **Brings the flow to rest, converting velocity head to pressure head: V = √(2gh)** ← |
| **NOZZLE and jet** | Pressure head converted to velocity head |
| **Flow over a WEIR or NOTCH** | Free surface flow with the same energy argument |
| **Siphon** | The pressure at the crest follows directly |

> **All of these are the same idea in different clothing: CONVERT ONE FORM OF HEAD INTO ANOTHER AND MEASURE THE DIFFERENCE.**

> **And every one of them needs a COEFFICIENT OF DISCHARGE, precisely because the real fluid is viscous while the derivation assumed it was not — the coefficient absorbs the assumption's failure.**

| Device | Typical C_d |
|---|---|
| **Venturimeter** | **0.95 to 0.99 — high, because the gradual expansion recovers most of the energy** ← |
| **Orifice meter** | **0.60 to 0.65 — low, because of the sharp contraction and the vena contracta** ← |
| **Sharp-edged orifice in a tank** | **0.62** |
| **Nozzle meter** | 0.95 to 0.98 |

> **The contrast between the venturimeter and the orifice meter is instructive and is a genuine engineering trade: the venturi is expensive to make and loses only about 10 per cent of the differential head permanently; the orifice plate is a cheap disc between flanges and loses 50 to 70 per cent.**

> **On a large water main pumped continuously, the venturi's higher cost is repaid in pumping energy within a year or two — so the choice between them is an economic calculation, not a matter of accuracy.**

**And the relationship of Bernoulli to the ENERGY and MOMENTUM equations, since all three appear together:**

| Equation | Based on | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTINUITY** | **Conservation of MASS** | Always applicable |
| **BERNOULLI / energy** | **Conservation of ENERGY** | **Where losses are small or known** ← |
| **MOMENTUM** | **Newton's second law** | **Where losses are UNKNOWN but FORCES are wanted — a hydraulic jump, a sudden enlargement, force on a bend** ← |

> **The MOMENTUM equation's advantage is the decisive one in the cases named: it needs no knowledge of what happens INSIDE the control volume, only of the conditions at its boundaries.**

> **A hydraulic jump dissipates an unknown amount of energy in violent turbulence, so the energy equation cannot be applied across it — but momentum can, which is exactly how the conjugate depth relation is derived.**

examTip.trick: **Steady, incompressible, non-viscous, along a STREAMLINE, with no energy added or removed.** Each term p/γ, V²/2g and z has the dimension of LENGTH.
examTip.trap: **The constant differs between streamlines unless the flow is also IRROTATIONAL.** And α, the kinetic energy correction, is **2 for LAMINAR** flow — a doubling that is easy to miss because it is ~1 for turbulent.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use MOMENTUM, not energy, where the losses are unknown but the forces are wanted** — a hydraulic jump, a sudden enlargement, force on a bend. And C_d: venturi 0.95-0.99 but expensive; orifice 0.62 but loses 50-70 % of the head permanently.

questions.stem: For two pipes connected in SERIES between a reservoir and an outlet:
options: The head loss is the same in each pipe and the discharges add
The discharge and the head loss are both the same in each pipe
The discharge is the same in each pipe and the head loss is the smaller of the two
The discharge is the same in each pipe and the total head loss is the sum of the individual losses
questions.solution:
**The DISCHARGE is the SAME through each pipe, and the total head loss is the SUM of the individual head losses.**

**Series against parallel — the complete contrast:**

| | SERIES | PARALLEL |
|---|---|---|
| **DISCHARGE** | **The SAME in every pipe** ← | **DIVIDES between the pipes; the discharges ADD to the total** ← |
| **HEAD LOSS** | **ADDS: h_L = h₁ + h₂ + …** ← | **The SAME across every pipe** ← |
| **Governing principle** | **Continuity** | **The two junctions have fixed heads, so every path between them loses the same head** ← |
| **Effect of adding a pipe** | **Increases the total resistance** | **DECREASES the total resistance** ← |

> **Option (a) states the PARALLEL case exactly, which makes it the designed distractor — and the two are constantly interchanged.**

> **The reliable way to keep them apart is to reason from CONTINUITY rather than to memorise: in series there is nowhere else for the water to go, so Q must be the same; in parallel the pipes share common end points, so the head difference between those points is the same for every route.**

> **It is exactly the electrical analogy — current the same in series, voltage the same in parallel — with discharge for current and head loss for voltage.**

**The EQUIVALENT PIPE, which is how a series system is simplified:**

> **An equivalent pipe is a single pipe that would carry the SAME discharge under the SAME total head loss as the system it replaces.**

> **Using Darcy-Weisbach, h_f = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵) for each pipe, and equating the sum to a single pipe of length L and diameter D:**

> **L / D⁵ = L₁/D₁⁵ + L₂/D₂⁵ + L₃/D₃⁵ + …**

> **This is DUPUIT'S equation, and it assumes the friction factor f is the same in all the pipes.**

> **A worked example: pipes of 300 m at 200 mm and 200 m at 150 mm in series, replaced by an equivalent 250 mm pipe.**

| Term | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **L₁/D₁⁵** | **300 / 0.2⁵ = 300/0.00032** | **937,500** ← |
| **L₂/D₂⁵** | **200 / 0.15⁵ = 200/0.0000759** | **2,634,000** ← |
| **Sum** | — | **3,571,500** |
| **Equivalent length at D = 0.25 m** | **L = 3,571,500 × 0.25⁵ = 3,571,500 × 0.000977** | **3,489 m** ← |

> **THE FIFTH-POWER DEPENDENCE IS THE STRIKING FEATURE OF THAT ARITHMETIC, and it is worth dwelling on:**

> **The 150 mm pipe is only 200 m long against the 200 mm pipe's 300 m, yet it contributes nearly THREE TIMES as much resistance.**

> **Because h_f ∝ 1/D⁵ at a given discharge, a modest reduction in diameter produces an enormous increase in head loss:**

| Diameter reduced by | Head loss multiplied by |
|---|---|
| **10 % (to 0.9 D)** | **1/0.9⁵ = 1.69** ← |
| **20 % (to 0.8 D)** | **1/0.8⁵ = 3.05** ← |
| **50 % (to 0.5 D)** | **1/0.5⁵ = 32** ← |

> **So HALVING a pipe's diameter multiplies its head loss THIRTY-TWO FOLD at the same discharge.**

> **That single relation explains a great deal of practical hydraulics: why a partially blocked or encrusted pipe loses capacity so dramatically, why undersizing a pipe is so costly in pumping energy, and why the economic diameter calculation is worth doing carefully.**

> **An old cast iron main whose bore has been reduced 20 per cent by tuberculation has three times the friction it was designed for — which is why rehabilitation by relining is often more valuable than it appears.**

**THE MINOR LOSSES, which the series calculation should include:**

| Fitting | Loss coefficient K, in h = K V²/2g |
|---|---|
| **Sharp entrance from a reservoir** | **0.5** ← |
| **Bell-mouthed entrance** | **0.05 — a tenth of the sharp value, for no extra cost of consequence** ← |
| **EXIT into a reservoir** | **1.0 — the ENTIRE velocity head is lost** ← |
| **Sudden enlargement** | **(V₁ − V₂)²/2g** |
| **90° bend, standard elbow** | 0.9 |
| **Gate valve, fully open** | **0.19** |
| **Gate valve, half open** | **5.6 — thirty times the open value** ← |
| **Globe valve, fully open** | **10** ← |

> **The EXIT LOSS of 1.0 is the one most often overlooked and it is not small: all the kinetic energy the flow carries is dissipated as it enters the receiving reservoir, and nothing recovers it.**

> **And the term "MINOR" losses is misleading in short pipe systems — in a pump house or a treatment works, where the pipework is short and full of bends and valves, the fitting losses commonly EXCEED the friction losses.**

> **They are minor only in a long transmission main, and calling them minor in a plant layout is how pumps come to be undersized.**

examTip.trick: **SERIES: same Q, head losses ADD. PARALLEL: same head loss, discharges ADD.** Option (a) is the parallel case. Reason from continuity, or use the electrical analogy — current in series, voltage in parallel.
examTip.trap: **Head loss goes as 1/D⁵** — so HALVING a diameter multiplies the loss THIRTY-TWO fold, and a 20 % bore reduction from encrustation triples the friction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dupuit: L/D⁵ = ΣLᵢ/Dᵢ⁵.** And "minor" losses are not minor in short pipework — exit loss alone is K = 1.0 (the whole velocity head), and a half-open gate valve is K = 5.6 against 0.19 open.

questions.stem: In the fully ROUGH TURBULENT zone of the Moody diagram, the Darcy friction factor f depends on:
options: The relative roughness only, and is independent of the Reynolds number
The Reynolds number only
Both the Reynolds number and the relative roughness
Neither — it is a constant for all pipes
questions.solution:
**The RELATIVE ROUGHNESS (k/D) only — it is INDEPENDENT of the Reynolds number.**

**The zones of the Moody diagram:**

| Zone | Reynolds number | f depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **LAMINAR** | **Re < 2,000** | **Re ONLY: f = 64/Re; roughness is irrelevant** ← |
| **Critical / transition** | **2,000 to 4,000** | **Unpredictable — this region is avoided in design** ← |
| **Smooth turbulent** | Above 4,000, low roughness | **Re only (Blasius: f = 0.316/Re^0.25)** ← |
| **Transitional turbulent** | Intermediate | **BOTH Re and k/D — the Colebrook-White region** ← (option c) |
