| **FULLY ROUGH turbulent** | High Re | **k/D ONLY** ← |

> **Options (b) and (c) describe the LAMINAR/smooth-turbulent and the TRANSITIONAL zones respectively — both real regions of the same diagram, offered for the rough-turbulent one.**

**Why roughness stops mattering in laminar flow, and why Reynolds number stops mattering in rough turbulent flow:**

> **The explanation for both lies in the VISCOUS SUB-LAYER — the thin film of essentially laminar flow that clings to the pipe wall even when the core is turbulent.**

| Condition | What happens |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR flow throughout** | **There is no turbulence to be disturbed; the roughness projections sit within an orderly flow and change nothing** ← |
| **Sub-layer THICKER than the roughness** | **The projections are SUBMERGED in the smooth film and the flow never "feels" them — HYDRAULICALLY SMOOTH** ← |
| **Sub-layer THINNER than the roughness** | **The projections PROTRUDE into the turbulent core and shed eddies; form drag dominates and viscosity becomes irrelevant — FULLY ROUGH** ← |

> **THE SUB-LAYER THINS AS THE REYNOLDS NUMBER RISES, which is what moves a pipe from smooth to rough behaviour as the velocity increases.**

> **So the SAME pipe can be hydraulically smooth at low flow and fully rough at high flow — "smooth" and "rough" are descriptions of the FLOW CONDITION, not fixed properties of the pipe.**

> **That is the point most often missed, and it is what makes the Moody diagram a diagram rather than a table.**

> **In the fully rough zone, resistance comes from form drag on the projections, which scales with V² exactly as the head loss formula assumes — so f becomes constant and h_f becomes truly proportional to V².**

**Typical roughness values, since k/D is what must be found:**

| Pipe material | Roughness k (mm) |
|---|---|
| **Drawn tubing, glass, plastic (PVC, HDPE)** | **0.0015 to 0.007 — effectively smooth** ← |
| **Commercial steel, wrought iron** | **0.045** ← |
| **Galvanised iron** | **0.15** |
| **Cast iron, new** | **0.26** ← |
| **Concrete** | **0.3 to 3.0** |
| **Riveted steel** | 0.9 to 9.0 |
| **Cast iron, heavily TUBERCULATED after decades** | **Up to 3 mm and more** ← |

> **The LAST ROW carries the practical warning: roughness is not a constant for a pipe over its life.**

> **An old cast iron main can have its effective roughness increase TENFOLD through tuberculation and corrosion products, and its bore reduced besides — so a system designed with new-pipe values will fall well short of its design capacity after thirty years.**

> **Good practice is to design with the roughness expected at the END of the design life, not at the beginning, which is a deliberately conservative choice that the fifth-power sensitivity of the previous question fully justifies.**

**The COLEBROOK-WHITE equation, which the Moody diagram plots:**

> **1/√f = −2 log₁₀ [ (k/3.7D) + (2.51/(Re√f)) ]**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is IMPLICIT in f** | **f appears on both sides, so it must be solved by ITERATION** ← |
| **The first term inside the bracket is the ROUGHNESS effect** | **Dominates at high Re → the fully rough zone** ← |
| **The second is the REYNOLDS effect** | **Dominates at low Re → the smooth zone** ← |
| **The Moody diagram is simply this equation plotted** | **Which is why the diagram existed — to avoid the iteration** ← |
| **Explicit approximations (Swamee-Jain, Haaland)** | **Now used in spreadsheets and software; accurate to within about 1-2 %** ← |

> **The structure of the equation makes the whole Moody diagram intelligible: it contains ONE term for roughness and ONE for viscosity, and whichever is larger determines which zone the flow is in.**

> **When the roughness term dominates, f depends on k/D alone — which is precisely this question's answer, now derived rather than recalled.**

**And the practical consequence for design:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Most water supply and sewerage flows lie in the TRANSITIONAL zone** | **So both Re and k/D matter, and Colebrook-White or the diagram is needed** ← |
| **Hazen-Williams is often used instead for water** | **h_f = 10.67 L Q^1.852/(C^1.852 D^4.87); simpler, but valid only for water at ordinary temperatures** ← |
| **Manning is used for open channels and part-full sewers** | **n rather than f** ← |
| **Darcy-Weisbach is the most general** | **Any fluid, any temperature, any regime — and dimensionally sound** ← |

> **The reason Hazen-Williams survives despite Darcy-Weisbach being more rigorous is that it is EXPLICIT — no iteration — and its coefficient C is a single number a designer can carry in their head for each pipe material.**

> **Its limitation is that C is not dimensionless and embeds an assumption about the fluid's viscosity, so it fails for anything other than water near 20 °C — which for water supply work it always is.**

examTip.trick: **Fully rough turbulent: f depends on k/D ONLY.** Laminar: f = 64/Re, roughness irrelevant. Transitional: both. Options (b) and (c) are the other zones.
examTip.trap: **"Smooth" and "rough" describe the FLOW, not the pipe** — the viscous sub-layer thins as Re rises, so the same pipe can be hydraulically smooth at low flow and fully rough at high flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **Colebrook-White has one ROUGHNESS term and one REYNOLDS term; whichever dominates fixes the zone.** And roughness grows over a pipe's life — tuberculated cast iron can reach 3 mm — so design with END-of-life values.

questions.stem: In open channel flow, the SPECIFIC ENERGY of a given discharge is a MINIMUM when the flow is at:
options: The normal depth
The sequent depth
Critical depth
The alternate depth
questions.solution:
**CRITICAL depth.**

**The specific energy curve, which is the whole of this topic:**

> **Specific energy E = y + V²/2g = y + Q²/(2gA²), measured from the CHANNEL BED rather than from a fixed datum.**

| Feature of the E-y curve for a constant Q | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is a curve with TWO limbs and a MINIMUM** | ← |
| **The UPPER limb: large y, small V** | **SUBCRITICAL (tranquil, streaming) flow; Fr < 1** ← |
| **The LOWER limb: small y, large V** | **SUPERCRITICAL (rapid, shooting) flow; Fr > 1** ← |
| **At the MINIMUM: y = y_c** | **CRITICAL flow; Fr = 1** ← |
| **For any E greater than E_min there are TWO depths** | **The ALTERNATE DEPTHS — one sub-, one supercritical** ← (option d) |
| **The upper limb approaches the 45° line E = y asymptotically** | Velocity head becomes negligible |
| **The lower limb approaches the E-axis** | Depth becomes negligible |

> **Option (d), the alternate depth, is the OTHER depth having the same specific energy — a real and closely related term. Option (b), the sequent (conjugate) depth, is the depth on the other side of a HYDRAULIC JUMP, which conserves MOMENTUM rather than energy. Option (a), the normal depth, is the uniform-flow depth for a given slope and roughness.**

> **All four are genuine depths in open channel hydraulics, which is what makes the option set demanding.**

**The critical depth relations, for a RECTANGULAR channel:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Critical depth** | **y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3), with q the discharge per unit width** ← |
| **Minimum specific energy** | **E_min = 1.5 y_c** ← |
| **Critical velocity** | **V_c = √(g y_c)** ← |
| **Velocity head at critical** | **y_c/2 — exactly half the depth** ← |
| **Froude number** | **Fr = V/√(gy) = 1 at critical** ← |

> **The relation E_min = 1.5 y_c follows immediately from the fourth row: E = y + V²/2g = y_c + y_c/2.**

> **And the general condition for critical flow in ANY channel shape is Q²T/(gA³) = 1, with T the top water surface width — which reduces to the above for a rectangle.**

**Why critical flow matters so much in practice:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A CONTROL SECTION** | **At critical flow there is a unique relation between depth and discharge — so measuring the depth gives the discharge** ← |
| **The basis of FLOW MEASUREMENT structures** | **Broad-crested weirs, flumes, Parshall flumes, free overfalls** ← |
| **It separates the two flow regimes** | **And determines the DIRECTION in which disturbances travel** ← |
| **Flow is UNSTABLE near critical** | **A small change in energy produces a large change in depth — the curve is flat at its minimum** ← |
| **Design should AVOID sustained near-critical flow** | **The water surface becomes wavy and unstable** ← |

> **THE DIRECTION-OF-CONTROL POINT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL IDEA IN OPEN CHANNEL HYDRAULICS, and it deserves stating fully:**

> **A surface disturbance travels at the wave celerity c = √(gy) relative to the water.**

| Regime | Velocity against celerity | Can a disturbance travel UPSTREAM? |
|---|---|---|
| **SUBCRITICAL (Fr < 1)** | **V < c** | **YES — so downstream conditions CONTROL the flow** ← |
| **CRITICAL (Fr = 1)** | **V = c** | **A disturbance stands still** ← |
| **SUPERCRITICAL (Fr > 1)** | **V > c** | **NO — so UPSTREAM conditions control** ← |

> **The practical consequence governs how any backwater computation is done: in SUBCRITICAL flow you compute the water surface profile working UPSTREAM from a downstream control; in SUPERCRITICAL flow you work DOWNSTREAM from an upstream control.**

> **Starting a gradually varied flow computation from the wrong end is a straightforward error that produces a plausible-looking and entirely wrong profile.**

> **And it explains everyday observation: a stone dropped into a slow river sends ripples in all directions, while in a fast shallow chute the ripples are swept downstream and nothing propagates back — the flow upstream cannot "know" what lies ahead.**

**The FLOW MEASUREMENT application, since it is the most common use:**

| Structure | How it works |
|---|---|
| **BROAD-CRESTED WEIR** | **The crest forces critical flow; measuring the upstream head gives Q, with Q = 1.705 C_d b H^1.5** ← |
| **VENTURI FLUME / Parshall flume** | **A contraction forces critical flow without a step — so it passes SEDIMENT, unlike a weir** ← |
| **Free overfall** | Critical depth occurs a short distance back from the brink |
| **Sluice gate** | Supercritical flow downstream |

> **The FLUME's advantage over the WEIR in the second row is a real and practical one, particularly in irrigation and sewerage: a weir ponds the flow behind it and traps sediment, which changes its calibration and eventually buries it.**

> **A flume contracts the channel horizontally instead of damming it vertically, so the velocity stays high, sediment passes through, and the calibration holds.**

> **That is why Parshall flumes are used at sewage works and on silt-laden irrigation canals where a weir would be unmaintainable.**

examTip.trick: **E is minimum at CRITICAL depth: y_c = (q²/g)^⅓, E_min = 1.5 y_c, Fr = 1.** All four options are real depths — alternate (same E), sequent (across a jump, same momentum), normal (uniform flow).
examTip.trap: **Compute SUBCRITICAL profiles working UPSTREAM from a downstream control, and SUPERCRITICAL profiles DOWNSTREAM from an upstream control** — because disturbances travel upstream only when V < √(gy).
examTip.mnemonic: **At critical, the velocity head is exactly HALF the depth**, which gives E_min = 1.5 y_c at once. And a FLUME beats a weir where sediment is carried: it contracts horizontally instead of damming, so the silt passes and the calibration holds.

questions.stem: A rectangular channel 4 m wide carries water at a depth of 1.5 m. Manning's n is 0.015 and the bed slope is 1 in 1000. The discharge is approximately:
options: 8.4 m³/s
questions.solution:
**About 11.4 m³/s.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Area A** | **4 × 1.5** | **6.00 m²** |
| **Wetted perimeter P** | **b + 2y = 4 + 2(1.5)** | **7.00 m** ← |
| **Hydraulic radius R** | **A/P = 6.00/7.00** | **0.857 m** |
| **R^(2/3)** | **0.857^0.6667** | **0.902** |
| **√S** | **√0.001** | **0.0316** |
| **Velocity V** | **(1/0.015) × 0.902 × 0.0316 = 66.67 × 0.902 × 0.0316** | **1.90 m/s** ← |
| **Discharge Q** | **A V = 6.00 × 1.90** | **11.4 m³/s** ← |

**Each distractor is a named wrong step:**

| Option | The error behind it |
|---|---|
| **8.4 m³/s** | **The FREE SURFACE included in the wetted perimeter (P = 4 + 2×1.5 + 4 = 11 m)** ← |
| **13.4 m³/s** | **P taken as b + y = 5.5 m — only ONE side counted** ← |
| **16.6 m³/s** | **R taken as the DEPTH y = 1.5 m, using the wide-channel approximation where it does not apply** ← |

> **The last of these deserves comment: R ≈ y is a legitimate simplification for a channel much wider than it is deep, but here b/y = 2.7, which is nowhere near wide enough. Using it overestimates the discharge by 45 per cent.**

> **The WETTED PERIMETER is the free surface's exception: it is the length of the boundary IN CONTACT WITH THE WATER, and the air-water surface exerts no friction, so it is never included.**

**MANNING'S EQUATION and its terms:**

> **V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2)  and  Q = (1/n) A R^(2/3) S^(1/2)**

| Term | Note |
|---|---|
| **n — Manning's roughness coefficient** | **Has awkward units (s/m^(1/3)) and is treated as an empirical constant for a surface** ← |
| **R — hydraulic radius = A/P** | **NOT the depth, and not the radius of anything for a non-circular channel** ← |
| **S — the slope of the ENERGY LINE** | **Equal to the bed slope only in UNIFORM flow** ← |

> **The third row deserves care: Manning's equation strictly relates velocity to the ENERGY slope. In uniform (normal) flow the bed, water surface and energy line are parallel, so the bed slope may be used — in gradually varied flow it may not.**

**Typical values of Manning's n:**

| Surface | n |
|---|---|
| **Glass, smooth plastic** | **0.010** |
| **Smooth concrete, trowelled** | **0.012 to 0.014** ← |
| **Concrete, ordinary finish; brickwork** | **0.015** ← |
| **Rubble masonry; corrugated metal** | 0.017 to 0.025 |
| **Earth channel, clean and straight** | **0.022** ← |
| **Earth channel, weedy or winding** | **0.030 to 0.040** ← |
| **Natural stream, clean and straight** | **0.030** |
| **Natural stream, sluggish, deep pools and weeds** | **0.070 to 0.100** ← |
| **Flood plain with heavy timber** | 0.10 to 0.15 |

> **Natural-channel n varies by a factor of three or more, and Q is INVERSELY proportional to n — so the choice of n is the dominant uncertainty in any river calculation, far exceeding the error in surveying the section or the slope.**

> **That is why a single gauged discharge measurement, used to CALIBRATE n for a particular reach, is worth more than a great deal of careful surveying, and why published tables are a starting point rather than an answer.**

**The HYDRAULIC RADIUS for the standard sections:**

| Section | A | P | R |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × y** | **by** | **b + 2y** | **by/(b+2y)** ← |
| **VERY WIDE rectangle (b ≫ y)** | by | **≈ b** | **≈ y — R equals the DEPTH** ← |
| **Trapezoid, side slope m:1** | **(b + my)y** | **b + 2y√(1+m²)** | — |
| **Circular, running FULL** | **πD²/4** | **πD** | **D/4** ← |
| **Circular, running HALF full** | πD²/8 | πD/2 | **D/4 — the SAME as full** ← |

> **The last two rows explain the result met in sewer hydraulics: a circular pipe running half full has the same hydraulic radius as one running full, and therefore by Manning the SAME VELOCITY.**

> **It carries half the discharge at the same velocity, which is why a sewer designed to run at 0.5 to 0.8 of full depth keeps its self-cleansing velocity over a wide range of flows.**

**And the relation to CHEZY, from which Manning derives:**

| Formula | Expression | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **CHEZY** | **V = C √(RS)** | **The original; C is not constant but varies with R** ← |
| **MANNING** | **V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2)** | **Equivalent to Chezy with C = R^(1/6)/n** ← |
| **Kutter, Bazin** | Empirical expressions for C | Largely superseded |

> **The relation C = R^(1/6)/n shows what Manning's contribution actually was: not a new theory, but an empirical description of how Chezy's C varies with the channel's size and roughness.**

> **And it explains why n is more nearly constant for a given surface than C is — n depends on the surface alone, while C depends on the surface AND the channel's dimensions.**

examTip.trap: **The FREE SURFACE is never part of the wetted perimeter** — air exerts no friction. And R ≈ y is valid only for a channel much wider than it is deep; at b/y = 2.7 it overestimates Q by 45 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **A circular pipe HALF full has the same R (= D/4) as one running FULL, hence the same velocity** — what keeps a part-full sewer self-cleansing. Chezy's C = R^(1/6)/n, which is why n is the more portable constant.

questions.stem: A structure is designed for a flood of 50-year RETURN PERIOD. The probability that this flood will be equalled or exceeded AT LEAST ONCE during a 20-year design life is approximately:
options: 2 per cent
40 per cent
20 per cent
33 per cent
questions.solution:
**About 33 per cent.**

**The computation:**

> **The probability of exceedance in any ONE year is P = 1/T = 1/50 = 0.02.**

> **The probability of NOT being exceeded in one year is (1 − P) = 0.98.**

> **The probability of not being exceeded in ANY of 20 years is (1 − P)ⁿ = 0.98²⁰ = 0.6676.**

> **So the RISK — the probability of at least one exceedance — is:**

> **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ = 1 − 0.6676 = 0.3324, or about 33 per cent** ←

| Distractor | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **2 %** | **1/T — the probability in a SINGLE year, not over the design life** ← |
| **40 %** | **n/T = 20/50 — the common but WRONG linear estimate** ← |
| **20 %** | Another mis-combination |

> **The 40 per cent distractor is the important one: simply dividing the life by the return period is the intuitive approach and it OVERESTIMATES the risk, because it double-counts the possibility of more than one exceedance.**

> **The linear estimate also fails catastrophically when n exceeds T — it would give a probability above 1, which is impossible, whereas the correct formula approaches 1 asymptotically and never reaches it.**

**A table of risk, which is where the practical lesson lies:**

| Design life n → | 10 years | 25 years | 50 years | 100 years |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **T = 25 years** | **34 %** | **64 %** | **87 %** | **98 %** |
| **T = 50 years** | **18 %** | **40 %** | **64 %** | **87 %** |
| **T = 100 years** | **10 %** | **22 %** | **39 %** | **63 %** ← |
| **T = 500 years** | 2 % | 5 % | 10 % | **18 %** |

> **THE DIAGONAL OF THIS TABLE IS THE RESULT WORTH REMEMBERING: when the design life EQUALS the return period, the risk is about 63 per cent — not 100 per cent, as intuition insists.**

> **The value is 1 − 1/e = 0.632 for large T, and it is the same for every pair where n = T.**

> **So a structure designed for the "100-year flood" and intended to last 100 years is MORE LIKELY THAN NOT to experience that flood during its life.**

> **The phrase "100-year flood" is therefore badly misleading to the public — it does not mean a flood that happens once a century, but one with a 1 per cent chance in any given year, and two of them can occur in successive years without anything being unusual.**

> **Some agencies now prefer the term "1 per cent annual exceedance probability (AEP)" for exactly that reason, and it is a better description.**

**How the return period is CHOSEN, since the risk table shows it is a deliberate decision:**

| Structure | Typical design return period |
|---|---|
| **Road side drains, minor culverts** | **5 to 25 years** ← |
| **Cross-drainage on a major highway** | **50 to 100 years** ← |
| **Bridges on important routes** | **100 years** |
| **Urban storm drainage** | **2 to 10 years for the minor system; 100 for the major flow path** ← |
| **Barrage and weir waterways** | 50 to 100 years |
| **Large DAM spillways** | **PROBABLE MAXIMUM FLOOD (PMF) — not a return period at all** ← |

> **The DAM entry is the important departure and its logic is worth stating: for most structures, failure means damage and disruption, and the return period is chosen by balancing the cost of provision against the expected cost of failure.**

> **For a large dam, failure means the catastrophic loss of a town downstream — a consequence so severe that no economic balance is acceptable, and the spillway is sized for the largest flood physically possible from the catchment's meteorology.**

> **So the design standard changes in KIND, not merely in degree, once the consequence of failure becomes unacceptable at any probability. That principle — that catastrophic consequences are treated deterministically rather than probabilistically — recurs across engineering.**

**And the URBAN DRAINAGE entry, which contains a similarly useful idea:**

> **A modern urban drainage system is designed as TWO systems:**

| System | Return period | Route |
|---|---|---|
| **MINOR (piped) system** | **2 to 10 years** | Underground pipes |
| **MAJOR (overland) system** | **100 years** ← | **Roads, swales and open channels, deliberately shaped to carry the excess safely** ← |

> **The insight is that piping every conceivable flood underground is prohibitively expensive, and unnecessary — because the excess will flow overland whether or not it was planned for.**

> **So the design accepts that the pipes will surcharge in a rare event, and PLANS the overland route: roads that act as channels, kerbs that guide the flow, and open space that floods harmlessly rather than water finding its own way through buildings.**

> **That is a far cheaper and more robust arrangement than oversized pipes, and its absence is exactly why unplanned urban growth floods so severely — the overland flow paths have been built over, and the water has nowhere to go.**

> **For Kathmandu and other rapidly urbanising Nepali towns, protecting the natural drainage lines and flow paths from encroachment is worth more than any amount of pipe capacity.**

examTip.trick: **Risk R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ = 1 − 0.98²⁰ = 33 %.** Option (b) 40 % is the tempting linear n/T, which overestimates and can exceed 1.
examTip.trap: **When the design life EQUALS the return period, the risk is 63 % (1 − 1/e), not 100 %** — so a 100-year structure designed for the 100-year flood is more likely than not to meet it.
examTip.mnemonic: **"100-year flood" means a 1 % ANNUAL exceedance probability — two can occur in successive years.** And large DAM spillways abandon return periods entirely for the PMF, because catastrophic consequences are treated deterministically.

questions.stem: For a beam carrying a UNIFORMLY VARYING (triangular) load, the bending moment diagram is a curve of degree:
options: First (linear)
Third (cubic)
Second (parabolic)
Zero (constant)
questions.solution:
**THIRD degree — a cubic.**

**The differential relations that generate the whole pattern:**

> **w = −dV/dx  and  V = dM/dx**

> **So each integration raises the degree of the curve by ONE, and the sequence load → shear → moment climbs two degrees.**

| Loading | Load w | SHEAR FORCE diagram | BENDING MOMENT diagram |
|---|---|---|---|
| **No load (between point loads)** | **Zero (degree −)** | **CONSTANT (degree 0)** | **LINEAR (degree 1)** ← |
| **POINT load** | — | **A sudden JUMP, then constant** ← | **Linear, with a KINK at the load** ← |
| **UNIFORMLY DISTRIBUTED load** | **Constant (degree 0)** | **LINEAR (degree 1)** | **PARABOLIC (degree 2)** ← |
| **UNIFORMLY VARYING (triangular) load** | **Linear (degree 1)** | **PARABOLIC (degree 2)** ← | **CUBIC (degree 3)** ← |
| **COUPLE applied** | — | No change | **A sudden JUMP in the moment** ← |

> **Options (a) and (c) are the correct answers for the no-load and UDL cases respectively — both real rows of the same table.**

> **The rule to carry: THE BMD IS ALWAYS TWO DEGREES HIGHER THAN THE LOAD, AND THE SFD ONE DEGREE HIGHER.**

**The other consequences of V = dM/dx, which are used constantly:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The bending moment is MAXIMUM where the SHEAR FORCE is ZERO or changes sign** ← | **Because dM/dx = 0 there — the standard method of locating maximum moment** ← |
| **The CHANGE in bending moment between two sections equals the AREA of the SFD between them** ← | **∫V dx = ΔM — often faster than computing moments directly** ← |
| **The change in shear between two sections equals the AREA of the load diagram** | **∫w dx = ΔV** |
| **A point of CONTRAFLEXURE is where the BM changes SIGN (passes through zero)** ← | Not where the shear is zero |
| **The BMD is CONCAVE toward the direction the load acts** | A useful shape check |

> **The SECOND ROW is the most useful computational shortcut in the subject: to find the moment at any section of a determinate beam, draw the SFD and take the area under it up to that section.**

> **For a simply supported beam with a UDL, the SFD is a triangle from wL/2 to zero over L/2, so the mid-span moment is ½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8 — obtained in one step without writing any equilibrium equation.**

**Worked confirmation of the cubic case, since it is the one asked:**

> **A cantilever of length L carries a triangular load, zero at the free end and w per metre at the fixed end.**

| Quantity | At a distance x from the FREE end | Degree |
|---|---|---|
| **Load intensity** | **w x / L** | **1** |
| **Total load to the left of x** | **½ (wx/L) x = w x²/(2L)** | **2** ← |
| **SHEAR FORCE** | **w x²/(2L)** | **2 — parabolic** ← |
| **BENDING MOMENT** | **(w x²/2L)(x/3) = w x³/(6L)** | **3 — cubic** ← |
| **At the fixed end (x = L)** | **V = wL/2, M = wL²/6** | ← |

> **The centroid of a triangle at x/3 from its base is what introduces the third power, and the results V = wL/2 and M = wL²/6 at the support are worth memorising alongside the UDL cantilever's wL and wL²/2.**

**The standard results, as a working set:**

| Beam and loading | Max shear | Max bending moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Cantilever, point load W at the free end** | **W** | **WL (at the fixed end)** ← |
| **Cantilever, UDL w** | **wL** | **wL²/2** ← |
| **Cantilever, triangular load (max at fixed end)** | **wL/2** | **wL²/6** ← |
| **Simply supported, central point load W** | **W/2** | **WL/4** ← |
| **Simply supported, UDL w** | **wL/2** | **wL²/8** ← |
| **Simply supported, triangular load (max at centre)** | **wL/4** | **wL²/12** ← |
| **Fixed both ends, UDL w** | wL/2 | **wL²/12 at supports, wL²/24 at mid-span** ← |
| **Fixed both ends, central point load W** | W/2 | **WL/8 at both supports and mid-span** ← |
| **Propped cantilever, UDL w** | — | **wL²/8 at the fixed end** ← |

> **A pattern worth noticing in the last three rows: FIXING the ends of a beam with a UDL reduces the maximum moment from wL²/8 to wL²/12 — a reduction of a third — by transferring moment to the supports.**

> **That is the structural benefit of continuity, and it is why continuous beams and rigid frames are more efficient than simply supported spans.**

> **The cost is that the fixed beam is INDETERMINATE, so it develops moments from support settlement and temperature change that a simply supported beam simply accommodates by rotating.**

> **Which is the standing trade in structural design: continuity buys efficiency and buys sensitivity to movement along with it.**

examTip.trick: **The BMD is TWO degrees higher than the load, the SFD one degree higher.** UDL → parabolic BMD; triangular load → CUBIC BMD. Options (a) and (c) are the no-load and UDL cases.
examTip.trap: **Maximum moment occurs where the SHEAR is zero; a point of CONTRAFLEXURE is where the MOMENT is zero.** These are different sections and are constantly confused.
examTip.mnemonic: **ΔM = area under the SFD** — the fastest route to any moment. Standard results: cantilever wL²/2 (UDL) and wL²/6 (triangular); simply supported wL²/8 and wL²/12; fixed-ended wL²/12 at supports.

questions.stem: A beam ABC is simply supported at A and B, 6 m apart, with an overhang BC of 2 m. It carries a point load of 30 kN at the free end C. The reaction at A is:
options: 10 kN downward
40 kN upward
20 kN upward
10 kN downward, and the reaction at B is 40 kN upward
questions.solution:
**10 kN DOWNWARD at A, with 40 kN upward at B.**

**The computation:**

> **Taking moments about B (clockwise positive), with A 6 m to the left of B and C 2 m to the right:**

> **R_A × 6 = −30 × 2**

> **R_A = −60/6 = −10 kN**

> **The negative sign means the reaction acts DOWNWARD.**

> **Then by vertical equilibrium: R_A + R_B = 30, so R_B = 30 − (−10) = 40 kN upward.** ←

| Check | Working |
|---|---|
| **ΣV** | **−10 + 40 = 30 ✓ equals the applied load** |
| **ΣM about A** | **40 × 6 − 30 × 8 = 240 − 240 = 0 ✓** ← |

> **Options (a) and (b) each state HALF of the correct answer, which is what makes option (d) the complete one — and reading the options carefully is part of the question.**

**Why the reaction at A is NEGATIVE — the physical picture:**

> **The load at the overhang end tries to rotate the beam about support B, lifting the far end A off its support.**

> **To maintain equilibrium, support A must therefore PULL DOWN — it must hold the beam down rather than hold it up.**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The support at A must be capable of TENSION (a hold-down)** ← | **A beam merely RESTING on A would LIFT OFF** ← |
| **In practice: anchor bolts, a counterweight, or a continuous member** | — |
| **If A cannot resist uplift, the structure is a MECHANISM and collapses** | ← |

> **THIS IS A REAL AND SERIOUS DESIGN CONSIDERATION, not an arithmetical curiosity:**

> **A cantilevered balcony, canopy or projecting slab loads its inner support in UPLIFT, and if that support is not anchored the structure overturns.**

> **Cantilever balcony failures — where the rear of the cantilever was not adequately held down or its top steel was misplaced — recur regularly, and this reaction calculation is where the requirement first appears.**

**The bending moment diagram for this beam, since the shape is characteristic:**

| Section | Bending moment |
|---|---|
| **At A** | **0 (simple support)** |
| **Between A and B, at distance x from A** | **−10x — NEGATIVE (hogging), increasing linearly** ← |
| **At B** | **−10 × 6 = −60 kN·m, or from the right: −30 × 2 = −60 kN·m ✓** ← |
| **Between B and C, at distance a from C** | **−30a — negative, increasing linearly toward B** |
| **At C** | **0** |

> **So the ENTIRE beam is in HOGGING (negative moment), with the maximum of 60 kN·m at the support B.**

> **There is NO point of contraflexure anywhere, and no sagging region at all — which is the distinctive feature of a beam whose only load is on the overhang.**

> **The practical consequence for reinforcement: the TENSION is at the TOP throughout, so the main steel runs along the top of the whole beam — the opposite of the usual arrangement, and a detailing error that is easy to make and impossible to correct after casting.**

**The general behaviour of overhanging beams, since the balance between spans matters:**

| Loading arrangement | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Load on the SPAN only** | **Sagging in the span; the overhang is unstressed** |
| **Load on the OVERHANG only** | **Hogging throughout; uplift at the far support** ← this question |
| **Load on BOTH** | **A point of CONTRAFLEXURE appears where the two effects cancel** ← |
| **The overhang chosen so the span moment equals the support moment** | **The most ECONOMICAL arrangement — the beam is used equally in both directions** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A GENUINELY USEFUL DESIGN IDEA and it is worth quantifying:**

> **For a beam with equal overhangs each side carrying a UDL over its whole length, the support and mid-span moments are made equal when the overhang is about 0.207 L, with L the central span.**

> **The maximum moment is then wL²/23.3 rather than wL²/8 for a simply supported beam of the same central span — a reduction of nearly two-thirds.**

> **That is why cantilevered overhangs are so often provided at the ends of continuous structures, and why the classical balanced-cantilever bridge form is so efficient: the overhang's hogging moment partly cancels the span's sagging moment, and the same section works far harder.**

> **The same reasoning gives the optimum position for the supports of a simply supported tank, a pipe on saddles or a beam being lifted by two slings — set the supports in from the ends by about a fifth of the length, and the maximum moment is minimised.**

examTip.trick: **Moments about B: R_A × 6 = −30 × 2, so R_A = −10 kN (DOWNWARD), and R_B = 40 kN.** Check ΣM about A: 40×6 − 30×8 = 0 ✓.
examTip.trap: **A negative reaction means the support must HOLD THE BEAM DOWN** — a beam merely resting there would lift off. Cantilevered balconies and canopies fail exactly this way when the rear support is not anchored.
examTip.mnemonic: **With load on the overhang only, the WHOLE beam hogs — tension on TOP throughout, no contraflexure at all.** And overhangs of about 0.207 L balance the support and span moments, cutting the maximum by nearly two-thirds.

questions.stem: In a COMPOSITE bar of two materials rigidly connected and carrying an axial load, the load is shared between the materials in proportion to their:
options: AE values (area × modulus of elasticity)
Cross-sectional areas only
Moduli of elasticity only
Yield strengths
questions.solution:
**Their AE values — the product of cross-sectional AREA and MODULUS OF ELASTICITY.**

**The derivation, which follows from a single compatibility statement:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **1 — COMPATIBILITY** | **The two materials are rigidly connected, so they undergo the SAME STRAIN: ε₁ = ε₂** ← |
| **2 — Hooke's law** | **σ₁/E₁ = σ₂/E₂, so σ₁/σ₂ = E₁/E₂** ← |
| **3 — Load in each** | **P₁ = σ₁A₁ and P₂ = σ₂A₂** |
| **4 — Therefore** | **P₁/P₂ = A₁E₁ / A₂E₂** ← |
| **5 — EQUILIBRIUM** | **P₁ + P₂ = P, the total load** |

> **So the load divides in proportion to AXIAL STIFFNESS (AE), which is exactly what one would expect: the stiffer path attracts more load.**

> **Option (b) would be right only if the two materials had the same E; option (c) only if they had the same area. Each is a special case of the correct answer, which is what makes them well-made distractors.**

> **Option (d) is wrong in principle: STRENGTH plays no part in how an elastic structure DISTRIBUTES load — only stiffness does. Strength determines when a member fails, not how much load it attracts.**

> **THAT DISTINCTION — STIFFNESS ATTRACTS LOAD, STRENGTH RESISTS IT — is one of the most important ideas in structural engineering, and it applies far beyond composite bars.**

**A worked example, since the numbers are instructive:**

> **A steel tube (A = 1,000 mm², E = 200 GPa) is filled with concrete (A = 10,000 mm², E = 25 GPa) and carries 600 kN.**

| Quantity | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **AE for steel** | **1,000 × 200,000** | **2.0 × 10⁸ N** ← |
| **AE for concrete** | **10,000 × 25,000** | **2.5 × 10⁸ N** ← |
| **Total AE** | — | **4.5 × 10⁸ N** |
| **Load in the STEEL** | **600 × 2.0/4.5** | **267 kN** ← |
| **Load in the CONCRETE** | **600 × 2.5/4.5** | **333 kN** |
| **Stress in the steel** | **267,000/1,000** | **267 MPa** ← |
| **Stress in the concrete** | **333,000/10,000** | **33.3 MPa** ← |
| **Ratio of stresses** | **267/33.3 = 8.0** | **= E_s/E_c = 200/25 ✓** ← |

> **The steel occupies only 9 per cent of the area and carries 44 per cent of the load — because it is eight times as stiff.**

> **And the stress ratio equals the MODULAR RATIO exactly, which is the check on any such calculation.**

**The MODULAR RATIO m = E_s/E_c, since it is the same idea in reinforced concrete:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **The TRANSFORMED SECTION method** | **Replace the steel area A_s by an equivalent concrete area m·A_s, then analyse as one homogeneous material** ← |
| **In a reinforced concrete COLUMN** | **The steel and concrete share load in proportion to AE, exactly as here** ← |
| **In working stress design of beams** | **m = 280/(3σ_cbc) in IS 456 — inflated above the true ratio to allow for CREEP** ← |

> **THE CREEP ADJUSTMENT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT REFINEMENT, and it matters for any long-term composite action:**

> **Concrete CREEPS under sustained load — it goes on shortening for years — while steel does not.**

> **In a composite column, that creep progressively TRANSFERS LOAD FROM THE CONCRETE TO THE STEEL, because the concrete relaxes while the steel continues to resist the same shortening.**

> **So the elastic distribution computed above is the SHORT-TERM one, and over years the steel's share rises substantially — sometimes by half as much again.**

> **The design allowance is to use an effective modulus for the concrete of roughly E_c/(1 + φ), where φ is the creep coefficient (commonly 1.6 to 3.0) — which is exactly what inflating the modular ratio achieves.**

> **A column designed on short-term stiffness alone will therefore have its steel overstressed in time, which is a slow and invisible failure mode.**

**And the same principle in other guises, since it recurs constantly:**

| Situation | Load attracted in proportion to |
|---|---|
| **Composite bar in tension or compression** | **AE** ← |
| **Beams sharing a load in parallel** | **EI / L³ — their FLEXURAL stiffness** ← |
| **Shear walls and frames in a building resisting wind** | **Their relative LATERAL stiffness** ← |
| **Springs in parallel** | Their spring constants |
| **Bolts in a group loaded eccentrically** | Their distance from the centroid |

> **THE SHEAR WALL ROW HAS A CONSEQUENCE THAT CAUSES REAL BUILDING FAILURES:**

> **A shear wall is far stiffer than a frame, so in a building containing both, the wall attracts nearly ALL the lateral load — often 80 to 95 per cent — even where the frame appears substantial.**

> **Designing the frame for a share of the load proportional to its STRENGTH, or splitting the load equally, badly under-designs the wall.**

> **And the reverse case is the SOFT STOREY met earlier: masonry infill panels are stiff and attract load until they fail, at which point the whole load transfers abruptly to the frame that was never designed for it.**

> **In each case the error is the same one — treating strength as if it governed distribution — and the rule that prevents it is the one in bold above.**

examTip.trick: **Same STRAIN (compatibility) → σ₁/σ₂ = E₁/E₂ → P₁/P₂ = A₁E₁/A₂E₂.** Options (b) and (c) are special cases where the other factor happens to be equal.
examTip.trap: **STIFFNESS attracts load; STRENGTH resists it.** Option (d) is wrong in principle — yield strength plays no part in how an elastic structure distributes load.
examTip.mnemonic: **Concrete CREEPS and steel does not, so load transfers from concrete to steel over years** — which is why IS 456 inflates the modular ratio to 280/(3σ_cbc). And a SHEAR WALL attracts 80-95 % of the lateral load because it is far stiffer than the frame.

questions.stem: The theoretical upper limit of POISSON'S RATIO for an isotropic elastic material is:
questions.solution:
**0.5.**

**Why 0.5 is the limit — the bulk modulus argument:**

> **E = 3K(1 − 2ν), which rearranges to K = E / [3(1 − 2ν)].**

| ν | (1 − 2ν) | Bulk modulus K |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | **1** | **E/3** |
| **0.25** | **0.5** | **2E/3** |
| **0.33** | **0.34** | **≈ E** |
| **0.5** | **ZERO** | **K → INFINITY** ← |
| **Above 0.5** | **NEGATIVE** | **K NEGATIVE — physically impossible** ← |

> **A material with ν = 0.5 has an INFINITE bulk modulus, meaning it cannot be compressed in volume at all — it is INCOMPRESSIBLE.**

> **A value above 0.5 would give a negative bulk modulus, which means the material would EXPAND when squeezed uniformly — a violation of energy conservation, since it would release energy on compression without limit.**

> **So 0.5 is not a conventional or empirical limit but a THERMODYNAMIC one, and it cannot be exceeded by any real stable material.**

> **Options (a) and (d) are typical VALUES for concrete and metals respectively — real numbers, offered for the limit.**

**Typical values, for calibration:**

| Material | Poisson's ratio |
|---|---|
| **Cork** | **≈ 0 — which is why a cork can be pushed into a bottle neck at all** ← |
| **CONCRETE** | **0.10 to 0.20** ← |
| **Glass** | 0.20 to 0.25 |
| **STEEL and most metals** | **0.25 to 0.33** ← |
| **Aluminium** | 0.33 |
| **Saturated CLAY, undrained** | **≈ 0.5 — it deforms at constant volume, since water cannot escape** ← |
| **RUBBER** | **0.49 to 0.4999 — very nearly incompressible** ← |

> **The CORK row explains a piece of everyday engineering: a cork has ν ≈ 0, so compressing it lengthwise does NOT make it bulge sideways, and it will therefore enter a bottle neck.**

> **A rubber bung with ν ≈ 0.5 bulges as much as it is compressed, and cannot be pushed in the same way — which is why bottles are corked and not rubbered.**

> **And the SATURATED CLAY row connects directly to the soil mechanics met earlier: undrained clay deforms at CONSTANT VOLUME because the water has nowhere to go, which is precisely the definition of ν = 0.5.**

> **That is the same fact as the φ_u = 0 condition, expressed in elastic rather than plastic terms — both follow from the impossibility of volume change without drainage.**

**The elastic constants and their relations:**

| Constant | Symbol | Defines |
|---|---|---|
| **Young's modulus** | **E** | **Direct stress ÷ direct strain** |
| **Modulus of rigidity (shear modulus)** | **G** | **Shear stress ÷ shear strain** |
| **Bulk modulus** | **K** | **Volumetric stress ÷ volumetric strain** |
| **Poisson's ratio** | **ν** | **Lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain** |

> **The relations connecting them:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **E = 2G(1 + ν)** ← | The most used |
| **E = 3K(1 − 2ν)** ← | Gives the 0.5 limit |
| **E = 9KG/(3K + G)** ← | Combining the two |
| **ν = (3K − 2G)/(2(3K + G))** | — |

> **ONLY TWO OF THE FOUR ARE INDEPENDENT for an isotropic material — knowing any two determines the other two, which is why the relations exist and why a single test measuring E and ν characterises the material completely.**

> **From E = 2G(1+ν), a useful working figure follows: for ν = 0.25, G = E/2.5 = 0.4E; and for ν = 0.3, G = E/2.6 ≈ 0.385E.**

> **So G is roughly 0.4 E for structural metals, which is worth carrying as an estimate.**

**The LOWER limit, and the curious materials that approach it:**

> **From E = 2G(1 + ν), a value of ν = −1 would make G infinite, so the theoretical range is −1 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5.**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Negative ν means the material gets FATTER when stretched** ← | **Counter-intuitive but not impossible** |
| **Such materials are called AUXETIC** ← | Certain foams, some crystals, engineered lattices |
| **No common structural material is auxetic** | So the practical range is 0 to 0.5 |

> **The practical importance for a civil engineer is small, but the theoretical range is worth knowing because it shows that the 0.5 limit is one end of a two-sided bound derived purely from requiring the moduli to be positive.**

**And the practical consequence of ν in structures, since it is easy to regard as a curiosity:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Volumetric strain under uniaxial stress** | **e_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2ν) — vanishes at ν = 0.5** ← |
| **CONFINEMENT of concrete** | **Concrete tries to expand laterally when compressed; spiral or hoop steel restrains it, generating triaxial compression and greatly increasing strength and ductility** ← |
| **Lateral earth pressure at rest** | **K₀ = ν/(1 − ν) from elasticity — giving 0.33 for ν = 0.25** ← |
| **Plane stress against plane strain** | **Plane strain effectively stiffens the material by 1/(1 − ν²)** ← |

> **The CONFINEMENT row is the most valuable application: the entire benefit of spiral reinforcement in a column, and of closely spaced hoops in a seismic design, arises from restraining the lateral expansion that Poisson's ratio produces.**

> **A confined concrete core can reach strains of 0.01 to 0.02 against the 0.0035 of unconfined concrete — a five-fold increase in ductility, obtained purely by preventing the material from doing what Poisson's ratio makes it want to do.**

examTip.trick: **0.5, from E = 3K(1 − 2ν)** — at ν = 0.5 the bulk modulus becomes INFINITE (incompressible), and above it K would be negative, which is impossible. Options (a) and (d) are typical values for concrete and metals.
examTip.trap: **Only TWO of E, G, K and ν are independent.** E = 2G(1+ν) = 3K(1−2ν), so G ≈ 0.4 E for structural metals.
examTip.mnemonic: **Saturated undrained clay has ν ≈ 0.5 — constant volume because water cannot escape**, the elastic statement of the same fact as φ_u = 0. And CONFINEMENT works by restraining exactly the lateral expansion ν describes: strains of 0.02 against 0.0035.

questions.stem: RANKINE'S formula for the crippling load of a column is preferred to Euler's because Rankine's formula:
options: Requires no knowledge of the end conditions
Is valid for both short and long columns
Always gives a higher load than Euler's
Applies only to columns of circular section
questions.solution:
**It is valid for BOTH short and long columns**, whereas Euler's formula applies only to long, slender ones.

**Rankine's formula:**

> **P_R = σ_c A / [1 + a (L_e/k)²]**

> **where σ_c is the crushing stress, A the area, L_e/k the slenderness ratio, and a = σ_c/(π²E) is Rankine's constant.**

**Why it works at both extremes — the key insight:**

> **Rankine's formula is constructed from the reciprocal relation:**

> **1/P_R = 1/P_c + 1/P_E**

> **where P_c is the pure CRUSHING load (σ_c A) and P_E is the EULER buckling load.**

| Column | Which term dominates | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **VERY SHORT** | **P_E is enormous, so 1/P_E → 0** | **P_R → P_c: pure CRUSHING** ← |
| **VERY LONG** | **P_c is large relative to P_E, so 1/P_c is small** | **P_R → P_E: pure EULER BUCKLING** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE** | **Both terms matter** | **A smooth transition between the two** ← |

> **So the formula automatically reduces to whichever mode governs, and interpolates smoothly between them — which is precisely what an empirical design formula should do.**

> **The reciprocal-addition form is the same device used for springs in series and for resistances in parallel, and it always produces a result SMALLER than either component — which is conservative and correct here, since a real column suffers a combination of both effects.**

**EULER'S formula and where it fails:**

> **P_E = π²EI/L_e² = π²EA/(L_e/k)²**

| Limitation of Euler's formula | Note |
|---|---|
| **It gives an INFINITE load as the length approaches zero** | **Absurd — the column would crush long before** ← |
| **It assumes the material remains ELASTIC** | **Fails once the stress exceeds the proportional limit** ← |
| **It assumes a PERFECTLY straight column, axially loaded, of homogeneous material** | **No real column is** ← |
| **It is valid only above a certain slenderness** | **For mild steel with σ_c = 320 MPa and E = 200 GPa, the limit is (L_e/k) ≈ 80** ← |

> **The critical slenderness in the last row follows from setting the Euler stress equal to the crushing stress:**

> **π²E/(L_e/k)² = σ_c, so (L_e/k) = π√(E/σ_c) = π√(200,000/320) = π × 25 = 78.5 ≈ 80**

> **Below that slenderness the Euler formula predicts a stress the material cannot reach, and it must not be used.**

**The classification of columns:**

| Column | Slenderness (L_e/k) | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| **SHORT** | **Below about 32 (or L/d < 12 per IS 456)** | **CRUSHING — pure compression** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE** | **32 to 80** | **INELASTIC buckling — the most complex case, and the most common in practice** ← |
| **LONG (slender)** | **Above about 80** | **ELASTIC (Euler) buckling** ← |

> **The INTERMEDIATE range is where most real columns lie, and it is exactly the range Euler cannot handle — which is the practical reason empirical formulae like Rankine's, the Perry-Robertson formula and the modern buckling curves exist at all.**

**The EFFECTIVE LENGTHS, since both formulae depend on them:**

| End conditions | Theoretical L_e | IS 456 recommended |
|---|---|---|
| **Both ends HINGED (pinned)** | **1.0 L** ← | 1.0 L |
| **Both ends FIXED** | **0.5 L** ← | **0.65 L** ← |
| **One fixed, one hinged** | **0.707 L** | **0.80 L** ← |
| **One fixed, one FREE (cantilever)** | **2.0 L** ← | **2.0 L** |

> **The Euler load varies as 1/L_e², so the fixed-fixed column carries FOUR TIMES the pinned one and the cantilever a QUARTER of it — a sixteen-fold range from end conditions alone.**

> **NOTE THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE THEORETICAL AND CODE VALUES in the second and third rows: the code figures are LARGER, and deliberately so.**

> **A joint described as "fixed" on a drawing is never perfectly rigid — the connection flexes, the foundation rotates slightly, the adjoining members are not infinitely stiff — so the code assumes less restraint than the idealisation promises.**

> **Using the theoretical 0.5 L where the code says 0.65 L overestimates the buckling load by (0.65/0.5)² = 1.69, that is by 69 per cent, which is a substantial and unsafe error.**

> **The general lesson is worth stating: IDEALISED BOUNDARY CONDITIONS ARE OPTIMISTIC, and codes systematically discount them. Where a designer must choose, assuming LESS restraint is the safe direction for a compression member.**

Euler's applies only to long slender columns.

examTip.trick: **1/P_R = 1/P_c + 1/P_E** — so Rankine reduces to CRUSHING for a short column and to EULER for a long one, interpolating smoothly between.
examTip.trap: **Euler's formula gives an INFINITE load as L → 0** and must not be used below (L_e/k) ≈ 80 for mild steel, from π√(E/σ_c). Most real columns are INTERMEDIATE — exactly the range Euler cannot handle.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effective lengths: 1.0 L pinned, 0.5 L fixed (code 0.65), 0.707 L (code 0.80), 2.0 L cantilever.** The code values are deliberately LARGER — idealised fixity is optimistic, and using 0.5 where 0.65 applies overestimates capacity by 69 %.

questions.stem: For a beam of solid CIRCULAR cross-section subjected to transverse shear, the ratio of the maximum shear stress to the mean shear stress is:
questions.solution:
**4/3 (about 1.33).**

**The ratios for the standard sections:**

| Section | τ_max / τ_mean | Where τ_max occurs |
|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE** | **3/2 = 1.5** ← (option a) | **At the NEUTRAL AXIS** |
| **CIRCLE (solid)** | **4/3 ≈ 1.33** ← | **At the neutral axis** |
| **Thin-walled circular TUBE** | **2.0** ← (option c) | At the neutral axis |
| **DIAMOND (square on edge)** | **9/8** | At 1/8 of the depth from the NA |
| **I-SECTION** | **Close to 1.0 for the WEB alone** ← (option b) | Web at the neutral axis |

> **Every distractor is the correct answer for a different section, which is what makes this set demanding.**

> **The value for the rectangle (1.5) is the most familiar and is the natural wrong answer here.**

**Where the ratios come from:**

> **The shear stress at any level is given by τ = V Q / (I b), where Q is the first moment of the area beyond the level considered and b the width there.**

| Section | Distribution |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE** | **PARABOLIC, zero at top and bottom, maximum at the neutral axis: τ_max = 1.5 V/A** ← |
| **CIRCLE** | **Also parabolic in form: τ_max = (4/3) V/A** |
| **I-SECTION** | **Small and roughly constant in the flanges, then a sudden JUMP at the flange-web junction, nearly uniform down the web** ← |

> **The JUMP in the I-section is caused by the sudden change in width b — the flange is wide and the web is narrow, so τ = VQ/(Ib) leaps as b collapses.**

> **That is why the WEB carries almost all the shear in an I-beam — commonly 90 to 95 per cent — and why the usual design simplification is:**

> **τ_avg = V / (d × t_w), the shear force divided by the WEB area alone.**

> **That approximation is accurate to within a few per cent and is what IS 800 and most steel codes use.**

**Why the shear stress is ZERO at the top and bottom fibres — the reason worth knowing:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **The top and bottom surfaces of the beam are FREE** | **No shear is applied to them** ← |
| **COMPLEMENTARY SHEAR requires that the shear stress on perpendicular planes be equal** ← | **τ on the horizontal plane = τ on the vertical plane at that point** |
| **Since the horizontal surface carries no shear, the vertical shear stress there must also be ZERO** ← | ← |

> **So the shear stress vanishes exactly where the BENDING stress is greatest, and is greatest at the neutral axis where the bending stress is zero.**

> **That complementary relationship between the two distributions is one of the neatest results in beam theory, and it explains why bending and shear rarely produce a critical combined stress at the same point.**

**Where shear governs, since bending usually does:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORT, DEEP beams** | **Shear grows as 1/L while bending grows as L — so short spans are shear-critical** ← |
| **Beams with heavy loads near the supports** | Large shear, small moment |
| **TIMBER beams** | **Timber is very weak in shear PARALLEL TO THE GRAIN — often the governing check** ← |
| **Thin-webbed plate girders** | **Web BUCKLING in shear, rather than shear yielding** ← |
| **RC beams near supports** | **DIAGONAL TENSION — the reason for stirrups** ← |
| **Bolted and welded connections** | Shear usually governs |

> **THE TIMBER CASE deserves the emphasis given because it is counter-intuitive and causes real failures:**

> **Wood's shear strength along the grain is perhaps a twentieth of its bending strength, so a timber beam that is comfortably adequate in bending may split horizontally along its neutral axis near the support.**

> **The failure appears as a long horizontal crack rather than as the vertical crack one expects from bending, and it is a shear failure of exactly the kind this stress distribution predicts.**

> **It is also why notching a timber beam at its support — a common carpentry expedient — is so damaging: the notch is precisely where the shear is greatest and it removes the material carrying it.**

**And the RC connection, since diagonal tension is the same phenomenon:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Shear does not fail concrete directly** | **The shear stress creates DIAGONAL PRINCIPAL TENSION at 45°, and concrete fails in TENSION** ← |
| **Hence the crack pattern near supports** | **Diagonal, running up toward the load at roughly 45°** ← |
| **Hence the reinforcement** | **Vertical STIRRUPS crossing the diagonal crack, or bent-up bars following the tension direction** ← |
| **Nominal shear stress** | **τ_v = V_u/(b d) in IS 456 — the MEAN value over the effective section** ← |

> **The code's use of the MEAN stress τ_v = V/(bd), rather than the true maximum of 1.5 times that, is worth noting: the design shear strength τ_c is CALIBRATED against that mean definition from test data.**

> **So the 1.5 factor is not omitted by oversight — it is absorbed into the empirical strength value, and applying it as well would double-count.**

> **That is a general caution about code formulae: a nominal stress and its permissible value form a matched pair, and refining one without the other makes the design wrong rather than more accurate.**

examTip.trick: **Circle 4/3; RECTANGLE 3/2; thin TUBE 2.0; I-section web ≈ 1.0.** Every distractor is the right answer for a different section — 1.5 (the rectangle) is the natural wrong choice.
examTip.trap: **Shear stress is ZERO at the extreme fibres and MAXIMUM at the neutral axis** — from complementary shear, since the free top and bottom surfaces carry none. So shear peaks exactly where bending vanishes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear governs in SHORT DEEP beams and in TIMBER** (weak along the grain — hence horizontal splitting, and why notching at supports is so damaging). In RC, shear fails as DIAGONAL TENSION, and IS 456's τ_v = V/(bd) is the MEAN, deliberately matched to a calibrated τ_c.

questions.stem: A flexible cable of span L carries a load w per unit horizontal length and hangs with a central dip h. The HORIZONTAL component of the cable tension is:
options: wL²/(8h)
wL²/(2h)
wL/(8h)
wL²/(4h)
questions.solution:
**H = wL² / (8h).**

**The derivation, which is a single moment equation:**

> **Take half the cable, from the lowest point to a support. The forces are the horizontal tension H at the lowest point, the vertical reaction wL/2, and the load wL/2 acting at its centroid L/4 from the support.**

> **Taking moments about the lowest point:**

> **H × h = (wL/2) × (L/4) = wL²/8**

> **H = wL²/(8h)** ←

> **The expression is identical in form to the mid-span bending moment of a simply supported beam (wL²/8) divided by the dip — and that is not a coincidence.**

**THE BEAM ANALOGY, which is the most useful idea here:**

| Statement | Note |
|---|---|
| **H × y = M_beam at every section** ← | **where y is the cable's dip below the chord at that section, and M_beam the bending moment in a simply supported beam of the same span and loading** ← |
| **At mid-span: H h = wL²/8** | **Which is the result above** ← |
| **Consequence** | **The cable's SHAPE is the BENDING MOMENT DIAGRAM of the equivalent beam, scaled by 1/H** ← |

> **So a cable under a UDL per horizontal metre hangs in a PARABOLA, because the beam's BMD for a UDL is a parabola.**

> **A cable under point loads hangs in straight segments with kinks at the loads, because the BMD for point loads is made of straight segments.**

> **And a cable under its OWN WEIGHT — which is uniform per unit length OF CABLE, not per horizontal metre — hangs in a CATENARY, a slightly different curve.**

| Curve | Loading | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PARABOLA** | **UDL per unit HORIZONTAL length** | **A suspension bridge deck; the usual engineering case** ← |
| **CATENARY** | **UDL per unit length OF THE CABLE** | **A cable hanging under its own weight; a power line** ← |
| **Difference between them** | **Negligible for dips up to about L/10** ← | **So the parabola is used in practice** |

**The rest of the cable's statics:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal tension H (constant throughout)** | **wL²/(8h)** ← |
| **Vertical component at the support** | **V = wL/2** |
| **MAXIMUM tension (at the SUPPORTS)** | **T_max = √(H² + V²) = H√(1 + 16h²/L²)** ← |
| **MINIMUM tension (at the LOWEST point)** | **= H, since V = 0 there** ← |
| **Length of a parabolic cable** | **≈ L(1 + 8h²/3L² − 32h⁴/5L⁴)** |

> **The HORIZONTAL COMPONENT IS CONSTANT ALONG THE WHOLE CABLE, because no horizontal force is applied anywhere between the supports — and that is the single most useful fact about cables.**

> **The tension therefore varies only through its vertical component, and is greatest at the supports where the cable is steepest.**

**THE DIP-TENSION TRADE, which governs every cable structure:**

> **Since H = wL²/(8h), the tension is INVERSELY proportional to the dip.**

| Dip h | H, as a multiple of wL² |
|---|---|
| **L/5 (a deep sag)** | **0.625 wL** |
| **L/10** | **1.25 wL** ← |
| **L/20** | **2.5 wL** ← |
| **L/50 (nearly straight)** | **6.25 wL** ← |

> **SO A NEARLY STRAIGHT CABLE CARRIES AN ENORMOUS TENSION, and a perfectly straight one would need infinite tension.**

> **That is why a horizontal cable can never be pulled truly straight, however hard it is tensioned, and why the sag of a power line or a suspension footbridge cannot be eliminated.**

> **The designer's trade is clear: a DEEPER sag means LESS cable tension, smaller cables and smaller anchorages — but taller towers and, for a bridge, more headroom needed beneath the deck.**

> **Suspension bridges settle on a dip of about L/10 as the economic compromise, and that ratio has been remarkably stable across a century of bridge building.**

**And the application most relevant to Nepal — the SUSPENDED (suspension) FOOTBRIDGE:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Nepal has built thousands of trail suspension bridges** | **Often the only crossing of a deep river gorge for many kilometres** ← |
| **Two types** | **SUSPENSION (deck hung from cables by hangers, cables in a shallow parabola above) and SUSPENDED (deck laid directly on the cables, which sag deeply)** ← |
| **The SUSPENDED type has a much larger dip** | **So a LOWER cable tension and smaller anchorages — cheaper, and simpler to build with local labour** ← |
| **Its disadvantage** | **The deck follows the sag, so the crossing dips steeply in the middle** ← |
| **ANCHORAGES are the critical element** | **They must resist H permanently; failures are almost always anchorage failures, not cable failures** ← |

> **The ANCHORAGE point in the last row is the practical lesson from this equation: the horizontal force H does not diminish, it acts continuously for the bridge's whole life, and it must be resisted by mass or by rock anchors.**

> **A cable is easy to inspect and its condition is visible; an anchorage is buried, its deterioration is invisible, and it is where the structure actually fails.**

> **Which is why the maintenance regime for these bridges concentrates on drainage around the anchor blocks and on corrosion at the cable-anchor interface, rather than on the spans that attract the attention.**

examTip.trick: **H = wL²/(8h)** — the simply supported beam's mid-span moment wL²/8 divided by the dip. **H × y = M_beam at every section**, so the cable's SHAPE is the beam's BMD scaled by 1/H.
examTip.trap: **H is CONSTANT along the whole cable; the tension is MAXIMUM at the supports** (T = √(H² + V²)) and equals H at the lowest point. A UDL per HORIZONTAL metre gives a parabola; self-weight gives a CATENARY.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tension is INVERSELY proportional to dip — a nearly straight cable needs an enormous force**, which is why sag can never be pulled out. Suspension bridges settle at h ≈ L/10, and it is the ANCHORAGES, not the cables, that fail.

questions.stem: Mohr's FIRST moment-area theorem states that the change in SLOPE between two points on a beam is equal to:
options: The deflection at the second point divided by the distance between them
The moment of the bending moment diagram about the second point
The area of the M/EI diagram between the two points
The area of the shear force diagram between the two points
questions.solution:
**The AREA of the M/EI diagram between the two points.**

**The two theorems, which are always used together:**

| Theorem | Statement | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| **FIRST** | **The change in SLOPE between two points = the AREA of the M/EI diagram between them** ← | **θ_AB = ∫(M/EI) dx** |
| **SECOND** | **The DEVIATION of a point from the TANGENT drawn at another point = the MOMENT of the M/EI area between them, taken about the point where the deviation is measured** ← | **t_AB = ∫(M/EI) x dx** |

> **Option (b) describes the SECOND theorem incompletely — it is the moment of the M/EI diagram (not the bending moment diagram) — which makes it the designed distractor.**

**Where the theorems come from:**

> **The governing differential equation of the elastic curve is:**

> **d²y/dx² = M/EI**

| Integration | Result |
|---|---|
| **Integrate ONCE** | **dy/dx (the SLOPE) = ∫(M/EI) dx — the AREA under the M/EI diagram** ← |
| **Integrate TWICE** | **y (the DEFLECTION) = ∫∫(M/EI) dx dx — which is the MOMENT of that area** ← |

> **So the two theorems are simply the first and second integrations of the elastic curve equation, given a geometric interpretation.**

> **That interpretation is what makes the method powerful: instead of integrating algebraically, one computes the AREA and the CENTROID of a diagram — quantities that can be read off by inspection for the standard shapes.**

**The areas and centroids needed, which is all the method requires:**

| Shape of the M/EI diagram | Area | Centroid from the vertical edge |
|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE, base b height h** | **bh** | **b/2** |
| **TRIANGLE** | **bh/2** | **b/3 from the vertical side** ← |
| **PARABOLA (2nd degree), vertex at the far end** | **bh/3** | **b/4** ← |
| **Parabola, vertex at the near end** | **2bh/3** | **3b/8** ← |
| **CUBIC, vertex at the far end** | **bh/4** | **b/5** ← |

> **The pattern is worth noticing: for a curve of degree n with its vertex at the far end, the area is bh/(n+1) and the centroid is at b/(n+2).**

> **That single rule generates the whole table and removes any need to memorise it.**

**A worked example — the classic cantilever:**

> **A cantilever of length L with a point load W at the free end. Find the free-end deflection.**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **BMD** | **Triangular, zero at the free end, −WL at the fixed end** |
| **M/EI diagram** | **Triangle of height WL/EI and base L** |
| **Area** | **½ × L × WL/EI = WL²/(2EI)** ← |
| **Slope at the free end (tangent at the FIXED end is horizontal)** | **θ = WL²/(2EI)** ← |
| **Centroid of the triangle from the FREE end** | **2L/3** ← |
| **Deflection = moment of the area about the free end** | **(WL²/2EI) × (2L/3) = WL³/(3EI)** ← |

> **Which is the standard result, obtained in two lines with no integration at all.**

> **THE CHOICE OF REFERENCE TANGENT IS WHAT MAKES THE METHOD EASY OR HARD, and it is the one piece of judgement it requires:**

| Beam | Best reference tangent |
|---|---|
| **CANTILEVER** | **At the FIXED end, where the slope is known to be ZERO** ← |
| **Simply supported, SYMMETRICAL loading** | **At MID-SPAN, where the slope is zero by symmetry** ← |
| **Simply supported, unsymmetrical** | **At a support — then use the second theorem twice** ← |

> **Choosing a tangent whose slope is already known turns the second theorem's "deviation from the tangent" directly into the deflection, which is what makes the cantilever and the symmetrical cases so quick.**

**The alternative methods, and when each is preferable:**

| Method | Best for |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE INTEGRATION** | **Simple loadings; gives the complete deflected shape as an equation** ← |
| **MACAULAY'S method** | **Several point loads — the bracket notation handles the discontinuities in one equation** ← |
| **MOMENT-AREA (Mohr)** | **Deflection and slope at SPECIFIC POINTS; cantilevers and symmetrical beams; VARIABLE EI** ← |
| **CONJUGATE BEAM** | **The same as moment-area, recast as a fictitious beam loaded with M/EI — often the most mechanical to apply** ← |
| **Unit load / virtual work** | **TRUSSES and frames; any single displacement component** ← |
| **CASTIGLIANO'S theorems** | Where strain energy is convenient; redundant structures |

> **THE VARIABLE-EI ADVANTAGE in the third row is the moment-area method's strongest claim: a beam of varying section is awkward to integrate algebraically, because EI is a function of x.**

> **In the moment-area method it is trivial — the M/EI diagram is simply drawn with its ordinates divided by the local EI, and the diagram is then treated in the ordinary way.**

> **A stepped beam produces a stepped M/EI diagram, which is a set of rectangles and triangles whose areas and centroids are immediate.**

> **That is a genuine practical advantage for haunched beams and stepped columns, and it is why the method survives alongside more general techniques.**

examTip.trick: **First theorem: change in SLOPE = AREA of the M/EI diagram. Second: DEVIATION from a tangent = MOMENT of that area.** They are the first and second integrations of d²y/dx² = M/EI.
examTip.trap: **It is the M/EI diagram, not the bending moment diagram** — which is exactly what makes the method handle VARIABLE EI so easily. Option (b) omits the EI.
examTip.mnemonic: **For a curve of degree n with the vertex at the far end: area = bh/(n+1), centroid at b/(n+2)** — that one rule generates the whole table. And choose a reference tangent where the slope is already ZERO: the fixed end, or mid-span by symmetry.

questions.stem: In the moment distribution method, the CARRY-OVER FACTOR for a prismatic member whose far end is FIXED is:
options: Zero
questions.solution:
**0.5** — half the balancing moment applied at the near end is carried over to the far end.

**The carry-over factors:**

| Far end condition | Carry-over factor | Stiffness of the member |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **1/2** ← | **k = 4EI/L** ← |
| **HINGED or free (pinned)** | **ZERO** ← (option d) | **k = 3EI/L — reduced to three quarters** ← |
| **Far end with a symmetrical arrangement** | — | 2EI/L |
| **Far end with an antisymmetrical arrangement** | — | 6EI/L |

> **Option (d) is the correct value for a HINGED far end, which makes it the designed distractor — and the two cases must be kept apart because they also change the member's stiffness.**

**Why the factor is exactly one half:**

> **Apply a moment M at end A of a prismatic member AB with B fixed. From the slope-deflection equations:**

> **M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B) and M_BA = (2EI/L)(2θ_B + θ_A)**

> **With B fixed, θ_B = 0:**

> **M_AB = 4EIθ_A/L  and  M_BA = 2EIθ_A/L**

> **So M_BA / M_AB = 2/4 = 1/2** ←

> **The result depends on the member being PRISMATIC (constant EI). For a haunched or tapered member the carry-over factor differs and must be computed or taken from tables.**

**The MODIFIED STIFFNESS for a hinged far end, since it accompanies the zero carry-over:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A member hinged at its far end has stiffness 3EI/L rather than 4EI/L** ← | **It is LESS stiff, because the far end is free to rotate** |
| **And nothing is carried over** | **There is no fixity at the far end to attract a moment** ← |
| **The practical use** | **For the END SPAN of a continuous beam simply supported at its outer end, using 3EI/L avoids having to balance and carry over at that support repeatedly** ← |

> **THE PRACTICAL USE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE POINT: applying the modified stiffness at the start collapses an infinite sequence of small balancing operations into a single adjustment, and the analysis converges far faster.**

> **It is a labour-saving device rather than a different theory, and using the unmodified 4EI/L is not wrong — merely slower.**

**The moment distribution procedure, so the carry-over is placed in context:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute the FIXED END MOMENTS for every member, treating each as fully fixed at both ends** ← |
| **2** | **Compute the DISTRIBUTION FACTORS at each joint: DF = k / Σk for the members meeting there** ← |
| **3** | **RELEASE a joint: the out-of-balance moment is distributed among its members in proportion to their DFs, with the sign reversed** ← |
| **4** | **CARRY OVER half of each distributed moment to the far end of that member** ← |
| **5** | **Repeat, joint by joint, until the carry-overs become negligible** ← |
| **6** | **SUM each column to obtain the final end moments** |

> **The method is ITERATIVE and converges because each cycle's carry-overs are half the size of the previous distribution — so the corrections diminish geometrically and three or four cycles usually suffice.**

> **Hardy Cross's insight, published in 1930, was that an indeterminate structure could be solved by successive approximation rather than by simultaneous equations — which, before computers, transformed what was practicable.**

> **A continuous beam that would have required solving five simultaneous equations could be handled with arithmetic on a single sheet, and the method dominated structural analysis for forty years.**

**The FIXED END MOMENTS that start the process, as a working set:**

| Loading on a member of span L, both ends fixed | FEM at each end |
|---|---|
| **UDL w over the whole span** | **wL²/12 at both ends** ← |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/8 at both ends** ← |
| **Point load W at distance a from A, b from B** | **M_AB = Wab²/L², M_BA = Wa²b/L²** ← |
| **UDL over half the span (from A)** | **11wL²/192 at A, 5wL²/192 at B** |
| **Triangular load, zero at A to w at B** | **wL²/30 at A, wL²/20 at B** ← |
| **Support SETTLEMENT δ** | **6EIδ/L² at both ends** ← |

> **THE SETTLEMENT ROW IS THE ONE WORTH DWELLING ON, because it is the price of indeterminacy:**

> **A settlement of one support induces moments throughout an indeterminate structure, with NO LOAD APPLIED AT ALL.**

> **The moment 6EIδ/L² is proportional to the STIFFNESS — so the stiffer the structure, the larger the moments a given settlement produces.**

> **That is a genuinely counter-intuitive result: making a structure stiffer makes it MORE vulnerable to support movement, not less.**

> **And it is why a determinate structure is sometimes deliberately preferred on poor ground — a simply supported span accommodates a settling pier by rotating, and develops no stress whatever, while a continuous beam over the same pier may crack.**

> **The same reasoning governs the choice between continuous and simply supported bridge decks on compressible foundations, and it is a real design decision rather than a textbook observation.**

examTip.trick: **0.5 for a FIXED far end (stiffness 4EI/L); ZERO for a HINGED far end (stiffness reduced to 3EI/L).** Option (d) is the hinged case — the two always change together.
examTip.trap: **The ½ holds only for a PRISMATIC member** — a haunched or tapered member has a different carry-over factor that must be taken from tables.
examTip.mnemonic: **FEMs: wL²/12 (UDL), WL/8 (central point load), Wab²/L², and 6EIδ/L² for SETTLEMENT.** That last one means a STIFFER structure suffers LARGER moments from a given support movement — which is why determinate spans are sometimes chosen on poor ground.

questions.stem: A single-bay, single-storey rigid portal frame with BOTH column bases FIXED has a degree of STATIC indeterminacy of:
questions.solution:
**3.**

**The computation:**

> **For a plane frame, the degree of EXTERNAL static indeterminacy is:**

> **D_se = r − 3, where r is the number of independent support reaction components and 3 is the number of equilibrium equations available (ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0, ΣM = 0).**

| Support | Reaction components |
|---|---|
| **FIXED base** | **THREE — horizontal, vertical and MOMENT** ← |
| **HINGED (pinned) base** | **TWO — horizontal and vertical** ← |
| **ROLLER** | **ONE — perpendicular to the surface** |

> **For the portal with two FIXED bases: r = 3 + 3 = 6, so D_se = 6 − 3 = 3** ←

> **The frame has no internal hinges and forms no closed loop below the beam, so the internal indeterminacy is zero and the total is 3.**

**The same frame with other support conditions:**

| Frame | r | D_s = r − 3 |
|---|---|---|
| **Both bases FIXED** | **6** | **3** ← |
| **Both bases HINGED** | **4** | **1** ← |
| **One fixed, one hinged** | **5** | **2** |
| **One fixed, one roller** | **4** | **1** |
| **Both hinged, PLUS an internal hinge at the crown** | **4, less 1 condition** | **0 — DETERMINATE (a three-hinged frame)** ← |

> **The last row is worth noticing: adding a third hinge makes the frame statically DETERMINATE, which is exactly the principle behind the three-hinged arch met earlier.**

> **Each internal hinge supplies one additional equation (the moment there is zero), so it reduces the indeterminacy by one.**

**The general formulae, for completeness:**

| Structure | Degree of static indeterminacy |
|---|---|
| **PLANE TRUSS** | **D_s = m + r − 2j** ← |
| **SPACE TRUSS** | **m + r − 3j** |
| **PLANE FRAME (rigid joints)** | **D_s = 3m + r − 3j, less the released conditions** ← |
| **Alternative for a plane frame** | **D_s = 3C − r_c, with C the number of closed loops and r_c the released conditions** ← |

> **Checking this portal with the loop formula: treating the frame plus the ground as forming ONE closed loop, D_s = 3 × 1 = 3 ✓ — which agrees and is often the quickest route for a frame.**

> **Each CLOSED LOOP in a rigid plane frame contributes THREE to the indeterminacy, which is a useful shortcut: a two-bay single-storey portal with fixed bases forms two loops and is 6 times indeterminate; a two-bay two-storey frame forms four loops and is 12 times indeterminate.**

> **The number rises quickly, which is why hand analysis of frames was so laborious and why moment distribution was so valued.**

**KINEMATIC indeterminacy, since it is the companion concept and is easily confused:**

| Concept | Definition |
|---|---|
| **STATIC indeterminacy (D_s)** | **The number of unknown FORCES in excess of the equilibrium equations** ← |
| **KINEMATIC indeterminacy (D_k)** | **The number of independent DISPLACEMENT components (degrees of freedom) at the joints** ← |

> **For this portal: each free joint of a plane frame has 3 degrees of freedom (two translations and one rotation). The two beam-column joints are free, and the fixed bases have none.**

> **So D_k = 6 if axial deformation is included; if the members are taken as AXIALLY RIGID — the usual assumption — the two joints share one horizontal sway and each has a rotation, giving D_k = 3.**

| Method | Uses |
|---|---|
| **FORCE (flexibility) methods — consistent deformation, three-moment, Castigliano** | **D_s as the number of unknowns — best when D_s is SMALL** ← |
| **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness) methods — slope-deflection, moment distribution, matrix stiffness** | **D_k as the number of unknowns — best when D_k is small, and the basis of ALL modern software** ← |

> **THE CHOICE BETWEEN THEM IS DECIDED BY WHICH NUMBER IS SMALLER, and that is the practical value of computing both.**

> **For this portal, D_s = 3 and D_k = 3 with axial rigidity — so either would serve.**

> **For a multi-storey building frame, D_s runs into the dozens while D_k grows more slowly, so displacement methods win decisively — which is why every structural analysis program is built on the stiffness method and none on the flexibility method.**

> **The stiffness method also has the property that made it suit computers: its formulation is entirely systematic, requiring no judgement about which redundants to release, so it can be coded once and applied to any structure.**

**And why indeterminacy is wanted at all, since it complicates the analysis:**

| Advantage of an indeterminate structure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Smaller maximum moments for the same span and load** | **Continuity redistributes moment to the supports** ← |
| **REDUNDANCY — alternative load paths** | **The failure of one member need not cause collapse** ← |
| **Greater stiffness and smaller deflections** | ← |
| **Moment REDISTRIBUTION after yielding** | **A ductile indeterminate structure can carry beyond first yield** ← |

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stresses from SUPPORT SETTLEMENT, temperature and shrinkage** | **A determinate structure develops none** ← |
| **More complex analysis** | Now trivial with software |
| **Lack of fit during erection induces stress** | **A member made slightly too short must be forced into place** ← |

> **THE REDUNDANCY ROW IS THE DECISIVE ADVANTAGE IN SAFETY TERMS, and it is why indeterminate structures are preferred wherever consequences are severe.**

> **A determinate structure has, by definition, exactly enough members to stand: remove any one and it becomes a mechanism and collapses entirely.**

> **An indeterminate structure has alternative paths, so local damage — a blast, a vehicle impact, a corroded member, a defective weld — can be absorbed rather than propagating into total collapse.**

> **That property is called ROBUSTNESS, and after the Ronan Point collapse in 1968 it became an explicit code requirement rather than an incidental benefit — structures must now be designed so that local failure does not lead to disproportionate collapse.**

examTip.trick: **D_se = r − 3.** Two FIXED bases give r = 6, so D_s = 3. Both HINGED gives r = 4 and D_s = 1; add a crown hinge and it becomes DETERMINATE.
