examTip.trap: **Each CLOSED LOOP of a rigid plane frame adds THREE to the indeterminacy** — a quick check that agrees here (3 × 1 = 3), and shows how fast the number grows in multi-storey frames.
examTip.mnemonic: **Choose the analysis method by which number is SMALLER — D_s (force methods) or D_k (displacement methods).** Modern software is all stiffness-based because D_k grows more slowly and needs no judgement about which redundants to release.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, when dead load and imposed load act together WITHOUT wind or earthquake, the load combination for the limit state of COLLAPSE is:
options: 1.5 (DL + IL)
1.2 (DL + IL)
questions.solution:
**1.5 (DL + IL).**

**The IS 456 partial safety factors for loads, limit state of COLLAPSE:**

| Combination | DL | IL (imposed) | WL / EL |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DL + IL** | **1.5** | **1.5** | — |
| **DL + WL/EL** | **1.5 (or 0.9 — see below)** | — | **1.5** |
| **DL + IL + WL/EL** | **1.2** | **1.2** | **1.2** ← |
| **DL alone, where DL is BENEFICIAL against overturning or uplift** | **0.9** ← | — | **1.5** |

> **Option (c), 1.2(DL + IL), is the factor for the THREE-load combination — real, and for a different case.**

> **Option (b), 1.0 DL + 1.0 IL, is the SERVICEABILITY combination, used for deflection and crack-width checks rather than for collapse.**

> **So both are genuine IS 456 combinations offered for the wrong limit state, which is what makes the option set work.**

**Why the three-load combination uses only 1.2:**

> **The probability that the FULL dead load, the FULL imposed load AND the FULL design wind or earthquake occur simultaneously is very small.**

> **Each load's characteristic value already has a low probability of being exceeded; requiring three of them at once compounds those small probabilities into a negligible one.**

> **So the code reduces the factor from 1.5 to 1.2 — not because the loads are less severe, but because their COINCIDENCE is less likely.**

> **That is the general logic of load combination in every modern code, and it is why a structure is never designed for the simple sum of every load's worst value.**

**Why the DL factor drops to 0.9 when dead load is BENEFICIAL:**

| Situation | Dead load's role | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| **A beam carrying its own weight** | **ADVERSE — it causes the moment** | **1.5** |
| **A retaining wall resisting OVERTURNING** | **BENEFICIAL — its weight resists** | **0.9** ← |
| **A light roof resisting wind UPLIFT** | **BENEFICIAL** | **0.9** ← |
| **A basement resisting FLOTATION** | **BENEFICIAL** | **0.9** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE IS THE ONE TO CARRY: A LOAD FACTOR EXCEEDS 1 WHEN THE LOAD'S EFFECT IS ADVERSE AND FALLS BELOW 1 WHEN IT IS BENEFICIAL.**

> **Overstating a helpful load is just as unsafe as understating a harmful one — and the 0.9 exists because the actual dead load may be LESS than calculated (a thinner screed, a lighter finish, a partition never built).**

> **The WIND UPLIFT case in the third row is where this most often bites: a light steel roof can be lifted bodily off its supports by suction, and checking it with the full 1.5 DL resisting would conceal the danger entirely.**

**The MATERIAL partial safety factors, which complete the limit state method:**

| Material | γ_m | Design strength |
|---|---|---|
| **CONCRETE** | **1.5** ← | **0.67 f_ck / 1.5 = 0.446 f_ck** ← |
| **STEEL** | **1.15** ← | **f_y / 1.15 = 0.87 f_y** ← |

> **The two figures differ for a reason worth stating: CONCRETE is made on site, its strength varies considerably between batches, and it is tested on cubes that may not represent the structure. STEEL is made under factory control to a tight specification and is far more predictable.**

> **So the greater uncertainty attracts the greater factor — 1.5 against 1.15 — and the origin of the familiar 0.87 f_y and 0.446 f_ck is simply those two numbers.**

> **The 0.67 in the concrete expression is separate: it accounts for the difference between the strength of a cube in the laboratory and the strength of concrete in an actual member under sustained load.**

**The LIMIT STATES themselves, since the combination depends on which is being checked:**

| Limit state | What it guards against | Load factors |
|---|---|---|
| **COLLAPSE (ultimate)** | **Flexure, shear, torsion, compression, overturning, sliding, buckling** | **1.5, 1.2, 0.9 as above** ← |
| **SERVICEABILITY** | **DEFLECTION, CRACKING, vibration** | **1.0 throughout — the structure must perform under REAL loads, not factored ones** ← |
| **Durability** | Cover, w/c ratio, grade | Not a load case |

> **The 1.0 factors in the serviceability row are not an oversight: deflection and cracking are about how the structure behaves IN SERVICE, under the loads it will actually carry.**

> **Applying 1.5 to a deflection check would ask whether the structure looks acceptable under a load it will almost certainly never see, which is not the question being asked.**

> **That distinction — factored loads for STRENGTH, unfactored loads for BEHAVIOUR — is the clearest way to keep the two limit states apart.**

examTip.trick: **1.5(DL+IL); 1.2(DL+IL+WL); 1.5(DL+WL); 0.9DL+1.5WL where DL is beneficial.** Option (c) is the three-load case; option (b) is the SERVICEABILITY combination.
examTip.trap: **The three-load factor drops to 1.2 because the COINCIDENCE of all three at full value is improbable** — not because any load is less severe.
examTip.mnemonic: **A factor exceeds 1 when the load is ADVERSE and falls below 1 when BENEFICIAL** — hence 0.9 DL against overturning, uplift and flotation. And γ_m: concrete 1.5 (site-made, variable), steel 1.15 (factory-controlled), giving 0.446 f_ck and 0.87 f_y.

questions.stem: In the IS 1893 expression for design seismic base shear, the RESPONSE REDUCTION FACTOR R represents:
options: The importance of the building's function
The amplification of ground motion by the soil
The ductility, redundancy and overstrength of the structural system
The reduction of load with increasing building height
questions.solution:
**The DUCTILITY, REDUNDANCY and OVERSTRENGTH of the structural system.**

**Where R sits in the expression:**

> **A_h = (Z/2) × (I/R) × (S_a/g)**

| Factor | Represents | Position |
|---|---|---|
| **Z** | **The site's seismic HAZARD** | Numerator |
| **I** | **The building's IMPORTANCE** ← (option a) | **Numerator — a more important building gets a HIGHER force** ← |
| **R** | **DUCTILITY and reserve capacity** ← | **DENOMINATOR — a more ductile system gets a LOWER force** ← |
| **S_a/g** | **DYNAMIC amplification with the period and SOIL type** ← (option b) | Numerator |

> **Options (a) and (b) name the importance factor I and the soil's effect within S_a/g — both real factors in the same equation, offered for R.**

**Typical values of R:**

| Structural system | R |
|---|---|
| **Unreinforced MASONRY** | **1.5 — the lowest; essentially no ductility** ← |
| **Ordinary RC moment-resisting frame (OMRF)** | **3.0** ← |
| **Ordinary RC shear wall** | **3.0** |
| **SPECIAL (ductile) RC moment-resisting frame (SMRF)** | **5.0** ← |
| **Ductile shear wall with SMRF** | **5.0** |
| **Steel frame with ductile detailing** | **5.0** |
| **Steel eccentrically braced frame** | 5.0 |

> **Since R is a DIVISOR, moving from an ordinary frame (R = 3) to a ductile detailed frame (R = 5) reduces the design force by 40 per cent.**

> **THAT REDUCTION IS THE COMMERCIAL INCENTIVE FOR DUCTILE DETAILING, and it is worth stating plainly: providing closely spaced confining hoops, proper anchorage and capacity-designed joints costs perhaps 2 to 3 per cent more in reinforcement, and buys a 40 per cent reduction in design seismic force.**

> **So ductile detailing is not merely safer — it is usually CHEAPER overall, because the reduction in member sizes and steel across the whole building exceeds the cost of the detailing.**

**What R actually means — and the point most often misunderstood:**

> **R does NOT mean the structure is designed for a smaller earthquake. The earthquake is the same.**

> **It means the structure is permitted to be designed for a FORCE SMALLER THAN THE ELASTIC DEMAND, on the understanding that it will YIELD and absorb the remaining energy through inelastic deformation.**

| Design approach | Force required | Behaviour in the design earthquake |
|---|---|---|
| **Fully ELASTIC design (R = 1)** | **The full elastic demand — enormous and uneconomic** | **No damage, and no yielding** ← |
| **Design with R = 5** | **One fifth of the elastic force** ← | **The structure YIELDS at chosen locations and dissipates energy; it is DAMAGED but does not collapse** ← |

> **So the R factor is a promise the designer makes: that the structure will be able to deform inelastically, repeatedly, without losing its capacity to carry gravity load.**

> **IF THAT PROMISE IS NOT HONOURED IN THE DETAILING, THE R FACTOR IS A LIE and the building is simply under-designed by a factor of five.**

> **That is precisely what happened in many non-engineered and poorly detailed reinforced concrete buildings in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake: the analysis used a ductile R value, and the construction provided no ductility at all.**

**What the detailing must deliver to justify R — the essentials of IS 13920:**

| Provision | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **CLOSELY SPACED CONFINING HOOPS at member ends and in joints** | **Confine the concrete core so it can sustain large strains without crushing** ← |
| **135° HOOKS with adequate extension, not 90°** | **A 90° hook opens out and the confinement is lost exactly when needed** ← |
| **STRONG COLUMN - WEAK BEAM: ΣM_column ≥ 1.4 ΣM_beam at a joint** | **Forces hinges to form in BEAMS, not columns — a beam hinge is local, a column hinge collapses the storey** ← |
| **Adequate ANCHORAGE and lap positions away from hinge regions** | Laps must not be where yielding occurs |
| **Limits on the shear span and on axial load ratio** | Preserve ductile behaviour |
| **CAPACITY DESIGN for shear: shear demand from the beam's flexural OVERSTRENGTH, not from the analysis** | **Shear failure is BRITTLE and must never precede flexural yielding** ← |

> **THE STRONG COLUMN - WEAK BEAM RULE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT OF THESE, and the reasoning is worth being able to state:**

> **A plastic hinge in a BEAM affects one span; the building sheds energy and remains standing.**

> **A plastic hinge at the top and bottom of every column in one storey creates a MECHANISM — the storey collapses and everything above it falls.**

> **So the design deliberately makes the beams weaker than the columns, ensuring the damage occurs where it is survivable.**

> **And the CAPACITY DESIGN principle in the last row generalises it: choose where you want the structure to yield, make that region ductile, and make everything else strong enough that it cannot fail first.**

> **It is the same reasoning as a fuse in an electrical circuit — a deliberate weak point, placed where failure is harmless and controlled.**

examTip.trick: **R is in the DENOMINATOR of A_h = (Z/2)(I/R)(S_a/g)** — so more ductility means a LOWER design force. Unreinforced masonry 1.5, OMRF 3.0, SMRF 5.0. Options (a) and (b) are I and the soil term.
examTip.trap: **R does not mean a smaller earthquake** — it means the structure may be designed for a fifth of the elastic force BECAUSE it will yield and absorb the rest. If the detailing does not deliver that ductility, the building is under-designed fivefold.
examTip.mnemonic: **STRONG COLUMN - WEAK BEAM (ΣM_col ≥ 1.4 ΣM_beam):** a beam hinge is local, a column hinge collapses the storey. That is CAPACITY DESIGN — choose where it yields, like a fuse, and make everything else stronger.

questions.stem: The CHARACTERISTIC COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH of concrete, f_ck, is defined as the strength below which not more than:
options: 5 per cent of the test results are expected to fall
10 per cent of the test results are expected to fall
1 per cent of the test results are expected to fall
50 per cent of the test results are expected to fall
questions.solution:
**5 per cent** of the test results are expected to fall.

**What that means statistically:**

> **f_ck is the 5 PER CENT FRACTILE of the strength distribution — the value exceeded by 95 per cent of results.**

> **It is deliberately NOT the average: designing to the mean would mean half of all concrete placed was below the design strength, which is plainly unacceptable.**

| Definition | Corresponding value |
|---|---|
| **MEAN strength, f_m** | **The 50 % fractile** ← (option d) |
| **CHARACTERISTIC strength, f_ck** | **The 5 % fractile** ← |
| **Relation** | **f_ck = f_m − 1.65 σ** ← |

> **The 1.65 is the standard normal deviate for a 5 per cent one-sided probability — so the definition and the formula are the same statement.**

> **Rearranged, it gives the TARGET MEAN STRENGTH the mix must be designed for:**

> **f_target = f_ck + 1.65 σ**

**The standard deviations assumed in IS 10262:**

| Grade | Assumed σ (N/mm²) |
|---|---|
| **M10, M15** | **3.5** |
| **M20, M25** | **4.0** ← |
| **M30 to M50** | **5.0** ← |

> **A worked example: for M25 with σ = 4.0, the target mean strength is 25 + 1.65 × 4.0 = 25 + 6.6 = 31.6 N/mm².**

> **So a mix nominally for "M25" must actually be designed to average nearly 32 N/mm² — and that margin of 6.6 N/mm² is the price of variability, not a safety factor.**

**THE MOST IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE, which is easy to miss:**

> **The margin depends on σ, and σ depends on the QUALITY OF SITE CONTROL — not on the concrete's ingredients.**

| Site control | Typical σ | Target mean for M25 | Cement needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EXCELLENT — weigh-batching, moisture correction, trained crew** | **3.0** | **29.9 N/mm²** | **Less** ← |
| **Average** | **4.0** | **31.6 N/mm²** | — |
| **POOR — volume batching, no moisture correction** | **6.0 or worse** | **34.9 N/mm²** ← | **Substantially more** ← |

> **SO POOR QUALITY CONTROL COSTS CEMENT — a badly run site must use a richer mix to deliver the same characteristic strength, because its results scatter more widely.**

> **That is a genuinely useful argument for investing in batching equipment and supervision: it is not merely a matter of quality but of direct material cost, and the saving is measurable.**

> **And it reverses the usual assumption that quality control is an overhead — for concrete, better control REDUCES the cement bill.**

**The ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA in IS 456, which apply the same statistics:**

| Criterion | Requirement for M20 and above |
|---|---|
| **Mean of any 4 consecutive test results** | **≥ f_ck + 0.825 σ, or f_ck + 3, whichever is GREATER** ← |
| **Any INDIVIDUAL test result** | **≥ f_ck − 3 N/mm²** ← |

> **A "test result" here is itself the average of THREE cube specimens, and no individual cube may differ from that average by more than 15 per cent.**

> **Note that the individual-result criterion PERMITS a result up to 3 N/mm² below f_ck — which follows directly from the 5 per cent definition: occasional low results are EXPECTED, and a specification demanding that every cube exceed f_ck would be statistically incoherent.**

> **That is the point most often argued about on site, and the statistics settle it: one low cube in twenty is the designed-for outcome, not evidence of failure.**

**And what to do when concrete genuinely fails the criteria:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1 — Check the TESTING first** | **Faulty curing of cubes, poor capping, a mis-calibrated machine, or wrong-sized moulds cause more "failures" than bad concrete** ← |
| **2 — CORE tests on the actual structure** | **The definitive evidence; corrected for the length-to-diameter ratio and for the direction of casting** ← |
| **3 — NON-DESTRUCTIVE testing** | **Rebound hammer (surface only) and ultrasonic pulse velocity — INDICATIVE, and not a substitute for cores** ← |
| **4 — LOAD TEST the member** | Where the analysis is inconclusive |
| **5 — Re-analyse at the lower strength** | **Often the member is adequate anyway, since strength rarely governs everything** ← |
| **6 — Strengthen, or remove and replace** | The last resort |

> **The FIRST step deserves the emphasis it is given: cubes left in the sun, cured in a bucket that dried out, or tested at the wrong age will fail regardless of the concrete's quality.**

> **Investigating the test regime before condemning the structure is both quicker and cheaper, and it resolves a large proportion of apparent failures.**

examTip.trick: **5 per cent — f_ck is the 5 % fractile, so f_ck = f_m − 1.65σ and the target mean is f_ck + 1.65σ.** Option (d), 50 %, is the MEAN strength.
examTip.trap: **IS 456 permits an individual result up to 3 N/mm² BELOW f_ck** — which follows directly from the 5 % definition. Demanding that every cube exceed f_ck is statistically incoherent.
examTip.mnemonic: **POOR SITE CONTROL COSTS CEMENT** — a larger σ means a higher target mean for the same f_ck (34.9 against 29.9 N/mm² for M25). Better batching reduces the cement bill, so quality control pays for itself directly.

questions.stem: For a singly reinforced rectangular section with Fe 415 steel, the LIMITING moment of resistance is:
options: 0.149 f_ck b d²
0.087 f_ck b d²
0.138 f_ck b d²
0.36 f_ck b d²
questions.solution:
**0.138 f_ck b d².**

**The limiting moment coefficients for each steel grade:**

| Steel grade | x_u,max / d | M_u,lim |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.531** | **0.149 f_ck b d²** ← (option a) |
| **Fe 415** | **0.479** | **0.138 f_ck b d²** ← |
| **Fe 500** | **0.456** | **0.133 f_ck b d²** |

> **Option (a) is the Fe 250 coefficient — a real value for a different grade, which is what makes it the designed distractor.**

> **Note that HIGHER strength steel gives a LOWER coefficient, which is counter-intuitive until the derivation is seen.**

**Where the coefficient comes from:**

> **M_u,lim = 0.36 f_ck b x_u,max (d − 0.42 x_u,max)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **0.36 f_ck b x_u** | **The total COMPRESSIVE force in the concrete stress block** ← (option d is this coefficient alone) |
| **0.42 x_u** | **The depth of the stress block's CENTROID below the top fibre** ← |
| **(d − 0.42 x_u)** | **The LEVER ARM between the compression and tension resultants** ← |

> **Substituting x_u,max/d = 0.479 for Fe 415:**

> **M_u,lim = 0.36 × 0.479 × (1 − 0.42 × 0.479) f_ck b d² = 0.1724 × (1 − 0.2012) f_ck b d²**

> **= 0.1724 × 0.7988 = 0.1377 ≈ 0.138 f_ck b d²** ←

> **So the coefficient is not an independent number to memorise — it follows from x_u,max/d, which itself follows from the strain compatibility met earlier (concrete at 0.0035, steel at 0.87f_y/E_s + 0.002).**

**Why higher-grade steel gives a LOWER limiting moment coefficient:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Higher f_y means a higher YIELD STRAIN** | **0.0038 for Fe 415 against 0.0031 for Fe 250** ← |
| **A higher steel strain, with the concrete fixed at 0.0035, means a SHALLOWER neutral axis** ← | **x_u,max/d falls from 0.531 to 0.479** |
| **A shallower neutral axis means a SMALLER concrete compression block** | **So less moment can be developed before the section becomes over-reinforced** ← |

> **The coefficient therefore measures how much moment the CONCRETE can supply before the ductility limit is reached — and higher-grade steel reaches that limit sooner.**

> **This does NOT mean Fe 500 is inferior. For the same moment it requires LESS steel by area, since the steel works at a higher stress. What it limits is how much moment a given CONCRETE SECTION can carry as a singly reinforced member.**

> **That distinction is the practical one: higher-grade steel saves steel, and does not enlarge the section's singly reinforced capacity.**

**How the coefficient is used — the three cases:**

| Condition | Section type | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **M_u < M_u,lim** | **UNDER-reinforced** | **Design as singly reinforced; the steel yields first — DUCTILE** ← |
| **M_u = M_u,lim** | **BALANCED** | The limiting case |
| **M_u > M_u,lim** | **Would be OVER-reinforced** | **NOT permitted. Either increase the depth, increase f_ck, or design as DOUBLY REINFORCED** ← |

> **The DOUBLY REINFORCED option is the usual answer where the depth is fixed by headroom or architecture:**

> **The section carries M_u,lim through the singly reinforced mechanism, and the EXCESS moment (M_u − M_u,lim) is carried by a couple formed between COMPRESSION steel near the top and additional TENSION steel.**

| Feature of doubly reinforced design | Note |
|---|---|
| **Compression steel must be RESTRAINED against buckling** | **By closely spaced stirrups, exactly as in a column** ← |
| **The stress in the compression steel depends on its strain** | **From the strain diagram at d′/x_u — it may not reach 0.87 f_y** ← |
| **It improves DUCTILITY and reduces long-term deflection** | **Compression steel resists creep, which is a real secondary benefit** ← |
| **It is LESS ECONOMICAL than increasing the depth** | **So it is used when the depth cannot be increased, not by preference** ← |

> **The CREEP benefit in the third row is worth knowing because it is often the real reason compression steel is provided: sustained compressive stress in concrete causes creep, and creep deflection can be two to three times the immediate deflection.**

> **Compression steel does not creep, so it progressively takes over the compressive force and restrains the section's continued curvature — reducing long-term deflection by 30 to 50 per cent.**

> **That is why IS 456's deflection modification factors give explicit credit for compression reinforcement, and why a beam that passes its strength check may still need compression steel to pass its deflection check.**

examTip.trick: **Fe 250 → 0.149; Fe 415 → 0.138; Fe 500 → 0.133 f_ck b d².** Option (a) is the Fe 250 value; option (d) is the 0.36 from the compression block alone.
examTip.trap: **HIGHER grade steel gives a LOWER coefficient** — its greater yield strain forces a shallower neutral axis (x_u,max/d falls 0.531 → 0.479 → 0.456), so less concrete is in compression.
examTip.mnemonic: **M_u,lim = 0.36 f_ck b x_u (d − 0.42 x_u)** — derive it from x_u,max/d rather than memorising. If M_u exceeds it, go DOUBLY reinforced; and compression steel also cuts long-term CREEP deflection by 30-50 %.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the MINIMUM area of tension reinforcement in a rectangular beam is given by:
options: A_st/bd = 0.85/f_y
A_st/bd = 4 %
questions.solution:
**A_st /(b d) = 0.85 / f_y**, with f_y in N/mm².

**The values that expression produces:**

| Steel grade | A_st,min / bd | As a percentage |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.85/250 = 0.0034** | **0.34 %** ← |
| **Fe 415** | **0.85/415 = 0.00205** | **0.205 %** ← |
| **Fe 500** | **0.85/500 = 0.0017** | **0.17 %** |

> **Option (c), 0.20 per cent, is very nearly the Fe 415 value — but it is the answer to a particular case rather than the general rule, which is what the question asks for.**

> **Option (a), 0.12 per cent, is the minimum for HYSD reinforcement in a SLAB (as a proportion of the GROSS area bD, not bd) — a real requirement for a different member.**

> **Option (d), 4 per cent, is the MAXIMUM tension steel (0.04 bD), which is the opposite limit.**

> **So all three distractors are genuine IS 456 reinforcement limits, and the question tests which applies where.**

**Why the minimum exists — the reasoning:**

> **An unreinforced concrete section has some flexural capacity from the concrete's own modest tensile strength — perhaps 3 N/mm² for M25.**

> **If the steel provided carries LESS than the moment at which the concrete cracks, then at the instant of cracking the steel is suddenly required to take the whole tension — and it immediately yields or fractures.**

| Situation | Behaviour at first crack |
|---|---|
| **A_st BELOW the minimum** | **The section fails SUDDENLY and completely the moment it cracks — a BRITTLE failure with no warning** ← |
| **A_st at or above the minimum** | **The steel takes up the tension released by cracking; the beam deflects and cracks visibly before failing** ← |

> **SO THE MINIMUM STEEL RULE EXISTS TO ENSURE THE CRACKING MOMENT DOES NOT EXCEED THE ULTIMATE MOMENT — that is, so that the beam gives warning.**

> **A very lightly reinforced beam is more dangerous than an unreinforced one, because it appears to be a reinforced beam and behaves like a plain one.**

> **That is the same class of reasoning as the prohibition on over-reinforced sections: both rules exist to guarantee a DUCTILE, WARNED failure rather than a brittle, sudden one — one attacking the problem from each end.**

**The full set of reinforcement limits in IS 456:**

| Member | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **BEAM, minimum tension steel** | **0.85 bd / f_y** ← |
| **Beam, MAXIMUM tension steel** | **0.04 bD (4 % of the GROSS area)** ← |
| **Beam, maximum compression steel** | **0.04 bD** |
| **Beam, side face reinforcement** | **0.1 % of the web area, where the web depth exceeds 750 mm** ← |
| **SLAB, minimum (mild steel)** | **0.15 % of bD** |
| **Slab, minimum (HYSD)** | **0.12 % of bD** ← |
| **COLUMN, minimum longitudinal steel** | **0.8 % of the gross area** ← |
| **Column, maximum** | **6 % (4 % where bars are lapped)** ← |

> **Two points deserve attention in this table.**

> **First, the beam minimum is expressed on the EFFECTIVE depth d, while the maximum and the slab minima are on the GROSS depth D. Mixing the two is a common slip.**

> **Second, the MAXIMUM limits exist for CONSTRUCTABILITY rather than for structural reasons: 4 per cent steel in a beam or 6 per cent in a column leaves too little room for the concrete to pass between the bars, and honeycombing results.**

> **The practical maximum in a column is nearer 4 per cent for that reason, and the code's note about lapped bars recognises that a lap doubles the local steel area and can double the congestion.**

**And the SIDE FACE reinforcement in the fourth row, which is easily overlooked:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Required where the web depth EXCEEDS 750 mm** | **0.1 % of the web area, distributed equally on the two faces** ← |
| **Spacing** | **Not exceeding 300 mm or the web thickness, whichever is less** |
| **Purpose** | **CRACK CONTROL on the side faces, not strength** ← |

> **The reason is the crack-width principle met earlier: in a deep beam, the tension steel at the bottom controls cracking only near itself, and midway up the web the cracks would open widely with nothing to restrain them.**

> **Those wide side cracks admit water and chlorides to the interior of the member, so the reinforcement is a DURABILITY provision — which is why it is required regardless of the calculated stresses, and why omitting it from a deep beam or a retaining wall stem is a real defect rather than a technicality.**

examTip.trick: **A_st,min/bd = 0.85/f_y** → 0.34 % for Fe 250, 0.205 % for Fe 415, 0.17 % for Fe 500. Option (a) is the SLAB minimum (0.12 % of bD), option (d) the MAXIMUM.
examTip.trap: **The beam minimum uses the EFFECTIVE depth d; the maximum and the slab minima use the GROSS depth D.** Mixing them is a routine slip.
examTip.mnemonic: **The minimum exists so the beam WARNS** — below it, the steel yields the instant the concrete cracks and the failure is sudden. A very lightly reinforced beam is more dangerous than a plain one, because it behaves like a plain one while looking reinforced.

questions.stem: The losses of prestress that occur in POST-TENSIONED members but NOT in pre-tensioned members are:
options: Creep and shrinkage of concrete
Relaxation of steel
Elastic shortening of concrete
Friction along the duct and anchorage slip
questions.solution:
**FRICTION along the duct and ANCHORAGE SLIP (draw-in).**

**The losses in each system:**

| Loss | PRE-tensioned | POST-tensioned |
|---|---|---|
| **ELASTIC SHORTENING of concrete** | **YES — full effect** ← | **Partial only; NIL if a single tendon, since it is stressed against the already-shortened member** ← |
| **CREEP of concrete** | **YES** | **YES** |
| **SHRINKAGE of concrete** | **YES — full, since the concrete is cast fresh around the tendon** ← | **LESS — much shrinkage has already occurred before stressing** ← |
| **RELAXATION of steel** | **YES** | **YES** |
| **FRICTION in the duct** | **NO — the tendon is straight and free** ← | **YES — wobble and curvature effects** ← |
| **ANCHORAGE SLIP (draw-in)** | **NO — the transfer is by bond** ← | **YES — the wedges pull in as the jack releases** ← |

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) all occur in BOTH systems, which is what makes them distractors rather than answers — the question asks specifically for what post-tensioning adds.**

**FRICTION LOSS in detail, since it is the larger of the two:**

> **P_x = P₀ e^(−(μα + kx))**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **μα — the CURVATURE effect** | **From the intended profile; μ is the coefficient of friction (0.25-0.55) and α the total angular change in radians** ← |
| **kx — the WOBBLE effect** | **From unintentional misalignment of the duct; k is 0.0015 to 0.005 per metre and x the length** ← |

> **The consequences are practical and important:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The prestress FALLS along the tendon, away from the jacking end** ← | **So the far end has the least force** |
| **In a LONG tendon the far end may receive very little** | ← |
| **Remedy 1 — stress from BOTH ENDS** | **Halves the effective length and the maximum friction loss** ← |
| **Remedy 2 — OVERSTRESS temporarily, then release** | Within the permissible limit |
| **Remedy 3 — grease or lubricate the tendon** | Reduces μ |
| **Remedy 4 — use a smoother, well-supported duct** | Reduces k |

> **ANCHORAGE SLIP behaves differently and is worth distinguishing: it is a FIXED amount of movement (typically 3 to 6 mm as the wedges seat), so its EFFECT is greatest on SHORT tendons.**

> **A 6 mm draw-in on a 5 m tendon is a strain of 0.0012 and a stress loss of about 240 N/mm²; on a 50 m tendon the same 6 mm is a tenth of that.**

> **So the two post-tensioning losses act oppositely with length: FRICTION dominates in LONG tendons and ANCHORAGE SLIP in SHORT ones — which is a satisfying and genuinely useful pairing.**

**The typical TOTAL losses:**

| System | Total loss |
|---|---|
| **PRE-tensioned** | **About 20 per cent** ← |
| **POST-tensioned** | **About 15 to 20 per cent** |

> **Pre-tensioning loses more from elastic shortening and shrinkage; post-tensioning loses more from friction and anchorage. The totals happen to come out similar by different routes.**

> **The losses are the reason HIGH-STRENGTH STEEL is essential to prestressing, and this is the single most important idea in the subject:**

| If mild steel (f_y = 250) were used at, say, 140 N/mm² working stress | If high-tensile steel is used at 1,000 N/mm² |
|---|---|
| **A total loss of 200 N/mm² would ERASE THE ENTIRE PRESTRESS** ← | **The same 200 N/mm² loss is 20 per cent, leaving 800 N/mm²** ← |

> **So prestressing with ordinary reinforcement is IMPOSSIBLE, not merely inefficient — the time-dependent losses are of the same magnitude as the whole available stress.**

> **High-tensile steel (1,600 to 1,860 N/mm² ultimate) is what makes prestressing work, and its development is what made prestressed concrete possible at all.**

**PRE- against POST-TENSIONING, to place the losses in context:**

| Aspect | PRE-tensioned | POST-tensioned |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequence** | **Tendon stressed FIRST, concrete cast around it, released when hardened** ← | **Concrete cast with DUCTS, hardened, then the tendon stressed and anchored** ← |
| **Force transfer** | **By BOND, over the transmission length** ← | **By END ANCHORAGES** ← |
| **Where done** | **FACTORY — needs a stressing bed with abutments** ← | **On SITE, or in a factory; suits large members** ← |
| **Tendon profile** | **Usually STRAIGHT (deflecting is possible but awkward)** ← | **CURVED and freely chosen — a great advantage** ← |
| **Suits** | **Mass-produced units: sleepers, poles, planks, hollow-core slabs** ← | **Large in-situ or segmental work: bridges, long-span beams, tanks, silos** ← |
| **Grouting** | Not required | **Required for bonded systems — protects the tendon and bonds it** ← |

> **The CURVED PROFILE in the fourth row is post-tensioning's decisive structural advantage: the tendon can be draped to follow the bending moment diagram, providing an upward load that opposes the applied load wherever it is greatest.**

> **And the GROUTING in the last row is the durability provision that matters most: an ungrouted duct leaves the tendon exposed to moisture, and a highly stressed high-tensile wire is exceptionally vulnerable to corrosion and to stress-corrosion cracking.**

> **Failures of post-tensioned bridges have been traced to voids in the grout at high points of the ducts, where a small amount of water collected and corroded the tendon invisibly from inside — which is why grouting procedures, vents at high points, and vacuum grouting have received so much attention.**

examTip.trick: **FRICTION (duct curvature + wobble) and ANCHORAGE SLIP are unique to POST-tensioning.** Creep, shrinkage, relaxation and elastic shortening occur in both — options (a), (b) and (c).
examTip.trap: **The two post-tensioning losses act oppositely with length: FRICTION dominates in LONG tendons, ANCHORAGE SLIP in SHORT ones** (a fixed 3-6 mm draw-in is a large strain on a short tendon).
examTip.mnemonic: **Prestressing REQUIRES high-tensile steel** — total losses of ~200 N/mm² would erase the entire prestress in mild steel but are only 20 % of 1,000 N/mm². And GROUT the ducts: voids at high points have corroded tendons invisibly and failed bridges.

questions.stem: In the design of a footing, the critical section for TWO-WAY (punching) shear is taken at a distance from the face of the column of:
options: d/2, where d is the effective depth
d
2d
At the face of the column itself
questions.solution:
**d/2 from the face of the column**, measured on a perimeter all round it.

**The two shear checks on a footing, which must be kept apart:**

| Check | Critical section | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **ONE-WAY (beam) shear** | **At a distance d from the column face, on a section across the FULL WIDTH of the footing** ← | **The footing acts as a wide beam cantilevering from the column** ← |
| **TWO-WAY (punching) shear** | **On a PERIMETER at d/2 all round the column** ← | **The column tends to PUNCH THROUGH the slab, pushing out a truncated pyramid of concrete** ← |

> **Option (b), d, is the ONE-WAY shear section — a real and adjacent critical section, which is what makes it the designed distractor.**

**Why the two distances differ:**

| Failure | Mechanism | Assumed crack |
|---|---|---|
| **One-way** | **A diagonal tension crack across the full width, as in a beam** | **Inclined at about 45°, so it reaches the soffit a distance d from the face** ← |
| **Two-way** | **A conical or pyramidal surface all round the column** | **Also at about 45°, but the code takes the perimeter at HALF that distance as an equivalent uniform check** ← |

> **The d/2 perimeter is a code convention that gives the right answer when used with the code's permissible punching stress — the pair is calibrated together, exactly as τ_v and τ_c are for beam shear.**

> **So the d/2 must not be "corrected" to d on the grounds of the 45° crack: doing so would use a section inconsistent with the permissible stress it is compared against.**

**The punching shear check:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Critical perimeter for a square column of side a** | **b₀ = 4(a + d)** ← |
| **For a rectangular column a × b** | **b₀ = 2(a + d) + 2(b + d)** |
| **Punching shear force** | **V = total upward soil pressure OUTSIDE the critical perimeter** ← |
| **Nominal punching stress** | **τ_v = V / (b₀ × d)** ← |
| **Permissible stress** | **τ_c = k_s × 0.25 √f_ck** ← |
| **k_s** | **= 0.5 + β_c, but not more than 1.0, where β_c is the ratio of the SHORTER to the LONGER side of the column** ← |

> **THE k_s FACTOR IS THE INTERESTING PROVISION: a very elongated column (small β_c) gets a REDUCED permissible punching stress.**

> **The reason is that for a long narrow column the shear is not distributed uniformly round the perimeter — it concentrates at the ends and along the short faces, so the average stress understates the peak.**

> **For a SQUARE column β_c = 1, so k_s = 1.5 capped at 1.0, and no reduction applies. For a column twice as long as it is wide, β_c = 0.5 and k_s = 1.0 — still no reduction. The reduction only bites for columns more elongated than about 1:2.**

**If punching shear is inadequate — the options:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **INCREASE the footing DEPTH** | **The usual and most effective answer — d appears twice, in both b₀ and the area** ← |
| **Increase the concrete grade** | **τ_c goes as √f_ck, so the benefit is modest** ← |
| **Provide SHEAR REINFORCEMENT** | **Possible but awkward in a footing; more usual in flat slabs** ← |
| **Enlarge the column, or add a PEDESTAL** | **Increases the perimeter b₀ directly** ← |
| **In flat slabs: a DROP PANEL or a COLUMN CAPITAL** | **The standard solution — increases both d and b₀ locally** ← |

> **The √f_ck dependence in the second row is worth noting: doubling the concrete grade from M20 to M40 increases the punching capacity by only √2 = 41 per cent, whereas increasing the depth by 41 per cent increases it by rather more, since d enters both terms.**

> **So DEPTH is almost always the more effective lever, and that is why footings are thick.**

**PUNCHING SHEAR IN FLAT SLABS, since it is the same check and a notorious failure mode:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A flat slab has no beams, so the whole load passes into the column through a small area** ← | **Punching is the governing check** |
| **The failure is SUDDEN and BRITTLE** | **The column punches through and the slab drops** ← |
| **PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE follows** | **The fallen slab lands on the floor below, which punches in turn — a pancake collapse through the whole building** ← |
| **INTEGRITY reinforcement** | **Bottom bars carried CONTINUOUSLY through the column, so a punched slab hangs rather than falls** ← |

> **THE INTEGRITY REINFORCEMENT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT DETAIL IN FLAT SLAB CONSTRUCTION, and its purpose is worth stating precisely:**

> **It does not prevent punching. It accepts that punching may occur and ensures the consequence is not catastrophic — bottom reinforcement passing through the column cage catches the slab and holds it in catenary action.**

> **The slab sags dramatically and does not fall, so the progressive collapse does not begin.**

> **That is the same ROBUSTNESS philosophy met in structural indeterminacy: the design does not assume nothing will fail, but ensures that a local failure stays local.**

> **Several well-documented flat slab collapses during construction — where the slab was loaded before the concrete had gained strength, and no integrity steel was present — have made this provision a code requirement rather than good practice.**

examTip.trick: **TWO-WAY (punching): a perimeter at d/2 all round the column. ONE-WAY (beam) shear: a section at d across the full width.** Option (b) is the one-way section.
examTip.trap: **The d/2 is a code CONVENTION matched to the permissible stress τ_c = k_s(0.25√f_ck)** — the pair is calibrated together, so "correcting" it to d for the 45° crack makes the check wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **DEPTH is the effective lever** — d appears in both b₀ and the area, while τ_c goes only as √f_ck. And in flat slabs, INTEGRITY BARS through the column do not prevent punching; they stop the pancake collapse that follows it.

questions.stem: The SHAPE FACTOR of a solid RECTANGULAR steel section in bending is:
questions.solution:
**1.5.**

**What the shape factor is:**

> **Shape factor S = Z_p / Z_e = plastic section modulus ÷ elastic section modulus**

> **It is the ratio of the fully PLASTIC moment to the moment at FIRST YIELD, and it measures the reserve strength a section has after its extreme fibre first yields.**

| Section | Shape factor |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE** | **1.5** ← |
| **Solid CIRCLE** | **16/(3π) = 1.70** ← (option b) |
| **DIAMOND (square on its diagonal)** | **2.0** ← (option d) |
| **TRIANGLE** | **2.34** |
| **I-SECTION, bending about the major axis** | **1.12 to 1.15** ← |
| **Thin circular TUBE** | **1.27** |

> **Options (b) and (d) are the circle and diamond values — real shape factors for other sections.**

**The derivation for a rectangle b × d:**

| Modulus | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **ELASTIC, Z_e = I/y_max** | **(bd³/12)/(d/2)** | **bd²/6** ← |
| **PLASTIC, Z_p** | **Two halves each of area bd/2, with their centroids d/4 above and below the axis: (bd/2)(d/4) × 2** | **bd²/4** ← |
| **Shape factor** | **(bd²/4)/(bd²/6) = 6/4** | **1.5** ← |

> **The plastic modulus is the FIRST MOMENT of the two half-areas about the equal-area axis — a much simpler calculation than the second moment of area, and worth noting for that reason.**

**Why the I-section's shape factor is so LOW, and why that matters:**

> **The shape factor measures how much material lies NEAR the neutral axis, waiting to be recruited after the extreme fibres yield.**

| Section | Material distribution | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE** | **Spread evenly through the depth, so a great deal is near the axis and lightly stressed elastically** | **A large reserve — shape factor 1.5** ← |
| **I-SECTION** | **Concentrated in the FLANGES, far from the axis, so almost all of it is near yield already** | **Little reserve — shape factor about 1.14** ← |

> **THIS PRODUCES AN APPARENT PARADOX WORTH RESOLVING: the I-section has the LOWEST shape factor, and it is the MOST EFFICIENT bending section.**

> **The resolution is that the shape factor measures the RESERVE beyond first yield, not the absolute capacity.**

> **The I-section is efficient precisely BECAUSE it wastes no material near the neutral axis — and having wasted none, it has none in reserve.**

> **A high shape factor is therefore a symptom of an INEFFICIENT elastic section, not a virtue. The rectangle's 1.5 reflects the fact that half its material was doing very little in the elastic range.**

**PLASTIC ANALYSIS, which the shape factor introduces:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **PLASTIC MOMENT M_p = f_y Z_p** | **The moment at which the whole section has yielded** ← |
| **PLASTIC HINGE** | **A region that has reached M_p and rotates at constant moment, like a rusty hinge** ← |
| **COLLAPSE MECHANISM** | **Enough hinges to turn the structure into a mechanism** ← |
| **Hinges required for collapse** | **D_s + 1, where D_s is the degree of static indeterminacy** ← |
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **Collapse load ÷ working load** |

> **The relation in the fourth row is the central result of plastic analysis: a DETERMINATE beam (D_s = 0) collapses on the FIRST hinge, while a fixed-ended beam (D_s = 2) needs THREE.**

> **That is the reserve of strength that indeterminacy provides, expressed in a single formula — and it is a further advantage of continuity beyond the reduced moments noted earlier.**

> **For a fixed-ended beam with a UDL, hinges form first at the two supports (where M = wL²/12), the moment there stays constant while the span moment grows, and collapse occurs when a third hinge forms at mid-span.**

> **The collapse load is 16 M_p/L², against a first-yield load of 12 M_p/L² — a reserve of 33 per cent beyond first yield, obtained purely from redistribution.**

**SECTION CLASSIFICATION, since plastic design requires it:**

| Class | Name | Can it reach M_p? | Can it ROTATE at M_p? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **PLASTIC** | **YES** | **YES — sufficient rotation for a mechanism to form** ← |
| **2** | **COMPACT** | **YES** | **NO — it buckles locally before rotating enough** ← |
| **3** | **SEMI-COMPACT** | **NO — reaches only the yield moment M_y** ← | No |
| **4** | **SLENDER** | **NO — buckles LOCALLY before even reaching M_y** ← | No |

> **The classification depends on the width-to-thickness ratios of the flange and web: a thin, wide plate element buckles locally before its material can yield.**

> **PLASTIC ANALYSIS MAY ONLY BE USED WITH CLASS 1 SECTIONS, because it requires hinges to rotate while other hinges form elsewhere.**

> **Using a plastic analysis on a compact or semi-compact section assumes a rotation capacity the section does not possess, and the structure will fail by local buckling at a load below the computed collapse load.**

> **That is why section classification is the FIRST step in any steel design to IS 800 — it determines which design method is even permissible before any calculation is done.**

examTip.trick: **Rectangle 1.5; circle 16/3π = 1.70; diamond 2.0; I-section 1.12-1.15.** S = Z_p/Z_e, and Z_p is the FIRST moment of the two half-areas about the equal-area axis.
examTip.trap: **The I-section has the LOWEST shape factor and is the MOST efficient** — a high shape factor signals an inefficient elastic section with material idling near the neutral axis, not a virtue.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hinges needed for collapse = D_s + 1** — a determinate beam fails on the first, a fixed-ended beam needs three. And plastic analysis requires CLASS 1 (plastic) sections: classification is the first step in IS 800, before any calculation.

questions.stem: In a steel plate girder, the principal function of INTERMEDIATE (transverse) STIFFENERS on the web is to:
options: Carry a share of the bending moment
Increase the web's resistance to shear buckling by dividing it into shorter panels
Transfer concentrated loads into the web
Connect the flanges to the web
questions.solution:
**To increase the web's resistance to SHEAR BUCKLING, by dividing the web into shorter panels.**

**The types of stiffener and what each does:**

| Stiffener | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **INTERMEDIATE (transverse) stiffeners** | **Divide the web into panels, raising its SHEAR BUCKLING resistance** ← |
| **BEARING (load-carrying) stiffeners** | **Transfer CONCENTRATED loads and reactions into the web, preventing web crippling and buckling** ← (option c) |
| **LONGITUDINAL (horizontal) stiffeners** | **Resist BENDING-induced buckling of the compression zone of a deep web** ← |
| **Torsional stiffeners** | Provide torsional restraint at supports |
| **Diagonal stiffeners** | Resist local distortion |

> **Option (c) describes the BEARING stiffener, which makes it the designed distractor — both are real stiffeners, and they are placed differently: bearing stiffeners at supports and point loads, intermediate stiffeners along the span.**

**Why a plate girder web buckles at all:**

> **A plate girder is deep and its web is thin — often with a depth-to-thickness ratio of 150 to 300, compared with perhaps 40 for a rolled beam.**

> **A thin plate under shear develops DIAGONAL COMPRESSION at 45°, and a slender plate in compression BUCKLES long before it yields.**

| Web slenderness d/t | Behaviour in shear |
|---|---|
| **Below about 67ε** | **Yields in shear before buckling — no stiffeners needed** ← |
| **Above that** | **BUCKLES first — stiffeners become worthwhile** ← |

> **The stiffeners work by reducing the PANEL SIZE: buckling strength depends on the panel's aspect ratio and its smaller dimension, so dividing a long web into shorter panels raises the buckling stress substantially.**

> **They carry no direct load themselves in the elastic range — their job is to provide a line of restraint, which is why they can be relatively light.**

**TENSION FIELD ACTION, which is what happens after buckling:**

| Stage | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **1 — Before buckling** | **The web carries shear as pure shear, in the ordinary way** |
| **2 — The web BUCKLES diagonally** | **The diagonal COMPRESSION capacity is exhausted** ← |
| **3 — But the girder does NOT fail** | **The web continues to carry load as a series of diagonal TENSION bands, like the diagonals of a truss** ← |
| **4 — The stiffeners act as the truss's VERTICAL STRUTS, and the flanges as its chords** ← | **The girder becomes, in effect, a Pratt truss** ← |
| **5 — Failure** | When the tension field and the flanges' anchoring capacity are exhausted |

> **TENSION FIELD ACTION IS ONE OF THE MOST ELEGANT IDEAS IN STEEL DESIGN, and it has a direct practical consequence: a plate girder's post-buckling strength can be TWO OR THREE TIMES its elastic buckling load.**

> **Designing to the elastic buckling load alone therefore wastes a great deal of capacity, and IS 800 and other modern codes permit the tension field method explicitly.**

> **The condition is that the stiffeners must be able to act as struts — so they must be designed for that compressive force, and the END PANEL needs special treatment because it has no adjacent panel to anchor its tension field against.**

> **The end panel is therefore either made stiffer, provided with a stronger end post, or designed without relying on tension field action at all.**

> **This is a good example of a structure being permitted to fail locally in one mode (web buckling) because a second, entirely different mechanism (the tension field) takes over — the same philosophy as plastic hinges and as integrity reinforcement.**

**When a plate girder is used at all:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Spans beyond the range of rolled sections** | **Rolled beams reach about 1 m depth; plate girders can be several metres** ← |
| **Heavy loads over long spans — bridges, crane gantries, transfer beams** | ← |
| **Where the section can be TAILORED along the span** | **Thicker flanges where the moment is greatest, thinner elsewhere — impossible with a rolled section** ← |
| **Where depth is available** | **A deep girder is efficient; if depth is limited a rolled or built-up section may be better** ← |

> **The TAILORING advantage in the third row is the plate girder's real economic case: a rolled beam must be sized for its worst section and carries that weight everywhere, while a plate girder can shed material where the moment is small.**

> **On a long-span bridge girder, curtailing the flange plates can save 15 to 25 per cent of the steel — which over a large structure repays the extra fabrication.**

> **And the fabrication itself is now largely automated: web-to-flange welds are made by submerged arc welding on an automatic gantry, so the labour penalty that once counted against plate girders has diminished considerably.**

examTip.trick: **INTERMEDIATE stiffeners divide the web into shorter panels to resist SHEAR BUCKLING. BEARING stiffeners (option c) transfer concentrated loads.** Longitudinal stiffeners resist bending-induced buckling.
examTip.trap: **A buckled web has not failed** — TENSION FIELD ACTION takes over, with the web acting as diagonal ties, the stiffeners as struts and the flanges as chords. Post-buckling strength can be 2-3 times the elastic buckling load.
examTip.mnemonic: **The END PANEL needs special treatment** — it has no neighbour to anchor its tension field against. And a plate girder's economy comes from TAILORING: curtailing flange plates saves 15-25 % of the steel a rolled section would carry everywhere.

questions.stem: In timber design, the permissible stresses given in the code may be INCREASED when the load is:
options: Applied for a long duration, such as dead load
Applied in a wet or exposed location
Applied to a member with knots and defects
Of short duration, such as wind or earthquake loading
questions.solution:
**Of SHORT DURATION** — wind or earthquake loading, for which the permissible stresses may be increased (commonly by 33⅓ per cent).

**Why timber's strength depends on the DURATION of the load:**

> **Timber exhibits pronounced CREEP RUPTURE: it will fail under a sustained load well below the stress it can carry briefly.**

| Duration of load | Permissible stress multiplier (typical) |
|---|---|
| **PERMANENT (dead load only)** | **About 0.9 — REDUCED** ← |
| **Long term (dead + sustained imposed)** | **1.0 — the base value** |
| **Medium term (normal imposed load)** | 1.15 |
| **Short term (snow, or a temporary load)** | 1.25 |
| **VERY SHORT (WIND, EARTHQUAKE, impact)** | **1.33 or more — INCREASED** ← |

> **Option (a) describes the opposite case — a long-duration load requires a REDUCTION, not an increase, which makes it the designed distractor.**

> **Options (b) and (c) also require REDUCTIONS: wet service conditions and the presence of defects both lower the permissible stress.**

> **So three of the four options are reduction factors and only one is an increase — the question turns on knowing the direction of each.**

**Why the effect is so much larger in timber than in steel or concrete:**

| Material | Sensitivity to load duration |
|---|---|
| **STEEL** | **Essentially none at ordinary temperatures** ← |
| **CONCRETE** | **Some — sustained loading reduces strength to about 0.85 of the short-term value, which is already in the 0.67 factor** ← |
| **TIMBER** | **LARGE — a permanent load capacity of roughly 60 per cent of the 5-minute strength** ← |

> **The mechanism is the progressive rupture of the cellulose microfibrils and the lignin matrix under sustained stress — a form of creep that ends in failure rather than merely in deflection.**

> **The practical rule known as the MADISON CURVE relates strength to the duration of loading, and it is the basis of the multipliers above.**

> **The consequence for design is that a timber member must be checked for the WORST COMBINATION of load magnitude AND duration, which is not necessarily the largest load.**

> **A member carrying a large but brief wind load may be governed instead by a smaller permanent load, because the permissible stress for the permanent case is so much lower.**

**The other modification factors applied to timber's permissible stresses:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **LOCATION / service condition** | **Inside (dry) — full value; Outside (exposed) — reduced; WET (permanently damp) — reduced further** ← |
| **Moisture content** | **Strength falls markedly as moisture rises up to the fibre saturation point** ← |
| **GRADE of timber** | **Select, Grade I, Grade II — reflecting knots, slope of grain, checks and shakes** ← |
| **SIZE / depth factor** | **Deeper members have a lower permissible bending stress — more volume, more chance of a critical defect** ← |
| **Form factor** | For non-rectangular sections |
| **Bearing length** | Short bearings permit higher stress |
| **TEMPERATURE** | Reduced at sustained high temperature |

> **The SIZE FACTOR in the fourth row rests on an idea worth knowing — the WEAKEST LINK principle.**

> **Timber's strength is governed by its defects: a knot, a sloping grain, a check. A larger member contains more volume and therefore a higher probability of containing a severe defect at a highly stressed location.**

> **So larger timber members are, statistically, weaker per unit area — which is the opposite of the size-independence assumed for steel, and it is why permissible stresses are tabulated against member depth.**

> **The same statistical reasoning explains why GLUED LAMINATED timber (glulam) is stronger and more reliable than solid timber of the same size: the laminations are thin, defects can be cut out or dispersed, and a knot in one lamination is surrounded by sound material in the others.**

**The characteristics of timber that follow from its structure:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strongly ANISOTROPIC** | **Strength along the grain is 10-20 times that across it** ← |
| **Weak in shear PARALLEL to the grain** | **Often governs, as noted in the beam shear discussion** ← |
| **Very weak in tension PERPENDICULAR to the grain** | **Avoid details that induce it — notches, curved members, eccentric connections** ← |
| **Strength varies inversely with MOISTURE up to the FSP** | **Roughly doubles from green to 12 per cent** ← |
| **Excellent strength-to-WEIGHT ratio** | **Comparable with steel on that basis** ← |
| **Combustible, but predictable in fire** | **Chars at about 0.6 mm/min, and the char layer PROTECTS the core** ← |

> **THE FIRE BEHAVIOUR IN THE LAST ROW IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND WORTH KNOWING: a large timber beam performs better in fire than an unprotected steel beam of equivalent capacity.**

> **Steel loses about half its strength at 550 °C and fails suddenly, whereas timber's char layer insulates the sound core beneath, which retains nearly its full strength.**

> **Fire design for timber is therefore a matter of SACRIFICIAL DEPTH: compute the char thickness for the required fire period (say 30 minutes × 0.6 mm/min = 18 mm from each exposed face) and design the residual section for the reduced loads present in a fire.**

> **That is a simple, predictable calculation, and it is why heavy timber construction has an unexpectedly good fire record — the danger in timber buildings is light framing and unprotected cavities, not large solid members.**

examTip.trick: **SHORT duration (wind, earthquake) permits an INCREASE of about 33⅓ %.** Options (a), (b) and (c) — long duration, wet location and defects — all require REDUCTIONS.
examTip.trap: **Timber's permanent-load capacity is only about 60 % of its short-term strength** (creep rupture), so a member may be governed by a SMALLER permanent load rather than by the largest wind load.
examTip.mnemonic: **Larger timber members are weaker per unit area — the WEAKEST LINK effect**, more volume meaning more chance of a severe defect. That is why glulam outperforms solid timber. And timber chars at ~0.6 mm/min, the char PROTECTING the core.

questions.stem: COLIFORM organisms are used as an indicator of the bacteriological quality of drinking water principally because they:
options: Are themselves the most dangerous pathogens found in water
Are always present in faecal matter, are far more numerous than pathogens, and are easily detected
Can survive indefinitely in water without any host
Are the only organisms that chlorine can destroy
questions.solution:
**They are always present in faecal matter, far MORE NUMEROUS than pathogens, and EASILY DETECTED.**

**Why an INDICATOR organism is used rather than testing for pathogens directly:**

| Difficulty with testing for pathogens | How the coliform test avoids it |
|---|---|
| **Pathogens are FEW in number, even in dangerous water** | **Coliforms are present in millions per gram of faeces, so contamination is detectable at far greater dilution** ← |
| **There are MANY different pathogens — bacteria, viruses, protozoa, helminths** | **One test covers the whole class of faecal contamination** ← |
| **Each needs its own test, which is slow, costly and needs specialist facilities** | **The coliform test is cheap, standard and can be done in a modest laboratory or in the field** ← |
| **Pathogens are INTERMITTENT — absent one day, present the next** | **Coliforms are ALWAYS present where faecal matter is** ← |
| **Culturing pathogens is HAZARDOUS to laboratory staff** | **Coliforms are largely harmless** ← |

> **So the coliform is a PROXY: its presence does not itself prove danger, but it proves that FAECAL MATTER HAS REACHED THE WATER — and where faeces can go, pathogens can follow.**

> **Option (a) inverts this: coliforms are mostly harmless, and that is part of why they are safe to use as a test organism.**

> **Option (c) is the opposite of what is wanted — an ideal indicator should survive in water for a SIMILAR time to the pathogens, so that its presence and absence track theirs. One that survived indefinitely would give false alarms long after the danger had passed.**

**The hierarchy of coliform tests:**

| Group | What it indicates |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL coliforms** | **A broad group, including species found naturally in soil and vegetation — so their presence does not necessarily mean faecal contamination** ← |
| **THERMOTOLERANT (faecal) coliforms** | **Grow at 44 °C; much more strongly associated with faecal matter** ← |
| **ESCHERICHIA COLI (E. coli)** | **Found ALMOST EXCLUSIVELY in the gut of warm-blooded animals — the DEFINITIVE indicator of faecal contamination** ← |
| **Faecal streptococci** | A confirmatory indicator; the ratio to faecal coliforms can suggest human against animal origin |

> **The progression is one of increasing SPECIFICITY: total coliforms may be a false alarm, E. coli is not.**

> **THE STANDARD IN EVERY DRINKING WATER GUIDELINE IS THE SAME AND IT IS ABSOLUTE: E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms must be ZERO in any 100 mL sample.**

> **That is not a limit to be approached but a requirement to be met, and it is the only water quality parameter expressed as zero — because any faecal contamination at all is unacceptable.**

**The test methods:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **MULTIPLE TUBE FERMENTATION (MPN)** | **Gives the MOST PROBABLE NUMBER per 100 mL, from a statistical table based on which tubes show growth** ← |
| **MEMBRANE FILTRATION** | **Water is filtered, the membrane incubated on a nutrient pad, and the COLONIES counted directly** ← |
| **Presence-absence tests (H₂S strip, chromogenic media)** | **Cheap field tests — no count, but a clear yes/no; valuable for rural surveillance** ← |

> **The MPN method's name is worth understanding: it does not COUNT the organisms but estimates their most probable concentration from the PATTERN of positive and negative tubes, using probability theory.**

> **Membrane filtration gives an actual count and is quicker, but it fails on turbid water where the membrane blocks — so MPN remains in use for raw and waste waters.**

**The other water quality parameters, for context:**

| Parameter | Desirable limit (typical drinking water standard) |
|---|---|
| **E. coli / thermotolerant coliforms** | **ZERO per 100 mL** ← |
| **Turbidity** | **1 NTU desirable, 5 NTU permissible** ← |
| **pH** | **6.5 to 8.5** ← |
| **Total hardness (as CaCO₃)** | 200 mg/L desirable |
| **Total dissolved solids** | 500 mg/L desirable |
| **Iron** | 0.3 mg/L |
| **Chloride** | 250 mg/L |
| **ARSENIC** | **0.01 mg/L (WHO); Nepal's interim standard 0.05 mg/L** ← |
| **Residual chlorine** | **0.2 mg/L minimum at the tap** |

> **The TURBIDITY limit deserves a note because it is not merely aesthetic: turbidity SHIELDS micro-organisms from disinfection, since particles physically shelter bacteria and viruses from the chlorine.**

> **So a turbid water cannot be reliably disinfected however much chlorine is added, and clarification must precede disinfection — which is why turbidity is a health parameter and not a cosmetic one.**

> **And the ARSENIC row is of particular importance in the Nepali Terai, where naturally occurring arsenic in shallow groundwater affects a substantial population.**

> **It is a case where the switch from surface water to "safe" tubewell water solved a bacteriological problem and created a chemical one — a reminder that water quality has several dimensions and that improving one can worsen another.**

examTip.trick: **Coliforms are a PROXY: numerous, always in faeces, cheap to detect, and harmless to handle.** Their presence proves faecal matter reached the water — where faeces go, pathogens can follow.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is the opposite of what is wanted** — a good indicator should survive in water for a SIMILAR time to the pathogens, not indefinitely, or it gives false alarms after the danger has passed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Total coliforms → thermotolerant → E. coli, in increasing specificity; the standard is ZERO per 100 mL** — the only parameter set at zero. And TURBIDITY shelters organisms from chlorine, so clarify BEFORE disinfecting.

questions.stem: In estimating the total water demand of a town, the FIRE DEMAND is:
options: Ignored, because fires are rare
The largest single component of the total demand
Taken as 50 per cent of the domestic demand
Small in annual volume but requiring a high rate of supply
questions.solution:
**SMALL in annual VOLUME but requiring a very HIGH RATE of supply**, and assumed to occur at the same time as the maximum daily demand.

**The distinction between volume and rate, which is the whole point:**

| Aspect of fire demand | Note |
|---|---|
| **Annual VOLUME consumed** | **Tiny — commonly taken as about 1 litre per capita per day when averaged over the year** ← |
| **Instantaneous RATE required** | **Very LARGE — a single hydrant may need 1,000 litres per minute, and a serious fire several times that** ← |
| **Consequence for DESIGN** | **It does not affect the SOURCE or the treatment plant appreciably, but it can GOVERN the size of the distribution mains and the service reservoir** ← |

> **THAT IS WHY FIRE DEMAND CANNOT BE IGNORED DESPITE BEING NEGLIGIBLE IN VOLUME: the water system must be able to DELIVER it, at pressure, at any moment, wherever the fire happens to be.**

> **Option (a) confuses volume with rate, and option (b) inverts the relationship entirely.**

**The empirical formulae, which give the required rate:**

| Formula | Expression (Q in litres/minute, P in THOUSANDS) |
|---|---|
| **KUICHLING's** | **Q = 3,182 √P** ← |
| **FREEMAN's** | **Q = 1,136 (P/5 + 10)** ← |
| **BUSTON's** | **Q = 5,663 √P** |
| **National Board of Fire Underwriters** | **Q = 4,637 √P (1 − 0.01 √P)** ← |

> **A worked comparison for a town of 100,000 (P = 100):**

| Formula | Working | Q (litres/min) |
|---|---|---|
| **Kuichling** | **3,182 × 10** | **31,820** ← |
| **Freeman** | **1,136 × (20 + 10)** | **34,080** |
| **NBFU** | **4,637 × 10 × (1 − 0.1)** | **41,733** ← |

> **So roughly 32,000 to 42,000 litres per minute — that is 32 to 42 m³/min, or about 0.5 to 0.7 m³/s, which is a substantial flow.**

> **Expressed as a daily volume it would be 46 to 60 million litres if sustained for 24 hours — but a fire is fought for hours, not days, so the reservoir must hold a few hours' worth and no more.**

> **The √P dependence in most of the formulae reflects a sensible idea: a larger town does not need proportionally more fire flow, because the fire occurs in one district and the rest of the town is unaffected.**

**The COINCIDENCE assumption, which is where the design decision lies:**

> **Fire demand is added to the MAXIMUM DAILY demand, not to the maximum hourly demand.**

| Combination | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **Maximum HOURLY demand alone** | **A normal peak — no fire** |
| **Maximum DAILY demand PLUS fire demand** | **The design case for distribution mains — a fire on a hot busy day** ← |
| **The mains are designed for the GREATER of these two** | ← |

> **Combining fire demand with the maximum HOURLY demand would be unnecessarily severe — it assumes the fire begins precisely at the evening peak, which is an unreasonable compounding of two independent low-probability events.**

> **Combining it with the maximum DAILY demand is the accepted compromise, and it is the same probabilistic reasoning that reduces load factors when three loads are combined in structural design.**

**The consequences for the distribution system:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Minimum residual PRESSURE at the hydrant during a fire** | **Typically 100 to 150 kPa (10-15 m) — enough for the fire pumps to draw on** ← |
| **Hydrant SPACING** | **90 to 150 m in built-up areas** ← |
| **Minimum main size where hydrants are fitted** | **100 mm, and 150 mm preferred** ← |
| **A GRID (looped) network rather than dead ends** | **So water can reach a hydrant from TWO directions** ← |
| **Fire storage in the service reservoir** | A few hours' supply at the fire rate |

> **THE LOOPED NETWORK IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT OF THESE, and its value is not confined to fire fighting:**

| Layout | Character |
|---|---|
| **DEAD END (tree) system** | **Simple and cheap; but water reaches each point by ONE route only** ← |
| **GRID IRON / looped system** | **Every point fed from two or more directions** ← |
| **RING (circular) system** | A loop around the district |
| **RADIAL system** | From district reservoirs outward |

| Advantage of a LOOPED system | Note |
|---|---|
| **A break can be ISOLATED without cutting off large areas** | **In a dead-end system everything beyond the break loses supply** ← |
| **No STAGNANT ends** | **Dead ends accumulate sediment, lose chlorine residual and develop taste and odour** ← |
| **Better pressure distribution and lower friction loss** | Flow arrives by two paths |
| **Fire flow can be delivered to any point** | ← |
| **Disadvantage** | **More pipe, more valves, higher cost; and analysis requires Hardy Cross or a network model** ← |

> **The STAGNATION point is the everyday problem that most often reaches the consumer: the last house on a dead-end main receives water that has sat in the pipe, lost its residual chlorine, warmed, and picked up taste from the pipe wall and its sediment.**

> **Regular flushing through a washout at the end of each dead-end main is the palliative; looping the network is the cure.**

And taken as coincident with the maximum daily demand.

examTip.trick: **Tiny in annual VOLUME (~1 lpcd) but a huge instantaneous RATE** — so it governs the MAINS and the reservoir, not the source or the treatment plant.
examTip.trap: **Fire demand is added to the maximum DAILY demand, not the maximum HOURLY** — combining it with the evening peak compounds two independent rare events unreasonably.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kuichling Q = 3,182√P (litres/min, P in thousands)** — the √P reflects that a fire affects one district, not the whole town. And LOOP the network: dead ends stagnate, lose chlorine residual, and cut off everything beyond a break.

questions.stem: Two identical centrifugal pumps are connected in SERIES. Compared with a single pump, the combination delivers:
options: The same discharge at approximately double the head
Double the discharge at the same head
Double the discharge at double the head
Half the discharge at double the head
questions.solution:
**The SAME discharge at approximately DOUBLE the head.**

**Series against parallel — the fundamental pairing:**

| Connection | Discharge | Head | Used when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SERIES** | **The SAME through both — the second pump takes the first's output** ← | **The HEADS ADD** ← | **HIGH HEAD is needed — a hill pumping main, a high-rise building** ← |
| **PARALLEL** | **The DISCHARGES ADD** ← | **The SAME across both — they share common suction and delivery** ← | **HIGH FLOW is needed at a modest head** ← |

> **Option (b) states the PARALLEL case exactly, which makes it the designed distractor.**

> **The logic is the same as for pipes in series and parallel, and for the electrical analogy: in series the through-quantity (discharge, current) is common and the driving quantity (head, voltage) adds; in parallel the reverse.**

**The important qualification — why "approximately":**

> **The combined head is exactly double ONLY if the discharge is unchanged, and the discharge is set by where the combined pump curve meets the SYSTEM CURVE.**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **PUMP characteristic curve** | **Head FALLS as discharge rises** ← |
| **SYSTEM curve** | **Head required RISES as discharge rises: H = static lift + friction (∝ Q²)** ← |
| **OPERATING POINT** | **Where the two curves INTERSECT — the pump delivers exactly this and nothing else** ← |

> **Adding a second pump in series raises the pump curve, so the operating point moves to a HIGHER head AND a somewhat HIGHER discharge — because the extra head overcomes more friction and pushes more water through.**

> **So two pumps in series give somewhat more than the single pump's discharge, and somewhat less than double its head.**

> **The same applies to parallel operation, and there the effect is more pronounced and more often misunderstood:**

| Expectation | Reality |
|---|---|
| **Two identical pumps in parallel give DOUBLE the discharge** | **They do NOT — usually 1.5 to 1.8 times** ← |
| **Why** | **Doubling the flow QUADRUPLES the friction head (∝ Q²), so the system demands much more head, and each pump backs off along its own curve** ← |

> **THAT IS THE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL POINT IN THIS TOPIC: parallel pumping gives diminishing returns, and the flatter the system curve (that is, the more the head is STATIC lift rather than friction), the closer the result comes to doubling.**

| System | Parallel operation |
|---|---|
| **Mostly STATIC lift, little friction — a short rising main to a high tank** | **Nearly DOUBLES the flow** ← |
| **Mostly FRICTION — a long transmission main** | **Adds relatively little; the second pump is largely wasted** ← |

> **So the decision to install duty and standby pumps in parallel, and whether running both together is worthwhile, depends entirely on the shape of the system curve — which is why the curve must be drawn rather than assumed.**

**The pump characteristics that follow from these curves:**

| Curve | Shape and use |
|---|---|
| **Head against discharge (H-Q)** | **Falls with Q; the principal curve** ← |
| **EFFICIENCY against discharge** | **Rises to a maximum at the BEST EFFICIENCY POINT (BEP), then falls** ← |
| **POWER against discharge** | **Rises with Q for a centrifugal pump** |
| **NPSH required against discharge** | **RISES with Q — so cavitation is most likely at HIGH flow** ← |

> **THE BEST EFFICIENCY POINT IS WHERE A PUMP SHOULD OPERATE, and running far from it is damaging as well as wasteful:**

| Operating well BELOW the BEP | Operating well ABOVE the BEP |
|---|---|
| **Recirculation within the impeller; vibration; bearing and seal wear; heating of the trapped water** ← | **CAVITATION (NPSH required rises); high power; motor overload** ← |

> **So a grossly oversized pump throttled back to suit the system is not merely inefficient — it is being damaged, and its bearings and seals will fail early.**

> **The correct remedies for an oversized pump are to TRIM THE IMPELLER, to fit a VARIABLE SPEED DRIVE, or to replace it with the right size — not to throttle the delivery valve permanently.**

**And the AFFINITY LAWS, which govern speed and impeller changes:**

| Quantity | Varies as |
|---|---|
| **Discharge Q** | **∝ N (speed), or ∝ D (impeller diameter)** ← |
| **Head H** | **∝ N², or ∝ D²** ← |
| **POWER P** | **∝ N³, or ∝ D³** ← |

> **THE CUBE LAW ON POWER IS THE BASIS OF EVERY VARIABLE-SPEED PUMPING SAVING, and its magnitude is striking: reducing the speed to 80 per cent gives 80 per cent of the flow at 0.8³ = 51 per cent of the power.**

> **So a modest reduction in flow halves the energy consumption — which is why variable speed drives are among the most reliably economic investments in any water or wastewater installation, and why throttling a valve (which wastes the surplus head as friction) is so much worse than slowing the pump.**

examTip.trick: **SERIES: same discharge, heads ADD (for high head). PARALLEL: same head, discharges ADD (for high flow).** Option (b) is the parallel case — the same logic as pipes and as the electrical analogy.
examTip.trap: **Two pumps in parallel do NOT double the flow — usually 1.5-1.8×** — because doubling Q QUADRUPLES the friction head, so each pump backs off along its curve. The flatter the system curve, the closer to doubling.
examTip.mnemonic: **AFFINITY LAWS: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³.** At 80 % speed you get 80 % flow for 51 % power — which is why variable speed drives pay, and why throttling a valve is the wrong way to reduce flow.

questions.stem: For a rural gravity water supply scheme in Nepal's hills, HDPE pipe is generally preferred to galvanised iron pipe chiefly because HDPE is:
options: Stronger in tension than steel
Able to withstand higher internal pressures for the same wall thickness
Light, flexible, corrosion-free and jointed by fusion, so it can be carried and laid in remote terrain
Completely resistant to damage by ultraviolet light
questions.solution:
**LIGHT, FLEXIBLE, CORROSION-FREE and jointed by FUSION** — so it can be head-loaded to a remote site and laid over irregular ground without heavy plant.

**Why each property matters in hill terrain:**

| Property | Consequence in a remote hill scheme |
|---|---|
| **LIGHT — about one seventh the weight of steel** | **Coils can be carried by porters or mules where no road exists** ← |
| **FLEXIBLE — supplied in long coils** | **Follows an irregular alignment with FAR FEWER JOINTS and fittings; bends without special pieces** ← |
| **CORROSION-FREE** | **No wrapping, painting or cathodic protection; unaffected by acidic hill soils** ← |
| **FUSION welded joints** | **A butt-fused or electrofusion joint is as strong as the pipe and cannot leak or pull apart** ← |
| **Tolerant of GROUND MOVEMENT** | **Bends rather than breaks where a slope creeps — a decisive advantage in unstable terrain** ← |
| **Smooth bore** | Lower friction; does not tuberculate |
| **Cheap and easily repaired** | Local artisans can be trained on fusion equipment |

> **THE GROUND MOVEMENT TOLERANCE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS MOST IN NEPAL, and it deserves stating plainly: hillsides creep, settle and slip, and a rigid pipeline crossing them fractures at its joints.**

> **A fused HDPE line has no joints to pull apart and deforms elastically with the ground, so it survives movement that would destroy a GI or DI line.**

> **That single property accounts for much of the difference in the long-term survival of hill schemes.**

**The claims in the distractors, and why each fails:**

| Option | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| **(a) Stronger in tension than steel** | **Far weaker — HDPE's tensile strength is perhaps 25 MPa against steel's 400** ← |
| **(b) Higher pressure for the same wall thickness** | **The reverse — HDPE needs a MUCH thicker wall for the same pressure** ← |
| **(d) Resistant to ultraviolet light** | **HDPE is DEGRADED by UV; it must be carbon-black stabilised and, better, BURIED or shaded** ← |

> **Option (d) states the OPPOSITE of an important practical limitation: HDPE left exposed on a hillside for years becomes brittle and cracks.**

> **Carbon black gives useful protection, but the reliable answer is to bury the pipe — which also protects it from impact, from animals, from theft and from freezing.**

**The pipe materials compared:**

| Material | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **HDPE / MDPE** | **Light, flexible, corrosion-free, fused joints, cheap** ← | **UV degradation if exposed; lower pressure rating per thickness; permeable to some hydrocarbons; needs fusion equipment** ← |
| **GI (galvanised iron)** | **Strong, rigid, resists impact and UV; good for EXPOSED lengths and river crossings** ← | **CORRODES, especially at threaded joints; heavy; threaded joints leak and loosen** ← |
| **DUCTILE IRON** | **Very strong and durable; high pressure; good for large mains** | **Heavy; needs plant to lay; expensive** |
| **uPVC** | Cheap, light, smooth | **BRITTLE, particularly in cold; UV sensitive; solvent joints need care** ← |
| **Steel** | Very high pressure and long spans | Corrosion; needs skilled welding |
| **RCC / PSC** | Large diameters, gravity mains | Very heavy; joints |

> **THE PRACTICAL ANSWER ON A NEPALI HILL SCHEME IS USUALLY A COMBINATION, and knowing where each belongs is the real skill:**

| Location | Pipe |
|---|---|
| **Buried along the main length** | **HDPE — the bulk of the scheme** ← |
| **EXPOSED sections: river crossings, rock faces, above ground where burial is impossible** | **GI — it tolerates UV, impact and vandalism** ← |
| **High-pressure reaches below a long fall** | **Higher PN HDPE, or GI where the head exceeds what HDPE can take** ← |
