| **Within structures — tanks, chambers, tapstands** | **GI — it takes threading and fittings, and resists rough handling** ← |

> **And the PRESSURE limitation from option (b) is a real design constraint that returns us to the break pressure tank: HDPE's pressure rating is what determines how many tanks a long fall requires.**

| HDPE class | Pressure rating | Maximum static head |
|---|---|---|
| **PN 6** | **6 bar** | **60 m** ← |
| **PN 10** | **10 bar** | **100 m** ← |
| **PN 16** | **16 bar** | **160 m** |

> **A pressure rating is quoted at 20 °C, and it must be DERATED at higher temperatures — a point occasionally overlooked in the Terai, where a shallow-buried or exposed pipe can reach 40 °C and lose perhaps 20 per cent of its rating.**

> **Burial deals with that as well, which is one more reason it is specified — a buried pipe is cooler, shaded, protected and stable, and nearly every one of HDPE's weaknesses is answered by putting it in the ground.**

examTip.trick: **Light, flexible, corrosion-free, fusion-jointed** — porters can carry coils where no road exists, and long coils mean far fewer joints on an irregular alignment.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is the reverse of the truth — HDPE is DEGRADED by ultraviolet light** and must be carbon-black stabilised and, preferably, BURIED. Options (a) and (b) also invert real weaknesses.
examTip.mnemonic: **HDPE buried for the main length, GI for EXPOSED sections** (river crossings, rock faces, inside chambers). HDPE's decisive Nepali advantage is tolerating GROUND MOVEMENT — a fused line bends where a rigid one fractures.

questions.stem: In the LIME-SODA process of water softening, SODA ASH (sodium carbonate) is required to remove:
options: Carbonate (temporary) hardness
NON-CARBONATE (permanent) hardness
Turbidity and colour
Dissolved iron and manganese
questions.solution:
**NON-CARBONATE (permanent) hardness.**

**The division of labour between the two chemicals:**

| Chemical | Removes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **LIME, Ca(OH)₂** | **CARBONATE (temporary) hardness** ← | **It supplies the hydroxide that converts bicarbonate to carbonate, which then precipitates as CaCO₃** |
| **SODA ASH, Na₂CO₃** | **NON-CARBONATE (permanent) hardness** ← | **It supplies the CARBONATE ion that the non-carbonate hardness lacks** ← |

> **THE REASON FOR THE SPLIT IS THE KEY IDEA, and it is worth stating clearly:**

> **Removing hardness means precipitating calcium as CaCO₃ and magnesium as Mg(OH)₂. To do that, each hardness ion needs a partner.**

| Hardness type | Associated anion | What is missing |
|---|---|---|
| **CARBONATE hardness** | **Bicarbonate, HCO₃⁻** | **Nothing — the carbonate is already present; it only needs to be converted, which LIME does** ← |
| **NON-CARBONATE hardness** | **Sulphate, chloride, nitrate** | **There is NO carbonate available, so it must be ADDED — which is soda ash's function** ← |

> **So lime alone can never remove permanent hardness, however much is added — the necessary anion simply is not there.**

**The reactions:**

| Reaction | Equation |
|---|---|
| **Free CO₂ (consumes lime, removes no hardness)** | **CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O** ← |
| **Calcium carbonate hardness** | **Ca(HCO₃)₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2CaCO₃↓ + 2H₂O** ← |
| **Magnesium carbonate hardness (needs TWICE the lime)** | **Mg(HCO₃)₂ + 2Ca(OH)₂ → Mg(OH)₂↓ + 2CaCO₃↓ + 2H₂O** ← |
| **Calcium non-carbonate hardness** | **CaSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄** ← |
| **Magnesium non-carbonate hardness** | **MgSO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → Mg(OH)₂↓ + CaSO₄; then CaSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄** ← |

> **Two features of this set are worth noting.**

> **First, FREE CARBON DIOXIDE consumes lime without removing any hardness at all — so a water high in CO₂ wastes chemical, and AERATION beforehand to strip the CO₂ can be economical.**

> **Second, MAGNESIUM needs TWICE the lime that calcium does, and magnesium non-carbonate hardness needs BOTH chemicals — so a magnesium-rich water is markedly more expensive to soften.**

> **Magnesium removal also requires a high pH (about 10.8 to 11.0), which is why EXCESS LIME is added beyond the stoichiometric requirement when magnesium must be removed.**

**What the process can and cannot achieve:**

| Aspect | Lime-soda | Ion exchange (zeolite) |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum hardness achievable** | **About 30-40 mg/L as CaCO₃ — the solubility limit of the precipitates** ← | **Essentially ZERO** ← |
| **Chemicals** | Lime and soda ash | **Salt (NaCl) for regeneration** |
| **Sludge produced** | **LARGE volumes of CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂ — a disposal problem** ← | **None; a salty regenerant waste instead** ← |
| **Effect on TDS** | **REDUCES it — the hardness is removed as solids** ← | **INCREASES sodium; TDS roughly unchanged** ← |
| **Suits** | **Large municipal plants; very hard water** | **Small installations, boiler feed, domestic softeners** |
| **Also removes** | **Some iron, manganese, heavy metals and bacteria, incidentally** ← | Hardness only |

> **THE SODIUM ROW IS A REAL HEALTH CONSIDERATION and is worth knowing: an ion exchange softener replaces every calcium ion with two sodium ions.**

> **For a very hard water this can add a significant sodium load, which matters for people on sodium-restricted diets — and it is why a softened supply is often provided with one unsoftened tap for drinking.**

> **And SOFTENING IS NOT ALWAYS DESIRABLE. Completely soft water is CORROSIVE, because it has no calcium carbonate to deposit a protective scale on pipe walls.**

| Water | Behaviour in pipes |
|---|---|
| **Slightly SUPERSATURATED with CaCO₃** | **Deposits a thin protective film — the ideal** ← |
| **Very SOFT / undersaturated** | **AGGRESSIVE — dissolves cement mortar linings, corrodes metal, and can leach lead from old plumbing** ← |
| **Very HARD** | Scales boilers and heaters, wastes soap |

> **The LANGELIER SATURATION INDEX measures which side of that balance a water sits on, and treatment aims for a slightly positive value rather than for the lowest possible hardness.**

> **So municipal softening typically targets 80 to 120 mg/L rather than the 30 to 40 the process could reach — deliberately leaving hardness in, because water that is too soft attacks the distribution system it flows through.**

> **That is a good example of a treatment objective being a BALANCE rather than a maximum, and of a parameter that can be both too high and too low.**

examTip.trick: **LIME removes CARBONATE (temporary) hardness; SODA ASH removes NON-CARBONATE (permanent).** Permanent hardness has no carbonate ion available, so it must be ADDED — lime alone can never remove it.
examTip.trap: **Free CO₂ consumes lime without removing any hardness, and MAGNESIUM needs TWICE the lime of calcium** (plus a high pH, hence excess lime). Both raise the chemical cost.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lime-soda bottoms out at ~30-40 mg/L; ion exchange reaches zero but ADDS SODIUM.** And do not over-soften: water with no CaCO₃ is AGGRESSIVE and attacks linings and pipes — aim for a slightly positive Langelier index.

questions.stem: AERATION of raw water in a treatment plant is carried out mainly to:
options: Kill pathogenic bacteria
Remove suspended solids by flotation
Reduce the hardness of the water
Add oxygen and strip out dissolved gases
questions.solution:
**To ADD oxygen and STRIP OUT dissolved gases**, thereby oxidising iron and manganese and removing many tastes and odours.

**The purposes of aeration, set out fully:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **ADD dissolved OXYGEN** | **Making the water palatable, and enabling oxidation reactions** ← |
| **OXIDISE IRON and MANGANESE** | **Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ and Mn²⁺ → Mn⁴⁺, which are INSOLUBLE and can then be settled and filtered out** ← |
| **REMOVE free CARBON DIOXIDE** | **Reduces corrosiveness and saves lime in softening** ← |
| **REMOVE HYDROGEN SULPHIDE** | **The rotten-egg smell of some groundwaters** ← |
| **Remove volatile organic compounds and methane** | Tastes and odours |
| **Remove RADON from groundwater** | Where it occurs |
| **Assist in removing ammonia at high pH** | Air stripping |

> **THE COMMON THREAD IS GAS TRANSFER IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: aeration brings the water toward EQUILIBRIUM with the atmosphere, so it ADDS what the water lacks (oxygen) and REMOVES what it holds in excess (CO₂, H₂S, volatiles).**

> **That single idea covers every entry in the table and makes the process easy to reason about.**

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) name disinfection, flotation and softening — all real treatment objectives, achieved by quite different processes.**

**Why GROUNDWATER so often needs aeration, and surface water rarely does:**

| Property | GROUNDWATER | SURFACE WATER |
|---|---|---|
| **Dissolved oxygen** | **LOW or absent — it has been isolated from the air** ← | **Near saturation from contact with air and from algae** |
| **Carbon dioxide** | **HIGH — from the decay of organic matter in the soil** ← | Low |
| **IRON and MANGANESE** | **Often HIGH — the anaerobic, high-CO₂ conditions keep them in their soluble reduced forms** ← | Usually low |
| **Hydrogen sulphide** | Sometimes present | Rare |
| **Turbidity and bacteria** | **LOW — filtered by the ground** ← | **HIGH — the main treatment problem** ← |
| **Temperature** | Constant | Variable |

> **THE CONTRAST IN THE LAST TWO ROWS DEFINES THE TWO TREATMENT TRAINS, and it is a genuinely useful organising idea:**

| Source | Typical treatment |
|---|---|
| **SURFACE water** | **Screening → coagulation → flocculation → sedimentation → filtration → disinfection** ← |
| **GROUNDWATER** | **AERATION → (settling) → filtration → disinfection — often no coagulation at all** ← |

> **A groundwater is generally clear and bacteriologically good but chemically loaded; a surface water is generally chemically clean but turbid and contaminated.**

> **So the two sources need almost opposite treatment, and choosing a source determines the plant.**

**The IRON AND MANGANESE removal sequence, since it is aeration's commonest application:**

| Step | Process |
|---|---|
| **1 — AERATION** | **Oxidises soluble Fe²⁺ to insoluble Fe³⁺** ← |
| **2 — REACTION / detention time** | **20 to 60 minutes; manganese is much SLOWER to oxidise than iron** ← |
| **3 — Sedimentation** | The floc settles |
| **4 — FILTRATION** | Catches the remainder |
| **5 — Where aeration alone is insufficient** | **A stronger oxidant — chlorine, potassium permanganate or ozone — particularly for manganese** ← |

> **The MANGANESE difficulty in the second and fifth rows is a real operational problem: manganese oxidises very slowly by air alone below about pH 9.5, so plants that remove iron successfully often pass manganese straight through.**

> **It appears at the consumer's tap days later as black staining of laundry and fittings — a complaint that is puzzling until the mechanism is understood, because the water leaves the works looking perfectly clear.**

**The types of aerator:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **CASCADE aerator** | **Water falls over a series of steps; simple, no moving parts, low maintenance — excellent for rural schemes** ← |
| **SPRAY aerator (nozzles)** | **Very efficient gas transfer; high head loss** ← |
| **TRAY aerator (with coke or stone media)** | **Compact and effective; the media also provides a surface for catalytic oxidation** ← |
| **DIFFUSED AIR** | Air blown through the water in a tank |
| **Mechanical (surface) aerator** | Paddles or turbines; used more in wastewater |

> **The CASCADE aerator's advantages match rural Nepali conditions exactly, and it is worth noting why: it needs NO POWER (gravity does the work), NO MOVING PARTS, and NO SPECIALIST MAINTENANCE.**

> **In a gravity scheme the head is already available and is otherwise simply dissipated, so aeration is obtained essentially free — the water is going to fall anyway, and making it fall over steps costs only the masonry.**

> **That is the same reasoning that makes the slow sand filter appropriate in the same settings: choose the process whose requirements the site already satisfies, rather than the process that performs best on paper.**

examTip.trick: **Aeration brings water toward EQUILIBRIUM WITH THE ATMOSPHERE — adding what it lacks (oxygen) and stripping what it holds in excess (CO₂, H₂S, volatiles).** That one idea covers every purpose.
examTip.trap: **MANGANESE oxidises far more slowly than iron** and often passes straight through a works that removes iron successfully — appearing later as black staining at the tap. It usually needs a stronger oxidant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Groundwater: low O₂, high CO₂, iron and manganese, but clear and clean — so AERATE, filter, disinfect. Surface water: turbid and contaminated but chemically clean — so COAGULATE, settle, filter, disinfect.** Opposite trains.

questions.stem: A DROP MANHOLE is provided in a sewerage system where:
options: An incoming (branch) sewer joins the main at a level appreciably higher than the main sewer's invert
The sewer changes direction
Two sewers of the same size and level meet
The sewer passes beneath a road
questions.solution:
**Where an incoming branch sewer joins at a level appreciably HIGHER than the main sewer's invert** — commonly a difference exceeding about 0.6 m.

**What the drop connection does and why it is needed:**

| Without a drop arrangement | With a drop manhole |
|---|---|
| **The sewage falls freely from the high inlet to the main's invert** | **It is carried down in a vertical DROP PIPE outside or inside the manhole** ← |
| **SPLASHING, turbulence and spray inside the manhole** ← | Contained |
| **EROSION of the benching and the manhole walls** ← | Prevented |
| **Release of H₂S and odour, and a corrosive atmosphere** ← | Greatly reduced |
| **A maintenance worker cannot safely enter** ← | **Safe access is preserved** ← |
| **Energy is dissipated destructively** | Controlled |

> **THE SAFE-ENTRY POINT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED: a manhole with sewage cascading through it cannot be entered for cleaning or inspection without the worker being soaked in it.**

> **Since a manhole exists precisely to be entered, an arrangement that makes entry impossible defeats its purpose — so the drop pipe is as much an access provision as a hydraulic one.**

> **Option (b) describes an ordinary manhole (one is provided at every change of direction), and options (c) and (d) describe conditions requiring no special manhole at all.**

**Where drop manholes are typically needed:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **STEEP terrain** | **The ground falls faster than the sewer's permissible gradient, so the level must be dropped in steps** ← |
| **A branch sewer laid at minimum depth joining a deep main** | **The commonest case in flat towns** ← |
| **Avoiding excessive excavation on a steep road** | **Rather than laying the sewer at the ground slope and exceeding the maximum velocity** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE NEPALI HILL CASE and it is the same problem met in road design: the ground is steeper than the design gradient permits.**

> **A sewer laid at the ground slope would exceed the maximum non-scouring velocity of 2.4 to 3.0 m/s and abrade its invert.**

> **So the sewer is laid at an acceptable gradient between manholes and the surplus fall is taken vertically inside them — converting a continuous steep slope into a series of flat runs and vertical drops.**

> **That is exactly the device used for roads (where the fall is taken in hairpins) and for canals (where it is taken in falls), and the three are the same solution to the same problem in three different systems.**

**MANHOLES generally, since the drop manhole is a special case:**

| Purpose of a manhole | Note |
|---|---|
| **INSPECTION and cleaning access** | **The primary purpose** ← |
| **At every CHANGE of direction, gradient, size or alignment** | **A sewer must be straight between manholes** ← |
| **At every JUNCTION of sewers** | ← |
| **VENTILATION of the sewer** | Through perforated covers, where used |
| **At intervals along straight runs** | See spacing below |

| Sewer diameter | Maximum manhole spacing |
|---|---|
| **Up to 0.3 m** | **45 m** ← |
| **0.3 to 0.6 m** | **75 m** |
| **0.6 to 0.9 m** | **90 m** |
| **Above 0.9 m** | **Up to 150 m and more** ← |

> **The spacing increases with size for a simple reason: larger sewers can be entered and travelled along internally, whereas a small sewer can only be rodded or jetted from a manhole and the equipment has a limited reach.**

> **The requirement that a sewer be STRAIGHT BETWEEN MANHOLES follows from the same practical need — rods and jetting hoses cannot negotiate bends, and a CCTV camera cannot see round one.**

**And the SAFETY point, which is where this topic becomes serious:**

| Hazard in a manhole or sewer | Note |
|---|---|
| **OXYGEN DEFICIENCY** | **The commonest killer; the atmosphere may simply lack oxygen** ← |
| **HYDROGEN SULPHIDE** | **Toxic, and it DEADENS THE SENSE OF SMELL — so the warning disappears as the concentration rises** ← |
| **METHANE** | **Explosive** |
| **Carbon dioxide, and other asphyxiants** | Heavier than air, collecting at the bottom |
| **Drowning in a sudden surge** | From upstream rainfall |
| **Infection** | Weil's disease (leptospirosis), hepatitis, tetanus |

> **THE PATTERN OF FATALITIES IN CONFINED SPACES IS ALWAYS THE SAME AND DESERVES TO BE STATED: one worker enters and collapses, and a second enters to rescue them and collapses too.**

> **A majority of confined-space deaths are would-be RESCUERS, which is why the rule is absolute — NEVER ENTER TO ATTEMPT A RESCUE without breathing apparatus, whatever the temptation.**

> **The required procedure is a PERMIT TO WORK, gas testing before and during entry, forced ventilation, a harness and lifeline with a person stationed outside, breathing apparatus available, and a planned rescue method that does not require anyone to enter.**

> **And the first principle remains the one from the hierarchy of control: wherever the work can be done from OUTSIDE the space — by rodding, jetting, camera or vacuum tanker — entry should not take place at all.**

examTip.trick: **Where a branch joins more than about 0.6 m above the main's invert.** The drop pipe prevents splashing, erosion and H₂S release — and preserves SAFE ENTRY, which is a manhole's whole purpose.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) describes an ORDINARY manhole** — one is required at every change of direction, gradient, size or junction, and the sewer must be STRAIGHT between manholes so rods and cameras can pass.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steep ground: lay the sewer at an acceptable gradient and take the surplus fall VERTICALLY in manholes** — the same device as hairpins on a road and falls on a canal. And in confined spaces, most fatalities are the RESCUERS.

questions.stem: A TRICKLING FILTER treats sewage by means of:
options: Straining the sewage through a bed of fine sand
A biological film (slime layer) growing on the surface of the media
Chemical precipitation of the organic matter
Settlement of solids in a deep quiescent tank
questions.solution:
**A BIOLOGICAL FILM — the slime layer or zoogleal film — growing on the surface of the media, which absorbs and oxidises the organic matter as the sewage trickles over it.**

**Why the name is misleading, and what actually happens:**

> **A trickling filter does NOT filter. Its media are coarse — 25 to 75 mm stone or plastic — with very large voids, and the sewage passes straight through.**

> **The treatment is entirely BIOLOGICAL, performed by the film that grows on the media's surface:**

| Layer of the biological film | What occurs |
|---|---|
| **The OUTER layer, in contact with the sewage** | **AEROBIC — bacteria absorb and oxidise the organic matter, using oxygen from the air passing through the bed** ← |
| **The INNER layer, next to the media** | **ANAEROBIC — oxygen cannot penetrate the thickening film** ← |
| **As the film THICKENS** | **The anaerobic layer loses its grip on the media** ← |
| **SLOUGHING (unloading)** | **The film detaches in sheets and is carried out, to be removed in the SECONDARY clarifier** ← |

> **The SLOUGHING in the last row is why a trickling filter MUST be followed by a secondary settling tank: the sloughed film is the process's sludge, and without settlement it would leave in the effluent.**

> **Option (a) is the natural misreading of the name, and option (d) describes the sedimentation tank that accompanies the filter rather than the filter itself.**

**ATTACHED GROWTH against SUSPENDED GROWTH — the fundamental division in biological treatment:**

| | ATTACHED growth (fixed film) | SUSPENDED growth |
|---|---|---|
| **Where the organisms live** | **On a fixed MEDIA surface** ← | **Freely suspended in the mixed liquor** ← |
| **Examples** | **Trickling filter, rotating biological contactor, submerged aerated filter** | **ACTIVATED SLUDGE, oxidation ditch, SBR** |
| **Sludge return** | **NOT required — the biomass stays put** ← | **ESSENTIAL — the biomass must be recycled** ← |
| **Power** | **LOW — gravity flow and natural draught** ← | **HIGH — continuous aeration** ← |
| **Operational skill** | **LOW — very tolerant** ← | **HIGHER — MLSS, F/M and sludge age must be managed** ← |
| **Shock loads and toxicity** | **TOLERANT — the film survives** ← | **SENSITIVE — the biomass can be killed** ← |
| **Effluent quality** | **Moderate; BOD removal 80-90 %** | **BETTER; 90-95 %** ← |
| **Land required** | Moderate | Less |
| **Problems** | **Ponding, odour, FILTER FLIES (Psychoda)** ← | **BULKING, foaming** ← |

> **THE THIRD, FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER MAKE THE CASE FOR TRICKLING FILTERS IN NEPALI CONDITIONS: no sludge recirculation to manage, little or no power, and great tolerance of neglect.**

> **An activated sludge plant that loses its power supply for a day may lose its biomass entirely and take weeks to recover; a trickling filter that loses power simply stops receiving sewage and its film survives.**

> **For a small town with intermittent electricity and no full-time process operator, that robustness is worth more than the better effluent an activated sludge plant would produce when it was working.**

**The operating problems named above:**

| Problem | Cause and remedy |
|---|---|
| **PONDING — the surface floods and the flow short-circuits** | **The voids clog with excessive film or fine media. Remedies: flooding and dosing the bed, increasing the hydraulic load, RECIRCULATION, or replacing the media** ← |
| **ODOUR** | **Anaerobic conditions from overloading or poor ventilation** ← |
| **FILTER FLIES (Psychoda)** | **Breed in the film; a nuisance to neighbours. Controlled by flooding the bed periodically or by continuous dosing** ← |
| **Freezing in cold weather** | Reduced efficiency at altitude |

> **RECIRCULATION appears as the remedy for several of these, and it is the process's principal control variable:**

| Benefit of recirculating effluent back over the filter | Note |
|---|---|
| **Dilutes a strong influent** | Protects the film |
| **Maintains a CONTINUOUS wetting and hydraulic load** | **Prevents the film drying out during low-flow periods, and prevents ponding and flies** ← |
| **Seeds the incoming sewage with organisms** | Improves performance |
| **Improves BOD removal** | For the same media volume |

> **The RECIRCULATION RATIO (recirculated flow ÷ raw flow) is typically 0.5 to 3 for a high-rate filter, and it is what distinguishes a high-rate filter from a standard-rate one as much as the loading does.**

**And the place of the trickling filter in the treatment train:**

> **Screening → grit removal → PRIMARY sedimentation → TRICKLING FILTER → SECONDARY sedimentation → disinfection → discharge**

> **With the sludges from both clarifiers going to a digester or drying beds.**

| Unit | BOD removal |
|---|---|
| **Primary sedimentation** | **30 to 35 per cent** ← |
| **Trickling filter plus secondary settling** | **A further 80 to 90 per cent of what remains** ← |
| **Overall** | **85 to 90 per cent** ← |

> **The PRIMARY tank is essential ahead of a trickling filter, and not merely helpful: settleable solids reaching the media would clog the voids and cause immediate ponding.**

> **So the sequence is not arbitrary — each unit protects the one after it, which is the organising principle of every treatment train and the reason the order must not be rearranged for convenience.**

examTip.trick: **A trickling filter does NOT filter** — the media are 25-75 mm with huge voids. Treatment is by the BIOLOGICAL FILM on their surface, aerobic outside and anaerobic within, which SLOUGHS off and is caught by the secondary clarifier.
examTip.trap: **ATTACHED growth needs NO sludge return** (the biomass stays put) and tolerates shock loads and power cuts; SUSPENDED growth (activated sludge) gives better effluent but needs constant aeration and skilled control.
examTip.mnemonic: **RECIRCULATION is the main control** — it dilutes strong influent, keeps the film wet, and prevents PONDING and filter flies. And a PRIMARY tank is essential first: settleable solids would clog the media at once.

questions.stem: The gas produced by the ANAEROBIC DIGESTION of sewage sludge consists mainly of:
options: Hydrogen and nitrogen
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide only
Methane (about 65 %) and carbon dioxide (about 35 %)
Oxygen and nitrogen, as in air
questions.solution:
**METHANE, about 60 to 70 per cent, and CARBON DIOXIDE, about 30 to 40 per cent**, with traces of hydrogen sulphide, nitrogen and water vapour.

**The composition and its value:**

| Component | Proportion | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **METHANE, CH₄** | **60 to 70 %** ← | **The fuel — calorific value about 35.8 MJ/m³ pure** |
| **CARBON DIOXIDE, CO₂** | **30 to 40 %** ← | **Inert; dilutes the gas** |
| **Hydrogen sulphide, H₂S** | **0 to 1 %** | **CORROSIVE and toxic; must be scrubbed before use in an engine** ← |
| **Nitrogen, hydrogen, water vapour** | Traces | — |
| **CALORIFIC VALUE of the mixture** | **20 to 25 MJ/m³** ← | **About two thirds that of natural gas** |
| **Gas yield** | **About 0.9 to 1.1 m³ per kg of volatile solids destroyed** ← | — |

> **Option (b) omits the methane, which is the whole point of the process, and options (a) and (d) name gases that are not significant products.**

**The four stages of anaerobic digestion:**

| Stage | Process | Organisms |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — HYDROLYSIS** | **Complex solids (fats, proteins, carbohydrates) broken into soluble molecules** ← | Hydrolytic bacteria |
| **2 — ACIDOGENESIS** | **Converted to VOLATILE FATTY ACIDS, alcohols, CO₂ and H₂** ← | Acid-forming bacteria |
| **3 — ACETOGENESIS** | **Converted to acetic acid, CO₂ and hydrogen** | Acetogens |
| **4 — METHANOGENESIS** | **Acetate and hydrogen converted to METHANE** ← | **METHANOGENS — slow-growing and highly sensitive** ← |

> **THE IMBALANCE BETWEEN STAGES 2 AND 4 IS WHERE DIGESTERS FAIL, and it is worth understanding:**

> **The acid-forming bacteria are ROBUST and FAST-GROWING; the methanogens are DELICATE and SLOW-GROWING.**

> **If the digester is overloaded, shocked by a temperature change, or receives a toxic input, the acid formers continue while the methanogens falter.**

> **VOLATILE FATTY ACIDS then ACCUMULATE, the pH FALLS, and the falling pH inhibits the methanogens further — a self-worsening spiral known as SOURING or acid stress.**

| Indicator | Healthy digester | Souring |
|---|---|---|
| **pH** | **6.8 to 7.4** ← | **Falling below 6.5** ← |
| **Volatile fatty acids** | **Below 250 mg/L** | **Rising sharply** ← |
| **VFA / alkalinity ratio** | **Below 0.3** ← | **Above 0.4 — the earliest warning** ← |
| **Gas methane content** | 60-70 % | **Falling; CO₂ rising** ← |

> **The VFA/ALKALINITY RATIO in the third row is the parameter operators actually watch, because it changes BEFORE the pH does — the alkalinity buffers the acids until it is exhausted, and by the time the pH falls the digester is already in trouble.**

> **The remedy is to reduce the feed, add alkalinity (lime or sodium bicarbonate), and allow the methanogens to recover — which takes weeks, since they grow so slowly.**

**The operating conditions:**

| Parameter | MESOPHILIC | THERMOPHILIC |
|---|---|---|
| **Temperature** | **30 to 38 °C, usually 35** ← | **50 to 57 °C** ← |
| **Detention time** | **20 to 30 days** ← | **12 to 15 days** ← |
| **Gas production** | Good | Higher |
| **PATHOGEN destruction** | Partial | **Much better — the sludge can be used on crops** ← |
| **Stability** | **More stable and forgiving** ← | **Sensitive to temperature change** ← |
| **Energy to heat** | Less | More |

> **MESOPHILIC digestion is the usual choice because it is forgiving, and the digester is heated using its OWN gas — which is the elegance of the process: it produces more energy than it consumes.**

**The benefits of digestion, which justify the plant:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **VOLUME reduction** | **Volatile solids reduced by 45-60 %, so far less sludge to dispose of** ← |
| **STABILISATION** | **The sludge no longer putrefies or smells** ← |
| **PATHOGEN reduction** | Substantial, especially thermophilic |
| **BIOGAS as a fuel** | **Often enough to heat the digester AND generate surplus power** ← |
| **Improved DEWATERING** | The digested sludge drains and filters better |
| **A usable soil conditioner** | Where the metal content permits |

> **AND THE SAME PROCESS AT DOMESTIC SCALE IS THE NEPALI BIOGAS PLANT, which is worth noting as a direct application of this chemistry:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Feedstock** | **Cattle dung, and often a latrine connection** ← |
| **Type** | **Fixed-dome (GGC model) buried masonry digester** ← |
| **Output** | **Gas for cooking and lighting, plus a high-quality SLURRY fertiliser** ← |
| **Scale of the programme** | **Hundreds of thousands of household plants installed in Nepal** ← |
| **Benefits beyond energy** | **Reduced firewood collection and deforestation; less indoor smoke and the respiratory illness it causes; sanitation; fertiliser** ← |

> **The INDOOR SMOKE benefit deserves its mention: cooking on an open wood fire inside an unventilated house is a major cause of respiratory disease among women and children in rural Nepal, and replacing it with a clean gas flame is a substantial health gain quite separate from the energy or the sanitation.**

> **It is a good illustration of an engineering intervention whose most valuable outcome is not the one it was designed for.**

examTip.trick: **About 65 % METHANE and 35 % CO₂, calorific value 20-25 MJ/m³** — roughly two thirds that of natural gas. Traces of H₂S must be scrubbed before use in an engine.
examTip.trap: **Digesters fail because ACID FORMERS are robust and METHANOGENS are delicate** — VFAs accumulate, pH falls, and the fall inhibits the methanogens further. Watch the VFA/ALKALINITY ratio: it moves before the pH does.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mesophilic 35 °C for 20-30 days is the forgiving standard; thermophilic 55 °C for 12-15 days destroys pathogens better but is sensitive.** The digester heats itself with its own gas — and the same chemistry is Nepal's household biogas plant.

questions.stem: In disaster risk management, RISK is conventionally expressed as a function of:
options: The magnitude of the hazard alone
The number of people living in the area alone
The cost of the infrastructure at stake alone
Hazard and vulnerability together, moderated by the capacity to cope
questions.solution:
**HAZARD and VULNERABILITY together, moderated by CAPACITY** — commonly written as:

> **RISK = (HAZARD × VULNERABILITY) / CAPACITY**

**What each term means:**

| Term | Definition | Can engineering change it? |
|---|---|---|
| **HAZARD** | **The potentially damaging natural or human-made event — an earthquake, a flood, a landslide** ← | **NO for natural hazards; the earthquake will happen** ← |
| **EXPOSURE** | **The people, property and systems located where the hazard occurs** | **YES — through LAND USE PLANNING** ← |
| **VULNERABILITY** | **The susceptibility to damage of what is exposed — weak buildings, poor drainage, fragile livelihoods** ← | **YES — this is where engineering acts most powerfully** ← |
| **CAPACITY** | **The resources and abilities available to cope: preparedness, early warning, emergency services, resilient institutions** ← | **YES — through planning and institutions** ← |

> **THE MOST IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE OF THIS EXPRESSION IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISSED: THE HAZARD CANNOT BE REDUCED, BUT THE RISK CAN.**

> **An engineer cannot prevent an earthquake. An engineer can make the buildings withstand it — which reduces vulnerability, and therefore reduces risk, without touching the hazard at all.**

> **That is why the phrase "natural disaster" is regarded as misleading: the HAZARD is natural, but the DISASTER is largely the product of how we have built and where.**

| Same hazard, different vulnerability | Outcome |
|---|---|
| **A magnitude 7 earthquake beneath a well-built, well-planned city** | **Damage, disruption, few deaths** ← |
| **The same earthquake beneath a city of unreinforced masonry on soft soil** | **Tens of thousands of deaths** ← |

> **The hazard is identical; the disaster is not — and the difference is entirely vulnerability and capacity, both of which are within human control.**

**The disaster management CYCLE, and where engineering contributes:**

| Phase | Activities | Engineering role |
|---|---|---|
| **MITIGATION (prevention)** | **Reducing vulnerability BEFORE the event: building codes, land use zoning, retrofitting, flood defences, slope stabilisation** ← | **THE LARGEST role, and the most cost-effective** ← |
| **PREPAREDNESS** | **Early warning systems, evacuation planning, drills, stockpiles, emergency plans** ← | Warning systems, safe shelters, escape routes |
| **RESPONSE** | **Search and rescue, relief, emergency medical care, temporary shelter** | Damage assessment, temporary works, restoring lifelines |
| **RECOVERY / RECONSTRUCTION** | **Rebuilding — ideally BUILD BACK BETTER, not merely as before** ← | Design and supervision of reconstruction |

> **THE COST-EFFECTIVENESS OF MITIGATION IS THE ARGUMENT THAT MATTERS FOR POLICY, and it is well supported: studies repeatedly find that each unit spent on mitigation saves something of the order of four to seven units in response and recovery.**

> **Yet mitigation attracts far less funding, because its benefit is INVISIBLE — a disaster that does not happen generates no photographs, no headlines and no political credit.**

> **Response, by contrast, is highly visible. So the incentives point away from the most effective action, which is a genuine structural problem in disaster policy rather than a failure of understanding.**

**The hazards Nepal faces, since the syllabus is Nepal-specific:**

| Hazard | Note |
|---|---|
| **EARTHQUAKE** | **The whole country is at high risk; the Main Himalayan Thrust accumulates strain continuously** ← |
| **LANDSLIDE** | **Monsoon-triggered; the most frequent cause of death in most years, and worsened by road construction and spoil disposal** ← |
| **FLOOD** | **Terai river floods, and flash floods in the hills** ← |
| **GLOF — glacial lake outburst flood** | **A moraine-dammed lake bursts and releases a catastrophic flood down a valley; the risk is rising as glaciers retreat** ← |
| **Fire** | Dense settlements with timber construction |
| **Drought, hailstorm, epidemic, avalanche** | — |

> **THE GLOF HAZARD IN THE FOURTH ROW IS DISTINCTIVELY HIMALAYAN AND IS WORTH A NOTE, because it connects climate change directly to engineering practice:**

> **Retreating glaciers leave meltwater lakes dammed by unconsolidated moraine. The moraine is weak, and it can fail — from an ice avalanche into the lake, from seepage, or from an earthquake.**

> **The resulting flood is far larger than any rainfall flood, arrives with little warning, and carries enormous quantities of debris down a valley.**

> **For hydropower schemes, roads and settlements downstream of such lakes, the GLOF is a design case that a conventional flood frequency analysis will never reveal — because it is not a rainfall event and does not appear in the gauged record at all.**

> **The engineering responses are to identify and monitor the dangerous lakes, to LOWER them artificially by controlled channels (as has been done at Tsho Rolpa), to site infrastructure above the credible GLOF level, and to install early warning.**

> **It is a good closing illustration of the risk equation: the hazard is growing and cannot be prevented, so the entire response must be through reduced exposure, reduced vulnerability and increased capacity.**

examTip.trick: **RISK = (HAZARD × VULNERABILITY) / CAPACITY.** Each distractor names one element alone — hazard, exposure or value at stake — and risk requires all of them together.
examTip.trap: **The HAZARD cannot be reduced; the RISK can.** An engineer cannot prevent an earthquake but can remove the vulnerability — which is why "natural disaster" is misleading: the hazard is natural, the disaster largely built.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mitigation → preparedness → response → recovery, and MITIGATION returns 4-7× its cost** — but attracts least funding because an averted disaster is invisible. In Nepal, note GLOF: a hazard no flood-frequency analysis will ever reveal.

questions.stem: The CONSUMPTIVE USE of a crop is:
options: The total water transpired by the plants plus that evaporated from the adjacent soil surface
The total water delivered at the head of the watercourse
The water lost by seepage from the canal system
The depth of water applied at each watering
questions.solution:
**The water TRANSPIRED by the plants plus that EVAPORATED from the adjacent soil, together with the small amount retained in the plant tissue** — that is, EVAPOTRANSPIRATION plus tissue water.

**The components:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **TRANSPIRATION** | **Water drawn up by the roots and released through the leaf stomata — the larger part** ← |
| **EVAPORATION from the soil surface** | **Significant early in the season when the crop canopy is sparse; small once the ground is shaded** ← |
| **Water retained in the plant TISSUE** | **Under 1 per cent of the total — usually neglected** ← |

> **Because the tissue fraction is negligible, CONSUMPTIVE USE and EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (ET) are used interchangeably in practice.**

> **The distinguishing feature is that consumptive use is water that LEAVES THE SYSTEM as vapour and cannot be recovered — unlike seepage or deep percolation, which return to the groundwater and may be pumped again.**

> **That is why it is the irreducible core of irrigation demand: every other loss can in principle be reduced, and this one cannot.**

**How it is estimated:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **BLANEY-CRIDDLE** | **TEMPERATURE and daylight hours only — the simplest, and widely used where data are scarce** ← |
| **PENMAN, and PENMAN-MONTEITH** | **A COMBINATION of the energy balance and an aerodynamic term; needs temperature, humidity, wind and radiation — the FAO standard** ← |
| **HARGREAVES** | Temperature and extraterrestrial radiation |
| **THORNTHWAITE** | Temperature; suits humid climates |
| **LYSIMETER** | **DIRECT measurement — a tank of soil with a crop, weighed or with its drainage measured; the reference against which the formulae are calibrated** ← |
| **Pan evaporation** | **Measured pan evaporation × a pan coefficient** ← |

> **BLANEY-CRIDDLE in metric form: U = k × f, where f = p (0.46 t + 8.13)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **U** | Consumptive use for the period, in mm |
| **k** | **The CROP COEFFICIENT — different for each crop and each growth stage** ← |
| **p** | Monthly percentage of the annual daytime hours |
| **t** | Mean monthly temperature in °C |

> **THE CROP COEFFICIENT k IS THE PRACTICAL HEART OF THE CALCULATION, and its variation through the season is the point most often overlooked:**

| Growth stage | Typical k |
|---|---|
| **INITIAL (bare soil, seedlings)** | **0.3 to 0.5 — LOW, since there is little leaf area** ← |
| **DEVELOPMENT** | Rising |
| **MID-SEASON (full canopy)** | **1.0 to 1.2 — the PEAK demand** ← |
| **LATE season (ripening, senescence)** | **0.6 to 0.9 — falling** ← |

> **So the crop's water demand is NOT uniform through its base period: it peaks at mid-season, when the canopy is complete and the plant is growing fastest.**

> **A canal system designed on the average demand will therefore be short of water at exactly the moment the crop is most sensitive — which is why the PEAK consumptive use, not the mean, sets the canal's capacity.**

> **And missing an irrigation at the CRITICAL growth stage (flowering and grain formation for most cereals) costs far more yield than missing one at any other time, which is the basis of DEFICIT IRRIGATION: where water is short, apply it at the critical stages and accept stress at the others.**

**The SOIL MOISTURE terms that determine how the water is stored and used:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **SATURATION** | All voids full of water |
| **FIELD CAPACITY (FC)** | **The moisture retained after gravity drainage has ceased — 2-3 days after wetting** ← |
| **PERMANENT WILTING POINT (PWP)** | **The moisture at which a plant wilts and cannot recover** ← |
| **AVAILABLE moisture** | **FC − PWP — the water the plant can actually use** ← |
| **READILY AVAILABLE moisture** | **Commonly 50 to 60 per cent of the available, before the plant suffers stress** ← |
| **Hygroscopic water** | Held too tightly to be extracted at all |

> **The available moisture depends strongly on soil texture, and the result is not what intuition suggests:**

| Soil | Field capacity | Wilting point | AVAILABLE moisture |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SAND** | **10 %** | **4 %** | **6 % — LOW** ← |
| **LOAM** | **25 %** | **10 %** | **15 % — the HIGHEST** ← |
| **CLAY** | **40 %** | **22 %** | **18 %, but much is held tightly** ← |

> **A LOAM holds the most readily usable water, which is why loams are the best agricultural soils — a sand drains too fast to store anything, and a clay holds a great deal that the plant cannot extract.**

> **So the frequency of irrigation follows from the soil as much as from the crop: a sandy soil must be irrigated LITTLE and OFTEN, and a loam or clay LARGER amounts LESS frequently.**

Together with the small quantity retained in the plant tissue.

examTip.trick: **Transpiration + evaporation from the soil + tissue water (under 1 %, so ET and consumptive use are used interchangeably).** It is the water that LEAVES as vapour and cannot be recovered — unlike seepage, which returns to groundwater.
examTip.trap: **The crop coefficient k VARIES through the season** — 0.3-0.5 initially, 1.0-1.2 at mid-season, falling late. So PEAK consumptive use, not the mean, sets the canal capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Available moisture = FC − PWP, and a LOAM holds the most usable water** (15 %, against sand's 6 %). Hence sandy soils need LITTLE and OFTEN. Blaney-Criddle needs only temperature; Penman-Monteith is the FAO standard.

questions.stem: A soil has a field capacity of 22 per cent and a permanent wilting point of 10 per cent, a dry unit weight of 15 kN/m³ and a root zone depth of 1.0 m. If irrigation is applied when 50 per cent of the available moisture has been used, and the consumptive use is 5 mm/day, the frequency of irrigation is about:
options: 9 days
12 days
18 days
37 days
questions.solution:
**About 18 days.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Available moisture, by weight** | **FC − PWP = 22 − 10** | **12 %** ← |
| **Apparent specific gravity of the soil** | **γ_d/γ_w = 15/9.81** | **1.529** ← |
| **Depth of AVAILABLE water in the root zone** | **1.529 × 1,000 mm × 0.12** | **183.5 mm** ← |
| **READILY available (50 % depletion permitted)** | **0.50 × 183.5** | **91.7 mm** ← |
| **Frequency** | **91.7 / 5** | **18.3 ≈ 18 days** ← |

**The general relation:**

> **Frequency = p × (γ_d/γ_w) × d × (FC − PWP) / (consumptive use rate)**

| Term | Note |
|---|---|
| **γ_d/γ_w** | **The soil's APPARENT SPECIFIC GRAVITY — typically 1.4 to 1.7** ← |
| **d** | **The ROOT ZONE depth — the depth the crop can actually draw from** ← |
| **(FC − PWP)** | **Available moisture as a fraction BY WEIGHT** ← |
| **p** | **The depletion permitted before stress — commonly 0.5** ← |

> **The γ_d/γ_w factor is essential and is the term most often dropped: the moisture contents are expressed by WEIGHT of dry soil, and converting them to a DEPTH of water requires the soil's density relative to water.**

**Each distractor is a named wrong step:**

| Option | The error behind it |
|---|---|
| **9 days** | **Depletion taken as 25 per cent instead of 50** ← |
| **12 days** | **The γ_d/γ_w conversion OMITTED: 0.12 × 1,000 × 0.5 / 5** ← |
| **37 days** | **The 50 per cent depletion factor omitted — the FULL available moisture used** ← |

> **The 12-day distractor is the one to watch, because omitting the density conversion is the commonest slip in this calculation and the answer it gives looks entirely reasonable.**

**How the ROOT ZONE DEPTH is chosen, since it drives the answer:**

| Crop | Effective root zone depth |
|---|---|
| **Rice (shallow-rooted, ponded)** | **0.3 to 0.5 m** ← |
| **Wheat, barley** | **1.0 to 1.5 m** ← |
| **Maize** | 1.0 to 1.7 m |
| **Sugarcane** | **1.2 to 2.0 m** |
| **Vegetables** | 0.3 to 0.6 m |
| **Orchards and deep-rooted trees** | **2.0 m and more** ← |

> **The root zone depth GROWS as the crop develops, so early in the season the plant can draw on only a shallow layer and must be irrigated more frequently even though its consumptive use is low.**

> **That is the practical reason young crops need light, frequent watering — not because they use more water, but because they can REACH less of it.**

**And the consequences of getting the interval wrong:**

| Interval | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **TOO FREQUENT (small applications)** | **High labour and distribution cost; more evaporation from the wetted surface; waterlogging risk** ← |
| **TOO INFREQUENT (large applications)** | **Moisture stress before the next watering; DEEP PERCOLATION beyond the root zone; possible runoff** ← |
| **The optimum** | **Apply the readily available moisture depth, at the interval that depth supports** ← |

> **THE DEEP PERCOLATION POINT WASTES MOST WATER IN PRACTICE: applying more than the root zone can hold sends the surplus below the roots, where the crop cannot reach it.**

> **It is not entirely lost — it recharges the groundwater and supplies the LEACHING FRACTION that carries salts away — but it is unavailable to the crop, and where the water table is already high it feeds waterlogging directly.**

> **So the depth applied at each irrigation should be matched to the root zone's capacity, which is exactly the quantity computed above, and that is why this calculation underlies any irrigation schedule.**

examTip.trick: **Frequency = p (γ_d/γ_w) d (FC − PWP) ÷ consumptive use** = (0.5)(1.529)(1000)(0.12)/5 = **18.3 days**.
examTip.trap: **The γ_d/γ_w conversion is the term most often dropped** — moisture contents are by WEIGHT of dry soil, so converting to a DEPTH of water needs the soil's density. Omitting it gives 12 days instead of 18.
examTip.mnemonic: **The root zone GROWS through the season**, so young crops need light frequent watering — they can REACH less, not use more. And applying more than the root zone holds is lost to deep percolation.

questions.stem: An INUNDATION canal differs from a PERENNIAL canal in that an inundation canal:
options: Takes off directly from a river without any weir or headworks, and flows only when the river is in high stage
Is always lined with concrete
Carries water throughout the year from a storage reservoir
Is used only for navigation
questions.solution:
**It takes off DIRECTLY from a river with NO weir or headworks, and therefore flows only when the river stage is high enough** — that is, during the monsoon.

**The classification of canals by their source of supply:**

| Type | Source | Availability |
|---|---|---|
| **INUNDATION canal** | **Direct offtake from a river, NO diversion structure** ← | **Only when the river is in flood — the monsoon months** ← |
| **PERENNIAL canal** | **From a permanent source through a WEIR or BARRAGE (a diversion headworks)** ← | **Throughout the year, so far as the river allows** ← |
| **Canal from a STORAGE reservoir** | **A dam with seasonal regulation** ← (option c) | **Year-round, including the dry season** |

> **Option (c) describes the storage-fed canal, which is a further category — so the option set distinguishes three real arrangements.**

**The characteristics of an inundation canal:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cost** | **VERY LOW — there is no headworks to build, which is the largest single cost of a diversion scheme** ← |
| **Reliability** | **POOR — it runs only when the river happens to be high, which may not coincide with the crop's need** ← |
| **Control of discharge** | **NONE — the canal takes whatever the river's stage delivers** ← |
| **SILTING** | **SEVERE — it draws from the river at its most sediment-laden stage, and has no undersluices or excluder** ← |
| **Maintenance** | **Heavy annual desilting of the head reach** ← |
| **Command** | **Limited — the water level cannot be raised, so only low-lying land can be commanded** ← |
| **Where still found** | **Older systems in the Indus and Gangetic plains; largely superseded** ← |

> **THE SILTING PROBLEM IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL DIFFICULTY, and its cause is worth naming: the canal draws during the flood, which is precisely when the river carries its heaviest sediment load, and it has none of the silt-control devices that a headworks provides.**

> **So the head reach silts every season and must be excavated afresh — a recurring cost that eventually exceeds what a proper headworks would have cost to build.**

> **That is the general case against the inundation canal: it is cheap to construct and expensive to keep, and its supply arrives when the river chooses rather than when the crop needs it.**

**The classification of canals by FUNCTION, which is the other axis:**

| Canal | Function |
|---|---|
| **MAIN canal** | **Takes off from the headworks; carries the full supply; NO direct irrigation from it** ← |
| **BRANCH canal** | **Carries more than about 5 cumecs; feeds distributaries; usually no direct irrigation** |
| **MAJOR DISTRIBUTARY** | **0.25 to 5 cumecs; feeds minors and watercourses** |
| **MINOR distributary** | **Below 0.25 cumecs; feeds watercourses directly** |
| **WATERCOURSE (field channel)** | **Built and maintained by the FARMERS, not the department** ← |

> **The boundary in the last row is administratively important and is where many systems fail: the department's responsibility usually ends at the OUTLET, and everything below it belongs to the water users.**

> **A well-built main system delivering into unlined, poorly maintained watercourses loses a large share of its water in the last few hundred metres — so the field-level channels, which receive the least engineering attention, often account for the greatest losses.**

**And the classification by ALIGNMENT, which governs the layout:**

| Canal | Alignment | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| **RIDGE (watershed) canal** | **Along the ridge line separating two drainages** ← | **Commands land on BOTH sides; NO cross-drainage works needed, since no drainage crosses a ridge** ← |
| **CONTOUR canal** | **Along a contour, at a slight slope** ← | **Commands land on ONE side only; CROSSES every drainage, so many cross-drainage works** ← |
| **SIDE SLOPE canal** | **Along the natural slope, at right angles to the contours** ← | **NO cross-drainage works, and NO irrigation possible from it — it is a carrier** ← |

> **THE RIDGE CANAL IS THE IDEAL AND IS ALWAYS PREFERRED WHERE THE TOPOGRAPHY ALLOWS, for the two reasons in its row: it irrigates both sides and needs no aqueducts or syphons.**

> **A contour canal is the usual necessity in hilly country, where no suitable ridge runs in the right direction — and every stream it crosses demands a structure, which is why cross-drainage works dominate the cost of hill irrigation schemes.**

> **The SIDE SLOPE canal's odd combination — no cross-drainage works but no irrigation either — follows from its alignment: running down the slope, it is always the highest point locally in the transverse direction, so nothing crosses it, and it is also always falling steeply, so it is used to carry water down to a lower system rather than to distribute it.**

examTip.trick: **No headworks at all — it flows only when the river stage is high.** Option (c) is the storage-fed canal, a third category.
examTip.trap: **Its fatal defect is SILTING** — it draws during the flood, when the river is most sediment-laden, with no undersluices or excluder. Cheap to build, expensive to keep.
examTip.mnemonic: **RIDGE canal: irrigates BOTH sides, NO cross-drainage works — always preferred. CONTOUR canal: ONE side, crosses every drainage. SIDE SLOPE: no cross-drainage works and no irrigation either.**

questions.stem: A BERM in a canal section is:
options: The vertical distance between the full supply level and the top of the bank
The slope of the canal's side
A horizontal strip left between the top edge of the cutting and the toe of the embankment (bank)
The depth of water at full supply
questions.solution:
**A horizontal STRIP left between the top edge of the excavated cutting and the toe of the bank (embankment).**

**What a berm is for:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevents the BANK's weight bearing directly on the cutting's edge** | **Which would cause the cutting slope to slip** ← |
| **Catches material from any SLIP of the bank** | **So it does not fall into the canal** ← |
| **Absorbs the canal's own EROSION over time** | **The section widens into the berm rather than into the bank** ← |
| **Provides a maintenance PATH** | **Access for inspection and desilting** ← |
| **Adds to the seepage path** | **Lengthening the route from the canal to the outside of the bank** ← |
| **Gives room for the bank to be RAISED later** | If the canal is remodelled |

> **Option (a) defines the FREEBOARD, which makes it the designed distractor — both are dimensions of the same cross-section and are routinely confused.**

**The elements of a canal cross-section, set out together:**

| Element | Definition | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **Bed width, B** | The width of the canal's floor | From the design |
| **Full supply depth, D** | **The depth at full supply level (FSL)** ← (option d) | From the design |
| **SIDE SLOPE** | **The slope of the cut or bank, expressed as m horizontal to 1 vertical** ← (option b) | **1:1 to 1.5:1 in cutting; 1.5:1 to 2:1 in filling** |
| **FREEBOARD** | **FSL to the top of the bank** ← | **0.3 m for small canals; 0.75 to 1.0 m for large** ← |
| **BERM** | **The horizontal strip between cutting and bank** ← | **Typically equal to the depth, or 1 to 3 m** |
| **Bank (dowla) top width** | For a service road or a footpath | 1.5 to 8 m |
| **Spoil bank / borrow pit** | Surplus excavation, or material taken for the bank | Set back from the canal |

**FREEBOARD, since it is the distractor and a real design quantity:**

| Canal discharge | Freeboard |
|---|---|
| **Below 0.75 cumec** | **0.30 m** ← |
| **0.75 to 1.5 cumec** | **0.45 m** |
| **1.5 to 85 cumec** | **0.60 m** |
| **Above 85 cumec** | **0.75 to 1.0 m** ← |

> **The freeboard guards against wave action, against a temporary surcharge when a downstream gate is closed, against settlement of the bank, and against the accumulation of silt that reduces the section.**

> **A canal running with inadequate freeboard will BREACH, and a breach in a large canal is a serious event — it empties the canal, floods the land below, interrupts the supply to everything downstream for weeks, and the repair must be made in flowing conditions.**

**The BALANCING DEPTH, which determines the economical section:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **A canal partly in cutting and partly in filling** | **The excavated material is used to build the banks** ← |
| **BALANCING DEPTH** | **The depth of cutting at which the excavated volume exactly equals the volume needed for the banks** ← |
| **Why it is the economical depth** | **No material need be imported, and none carted away** ← |
| **Shallower than balancing depth** | **Borrow material must be brought in for the banks** ← |
| **Deeper than balancing depth** | **Surplus spoil must be disposed of** ← |

> **The balancing depth is therefore the point at which HAULAGE — the most expensive part of any earthwork — is minimised, and the canal's bed level is chosen accordingly wherever the command permits.**

> **It is the same reasoning as the mass haul diagram in road construction: move earth the shortest distance possible, and balance cut against fill locally.**

**And the SEEPAGE path point in the first table, which links to canal lining:**

> **Water seeping from an unlined canal travels through the bed and banks, and the berm lengthens the shortest path from the water surface to the outer toe of the bank.**

| Consequence of a short seepage path | Note |
|---|---|
| **High seepage LOSS** | The water is gone |
| **Saturation of the bank, reducing its stability** | **A saturated bank can slump** ← |
| **PIPING through the bank** | **The same runaway mechanism as beneath a weir — and it destroys canal banks in exactly the same way** ← |
| **Waterlogging of the land immediately outside** | ← |

> **The PIPING row deserves the emphasis: a canal bank is a small earth dam, permanently retaining water, and it fails by the same mechanisms — overtopping, slope instability, and internal erosion.**

> **Rat and crab burrows through canal banks are a well-documented cause of breaches in the subcontinent, because a burrow provides a ready-made pipe through the bank and the flow enlarges it rapidly once it begins.**

> **Regular inspection of banks for burrows, seepage and wet patches on the outer slope is therefore a routine maintenance duty rather than an optional refinement, and a wet patch appearing on the outside of a bank is an emergency rather than a nuisance.**

examTip.trick: **A BERM is the horizontal strip between the cutting's top edge and the bank's toe.** Option (a) is the FREEBOARD, option (b) the side slope, option (d) the full supply depth — all dimensions of the same section.
examTip.trap: **Freeboard: 0.30 m below 0.75 cumec, rising to 0.75-1.0 m above 85 cumec.** Inadequate freeboard leads to a BREACH, which empties the canal and floods the land below.
examTip.mnemonic: **BALANCING DEPTH is where the cutting exactly supplies the banks** — no borrow, no spoil, minimum haulage. And a canal bank is a small EARTH DAM: it fails by overtopping, slumping and PIPING, and burrows through it are a real cause of breaches.

questions.stem: The AFFLUX caused by a weir or barrage across a river is:
options: The scour depth below the structure's floor
The rise in the maximum flood level upstream of the structure, caused by the obstruction
The head loss through the undersluices
The difference between the pond level and the canal's full supply level
questions.solution:
**The RISE in the maximum flood level UPSTREAM of the structure**, caused by the obstruction the structure presents to the flood flow.

**Why afflux matters — its consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The flood level rises over a LONG REACH upstream** | **The backwater curve extends for kilometres in a flat river** ← |
| **Land and villages are SUBMERGED that were not before** | ← |
| **MARGINAL BUNDS must be built to contain the raised flood** ← | **A substantial cost, and they must extend far upstream** |
| **The structure's own design is affected** | **A greater head difference means a longer creep path and a deeper cut-off** ← |
| **Increased upstream SILTING** | **The backwater slows the flow, so sediment deposits** ← |
| **The waterway can be reduced if more afflux is accepted** | **A shorter, cheaper structure — the trade** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS THE DESIGN DECISION: afflux and waterway width are traded against one another.**

| Choice | Effect |
|---|---|
| **A WIDE waterway** | **Low afflux; less land submerged and shorter bunds — but a longer, more expensive structure** ← |
| **A NARROW waterway** | **A cheaper structure — but greater afflux, more submergence, longer marginal bunds and higher velocities requiring more scour protection** ← |

> **So the economical waterway is found by balancing the structure's cost against the cost of the afflux it creates, and the permissible afflux is usually fixed by what land can acceptably be submerged.**

> **Typical design afflux for a barrage on an alluvial river is around 1 m, and for a bridge rather less.**

**LACEY'S regime perimeter, which usually fixes the waterway:**

> **P = 4.75 √Q**

> **A river in regime adopts this wetted perimeter naturally, so a structure providing that width causes minimal disturbance — the flow neither contracts nor expands appreciably.**

| Waterway provided | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Equal to Lacey's P** | **The river passes through in regime; minimal afflux and minimal scour** ← |
| **LESS than Lacey's P (constricted)** | **Higher velocities, DEEPER SCOUR, and greater afflux** ← |
| **MORE than Lacey's P** | **Silting within the structure; the river forms its own channel and abandons part of the waterway** ← |

> **The last row is worth noting because it is counter-intuitive: an OVER-WIDE waterway is not simply wasteful, it is harmful.**

> **The river will not spread to fill it; it will meander within it, silting the unused portion and attacking one flank — which is precisely why guide bunds are needed to hold the flow in the centre of the waterway.**

**Where afflux enters the structure's own design — the connection to seepage:**

| Quantity | Note |
|---|---|
| **The SEEPAGE HEAD** | **The difference between the upstream and downstream water levels** ← |
| **Under pond conditions (no flood)** | **Pond level minus downstream bed level — usually the maximum static head** ← |
| **Under high flood** | **Roughly equal to the AFFLUX, since both sides are high** ← |
| **The design creep length L = C × H** | **Uses the WORST of these heads** ← |

> **So afflux is not merely an environmental and land-acquisition matter — it enters directly into Bligh's and Khosla's calculations and thus into the length of the impervious floor and the depth of the cut-offs.**

> **A designer who chooses a narrower waterway to save on the structure's width therefore pays for it partly in a longer floor and deeper piles, which offsets some of the saving.**

**The TYPES OF WEIR, since the structure's form follows from its foundation:**

| Type | Description | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **VERTICAL DROP weir** | **A masonry or concrete body wall with a vertical downstream face, on an impervious floor** ← | **Firm clay or rock foundations; low weirs** |
| **SLOPING GLACIS weir (Sarda type)** | **A downstream sloping glacis on which a HYDRAULIC JUMP is formed and held** ← | **SANDY (alluvial) foundations — the usual Indian and Nepali case** ← |
| **OGEE weir** | **An S-shaped crest following the nappe of a free overfall** | **Sound rock foundations; also dam spillways** ← |
| **Rockfill / dry stone weir** | Boulders in a series of steps | Where boulders are plentiful and heads are low |

> **THE SLOPING GLACIS TYPE IS THE STANDARD FOR ALLUVIAL RIVERS FOR ONE REASON: the hydraulic jump.**

> **A vertical drop weir dissipates energy by the falling nappe striking a cistern, which is violent and erosive. A sloping glacis forms a controlled hydraulic jump on the glacis itself, dissipating 60 to 70 per cent of the energy in a predictable location.**

> **Since an alluvial bed will scour severely under any concentrated energy release, holding the jump in a designed, protected position is essential — and the glacis is what achieves it.**

> **The same reasoning appeared in the discussion of canal falls, where the progression from ogee to glacis to baffle falls was driven by exactly this problem of controlling where the jump occurs.**

examTip.trick: **Afflux is the RISE in upstream flood level caused by the obstruction** — it extends kilometres upstream as a backwater curve, submerging land and requiring marginal bunds.
examTip.trap: **Afflux is TRADED against waterway width** — a narrower structure is cheaper but affluxes more, needs longer bunds, scours deeper AND needs a longer creep path. Some of the saving is given straight back.
examTip.mnemonic: **Provide Lacey's P = 4.75√Q** — narrower means scour and afflux, WIDER means silting and the river attacking one flank. And on alluvial (sandy) beds use a SLOPING GLACIS weir, to hold the hydraulic jump where it is protected.

questions.stem: The principal function of a FISH LADDER at a diversion headworks is to:
options: Trap fish for commercial harvesting
Prevent fish from entering the canal system
Filter fine sediment from the water entering the canal
Enable migratory fish to pass the barrier and reach their spawning grounds upstream
questions.solution:
**To enable MIGRATORY FISH to pass the barrier** and reach their upstream spawning grounds.

**How a fish ladder works:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A series of small POOLS in steps, each slightly higher than the last** ← | **The total head is divided into small drops fish can negotiate** ← |
| **Drop between successive pools** | **Kept SMALL — typically 150 to 300 mm** ← |
| **Velocity in the connecting slots** | **Low enough for the target species to swim against — commonly under 2 m/s** ← |
| **Pool size** | **Large enough for the fish to REST between jumps** ← |
| **Continuous flow, at all seasons of migration** | **A dry ladder is useless** ← |
| **Position** | **Adjacent to the undersluices, where a flow is always maintained and where fish naturally congregate** ← |

> **THE POSITION IN THE LAST ROW MATTERS MORE THAN THE LADDER'S DESIGN, and it is where fish passes most often fail:**

> **Fish find their way upstream by following the strongest current. If the ladder's entrance is tucked away at the bank while the main flow pours over the weir or through the sluices, the fish will congregate at the base of the weir and never find the ladder.**

> **So the ladder must be sited where the fish will naturally arrive, and it must discharge enough flow (an "attraction flow") to draw them in.**

> **A well-designed ladder in the wrong place passes no fish at all, and many older installations are effectively ornamental for exactly this reason.**

**Why fish passage matters — the ecological and human consequences:**

| Consequence of blocking migration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Migratory species cannot reach their SPAWNING grounds** | **Their reproduction fails and the population collapses** ← |
| **The upstream fishery is lost** | **Often a significant local food source and livelihood** ← |
| **Genetic isolation of populations** | Long-term loss of diversity |
| **Loss of a species from a whole river system** | **Not merely upstream of the dam — the population depends on the whole cycle** ← |

> **In Nepal this is a live issue for hydropower and irrigation development: several native species including the GOLDEN MAHSEER migrate long distances up the Himalayan rivers to spawn, and they are already in decline.**

> **A run-of-river hydropower scheme presents a double barrier: the diversion weir blocks the passage, and the DEWATERED REACH between the intake and the powerhouse may be impassable even if the weir is not.**

> **That is why the ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW requirement and fish passage must be considered together — a fish pass over the weir achieves nothing if the river below it is dry.**

**The other environmental provisions at a headworks or hydropower diversion:**

| Provision | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **FISH LADDER or fish pass** | **Upstream migration** ← |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL (compensation) FLOW** | **A minimum release to the dewatered reach — commonly 10 per cent of the minimum monthly average flow, or from a specific study** ← |
| **Fish SCREENS at the intake** | **Prevent fish being drawn into the canal or turbines — option (b)'s function, which is a REAL and separate provision** ← |
| **Downstream passage** | **Often harder than upstream; fish must descend past the structure safely** ← |
| **Sediment flushing timed to avoid spawning** | Reduces smothering of eggs |

> **Option (b) names the FISH SCREEN, which is a genuine and different device — so the option set contains two real fish-related provisions with opposite purposes: the ladder lets fish PAST the structure, and the screen keeps them OUT of the canal.**

> **Both may be needed at the same headworks, and confusing them is a natural error.**

**And the DOWNSTREAM passage difficulty, since it is less obvious:**

| Hazard to descending fish | Note |
|---|---|
| **Passing through TURBINES** | **High mortality — blade strike, pressure change and shear** ← |
| **Falling over a high spillway** | Impact injury |
| **Being drawn into the intake** | Screens help, but the fish must then find another route |
| **Disorientation in a reservoir** | **A migrating juvenile navigating by current cannot find its way across still water** ← |

> **The last row is an under-appreciated effect: young fish descending a river follow the current, and a reservoir has none. They circle, are predated, and never reach the outlet.**

> **So a storage scheme can block downstream migration as effectively as upstream migration, without any physical barrier being involved — which is why fish passage is a harder problem for large dams than a ladder alone can solve, and why for some rivers it has not been solved at all.**

examTip.trick: **A stepped series of pools with small drops (150-300 mm) letting migratory fish reach their spawning grounds.** Option (b) is the FISH SCREEN — a real, separate device with the opposite purpose.
examTip.trap: **Position matters more than design** — fish follow the strongest current, so a ladder tucked at the bank while the flow pours over the weir passes no fish at all. It needs an attraction flow at the right place.
examTip.mnemonic: **A fish pass is useless if the reach below is DRY** — passage and ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW must be designed together. And downstream passage is the harder half: turbine mortality, and juveniles unable to navigate a still reservoir.

questions.stem: CATCHMENT AREA TREATMENT (watershed management) upstream of a reservoir is undertaken principally to:
options: Reduce the sediment inflow, moderate flood peaks and sustain dry-season flows
Increase the total annual runoff into the reservoir
Raise the reservoir's full supply level
Reduce the cost of the dam's spillway
questions.solution:
**To reduce the SEDIMENT inflow, moderate flood peaks and sustain dry-season flows.**

**The measures involved:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **AFFORESTATION and reforestation** | **Roots bind the soil; the canopy intercepts rainfall and breaks its erosive impact** ← |
| **CONTOUR BUNDING and contour trenching** | **Intercept runoff on the slope, reduce its velocity and let it infiltrate** ← |
| **TERRACING of cultivated slopes** | **Converts a long slope into a series of short, level ones** ← |
| **CHECK DAMS and gully plugging** | **Trap sediment in the gullies and raise their beds, arresting head-cut erosion** ← |
| **Stream bank protection; bio-engineering** | **Vegetative and live-cutting techniques suited to Nepali slopes** ← |
| **Controlled GRAZING and fodder plots** | **Overgrazing is a major cause of degradation** ← |
| **Improved farming practice; agroforestry** | Contour ploughing, strip cropping, mulching |
| **Road spoil management and slope stabilisation** | **Since road building is itself a major sediment source** ← |

> **THE COMMON MECHANISM IS TO SLOW THE WATER DOWN: slower water carries less sediment, infiltrates more, and arrives later and more gradually.**

> **That single idea explains every measure in the table, and it explains all three benefits at once — less sediment, lower flood peaks, and more sustained dry-season flow from the infiltrated water.**

**Why option (b) is wrong, and it is the most instructive distractor:**

> **Catchment treatment generally REDUCES the total annual runoff, not increases it.**

| Effect | Reason |
|---|---|
| **More INFILTRATION** | Less water runs off directly |
| **More EVAPOTRANSPIRATION from the new vegetation** | **Trees use water — a mature forest transpires a great deal** ← |
| **Net effect on TOTAL annual yield** | **Usually a slight REDUCTION** ← |
| **Net effect on the DISTRIBUTION of that yield** | **Greatly improved — less in the flood peak, MORE in the dry season** ← |

> **SO CATCHMENT TREATMENT REDISTRIBUTES THE WATER IN TIME RATHER THAN INCREASING IT, and that redistribution is precisely what is wanted.**

> **A reservoir does not benefit from a larger flood peak — it spills the surplus. It benefits enormously from higher flows in the dry months, when its storage is being drawn down.**

> **This is worth stating clearly because "planting trees increases water supply" is a widely held belief and is generally not true of total yield. What planting trees does is even out the flow, reduce erosion, and improve water quality — which are substantial benefits, correctly described.**

**Why SEDIMENT is the dominant concern for a Himalayan reservoir:**

| Fact | Note |
|---|---|
| **Himalayan rivers carry among the world's highest sediment loads** | **Young, rapidly rising, steep, seismically shattered mountains under intense monsoon rain** ← |
| **Reservoirs trap that sediment** | **The TRAP EFFICIENCY of a large reservoir approaches 100 per cent** ← |
| **DEAD STORAGE fills first, then LIVE storage** | **The regulating capability declines year by year** ← |
| **Design lives of 100 years have proved to be 30-40 in some cases** | ← |
| **Removing deposited sediment is extremely difficult and costly** | **Dredging a large reservoir is rarely economic** ← |

> **So catchment treatment is not a peripheral environmental gesture but a direct protection of the project's own asset — every tonne of soil kept on the hillside is a tonne that does not occupy the reservoir.**

> **The difficulty is that the treatment must be carried out over a very large area, by and with the cooperation of the communities living there, and its benefits accrue to the project downstream.**

> **That mismatch between who bears the effort and who receives the benefit is the central institutional problem of watershed management, and it is why BENEFIT SHARING — royalties or funds directed to upstream communities — has become part of hydropower policy in Nepal.**

**The other sediment management measures at the reservoir itself:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLUICING / drawdown FLUSHING** | **Lower the reservoir during the flood so the river's own current scours deposits through low-level outlets** ← |
| **DENSITY CURRENT VENTING** | **A turbid underflow travels along the bed to the dam; vent it out before it settles** ← |
| **Bypass tunnels** | **Divert the sediment-laden flood around the reservoir entirely** ← |
| **Setting the intake HIGH above the dead storage** | Delays the effect on operations |
| **Providing generous dead storage** | Accepts rather than prevents the problem |
| **Dredging** | Rarely economic at scale |

> **DRAWDOWN FLUSHING in the first row is the most effective of these and it has a real cost: the reservoir must be emptied during the monsoon, forgoing generation and storage precisely when water is abundant.**

> **It also releases a slug of sediment-laden water downstream, which can damage the river ecology severely if done carelessly — so it must be timed and managed rather than simply carried out.**

> **The general lesson is the one this question began with: it is far easier and cheaper to keep the sediment out of the reservoir than to get it out afterwards, which is the case for treating the catchment.**

examTip.trick: **Every measure works by SLOWING THE WATER DOWN** — slower water carries less sediment, infiltrates more, and arrives later. That one mechanism gives all three benefits.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is a widely held error: catchment treatment usually REDUCES total annual runoff** (more infiltration, more transpiration). It REDISTRIBUTES the water in time — less flood peak, more dry-season flow — which is what a reservoir actually wants.
examTip.mnemonic: **Trap efficiency of a large reservoir approaches 100 %, and Himalayan design lives of 100 years have proved to be 30-40.** Keeping sediment OUT is far cheaper than getting it out — drawdown flushing costs monsoon generation and harms the river below.

questions.stem: A canal outlet whose discharge is INDEPENDENT of the water levels in BOTH the distributary and the watercourse is classified as:
options: Non-modular
Semi-modular (flexible)
Modular (rigid)
Proportional
questions.solution:
**MODULAR (rigid)** — its discharge is constant, independent of the levels on both sides.

**The three classes of outlet:**

| Class | Discharge depends on | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR** | **BOTH the distributary level AND the watercourse level** ← | **Open sluice, submerged pipe outlet** ← |
| **SEMI-MODULAR (flexible)** | **The DISTRIBUTARY level ONLY — independent of the watercourse** ← | **Open flume, orifice semi-module, Kennedy's gauge outlet** ← |
| **MODULAR (rigid)** | **NEITHER — the discharge is essentially CONSTANT** ← | **Gibb's module, Khanna's module** ← |

> **The distinction rests on whether the outlet drowns: a SEMI-MODULE works with a free (unsubmerged) discharge, so conditions downstream cannot influence it, while a NON-MODULAR outlet runs submerged and both levels matter.**

> **Option (d), "proportional", is a different property altogether — see below — which makes it the subtlest distractor.**

**The advantages and drawbacks of each:**

| Class | Advantage | Drawback |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-modular** | **Cheap; simple; passes SILT well; works at very small head** ← | **The cultivator can increase the supply by lowering the watercourse level — TAMPERING is easy** ← |
| **Semi-modular** | **Fair control; moderate cost; reasonably silt-tolerant** ← | Needs a working head; discharge still varies with the distributary level |
| **Modular** | **The FAIREST distribution — everyone gets their fixed share whatever happens** ← | **Expensive; needs a LARGE working head; liable to SILT UP; no flexibility in operation** ← |

> **THE MODULAR OUTLET'S APPARENT PERFECTION IS ALSO ITS PROBLEM, and the reason is worth understanding:**

> **A rigid module delivers its fixed discharge REGARDLESS of the supply available in the distributary.**

> **So when the canal runs short — as it does in a dry year — the head-end modules continue to take their full share, and the shortage falls ENTIRELY on the tail-end farmers, who receive nothing.**

> **A PROPORTIONAL outlet, by contrast, shares the shortage: if the distributary runs at 70 per cent, every outlet delivers about 70 per cent, and the hardship is distributed equitably.**

> **That is why the proportional (rather than the rigid) outlet is usually preferred in practice, and it is a case where the technically superior device produces the socially worse outcome.**

**FLEXIBILITY, which is the property option (d) names:**
