> **Flexibility F = (dq/q) / (dQ/Q) — the proportionate change in the OUTLET's discharge for a given proportionate change in the DISTRIBUTARY's discharge.**

| Flexibility | Name | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **F = 1** | **PROPORTIONAL outlet** ← | **The outlet takes a constant SHARE — shortages and surpluses are shared equally** ← |
| **F > 1** | **HYPER-PROPORTIONAL** | **The outlet's share RISES when the canal runs full and FALLS when it runs low — it exaggerates the variation** ← |
| **F < 1** | **SUB-PROPORTIONAL** | **The outlet's share is more stable than the canal's** ← |
| **F = 0** | **RIGID (modular)** ← | No response at all |

> **The SETTING of an outlet — the ratio of its depth below the distributary's full supply level to the distributary's full supply depth — is what determines its flexibility.**

| Setting | Flexibility |
|---|---|
| **Outlet set HIGH (near the water surface)** | **HYPER-proportional — a small fall in level cuts its supply sharply** ← |
| **Outlet set at the PROPORTIONAL depth** | **F = 1** |
| **Outlet set LOW (deep below the surface)** | **SUB-proportional — a change in level affects it little** ← |

> **So the designer controls the equity of distribution simply by choosing the SILL LEVEL of each outlet, which is an elegant piece of hydraulic design with a direct social consequence.**

**SILT DRAWING, the other property that governs outlet design:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **The problem** | **If an outlet draws a greater PROPORTION of silt than of water, the distributary silts up; if less, the distributary scours** ← |
| **The requirement** | **The outlet should draw silt in the SAME proportion as water** ← |
| **How it is influenced** | **By the outlet's SETTING — a low sill draws the silt-laden bottom water, a high sill draws clearer surface water** ← |

> **THIS PULLS AGAINST THE FLEXIBILITY REQUIREMENT, and that tension is the real difficulty of outlet design:**

> **A HIGH setting gives good flexibility behaviour but draws clear water, so the distributary progressively SILTS.**

> **A LOW setting draws its fair share of silt but is sub-proportional, so it takes more than its share when the canal is short.**

> **The designer must therefore balance equity of water distribution against the silt regime of the channel — and since a silted distributary eventually delivers nothing to anybody, neither consideration can simply be given priority.**

> **That is the same class of trade met throughout this chapter: the silt excluder against the ejector, the waterway against the afflux, the lining against the drainage. In canal engineering the water and the sediment must both be managed, and a design that considers only the water will not survive its first monsoon.**

examTip.trick: **NON-MODULAR: both levels matter. SEMI-MODULAR: only the distributary. MODULAR: neither.** Option (d), proportional, describes FLEXIBILITY (F = 1), a different property.
examTip.trap: **A rigid module is technically superior and socially worse** — it takes its full share in a shortage, so the whole deficit falls on the TAIL-END farmers. A PROPORTIONAL outlet shares the shortage.
examTip.mnemonic: **The SETTING (sill depth) fixes both flexibility and silt drawing, and they pull opposite ways** — a HIGH sill is hyper-proportional and draws clear water (silting the distributary); a LOW sill draws its share of silt but is sub-proportional.

questions.stem: A LEVEL CROSSING as a cross-drainage arrangement is one in which:
options: The canal is carried over the drainage on an aqueduct
The canal and the drainage meet at the same level and their waters are allowed to INTERMIX
The drainage is carried over the canal
The canal passes under the drainage as a syphon
questions.solution:
**The canal and the drainage MEET AT THE SAME LEVEL and their waters INTERMIX**, with a regulator on the canal downstream of the junction and a cross regulator or escape on the drainage.

**When a level crossing is adopted:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal's bed and the drainage's bed are at NEARLY THE SAME LEVEL** ← | **So neither can pass over the other without excessive works** |
| **The drainage carries a LARGE discharge** | **Too large to be taken through a culvert or syphon economically** ← |
| **The drainage water is reasonably CLEAN** | **It will enter the canal and be delivered to the fields** ← |
| **Where the extra water can be USED or safely escaped** | ← |

> **The arrangement is simple: the two channels are joined in a common pool, a regulator on the canal downstream admits the required discharge, and a regulator or escape on the drainage passes the surplus onward.**

> **Options (a), (c) and (d) describe the aqueduct, super-passage and canal syphon — the other members of the cross-drainage family, which are the alternatives a level crossing is chosen instead of.**

**The complete family, for comparison:**

| Work | What passes over | Flow condition below |
|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **The CANAL** | Free surface |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | **The CANAL** | **Under PRESSURE** |
| **SUPER-PASSAGE** | **The DRAINAGE** | Free surface |
| **CANAL SYPHON** | **The DRAINAGE** | **Under PRESSURE** |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** | **NEITHER — they meet and mix** ← | — |
| **INLET and OUTLET** | **The drainage is ADMITTED into the canal and taken out downstream** ← | — |

> **The INLET-AND-OUTLET arrangement in the last row is the level crossing's smaller cousin: a minor drainage is simply let into the canal at one point and an outlet further along discharges the surplus back to the natural channel.**

> **It suits a SMALL, clean drainage where building any structure would be disproportionate, and it is the cheapest arrangement of all.**

**The disadvantages of a level crossing, which are why it is a last resort:**

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal receives the drainage's SILT and DEBRIS** ← | **Which then deposits in the canal downstream** |
| **Flood water may enter the canal in uncontrolled quantity** | **Requiring careful regulation and an escape** ← |
| **Contamination** | **The drainage may carry pollutants, and the canal may supply drinking water as well as irrigation** ← |
| **It demands ACTIVE OPERATION** | **Two sets of gates must be worked during every flood — an unattended crossing is dangerous** ← |
| **Loss of independent control** | The two systems become coupled |

> **THE OPERATIONAL DEMAND IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE OBJECTION IN PRACTICE: every other cross-drainage work is PASSIVE — an aqueduct carries the canal over the drainage whether anyone is present or not.**

> **A level crossing requires a gate operator to be there, and to act correctly, during the flood — which is exactly when access is difficult and attention is divided.**

> **An unattended level crossing during a large flood admits the flood into the canal, which then overtops and breaches, and the damage extends far beyond the crossing itself.**

> **So the choice between a level crossing and an aqueduct is partly a judgement about the reliability of OPERATION, not only about levels and cost — and where operation cannot be assured, the passive structure is worth its extra cost.**

**Choosing between the cross-drainage works — the governing factors:**

| Factor | Influence |
|---|---|
| **RELATIVE LEVELS of the canal and the drainage** | **The dominant factor — see the table above** ← |
| **Relative DISCHARGES** | **A large drainage and a small canal favours a super-passage or syphon; the reverse favours an aqueduct** ← |
| **Nature of the drainage's flow** | **A flashy, debris-laden torrent argues against anything the debris can block** ← |
| **Foundation conditions** | Affects cost |
| **Cost of the alternatives** | Compared on a whole-life basis |
| **Whether the drainage water can be USED** | **If it is clean and useful, a level crossing or an inlet becomes attractive** ← |

> **The third row is particularly relevant in Nepal: a hill drainage in the monsoon is not a gentle stream but a debris-laden torrent carrying boulders.**

> **A syphon barrel beneath such a drainage will block; a culvert will block; and even an aqueduct's piers are vulnerable to impact and scour.**

> **The safest arrangement where debris flow is credible is to carry the canal WELL ABOVE the drainage on an aqueduct with a generous clear waterway and no obstruction in the flood path — accepting the cost, because a blocked structure in a debris flow does not merely fail, it dams the torrent and then releases it.**

Regulators controlling both.

examTip.trick: **A level crossing lets the canal and drainage MEET AND MIX at the same level, controlled by regulators on both.** Options (a), (c) and (d) are the aqueduct, super-passage and canal syphon.
examTip.trap: **Its decisive drawback is that it demands ACTIVE OPERATION during every flood** — every other cross-drainage work is passive. An unattended crossing admits the flood into the canal, which then breaches.
examTip.mnemonic: **INLET-and-OUTLET is the cheapest arrangement** — a small clean drainage let into the canal and taken out downstream. And where a monsoon DEBRIS FLOW is credible, carry the canal well above on an aqueduct: a blocked structure dams the torrent and then releases it.

questions.stem: In a SUBSURFACE (tile) drainage system for waterlogged agricultural land, the SPACING of the drains depends principally on the:
options: Length of the field
Type of crop grown
Cost of the drainage pipe
Permeability of the soil and the depth at which the water table must be held
questions.solution:
**The PERMEABILITY of the soil and the DEPTH at which the water table is to be maintained** (together with the drain depth and the recharge rate).

**Why permeability governs:**

| Soil | Permeability | Drain spacing |
|---|---|---|
| **SAND and gravel** | **HIGH** | **WIDE — 50 to 100 m or more** ← |
| **Sandy loam** | Moderate | 25 to 50 m |
| **Loam** | Moderate to low | 15 to 30 m |
| **CLAY** | **VERY LOW** | **CLOSE — 8 to 15 m, and subsurface drainage may be uneconomic altogether** ← |

> **The relation is intuitive once seen: in a permeable soil, water can travel a long way laterally to reach a drain, so the drains can be far apart. In a clay it can barely travel at all, so they must be close together — and at some point so close that the system costs more than the land is worth.**

> **That is why subsurface drainage is often ruled out for heavy clays, and SURFACE drainage or mole drainage used instead.**

**HOOGHOUDT'S equation, which formalises the relation:**

> **S² = (4K/q)(2 d_e h + h²)** approximately, where:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S** | **Drain SPACING** ← |
| **K** | **Hydraulic conductivity (PERMEABILITY) of the soil** ← |
| **q** | **The DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT — the recharge rate to be removed, in m/day** ← |
| **h** | **The height of the water table MIDWAY between drains, above the drain level** ← |
| **d_e** | **The EQUIVALENT depth to the impermeable layer below the drains** ← |

> **The essential relationships that fall out of it:**

| If this increases | The spacing |
|---|---|
| **Permeability K** | **INCREASES (as √K)** ← |
| **Drainage coefficient q (more water to remove)** | **DECREASES** ← |
| **Permitted water table height h** | **INCREASES** ← |
| **Depth to the impermeable layer** | **INCREASES — more soil for the water to flow through** ← |

> **The √K dependence in the first row means that permeability must be estimated within a factor of about four to fix the spacing within a factor of two — so a rough field measurement (an auger-hole test) is usually adequate, which is fortunate, since permeability is notoriously variable.**

**The DEPTH of the drains, which is the other main decision:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The water table must be held BELOW the root zone** | **Typically 1.2 to 1.5 m below the surface for most crops** ← |
| **Deeper drains permit WIDER spacing** | **So fewer drains — often the cheaper combination despite the deeper trench** ← |
| **But excavation cost rises steeply with depth** | And machinery limits apply |
| **And an impermeable layer may limit the depth** | ← |
| **Typical depth** | **1.5 to 2.5 m** ← |

> **The economic optimum trades DEPTH against SPACING: a deeper, wider-spaced system and a shallower, closer-spaced one may cost the same, and the choice then rests on soil conditions and available machinery.**

**The components of the system:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **LATERALS (field drains)** | **Perforated pipe — formerly clay tiles, now corrugated PVC** ← |
| **A FILTER envelope round the pipe** | **Gravel, or a synthetic wrap — ESSENTIAL, and it is where these systems fail** ← |
| **COLLECTORS and mains** | Carry the water to the outfall |
| **Manholes and inspection chambers** | Access for flushing |
| **The OUTFALL** | **Gravity to a drain or river, or a PUMPED sump where the land is too low** ← |

> **THE FILTER ENVELOPE DESERVES THE EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS THE COMMONEST CAUSE OF FAILURE, and the reason is the one met with retaining walls:**

> **Water entering the pipe carries fine soil with it. Without a properly graded filter, the fines pass through the perforations, the pipe silts up, and the system stops working — invisibly, since it is buried.**

> **A tile drainage scheme that has silted gives no external sign until the land waterlogs again, by which time the cause is not obvious and the remedy is to excavate and replace.**

> **The same Terzaghi filter criteria apply as behind a retaining wall, and the same conclusion holds: wherever water leaves soil, it will try to take the soil with it.**

**And MOLE DRAINAGE, the alternative for clays:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **An unlined channel drawn through the subsoil by a bullet-shaped "mole" plough** ← |
| **Suits** | **Heavy CLAY soils, which are stable enough to hold an unlined channel open** ← |
| **Depth and spacing** | **0.5 to 0.7 m deep, 2 to 5 m apart** ← |
| **Life** | **A few years only — the channels collapse and must be redrawn** ← |
| **Cost** | **VERY LOW — one pass of a tractor, no materials at all** ← |

> **The mole drain's economics are the reverse of the tile system's: it is cheap and short-lived rather than expensive and permanent, and it works in precisely the soil where tile drains are uneconomic.**

> **The two are therefore complements rather than competitors, and mole drains are often drawn ACROSS a widely spaced permanent tile system — the moles collecting water over the clay and delivering it to the tiles, which carry it away.**

> **That combination gets the close spacing a clay needs at the cost of the cheap component, and it is a neat resolution of the spacing problem this question began with.**

examTip.trick: **Permeability and the required water table depth.** Sands: 50-100 m spacing; clays: 8-15 m, often uneconomic. Hooghoudt: S² = (4K/q)(2d_e h + h²), so S varies as √K.
examTip.trap: **Deeper drains permit WIDER spacing** — so a deeper, sparser system is often cheaper overall despite the deeper trench. The economic optimum trades depth against spacing.
examTip.mnemonic: **The FILTER ENVELOPE is where these systems fail** — fines wash in, the pipe silts, and nothing shows until the land waterlogs again. And for heavy clays use MOLE drains: cheap, unlined, 2-5 m apart, lasting a few years — often feeding a permanent tile system.

questions.stem: A PUMPED STORAGE hydropower plant:
options: Generates more energy than it consumes, and is therefore a net energy source
Pumps water to an upper reservoir during OFF-PEAK hours and generates during peak hours, consuming more energy overall than it produces
Operates without any upper reservoir
Is used only for irrigation water supply
questions.solution:
**It PUMPS water to an upper reservoir during off-peak hours and GENERATES during peak hours, and it consumes MORE energy overall than it produces.**

**Why a net energy CONSUMER is nevertheless valuable:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Round-trip efficiency** | **70 to 80 per cent — so it returns about three quarters of the energy it takes** ← |
| **It is therefore a net CONSUMER of energy** | **It stores energy; it does not create it** ← |
| **But it converts CHEAP off-peak energy into VALUABLE peak energy** ← | **And the price difference greatly exceeds the 20-30 per cent lost** ← |

> **THAT PRICE ARBITRAGE IS THE WHOLE ECONOMIC CASE: if peak energy is worth three times off-peak energy, then losing a quarter of it in the round trip is comfortably profitable.**

> **Option (a) states the impossible — no storage device can return more than it receives — and it is the natural misreading of "hydropower plant".**

**The other services a pumped storage plant provides, which are now often worth more than the arbitrage:**

| Service | Note |
|---|---|
| **PEAKING capacity** | **Very rapid start — from standstill to full output in a minute or two** ← |
| **FREQUENCY regulation and spinning reserve** | **It can absorb or deliver power almost instantly, stabilising the grid** ← |
| **Absorbing surplus GENERATION** | **Which is the modern driver — see below** ← |
| **Black start capability** | Restarting a collapsed grid |
| **Deferring transmission investment** | Storage near the load reduces peak transmission demand |

> **THE THIRD ROW HAS BECOME THE DOMINANT REASON FOR BUILDING PUMPED STORAGE WORLDWIDE, and it is worth explaining:**

> **Solar and wind generate when the sun shines and the wind blows, not when demand occurs. A grid with a large renewable share therefore has SURPLUS at midday and a DEFICIT in the evening.**

> **Pumped storage absorbs the midday surplus that would otherwise be wasted and returns it in the evening peak — which is exactly the shape of the problem.**

> **It remains, by a large margin, the world's dominant form of grid-scale energy storage, holding far more capacity than all batteries combined, because it is cheap per unit of ENERGY stored (unlike batteries, which are cheap per unit of POWER).**

**Relevance to Nepal, which is a genuine and current question:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Nepal's system is dominated by RUN-OF-RIVER hydro** | **Surplus in the monsoon, deficit in the dry season and at the evening peak** ← |
| **Pumped storage would address the DAILY peak** | **Storing overnight surplus for the evening** ← |
| **It does NOT address the SEASONAL deficit** | **A daily cycle cannot bridge a five-month dry season — only true STORAGE can** ← |
| **Topography is highly favourable** | **Steep terrain gives large head over short distances, which is exactly what pumped storage needs** ← |
| **Several sites have been identified and studied** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL QUALIFICATION AND IT IS OFTEN GLOSSED OVER: pumped storage is a DAILY (or at most weekly) storage device.**

> **Its upper reservoir holds perhaps six to twelve hours of generation. It cannot store monsoon water for use in April, because that would require a reservoir hundreds of times larger — at which point it is simply a conventional storage scheme.**

> **So pumped storage and seasonal storage solve DIFFERENT problems, and proposing the first as an answer to the second is a category error.**

**The machinery, since it distinguishes these plants:**

| Arrangement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Separate pump and turbine** | Simple, but two machines and two sets of civil works |
| **REVERSIBLE PUMP-TURBINE** | **One machine, run in reverse to pump — the standard modern arrangement, usually a FRANCIS type** ← |
| **Ternary set (turbine, pump and motor-generator on one shaft)** | Fast transition between modes |

> **The reversible Francis machine is a genuine engineering compromise: a pump and a turbine want slightly different runner geometries, so a reversible unit is somewhat less efficient than either would be alone.**

> **The saving in capital cost and civil works more than repays that, which is why virtually all modern pumped storage uses reversible units.**

**And the classification of hydropower plants generally, to place this one:**

| Basis | Categories |
|---|---|
| **By HEAD** | **Low (below 30 m), medium (30-300 m), high (above 300 m)** ← |
| **By CAPACITY** | **Micro (below 100 kW), mini (100 kW-1 MW), small (1-10 MW), medium, large** ← |
| **By STORAGE and regulation** | **Run-of-river, PEAKING run-of-river (daily pondage), STORAGE (seasonal), PUMPED STORAGE** ← |
| **By LOAD served** | **BASE load, PEAK load** ← |
| **By interconnection** | Isolated, or grid-connected |

> **Pumped storage occupies a distinctive place in this scheme: it is the only category that generates no NEW energy at all, and it is classified with the others because it uses identical civil and mechanical engineering to serve an entirely different purpose — managing WHEN energy is available rather than producing it.**

examTip.trick: **Pump off-peak, generate on-peak, round-trip efficiency 70-80 % — a net CONSUMER of energy.** Option (a) is impossible: no store returns more than it receives.
examTip.trap: **It stores DAILY, not SEASONALLY** — six to twelve hours of generation. It cannot bridge Nepal's five-month dry season; only true storage can. Proposing it for that is a category error.
examTip.mnemonic: **The modern driver is absorbing SURPLUS renewables** — solar peaks at midday, demand in the evening. Pumped storage remains the world's dominant grid storage because it is cheap per unit of ENERGY, where batteries are cheap per unit of POWER.

questions.stem: Compared with a thermal power station, a hydropower station is characterised by:
options: Low capital cost and high running cost
A long starting time and slow response to load changes
A short useful life requiring frequent replacement
High capital cost, very low running cost, rapid starting and a long useful life
questions.solution:
**HIGH capital cost, very LOW running cost, RAPID starting and a LONG useful life.**

**The comparison in full:**

| Aspect | HYDRO | THERMAL |
|---|---|---|
| **CAPITAL cost per kW** | **HIGH — dams, tunnels, civil works dominate** ← | **Lower** |
| **RUNNING cost** | **VERY LOW — no fuel; the water is free** ← | **HIGH — fuel is the dominant cost** ← |
| **STARTING time** | **MINUTES, or less — a hydro set can be synchronised in about two minutes** ← | **HOURS from cold — boilers must be raised slowly** ← |
| **Response to LOAD change** | **Very rapid** ← | Slow |
| **Useful LIFE** | **50 to 100 years and more — civil works are extremely durable** ← | **25 to 30 years** ← |
| **Efficiency** | **85 to 90 per cent** ← | **35 to 45 per cent** ← |
| **Staff required** | Few | Many |
| **Maintenance** | Low | High |
| **Emissions** | **None in operation** | **CO₂, SO₂, NOₓ, particulates, ash** ← |
| **Location** | **Fixed by topography and hydrology — often remote** ← | **Flexible — near the load or the fuel** ← |
| **Dependability** | **Varies with HYDROLOGY — a dry year reduces output** ← | **Independent of weather, dependent on fuel supply** ← |
| **Environmental and social cost** | **Submergence, resettlement, river ecology** ← | Air pollution, water for cooling, ash disposal |

> **Each distractor inverts one of these: option (a) reverses the cost structure, option (b) the starting time, and option (c) the life.**

**Why the STARTING TIME matters so much — the system consequence:**

> **A power system must match generation to demand INSTANTANEOUSLY and continuously. A plant that takes hours to start cannot follow a load that changes in minutes.**

| Plant type | Role in the system |
|---|---|
| **BASE LOAD** | **Runs continuously at high output; low running cost, slow to start** — coal, nuclear, run-of-river hydro ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE (load following)** | Follows the daily pattern |
| **PEAKING** | **Runs a few hours a day; must start FAST; high running cost is acceptable because it runs so little** — gas turbines, PUMPED STORAGE, peaking hydro ← |

> **HYDRO WITH STORAGE IS ALMOST UNIQUELY SUITED TO PEAKING, because it combines the two properties that are usually opposed: very rapid starting AND very low running cost.**

> **A gas turbine also starts fast but burns expensive fuel; a coal plant is cheap to run but cannot start quickly. Storage hydro is fast AND cheap, which is why it commands a premium in any mixed system.**

> **That is the economic reason a PEAKING run-of-river plant earns more per unit than a plain run-of-river plant of the same annual energy — the same electricity delivered at a more valuable moment.**

**The EFFICIENCY row deserves a note, since the difference is so large:**

> **A thermal plant is limited by the CARNOT efficiency — it converts heat to work, and the second law of thermodynamics caps what is achievable at the temperatures available.**

> **A hydro plant converts MECHANICAL energy (a falling mass) directly to mechanical rotation, with no thermal step at all — so it is not subject to that limit and loses only to friction and hydraulic losses.**

> **That is why 90 per cent is routine for hydro and unreachable for any heat engine, and it is a fundamental distinction rather than a matter of engineering refinement.**

**The disadvantages of hydro, stated fairly:**

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very high CAPITAL cost and long construction period** | **Which makes financing difficult and interest during construction substantial** ← |
| **Dependent on HYDROLOGY** | **A dry year cuts output; climate change adds uncertainty** ← |
| **SITE-SPECIFIC** | **The site is where the river is, often far from the load — requiring transmission** ← |
| **Submergence, displacement and resettlement** | **The principal social cost, and often the decisive obstacle** ← |
| **River ecology, fish passage, sediment regime** | ← |
| **SEDIMENTATION shortens a reservoir's life** | Particularly in the Himalaya |
| **Dam failure risk** | Low probability, catastrophic consequence |

> **The CAPITAL COST and LONG CONSTRUCTION PERIOD in the first row interact badly and are worth understanding together:**

> **A hydropower project may take five to eight years to build, during which the borrowed capital accrues interest with no revenue at all.**

> **That INTEREST DURING CONSTRUCTION can amount to 15 to 25 per cent of the total project cost, and a delay of a year adds directly to it.**

> **So schedule discipline matters more in hydropower than in almost any other kind of construction, and the geological surprises discussed earlier are expensive twice over — once for the extra excavation and once for the interest on the delay.**

> **This is also why the appraisal methods of the earlier chapter matter here: a project whose benefits arrive only after eight years, and continue for eighty, is exactly the case where the choice of discount rate determines whether it appears worthwhile.**

examTip.trick: **High capital, near-zero running cost, starts in MINUTES, lasts 50-100 years, 85-90 % efficient.** Each distractor inverts one of these.
examTip.trap: **Hydro with storage is almost uniquely FAST to start AND CHEAP to run** — a gas turbine is fast but costly to run, coal is cheap but slow. That combination is why peaking hydro earns a premium.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hydro escapes the CARNOT limit entirely** — no heat engine step — which is why 90 % is routine against a thermal plant's 40 %. And INTEREST DURING CONSTRUCTION is 15-25 % of project cost over a 5-8 year build, so delays are expensive twice over.

questions.stem: In a power system, a BASE LOAD plant is one that:
options: Operates continuously at a high capacity factor
Operates only during the hours of maximum demand
Is kept as a standby and rarely operated
Supplies only the transmission losses of the system
questions.solution:
**One that operates CONTINUOUSLY at a high capacity factor, supplying the portion of the demand that is present at all times.**

**Base load against peak load:**

| | BASE LOAD plant | PEAK LOAD plant |
|---|---|---|
| **Operation** | **CONTINUOUS, at or near full output** ← | **A few hours a day, intermittently** ← (option b) |
| **Capacity factor** | **HIGH — 60 to 90 per cent** ← | **LOW — 5 to 25 per cent** ← |
| **Required characteristic** | **LOW RUNNING COST — it runs all the time, so fuel dominates** ← | **FAST STARTING — running cost matters less, since it runs so little** ← |
| **Capital cost** | **High capital is acceptable, spread over many units generated** ← | **LOW capital preferred, since few units are generated to pay for it** ← |
| **Typical plants** | **Run-of-river hydro, coal, nuclear, geothermal** ← | **Gas turbines, PUMPED STORAGE, peaking (storage) hydro, diesel sets** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN THE WHOLE OF PLANT SELECTION, and the logic is purely economic:**

> **A plant running 8,000 hours a year generates a great many units, so a small saving per unit repays a large capital outlay. LOW RUNNING COST is what matters.**

> **A plant running 500 hours a year generates few units, so a high capital cost cannot be recovered. LOW CAPITAL COST is what matters, and an expensive fuel is tolerable.**

> **That is why a system contains a MIX of plant types rather than only the cheapest kind — the cheapest plant to run is rarely the cheapest to build, and a system of nothing but base load plant could not follow its own demand.**

**The LOAD CURVE, which is what the mix is designed against:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **CHRONOLOGICAL LOAD CURVE** | **Demand plotted against time of day — shows WHEN the peaks occur** ← |
| **LOAD DURATION CURVE** | **The same data with the loads arranged in DESCENDING order — shows FOR HOW LONG each level is demanded** ← |
| **The AREA under either curve** | **The same: the total ENERGY demanded** ← |
| **The BASE of the load duration curve** | **The load present 100 per cent of the time — served by base load plant** ← |
| **The narrow TOP of the curve** | **Demanded for only a few hours — served by peaking plant** ← |

> **THE LOAD DURATION CURVE IS THE TOOL FOR SIZING THE PLANT MIX, and reading it is straightforward: draw a horizontal line at any output, and the area below it is the energy the base plant supplies while the area above is the energy the peaking plant must supply.**

> **Moving that line up assigns more energy to cheap base plant (good) but leaves the base plant idle for part of the year (bad). The economic split is where the marginal costs of the two balance.**

**The performance factors, since they describe how the plants are used:**

| Factor | Definition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load ÷ PEAK load** | **A high load factor means a flat demand, which is economical to serve** ← |
| **CAPACITY (plant) factor** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY** ← | Measures how hard the plant is worked |
| **UTILISATION factor** | **Maximum load reached ÷ installed capacity** | How much of the plant is ever used |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | **Sum of individual maximum demands ÷ the system's coincident maximum** | **ALWAYS greater than 1** ← |
| **DEMAND factor** | **Maximum demand ÷ total connected load** | Always less than 1 |

> **A HIGH LOAD FACTOR IS THE GOAL OF EVERY UTILITY, and the reason is worth stating: the system's capacity must be built for the PEAK, while its revenue comes from the ENERGY sold.**

> **A system with a peak of 1,000 MW and an average load of 400 MW (load factor 0.4) has built 1,000 MW of plant to sell the output of 400 MW — an expensive way to operate.**

> **Raising the load factor to 0.7 would sell 750 MW average from the same plant, nearly doubling the revenue from the same investment.**

> **That is why utilities offer cheap OFF-PEAK tariffs, encourage industrial night operation, and invest in storage — every one of those measures raises the load factor and improves the return on capacity already built.**

> **And it is why pumped storage is valuable to the SYSTEM even though it consumes energy: it fills the trough and shaves the peak, raising the load factor of everything else.**

**And Nepal's particular difficulty, which follows from all of this:**

| Feature of the Nepali system | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Dominated by RUN-OF-RIVER hydro** | **These are inherently BASE LOAD plants — they generate what the river gives, whenever it gives it** ← |
| **A pronounced EVENING peak** | **Which run-of-river plants cannot follow** ← |
| **Very little storage or peaking capacity** | ← |
| **The result** | **Surplus energy at night that cannot be sold, and a shortage at the evening peak** ← |

> **So Nepal's problem is not only a shortage of ENERGY but a shortage of the RIGHT KIND of capacity — and adding more run-of-river plants adds to the night-time surplus without addressing the evening peak.**

> **The remedies are storage and peaking-run-of-river schemes, regional trade (exporting the surplus and importing at the peak), and demand management — and recognising that the problem is one of TIMING rather than of total quantity is the first step in choosing among them.**

examTip.trick: **BASE LOAD: continuous, high capacity factor, needs LOW RUNNING COST. PEAK LOAD: a few hours, needs FAST START and LOW CAPITAL.** Option (b) describes the peaking plant.
examTip.trap: **The economics are purely about hours run** — 8,000 hours a year repays capital through fuel savings; 500 hours cannot repay capital at all. That is why a system needs a MIX.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capacity is built for the PEAK; revenue comes from the ENERGY** — so a HIGH LOAD FACTOR is the goal, and off-peak tariffs and storage exist to raise it. Nepal's problem is TIMING, not total quantity: run-of-river plants cannot follow an evening peak.

questions.stem: In fixing the INSTALLED CAPACITY of a run-of-river hydropower plant, increasing the design discharge beyond a certain point becomes uneconomic because:
options: The net head increases with discharge
The turbine efficiency rises indefinitely with size
The additional capacity is used for fewer hours each year
The construction cost falls as the plant gets larger
questions.solution:
**The ADDITIONAL capacity is usable for FEWER HOURS each year**, so each extra kilowatt installed earns progressively less energy and eventually cannot repay its cost.

**The reasoning, read off the flow duration curve:**

| Design discharge | Available for | Extra energy from the last increment |
|---|---|---|
| **Q₈₀ (a small plant)** | **80 % of the year** | — |
| **Q₅₀** | **50 % of the year** | Substantial |
| **Q₄₀** | **40 % of the year** | **Moderate — the usual Nepali design point** ← |
| **Q₃₀** | **30 % of the year** | Smaller |
| **Q₁₀** | **10 % of the year** | **Very small — that capacity stands idle nine months a year** ← |

> **Each increment of installed capacity costs roughly the SAME to provide — the same turbine, generator, penstock and powerhouse volume per kilowatt.**

> **But each increment is usable for LESS of the year, so it generates less energy and earns less revenue.**

> **THE OPTIMUM IS WHERE THE MARGINAL COST OF THE LAST KILOWATT EQUALS THE MARGINAL VALUE OF THE ENERGY IT WILL GENERATE — the standard marginal-analysis result, applied to a flow duration curve.**

**Why option (a) is wrong, and importantly so:**

> **The net head does not rise with discharge — it FALLS.**

> **A larger discharge through the same conveyance means higher velocities and therefore GREATER FRICTION LOSSES, so the net head available at the turbine DECREASES as the discharge increases.**

> **That makes the diminishing return steeper still: the extra discharge is available for fewer hours AND generates at a slightly lower head, so the last increment of capacity is doubly disadvantaged.**

**What shifts the optimum, which is where judgement enters:**

| Factor | Effect on the optimum design discharge |
|---|---|
| **A high tariff for PEAK energy** | **RAISES it — extra capacity is worth more if it can be sold at peak rates** ← |
| **A FLAT tariff paid for all energy** | Lowers it — only the energy matters, not the capacity |
| **A CAPACITY payment in the PPA** | **RAISES it — the plant is paid for being available, not only for generating** ← |
| **A FLAT flow duration curve (snow-fed river)** | **RAISES it substantially — the higher flows persist for much longer** ← |
| **A STEEP curve (rain-fed, flashy river)** | **LOWERS it — high flows last only weeks** ← |
| **High civil cost per unit of capacity** | Lowers it |
| **Transmission capacity limits** | **Caps it, regardless of the hydrology** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE MOST IMPORTANT AND CONNECT BACK TO THE FLOW DURATION CURVE'S SHAPE:**

> **A snow- and glacier-fed Himalayan river sustains substantial flows well into the dry season, so a larger plant is justified — the extra capacity works for much of the year.**

> **A purely rain-fed Middle Hills river may carry fifty times its dry-season flow for a few monsoon weeks, and capacity sized for that would be idle for ten months.**

> **So two rivers with the SAME mean annual flow can justify quite different installed capacities, and the flow duration curve — not the mean flow — is what determines it.**

**The methods used in practice:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Percentage-of-time rule of thumb** | **Design for Q₃₀ to Q₅₀; in Nepal, Q₄₀ is conventional** ← |
| **INCREMENTAL (marginal) economic analysis** | **Compute the NPV at a range of design discharges and select the maximum — the rigorous method** ← |
| **Constraint-driven** | **Set by the transmission line, the PPA's contracted capacity, or the available finance** ← |
| **Firm power requirement** | Where a guaranteed output is contracted |

> **The INCREMENTAL analysis is the correct approach and is straightforward in principle: for each candidate design discharge, compute the capital cost and the annual energy from the flow duration curve, discount both, and plot the NPV.**

> **The NPV curve rises, reaches a maximum and falls — and its peak is the answer. The rule-of-thumb Q₄₀ is simply where that peak usually falls for typical Nepali hydrology and tariffs.**

> **The value of understanding the derivation rather than the rule is that when the tariff structure or the hydrology is unusual, the rule of thumb will be wrong and only the analysis will show it.**

**And the SPILL that necessarily results, which is the visible consequence:**

| Observation | Note |
|---|---|
| **For flows ABOVE the design discharge, the surplus is SPILLED** ← | **The plant cannot use it** |
| **In the monsoon, a Q₄₀ plant spills a great deal of water** | **Which looks wasteful and is not** ← |
| **The alternative — capacity to use it — would stand idle most of the year** | ← |

> **Spilled water at a run-of-river plant is therefore not a design failure but the deliberate and correct consequence of an economic optimisation — a point worth being able to explain, since it is frequently raised as a criticism by observers who see the spillway running.**

Each extra kilowatt earns progressively less energy.

examTip.trick: **Each extra kilowatt costs the same but is usable for FEWER HOURS**, so its energy and revenue fall. The optimum is where marginal cost equals marginal value — usually around Q₄₀ in Nepal.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is backwards — net head FALLS as discharge rises** (greater friction losses), so the last increment of capacity is doubly disadvantaged.
examTip.mnemonic: **The SHAPE of the flow duration curve sets the optimum, not the mean flow** — a snow-fed river justifies a larger plant than a flashy rain-fed one of the same mean. And SPILL at a run-of-river plant is the correct result of the optimisation, not a failure.

questions.stem: A SKI-JUMP (flip) bucket is preferred to a stilling basin for dissipating the energy of a spillway discharge when:
options: The head is low and the tailwater is deep
The head is high and the river bed downstream is sound rock
The spillway discharge is very small
The foundation consists of soft alluvium
questions.solution:
**When the head is HIGH and the downstream bed is SOUND ROCK**, so the jet can be thrown clear of the structure to land in a plunge pool well away from the dam's toe.

**How a ski-jump works, and what it requires:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A curved bucket at the toe deflects the jet UPWARD and OUTWARD** ← | **The jet leaves as a free trajectory** |
| **The jet breaks up in the AIR, entraining air and spreading** | **Dissipating some energy before it lands** ← |
| **It lands in a PLUNGE POOL well downstream** | **Which the jet scours out for itself, and which then cushions further impact** ← |
| **Requirement: SOUND ROCK at the impact point** ← | **The jet will excavate a deep pool; in erodible material the scour would work back toward the dam** ← |
| **Requirement: HIGH head** | **Enough energy to throw the jet clear** ← |
| **Requirement: adequate space downstream** | The trajectory needs room |

> **THE ROCK REQUIREMENT IS ABSOLUTE, and option (d)'s soft alluvium is precisely the condition that forbids a ski-jump: the scour hole would deepen without limit and migrate upstream until it undermined the dam itself.**

> **So the choice between the two dissipators is made by the FOUNDATION as much as by the head.**

**The comparison:**

| | STILLING BASIN | SKI-JUMP BUCKET |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | **A HYDRAULIC JUMP formed and held within a concrete basin** ← | **The jet thrown clear, dissipating in the air and in a plunge pool** ← |
| **Suits** | **LOW to MEDIUM head; any foundation, including alluvium** ← | **HIGH head; SOUND ROCK only** ← |
| **Cost** | **HIGH — a long, thick, heavily reinforced concrete structure** ← | **LOW — a short bucket, with no basin at all** ← |
| **Tailwater** | **Must be adequate to hold the jump; a deficiency sweeps the jump out** ← | **Not critical** ← |
| **Downstream scour** | **Controlled** | **A deep plunge pool forms and is accepted** ← |
| **Spray and noise** | Modest | **Considerable — spray can reach the powerhouse and switchyard** ← |

> **THE COST DIFFERENCE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ATTRACTION OF THE SKI-JUMP: a stilling basin for a high dam is an enormous structure, and eliminating it saves a great deal.**

> **On a high dam in a narrow rock gorge — which is the typical Himalayan site — the ski-jump is usually both cheaper and more appropriate, and it is very widely used on Nepali and Indian projects for exactly that reason.**

**THE STILLING BASIN, since it is the alternative:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Principle** | **Force a HYDRAULIC JUMP, which dissipates 60 to 70 per cent of the energy in a short length** ← |
| **Appurtenances** | **CHUTE BLOCKS at the entry, BAFFLE BLOCKS in the basin, and an END SILL** ← |
| **What the blocks do** | **Stabilise the jump's position, shorten the basin, and reduce the tailwater depth needed** ← |
| **USBR standard types** | **Types I to IV, selected by the incoming Froude number** ← |
| **The critical requirement** | **The TAILWATER depth must at least equal the sequent depth of the jump** ← |

> **THE TAILWATER CONDITION IS WHERE STILLING BASINS FAIL, and the failure mode is worth knowing:**

| Tailwater | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **EQUAL to the sequent depth** | **The jump forms exactly at the toe — the design condition** ← |
| **INSUFFICIENT** | **The jump is SWEPT DOWNSTREAM out of the basin, and the high-velocity jet attacks the unprotected river bed** ← |
| **EXCESSIVE** | **The jump is DROWNED — it moves back onto the spillway face, dissipating little energy and leaving a fast current along the bed** ← |

> **So a stilling basin works only within a range of tailwater depths, and since the tailwater varies with the discharge, the basin must be checked across the whole range of operation — not merely at the design flood.**

> **A basin adequate at the design flood may sweep out at a partial discharge, which is a common and damaging oversight because partial discharges occur far more often than the design flood ever will.**

**And the other energy dissipators, to complete the set:**

| Device | Note |
|---|---|
| **STILLING BASIN (jump type)** | The general-purpose solution |
| **SKI-JUMP / flip bucket** | **High head on rock** ← |
| **ROLLER BUCKET (solid or slotted)** | **Where the tailwater is DEEPER than the sequent depth — a submerged roller dissipates the energy** ← |
| **PLUNGE POOL** | Free fall from an overflow, into a pool |
| **Impact and baffled-chute dissipators** | Small structures and outlets |
| **Stepped spillway** | **Steps dissipate energy progressively down the face — increasingly used with roller-compacted concrete dams** ← |

> **The STEPPED SPILLWAY in the last row is worth noting as a modern development: it dissipates a large proportion of the energy on the way down rather than all at once at the bottom, so the stilling basin at the toe can be much smaller.**

> **It became practical with roller-compacted concrete construction, where the steps arise naturally from the placing method rather than having to be formed — a good example of a construction technique enabling a hydraulic solution that was previously uneconomic.**

examTip.trick: **Ski-jump: HIGH head, SOUND ROCK, jet thrown clear into a plunge pool.** Option (d)'s soft alluvium is precisely the condition that forbids it — the scour hole would migrate back and undermine the dam.
examTip.trap: **A stilling basin works only within a RANGE of tailwater depths** — too little and the jump SWEEPS OUT, too much and it DROWNS. Check the whole discharge range, not just the design flood, since partial flows occur far more often.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ski-jump's attraction is COST** — it eliminates a huge concrete basin, which is why it suits high dams in narrow Himalayan rock gorges. And STEPPED spillways (from RCC construction) dissipate on the way down, shrinking the basin at the toe.

questions.stem: In an EARTH DAM, the principal purpose of a CHIMNEY DRAIN (a vertical filter within the embankment) is to:
options: Provide access for inspection of the dam's interior
Ventilate the core and allow it to dry
Increase the dam's weight and hence its stability
Intercept seepage passing through the core and carry it safely to the toe drain
questions.solution:
**To INTERCEPT the seepage passing through the core and carry it safely down to the toe drain, keeping the downstream shell UNSATURATED.**

**Why that matters so much:**

| Consequence of a SATURATED downstream shell | Note |
|---|---|
| **The phreatic (seepage) line emerges on the downstream FACE** ← | **Water appears on the slope, softening and eroding it** |
| **Pore pressures reduce the EFFECTIVE STRESS in the shell** | **So its shear strength falls and the slope's factor of safety drops sharply** ← |
| **PIPING may begin at the point of emergence** | **The classic internal erosion failure** ← |
| **Sloughing and progressive slope failure** | ← |

> **THE CHIMNEY DRAIN'S FUNCTION IS THEREFORE TO CONTROL WHERE THE WATER GOES, not to stop it: seepage through an earth dam cannot be prevented, only intercepted and drained safely.**

> **By placing a vertical filter immediately downstream of the core, the phreatic line is DRAWN DOWN to the drain and the entire downstream shell stays dry — so its full shear strength is available and the slope can be steeper and the dam cheaper.**

> **A chimney drain also guards against a defect in the core: if the core cracks or is imperfectly compacted, the concentrated leak is intercepted by the filter rather than eroding its way through the shell.**

**The seepage-control elements of an earth dam:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **Impervious CORE (central or inclined)** | **The principal barrier — reduces the quantity of seepage** ← |
| **CUT-OFF trench or grout curtain** | **Extends the barrier into the FOUNDATION, which would otherwise be bypassed** ← |
| **CHIMNEY (vertical) DRAIN** | **Intercepts seepage through the core** ← |
| **BLANKET drain (horizontal, at the base)** | **Carries the intercepted water downstream to the toe** ← |
| **TOE DRAIN / rock toe** | **Collects and discharges it, and buttresses the toe** ← |
| **Upstream impervious BLANKET** | Lengthens the seepage path where a full cut-off is impractical |
| **Relief wells downstream** | Reduce uplift in a pervious foundation |

> **THE FILTER DESIGN IS WHAT MAKES ALL OF THESE WORK, and the criteria are exactly Terzaghi's, met earlier behind a retaining wall:**

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **PERMEABILITY** | **D₁₅(filter) ≥ 4-5 × D₁₅(soil) — it must drain freely** ← |
| **RETENTION** | **D₁₅(filter) ≤ 4-5 × D₈₅(soil) — it must not let the core wash through** ← |

> **A drain that fails the retention criterion does not merely leak — it actively removes the core, which is the mechanism of internal erosion.**

> **So the filter is the single most safety-critical element of an earth dam, and filter failures have destroyed dams: the Teton Dam failure of 1976 is the standard case, in which seepage through a poorly protected core eroded rapidly and the dam was lost within hours.**

**The modes of earth dam failure, since this is what the drainage guards against:**

| Mode | Share of failures | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| **HYDRAULIC — OVERTOPPING** | **About a third** ← | **Inadequate spillway capacity, or a blocked spillway; an earth dam is destroyed rapidly once overtopped** ← |
| **SEEPAGE — piping and internal erosion** | **About a third** ← | **Inadequate filters, cracked core, foundation seepage, animal burrows, conduits through the embankment** ← |
| **STRUCTURAL — slope failure** | **The remainder** | **Slides during construction, on sudden drawdown, or during an earthquake** ← |

> **THE OVERTOPPING SHARE IS THE REASON EARTH DAMS ARE GIVEN SUCH GENEROUS SPILLWAYS: a concrete dam can be overtopped and survive, and an earth dam cannot.**

> **Water flowing over an embankment erodes a notch, the notch concentrates the flow, and the flow deepens the notch — the same runaway geometry as piping, and it can breach a large dam in hours.**

> **That single vulnerability governs the whole design philosophy: freeboard is generous, wave run-up is calculated, and the spillway is sized for an extreme flood rather than an economic one.**

**And SUDDEN DRAWDOWN, the structural case that is easiest to overlook:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Reservoir full for a long period** | **The UPSTREAM shell becomes saturated** ← |
| **The reservoir is drawn down rapidly** | **The water supporting the upstream slope is removed** ← |
| **But the pore water inside the shell CANNOT drain as fast** | **So the pore pressures remain high while the external support has gone** ← |
| **Result** | **The upstream slope's effective stress collapses and it SLIDES** ← |

> **This is the mirror image of the clay-cutting problem met in soil mechanics: there, unloading generated NEGATIVE pore pressures that dissipated over years; here, the external support is removed faster than the POSITIVE pore pressures can dissipate.**

> **In both cases the danger lies in the mismatch between the speed of the load change and the speed of drainage — which is the recurring theme of effective stress analysis, and the reason the CU triaxial test exists.**

> **The remedies are to use free-draining material in the upstream shell, to limit the permitted rate of drawdown by operating rule, and to flatten the upstream slope.**

examTip.trick: **It intercepts seepage through the core and draws the PHREATIC LINE down, keeping the downstream shell UNSATURATED** — so its full shear strength is available and the slope can be steeper.
examTip.trap: **Seepage cannot be prevented, only controlled** — and a drain failing the RETENTION criterion actively removes the core. Filters are the most safety-critical element of an earth dam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Failures: about a third OVERTOPPING, a third SEEPAGE/piping, the rest structural.** An earth dam cannot survive overtopping as a concrete dam can, which is why its spillway is sized for an extreme rather than an economic flood.

questions.stem: At the intake of a hydropower scheme, the approach velocity through the TRASHRACK is normally limited to about 0.6 to 1.0 m/s in order to:
options: Limit the head loss through the rack and allow trash to be raked off rather than being pinned against the bars
Increase the discharge entering the intake
Prevent the water from freezing
Ensure the rack bars remain in tension
questions.solution:
**To limit the HEAD LOSS through the rack, and to allow accumulated trash to be RAKED off rather than being pinned immovably against the bars by the flow.**

**Why the velocity limit matters:**

| Consequence of an excessive approach velocity | Note |
|---|---|
| **HEAD LOSS rises as the SQUARE of the velocity** | **And head lost at the intake is lost for the plant's whole life** ← |
| **Trash is PRESSED against the bars and cannot be raked off** ← | **A rake cannot dislodge debris held by the flow's full force** |
| **The rack blocks progressively, raising the velocity through what remains** | **A self-worsening cycle** ← |
| **Structural load on the bars increases** | **A fully blocked rack can carry the full differential head and collapse** ← |
| **Fish are drawn onto the rack and cannot escape** | **IMPINGEMENT — a real ecological concern** ← |
| **Vortices and air entrainment** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES THE FAILURE SEQUENCE THAT ACTUALLY OCCURS: a partly blocked rack has a smaller open area, so the velocity through it rises, which presses the trash harder and catches more, which blocks it further.**

> **During a monsoon flood carrying leaves, branches and plastic, a rack can go from clear to fully blocked in a short time — and a fully blocked rack either collapses under the head difference or starves the turbines.**

> **That is why the velocity is kept low and why mechanical raking is provided on any plant of consequence: the rack must be cleanable while it is working.**

**The design of a trashrack:**

| Feature | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Approach velocity** | **0.6 to 1.0 m/s** ← |
| **Bar spacing — PELTON turbines** | **Finest, since a small object can damage a needle or a bucket — often 20 to 50 mm** ← |
| **Bar spacing — FRANCIS** | **50 to 100 mm** |
| **Bar spacing — KAPLAN** | **Coarsest, 100 to 150 mm — the large passages tolerate debris** ← |
| **Inclination to the horizontal** | **1:4 to 1:5 (about 70-80°), so a rake can be drawn up the face** ← |
| **Head loss** | **Typically 0.1 to 0.3 m when clean** ← |

> **The BAR SPACING follows the turbine's tolerance, and the pattern is consistent: the smaller and faster the passages in the machine, the finer the rack must be.**

> **A Pelton's needle and buckets are precisely machined and run at very high velocity, so a small hard object does great damage; a Kaplan's passages are large and its blades robust.**

> **The cost of the finer rack is a greater head loss and more frequent cleaning, so the requirement is not made stricter than the machine needs.**

**KIRSCHMER'S formula for the head loss, since it shows what the designer controls:**

> **h_L = K_t (t/b)^(4/3) (V²/2g) sin θ**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **K_t** | **A shape factor for the bar section — 2.42 for a rectangular bar, 1.79 for a round-nosed, 1.67 for a streamlined bar** ← |
| **t/b** | **The ratio of bar THICKNESS to clear SPACING** ← |
| **V** | The approach velocity |
| **θ** | The rack's inclination |

> **The (t/b)^(4/3) term is the one the designer can most easily improve: thinner bars at wider spacing reduce the loss substantially.**

> **And the SHAPE FACTOR shows that a streamlined or round-nosed bar loses about a third less head than a plain rectangular one — for no change in strength or spacing, and at very little extra cost.**

> **That is a cheap and permanent efficiency gain, and it is regularly overlooked in small schemes where flat bar is used simply because it is what the fabricator has.**

**The intake's other requirements, since the trashrack is one element:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adequate SUBMERGENCE** | **To prevent a vortex drawing AIR into the conduit — at least 1.5 to 2 times the conduit diameter** ← |
| **Exclusion of BED LOAD** | **A raised sill, a gravel trap, or an orientation that draws from above the bed** ← |
| **A BELL-MOUTHED entry** | **Reduces the entry loss from K = 0.5 to about 0.05** ← |
| **A control GATE, and a stoplog slot upstream of it** | For isolation and maintenance |
| **An AIR VENT downstream of the gate** | **To admit air when the gate is closed and the conduit drains — or the conduit collapses** ← |
| **Accessibility for raking and gate operation** | Especially in flood conditions |

> **THE AIR VENT IN THE FIFTH ROW IS A SMALL ITEM WITH A LARGE CONSEQUENCE, and its omission has destroyed conduits:**

> **When the intake gate is closed while water continues to flow away downstream, a partial vacuum forms in the conduit behind it.**

> **A steel penstock or a thin lining has very little resistance to EXTERNAL pressure and will buckle inward — a failure that occurs during an ordinary shutdown rather than under any extreme condition.**

> **The vent costs almost nothing and must be sized to admit air as fast as the water can leave, which is a straightforward calculation and an easy one to neglect.**

examTip.trick: **0.6-1.0 m/s limits head loss (∝ V²) and keeps trash rakeable** — above that the debris is pinned against the bars and cannot be removed.
examTip.trap: **Blocking is self-worsening** — less open area raises the velocity, which catches and holds more debris. A fully blocked rack can carry the whole differential head and collapse.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bar spacing follows the turbine: PELTON finest (20-50 mm), Francis 50-100, KAPLAN coarsest (100-150).** Kirschmer: loss ∝ (t/b)^(4/3)V², and a streamlined bar loses a third less than a rectangular one for nothing.

questions.stem: A CIRCULAR cross-section is preferred to a D-shaped or horseshoe section for a hydropower tunnel when the tunnel:
options: Is very short
Is excavated in soft ground requiring immediate support
Carries water under high internal pressure
Must accommodate a roadway during construction
questions.solution:
**When it carries water under HIGH INTERNAL PRESSURE.**

**Why a circle suits internal pressure:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **A circular lining under uniform internal pressure carries it as pure HOOP TENSION** ← | **With NO bending at all** ← |
| **Any other shape develops BENDING MOMENTS** | **A flat invert or a straight wall must bend to resist pressure, which concrete does poorly** ← |
| **Hoop tension is resisted efficiently** | **By circumferential reinforcement, or by the surrounding rock's confinement** ← |
| **A circle also has the best HYDRAULIC efficiency** | **The maximum area for the least perimeter, so the least friction** ← |

> **THE ABSENCE OF BENDING IS THE DECISIVE STRUCTURAL POINT: a shape that resists load purely in direct tension or compression uses its material far more efficiently than one that must bend, exactly as an arch does in compression.**

> **So the circular pressure tunnel is the hydraulic equivalent of the arch — the shape matched to the loading.**

**When the other shapes are used:**

| Shape | Suits |
|---|---|
| **CIRCULAR** | **HIGH internal pressure; also high external rock pressure from all directions; TBM excavation** ← |
| **D-SHAPED (flat invert, arched roof)** | **LOW or no internal pressure — headrace tunnels above the hydraulic grade line, and access and diversion tunnels** ← |
| **HORSESHOE** | **A compromise — a curved invert giving some pressure capacity with a nearly flat floor for construction** ← |
| **Rectangular** | Only in very sound rock at low pressure; rare |
| **Egg-shaped / oval** | Where vertical rock pressure greatly exceeds horizontal |

> **THE FLAT INVERT IS THE ATTRACTION OF THE D AND HORSESHOE SHAPES, and its value is purely constructional:**

> **A flat floor lets vehicles, muck cars and equipment run through the tunnel during excavation, which a circular section does not — a circular tunnel needs a temporary invert filled in and later removed.**

> **So the choice is between the structural efficiency of the circle and the constructional convenience of the flat invert, and the decision follows from whether internal pressure exists.**

> **A drill-and-blast headrace tunnel operating with a free surface will normally be D-shaped or horseshoe; a pressure shaft or a pressure tunnel will be circular.**

**TUNNEL LINING, since the shape and the lining are decided together:**

| Purpose of a lining | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRUCTURAL support of the rock** | Where the rock cannot stand unsupported |
| **Reduce FRICTION** | **A concrete lining has n ≈ 0.014 against 0.030-0.040 for rough blasted rock — more than halving the head loss** ← |
| **Prevent LEAKAGE out of the tunnel** | **Critical where the internal pressure exceeds the external ground water pressure** ← |
| **Prevent water entering the rock and destabilising it** | **Hydraulic jacking, and the softening of weak rock** ← |
| **Protect erodible rock from scour** | ← |

> **THE FRICTION ITEM IS OFTEN THE ONE THAT PAYS FOR THE LINING: an unlined blasted tunnel is very rough, and over several kilometres the extra head loss is a permanent reduction in output.**

> **The economic comparison is the familiar one — capital cost of the lining against the capitalised value of the head saved over the plant's life — and for a long tunnel on a high-value scheme the lining usually wins on hydraulics alone, before any structural need is considered.**

> **Where the rock is sound and the tunnel short, an UNLINED tunnel is entirely acceptable and is used — Norway in particular has built extensive unlined pressure tunnels, relying on the rock's own confinement.**

**The CONFINEMENT CRITERION, which decides whether an unlined or lightly lined pressure tunnel is safe:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **The internal water pressure tries to lift and split the rock** | **HYDRAULIC JACKING** ← |
| **It is resisted by the WEIGHT of rock above** | ← |
| **The rule of thumb (Norwegian criterion)** | **The vertical rock cover must exceed the internal pressure head, with a factor of safety — and the SIDE cover matters in a valley** ← |
| **In a steep valley the critical direction is toward the VALLEY SIDE, not vertically** ← | **Because the rock cover measured perpendicular to the slope is far less than the vertical depth** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT THAT MATTERS IN HIMALAYAN TERRAIN AND IS EASY TO MISS: in a steep-sided valley, a tunnel with 300 m of rock vertically above it may have only 80 m of cover toward the valley side.**

> **The pressure will find the shortest path, so it is the MINIMUM cover in any direction that governs — and a pressure tunnel following a valley wall must be set far enough into the hillside, not merely deep enough below the surface.**

> **Failures have occurred where this was assessed vertically: the water jacked its way out through the valley side, emptying the tunnel and destabilising the slope.**

> **The remedy where cover is insufficient is a STEEL LINER embedded in concrete, which carries the pressure structurally and does not rely on the rock at all — expensive, and the standard solution for the final reach of a pressure shaft near the powerhouse, where cover is always least.**

examTip.trick: **A circle carries uniform internal pressure as pure HOOP TENSION with NO bending** — any other shape must bend, which concrete does poorly. It is also hydraulically the most efficient.
examTip.trap: **The D and horseshoe shapes exist for CONSTRUCTIONAL convenience** — a flat invert lets vehicles run through during excavation. So free-surface headrace tunnels are D-shaped; pressure tunnels are circular.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lining often pays on FRICTION alone** (n from 0.035 blasted to 0.014 lined). And for an unlined pressure tunnel it is the MINIMUM rock cover in ANY direction that governs — in a steep valley that is toward the valley SIDE, not vertically.

questions.stem: The ECONOMIC DIAMETER of a penstock is that which:
options: Gives the maximum possible velocity of flow
Minimises the sum of the penstock's capital cost and the capitalised value of the energy lost to friction over the plant's life
Is the smallest diameter the available steel plate permits
Makes the head loss exactly zero
questions.solution:
**The diameter that MINIMISES the SUM of the penstock's capital cost and the capitalised value of the energy lost to friction over the plant's life.**

**The two opposing costs:**

| As the diameter INCREASES | Effect |
|---|---|
| **CAPITAL cost** | **RISES — more steel, larger anchor blocks, bigger supports, more excavation** ← |
| **FRICTION head loss** | **FALLS steeply — as 1/D⁵ at a given discharge** ← |
| **Energy lost over the life** | **Falls with it** ← |
| **The SUM of the two** | **Falls, reaches a MINIMUM, then rises — and that minimum is the economic diameter** ← |

> **The 1/D⁵ dependence makes the friction curve very steep at small diameters and very flat at large ones, so the total-cost curve is ASYMMETRIC: it falls sharply on the left and rises gently on the right.**

> **The practical consequence is worth knowing: IF IN DOUBT, ERR ON THE LARGE SIDE. A penstock slightly larger than the optimum costs a little extra capital; one slightly smaller wastes energy for fifty years.**

**Why the loss is capitalised rather than merely noted:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The head loss is PERMANENT** | **Every hour the plant runs, for its whole life** ← |
| **A capital cost is paid ONCE** | ← |
| **So the two must be brought to a common basis** | **Either capitalise the annual energy loss, or annualise the capital cost** ← |
| **The capitalisation uses the discount rate and the plant's life** | **Which is exactly the equivalent annual cost calculation of engineering economics** ← |

> **A worked feel for the magnitudes: a permanent head loss of 1 m on a plant of 10 m³/s at 85 per cent efficiency costs 9.81 × 10 × 1 × 0.85 = 83 kW.**

> **At a 55 per cent capacity factor that is 83 × 8,760 × 0.55 = 400,000 kWh a year — and over fifty years, discounted, a very substantial sum.**

> **So a metre of head casually lost at the design stage is a permanent charge on the project, and it is why the economic diameter calculation is worth doing properly rather than adopting a rule of thumb.**

**The empirical rules, for a first estimate:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Economic VELOCITY of 3 to 5 m/s** | **The commonest quick check** ← |
| **Head loss limited to 3 to 5 per cent of the gross head** | **Another common target** ← |
| **Bondschu's, Sarkaria's and similar formulae** | Empirical expressions in terms of head, discharge and power |

> **These are starting points for the iteration, not substitutes for it — and they diverge for unusual cases, such as a very long penstock or an unusually high energy value.**

**The NUMBER of penstocks, which is the related decision:**

| Arrangement | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| **ONE large penstock with a manifold to several units** | **Cheaper — the cost per unit of capacity falls with size; less excavation and fewer anchors** ← | **A single point of failure — a penstock fault shuts the WHOLE plant** ← |
| **SEPARATE penstocks, one per unit** | **Redundancy; a unit can be isolated for maintenance while the others run** ← | More expensive |

> **The usual compromise on a larger plant is a single penstock down the hillside branching into a manifold near the powerhouse, with a valve on each branch — which gives most of the economy of the single pipe and most of the maintenance flexibility of separate ones.**

**And the other design decisions that accompany the diameter:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **WALL THICKNESS** | **From the design pressure (static head PLUS the water hammer surge), with a minimum for handling and corrosion allowance** ← |
| **Surface or BURIED** | **Buried is protected from temperature change, impact and vandalism, and needs no expansion joints — but is inaccessible for inspection** ← |
| **ANCHOR blocks at every bend** | Resist the unbalanced thrust |
| **EXPANSION joints between anchors** | **For an exposed penstock — a 500 m run moves over 100 mm** ← |
| **Air valve at the top** | **Admits air on draining, or the pipe collapses** ← |
| **Corrosion protection** | Coating internally and externally; cathodic protection if buried |

> **THE BURIED-AGAINST-EXPOSED CHOICE IN THE SECOND ROW IS A REAL ONE IN NEPALI CONDITIONS, and the arguments run both ways:**

> **Burying protects the pipe from the very large diurnal temperature range at altitude, removes the need for expansion joints and rollers, protects it from rockfall and from theft of the steel, and is less visually intrusive.**

> **Exposing it allows inspection and painting, avoids the excavation cost on a steep slope, and permits repair without excavation.**

> **The decisive factor is often SLOPE STABILITY: a buried penstock on a creeping hillside is strained by ground movement it cannot be seen to be suffering, while an exposed one on piers can be re-levelled — so on unstable ground, exposure is frequently the safer choice despite its other disadvantages.**

examTip.trick: **Minimise (capital cost + capitalised friction energy loss).** Capital rises with D; friction falls as 1/D⁵ — the sum has a minimum, and that is the economic diameter.
examTip.trap: **The total-cost curve is ASYMMETRIC — steep on the small side, flat on the large.** If in doubt, err LARGE: a slightly big penstock costs a little capital, a slightly small one wastes energy for fifty years.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quick check: economic velocity 3-5 m/s, or head loss 3-5 % of gross.** And on unstable Nepali hillsides an EXPOSED penstock is often safer than a buried one — ground movement can be seen and the pipe re-levelled.

questions.stem: Compared with a Francis turbine, a PELTON turbine and a KAPLAN turbine both maintain good efficiency at PART LOAD because:
options: They run at a much higher rotational speed
They operate with a completely submerged runner
Their efficiency is independent of the head
They have adjustable control elements
questions.solution:
**Because both have ADJUSTABLE control elements** — the Pelton's spear (needle) valve, and the Kaplan's adjustable runner BLADES in addition to its guide vanes.

**The part-load efficiency curves compared:**

| Turbine | Efficiency curve | Efficiency at 40 % load |
|---|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **VERY FLAT — excellent over a wide range** ← | **About 85 per cent** ← |
| **KAPLAN (double regulated)** | **VERY FLAT** ← | **About 88 per cent** ← |
| **FRANCIS** | **PEAKY — falls away below about 60 per cent load** ← | **About 65 per cent** ← |
| **PROPELLER (fixed blades)** | **VERY PEAKY — the worst** ← | **About 40 per cent** ← |

> **The PROPELLER row is the instructive comparison: a Kaplan IS a propeller turbine with adjustable blades, and the difference between the two rows is entirely due to that adjustment.**

**Why adjustability matters — the underlying mechanism:**

> **A turbine is most efficient when the water enters the runner at the blade's designed angle, without shock or separation.**

| Turbine | What happens at part load |
|---|---|
| **FIXED blades (Francis, propeller)** | **The guide vanes close, changing the direction of the incoming flow — but the runner blade angle CANNOT change to match, so the water strikes at the wrong angle. SHOCK LOSSES and separation follow** ← |
| **KAPLAN (double regulation)** | **BOTH the guide vanes and the runner blades adjust together, so the entry angle stays correct at every load** ← |
| **PELTON** | **The needle simply reduces the jet's SIZE, not its VELOCITY or its direction — so the bucket sees exactly the same conditions, merely less water** ← |

> **THE PELTON'S BEHAVIOUR IS THE MOST ELEGANT OF THE THREE AND IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING PROPERLY:**

> **Closing the needle narrows the jet, but the jet's VELOCITY depends only on the head (V = √(2gH)), which is unchanged.**

> **So the jet still strikes the buckets at the same speed and the same angle, and the bucket's hydraulics are unaltered — the machine is simply processing a smaller stream of identical water.**

> **That is why a Pelton's efficiency curve is almost flat down to about 20 per cent load, and it makes the Pelton exceptionally well suited to a run-of-river scheme whose flow varies through the year — which is precisely the Nepali high-head case.**

**The practical consequences for plant design:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A FRANCIS plant on a variable river benefits greatly from MULTIPLE UNITS** ← | **Shut some down and run the others near their best point** |
| **A PELTON plant needs multiple units less urgently** | **A single unit performs well across the range; though multi-JET machines give further flexibility** ← |
| **A Kaplan suits a low-head river with variable flow** | **Its double regulation handles both** ← |
| **A fixed-blade PROPELLER suits only a steady flow** | **Which is why it is used mainly where the discharge is regulated** ← |

> **The MULTI-JET Pelton in the second row deserves a note: a Pelton may have up to six jets, and jets can be shut off individually.**

> **So a six-jet machine running on two jets is operating each of those two at its full design condition — giving essentially full efficiency at one third load, which no single-runner reaction turbine can approach.**

**The cost of the Kaplan's adjustability, since nothing is free:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Mechanical complexity** | **A hub mechanism, oil supply and linkages inside the rotating runner** ← |
| **Cost** | **Significantly more than a fixed propeller** |
| **Maintenance** | **Oil leakage from the hub into the river is a real environmental concern** ← |
| **Reliability** | More parts to fail |

> **So the choice between a Kaplan and a fixed propeller is exactly the choice between part-load efficiency and simplicity — and where the flow is steady, the simpler machine is correct.**

**And the SEMI-KAPLAN, which is the intermediate:**

| Machine | Regulation |
|---|---|
| **Propeller** | **Neither adjustable — SINGLE speed, single flow** |
| **SEMI-KAPLAN** | **Adjustable BLADES, FIXED guide vanes — good part-load performance at lower cost** ← |
| **Full KAPLAN** | **DOUBLE regulated — both adjustable** ← |

> **The semi-Kaplan is common in small hydropower because it captures most of the part-load benefit at a fraction of the complexity — and in a small plant with a simple control system, dispensing with adjustable guide vanes also removes a governor requirement.**

> **That combination of adequate performance and mechanical simplicity is the recurring theme in small hydropower generally, and it is why the CROSSFLOW turbine — which is inefficient at its best point but flat across its range, and can be built in a modest workshop — remains widely used in Nepal despite being outperformed by every other type on paper.**

The Pelton's needle, and the Kaplan's adjustable BLADES as well as its guide vanes.

examTip.trick: **Adjustable elements keep the flow entering at the correct blade angle.** A Kaplan IS a propeller with adjustable blades — and at 40 % load they give about 88 % and 40 % efficiency respectively.
examTip.trap: **The Pelton's needle changes the jet's SIZE, not its VELOCITY or direction** — jet speed depends only on head. So the buckets see identical conditions and efficiency stays flat down to ~20 % load.
examTip.mnemonic: **Francis on a variable river needs MULTIPLE UNITS; a Pelton does not.** A six-jet Pelton on two jets runs those two at full design condition. And in Nepali small hydro, the CROSSFLOW survives because it is flat across its range and workshop-buildable.

questions.stem: In highway alignment, OBLIGATORY POINTS are:
options: Points through which the alignment must pass, or which it must avoid
The points at which the gradient changes
The chainage marks set out along the centre line
The points at which the road crosses a contour
questions.solution:
**Points through which the alignment MUST PASS, or which it must AVOID.**

**The two classes:**

| Points the alignment MUST PASS THROUGH | Points it must AVOID |
|---|---|
| **A BRIDGE SITE — a narrow, stable, straight reach of river** ← | **Unstable slopes, active landslides and slip zones** ← |
| **A mountain PASS or saddle** ← | **Marshy and poor ground** |
| **Intermediate towns and villages to be served** | **Religious, cultural and archaeological sites** ← |
| **An existing road, bridge or terminal to be connected** | **Forest and protected areas** |
| **A stable bench or ridge** | **Expensive land and built-up property** |
| **Sources of construction material** | **Very steep rock faces requiring heavy cutting** |
| **A junction with another route** | Water bodies and flood plains |

> **The obligatory points are settled FIRST, before any gradient or curvature is considered — they define the corridor within which the alignment must be found.**

**Why the BRIDGE SITE is usually the strongest constraint:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A bridge costs FAR MORE per metre than road** | **So its length must be minimised** ← |
| **A good crossing requires a NARROW, STABLE, STRAIGHT reach with firm banks and a non-migrating channel** | **Such places may occur only once or twice along a river** ← |
| **The approach must be reasonably straight and level** | Adding a further constraint |

> **SO THE PRACTICE IS TO FIX THE BRIDGE SITES FIRST AND ALIGN THE ROAD TO REACH THEM — the reverse of the intuitive order, in which one would lay out the road and cross wherever it arrived.**

> **A road aligned first and bridged second will cross at whatever point it happens to meet the river, which may be a wide braided reach requiring a structure several times longer than necessary.**

**The requirements of a good alignment, once the obligatory points are fixed:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORT** | **The shortest route is the cheapest to build and to use — but rarely achievable** ← |
| **EASY to construct and to maintain** | ← |
| **SAFE — for both construction and traffic** | **Adequate sight distance, gentle curvature, stable slopes** ← |
| **ECONOMICAL — on a whole-life basis** | **Construction plus maintenance plus vehicle operating cost** ← |

> **THESE FOUR PULL AGAINST ONE ANOTHER, and the tension between the first and the rest is the substance of route location:**

> **The SHORTEST route in hill country is a straight line over the ridges — which would be impossibly steep, expensive and unsafe.**

> **The EASIEST route follows the valley or the contour — which is far longer, and may be exposed to floods and debris flows.**

> **The economical alignment is the compromise, and it is found by comparing several candidate routes rather than by optimising one.**

**The factors CONTROLLING alignment, in the order they are considered:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **OBLIGATORY points** | **Considered first — they define the corridor** ← |
| **TRAFFIC — its origin, destination and volume** | **The road must serve the desire lines, not merely connect two points** ← |
| **GEOMETRIC design standards** | Gradient, curvature, sight distance |
| **ECONOMY** | Construction, maintenance and operating costs together |
| **Other considerations** | **Drainage, geology, hydrology, political and environmental factors, material sources** ← |

> **The special controls in HILLY terrain, which govern Nepali practice:**

| Control | Note |
|---|---|
