| **STABILITY of the slopes** | **The dominant factor — an alignment through unstable ground will never be maintainable at any cost** ← |
| **Geology, and the DIP of the strata relative to the slope** | **Cut AGAINST the dip wherever there is a choice** ← |
| **Drainage crossings** | Every stream is a structure and a maintenance point |
| **RESISTANCE TO CUTTING and filling** | Rock is expensive to cut, and fill on a steep slope is unstable |
| **Spoil DISPOSAL sites** | **Must be identified as part of the alignment, not left to the contractor** ← |

> **THE STABILITY REQUIREMENT DESERVES ITS PRIMACY, and the reason is economic as much as technical: a road through an unstable slope is not merely expensive to build but permanently expensive to keep.**

> **It will be blocked every monsoon, its retaining works will fail repeatedly, and its maintenance cost over thirty years can exceed its construction cost several times over.**

> **A longer alignment on stable ground is therefore frequently the cheaper option on a whole-life basis, and the comparison must be made on that basis rather than on construction cost alone.**

> **That is the single most consequential judgement in Nepali hill road location, and it is the one most often decided the wrong way, because the construction budget and the maintenance budget belong to different institutions and different years.**

examTip.trick: **Points the alignment must PASS THROUGH (bridge sites, passes, towns) or must AVOID (unstable slopes, forests, cultural sites).** They are fixed FIRST and define the corridor.
examTip.trap: **Fix the BRIDGE SITES first and align the road to reach them** — the reverse of the intuitive order. A road aligned first will cross wherever it happens to arrive, which may need a structure several times longer.
examTip.mnemonic: **A good alignment is SHORT, EASY, SAFE and ECONOMICAL — and the first pulls against the others.** In hills, SLOPE STABILITY dominates: a longer route on stable ground is usually cheaper over thirty years, though the construction budget will not show it.

questions.stem: CAMBER is provided on a road's carriageway principally to:
options: Counteract the centrifugal force on curves
Increase the sight distance
Drain rain water rapidly from the surface to the sides
Allow vehicles to overtake more easily
questions.solution:
**To DRAIN rain water rapidly from the surface to the sides.**

**Why rapid surface drainage matters so much:**

| Consequence of water standing on the carriageway | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water enters the pavement through cracks and joints** | **Weakening the base, sub-base and subgrade** ← |
| **STRIPPING of the bitumen from the aggregate** | **Water displaces the binder film — the mechanism met in the bitumen discussion** ← |
| **PUMPING at joints and cracks under traffic** | **Fines are ejected and voids form beneath** ← |
| **AQUAPLANING and loss of skid resistance** | **A safety hazard at speed** ← |
| **Splash and spray, reducing visibility** | ← |
| **Frost damage at altitude** | ← |

> **THE FIRST THREE ARE THE STRUCTURAL CASE AND THEY RETURN TO THE PRINCIPLE STATED IN PAVEMENT DESIGN: the three most important things are drainage, drainage and drainage.**

> **Camber is the first line of that drainage — it removes the water before it can enter — and it is the cheapest element of the whole drainage system, costing nothing but the shaping of the surface.**

> **Option (a) describes SUPERELEVATION, which is a different provision on curves; the two are related in form and quite different in purpose, and camber is a distractor for superelevation as often as the reverse.**

**The recommended camber values, which depend on the SURFACE and the RAINFALL:**

| Surface type | Camber in LOW rainfall | Camber in HEAVY rainfall |
|---|---|---|
| **Cement concrete and high-quality bituminous** | **1 in 60 (1.7 %)** | **1 in 50 (2.0 %)** ← |
| **Thin bituminous surfacing** | **1 in 50 (2.0 %)** | **1 in 40 (2.5 %)** ← |
| **Water bound macadam, gravel** | **1 in 40 (2.5 %)** | **1 in 33 (3.0 %)** ← |
| **EARTH roads** | **1 in 33 (3.0 %)** | **1 in 25 (4.0 %)** ← |

> **THE PATTERN IS CONSISTENT AND EASY TO REASON FROM: the ROUGHER and more PERMEABLE the surface, the STEEPER the camber must be.**

> **A smooth impermeable concrete surface sheds water readily and needs little slope; a rough gravel surface holds water in its irregularities and admits it readily, so it needs much more.**

> **And heavier rainfall requires a steeper camber for the same surface, for the obvious reason.**

**Why the camber must not be EXCESSIVE, which is the other half of the design:**

| Consequence of too steep a camber | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vehicles tend to drift toward the EDGE of the carriageway** | **Drivers correct by moving to the crown, concentrating traffic there** ← |
| **Traffic CONCENTRATES along the crown** | **Rutting and wear along the centre line** ← |
| **Overturning risk for high vehicles, especially on a curve** | ← |
| **Discomfort to occupants; strain on the vehicle's springs** | ← |
| **Transverse erosion of an unsurfaced shoulder** | **Water running off fast enough to scour** ← |

> **So camber is bounded on both sides: too little and the water stands, too much and the traffic misbehaves — and the values in the table are the compromise for each surface.**

**The SHAPES of camber:**

| Shape | Note |
|---|---|
| **PARABOLIC (barrel)** | **Steeper at the edges and flatter at the crown; comfortable for fast traffic, but the flat crown drains slowly** ← |
| **STRAIGHT LINE (two planes meeting at the crown)** | **Uniform slope throughout; simple to construct and to check; a sharp crown that wears** ← |
| **COMBINATION — straight with a parabolic crown** | **The usual modern compromise: uniform drainage with a rounded crown** ← |

> **On modern high-speed roads a straight-line camber is generally preferred because its uniform slope drains the whole width equally, and it is far easier to set out and to verify with a straight edge.**

**And the CROSS-SECTION as a whole, since camber is one element of it:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **CARRIAGEWAY** | **3.75 m for a single lane; 7.0 m for two lanes; 3.5 m per lane on multi-lane roads** ← |
| **SHOULDERS** | **Minimum 2.5 m on a national highway; 0.9 m minimum on a hill road** ← |
| **Shoulder CAMBER** | **STEEPER than the carriageway's — typically 0.5 % more, so water carries on outward** ← |
| **KERB** | Separates the carriageway from the shoulder or footpath |
| **SIDE DRAINS** | **Below the subgrade level, so they drain the pavement and not merely the surface** ← |
| **ROAD MARGIN — footpath, cycle track, parking, guard rail** | — |
| **RIGHT OF WAY** | The land width acquired |

> **THE SIDE DRAIN'S DEPTH IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE DETAIL MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND IT MATTERS GREATLY: a side drain whose invert is above the subgrade level removes the surface water and leaves the pavement's foundation saturated.**

> **The drain must be deep enough to lower the water table below the subgrade — otherwise the road sits in a bath, and the camber's careful work is undone.**

> **On Nepali roads, side drains that are silted up, built too shallow, or discharged nowhere are among the commonest causes of premature pavement failure — and they are also the cheapest defect to remedy, which is why routine drain clearance is the highest-value maintenance activity there is.**

examTip.trick: **Camber drains the surface; SUPERELEVATION (option a) counteracts centrifugal force on curves.** The two are similar in form and quite different in purpose.
examTip.trap: **The ROUGHER and more PERMEABLE the surface, the STEEPER the camber** — concrete 1.7-2 %, thin bituminous 2-2.5 %, WBM 2.5-3 %, earth 3-4 %. And too MUCH camber concentrates traffic along the crown.
examTip.mnemonic: **The SIDE DRAIN must be BELOW subgrade level, not merely below the surface** — otherwise the pavement sits in a bath and the camber's work is undone. Clearing silted drains is the highest-value road maintenance there is.

questions.stem: The SET-BACK DISTANCE at a horizontal curve is the:
options: Distance by which the road is widened on the inside of the curve
Length of the transition curve at each end
Distance between the tangent point and the apex of the curve
Clearance required from the centre line of the inner lane to any obstruction on the inside of the curve
questions.solution:
**The CLEARANCE required from the centre line of the inner lane to any obstruction on the INSIDE of the curve**, so that the required sight distance is actually available.

**Why the provision is needed:**

> **On a horizontal curve, the driver's line of sight is a CHORD, while the road is an ARC — so the line of sight cuts ACROSS the inside of the bend.**

> **Anything standing on the inside of the curve therefore blocks it: a cut face, a wall, a parapet, a building, a hedge, a line of trees, or a parked vehicle.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The available sight distance can be FAR LESS than the stopping sight distance** ← | **Even though the road's geometry is otherwise perfectly adequate** |
| **The deficiency is invisible in plan unless it is specifically checked** ← | ← |
| **It is a leading cause of accidents on hill roads** | ← |

> **Option (a) describes EXTRA WIDENING, which is also provided on the inside of a curve — so the two are easily confused, and both are real provisions at the same location.**

**The expression for the set-back:**

> **For a curve LONGER than the sight distance S, and with R the radius of the centre line of the road and d the distance from the centre line to the inner lane's centre line:**

> **m = R − (R − d) cos(θ/2), where θ = S/(R − d) radians**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **m grows as the RADIUS decreases** | **A sharp curve needs much more clearance** ← |
| **m grows as the SIGHT DISTANCE required increases** | **So a higher design speed demands far more** ← |
| **For a curve SHORTER than S, a different expression applies** | The chord extends beyond the curve |

> **A worked feel for the magnitude: for R = 100 m, a two-lane road (d = 1.875 m) and an SSD of 80 m:**

> **θ = 80/98.125 = 0.8153 rad; cos(θ/2) = cos(0.4077) = 0.9180**

> **m = 100 − 98.125 × 0.9180 = 100 − 90.08 = 9.9 m** ←

> **So nearly TEN METRES of clearance is needed from the inner lane's centre line — which on a hill road means cutting the slope back very substantially, and it is a large and often unwelcome quantity.**

**Why this is so difficult in hill terrain:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **The obstruction is usually the CUT SLOPE itself** | **It cannot simply be removed — it is the hillside** ← |
| **Cutting back 10 m into a steep slope is an enormous excavation** | **And it creates a higher, less stable cut face** ← |
| **The spoil must be disposed of** | Adding to the environmental cost |
| **A higher cut face is more prone to failure and rockfall** | **So the remedy for one hazard creates another** ← |

> **THAT LAST ROW IS THE GENUINE DILEMMA OF HILL ROAD DESIGN, and it has no clean resolution:**

> **Providing full sight distance requires a deep cut; a deep cut is unstable and sheds rock onto the road; and rockfall is itself a serious hazard.**

> **The practical resolution is a combination — accept a lower design speed on the curve, post a warning and a speed restriction, provide a convex MIRROR at the sharpest bends, sound the horn (which is why Nepali hill roads carry "Blow Horn" signs at every bend), and cut back only as far as stability allows.**

> **This is a case where the geometric standard genuinely cannot be met economically, and the honest response is to reduce the design speed rather than to pretend the standard has been achieved.**

**The associated provisions at a horizontal curve, so the whole set is together:**

| Provision | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **SUPERELEVATION** | Counteracts centrifugal force |
| **EXTRA WIDENING** | **Mechanical off-tracking plus a psychological allowance** ← |
| **TRANSITION curve** | **Introduces curvature, superelevation and widening gradually** ← |
| **SET-BACK (clearance) on the inside** | **This question — sight distance** ← |
| **GRADE COMPENSATION** | **Reduces the gradient through a sharp curve, since curve resistance adds to grade resistance** ← |
| **Adequate radius** | From e + f = V²/(127R) |

> **All six are required together at any sharp curve, and the set-back is the one most often omitted from an estimate because it appears as EARTHWORK rather than as a geometric item.**

> **A curve set out correctly in plan, superelevated and widened, can still be unsafe because nobody costed the clearing of its inside — and the deficiency only becomes apparent when the road is open and drivers cannot see round the bend.**

> **Checking sight distance on the DRAWING, by scaling the chord across each curve, takes minutes and prevents exactly that outcome.**

The required sight distance is available.

examTip.trick: **m = R − (R − d) cos(θ/2), with θ = S/(R − d) radians.** The line of sight is a CHORD while the road is an ARC, so anything on the inside of the bend blocks it.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is EXTRA WIDENING** — also provided on the inside of a curve, and constantly confused with the set-back.
examTip.mnemonic: **For R = 100 m and SSD 80 m, the set-back is nearly 10 m** — an enormous cut on a hillside, which then becomes unstable and sheds rock. Where it cannot be met, REDUCE THE DESIGN SPEED honestly rather than pretend the standard is achieved.

questions.stem: The LOS ANGELES ABRASION test on road aggregate measures its:
options: Resistance to wear and abrasion by rubbing and impact
Resistance to crushing under a gradually applied load
Water absorption
Resistance to freezing and thawing
questions.solution:
**Its resistance to WEAR and ABRASION** — by the combined rubbing, grinding and impact action of steel balls tumbling with the aggregate in a rotating drum.

**The test:**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Apparatus** | **A hollow steel cylinder rotating about a horizontal axis, with an internal shelf** ← |
| **Abrasive charge** | **Cast iron or steel spheres, 12 of them for the standard grading** ← |
| **Rotation** | **500 to 1,000 revolutions at 30 to 33 rpm** ← |
| **Measurement** | **The percentage of material passing a 1.7 mm sieve after the test** ← |
| **Result** | **The LOS ANGELES ABRASION VALUE — a LOWER value means a TOUGHER aggregate** ← |

> **The permissible values by application:**

| Application | Maximum LA abrasion value |
|---|---|
| **Bituminous CONCRETE wearing course** | **30 per cent** ← |
| **Bituminous macadam, base courses** | **40 per cent** |
| **Water bound macadam, sub-base** | **50 per cent** ← |
| **Cement concrete pavement wearing surface** | **30 per cent** |

> **The pattern is straightforward: the nearer the surface and the more direct the traffic contact, the TOUGHER the aggregate must be.**

**The family of aggregate strength tests, since each measures something different:**

| Test | Measures | Applied load |
|---|---|---|
| **LOS ANGELES ABRASION** | **Combined abrasion, attrition and impact** ← | **Tumbling with steel balls** |
| **AGGREGATE CRUSHING VALUE** | **Resistance to CRUSHING under a GRADUAL load** ← (option b) | **400 kN applied over 10 minutes** ← |
| **AGGREGATE IMPACT VALUE** | **Resistance to sudden SHOCK or impact** ← | **A hammer dropped 15 times** ← |
| **Deval attrition test** | Abrasion, without the impact of steel balls | Older, superseded |
| **Soundness test (sodium/magnesium sulphate)** | **Resistance to WEATHERING — crystallisation of salts simulates freeze-thaw** ← (option d) | Cycles of soaking and drying |
| **Water absorption** | **Porosity and durability** ← (option c) | Soaking |
| **Polished stone value** | **Resistance to POLISHING under traffic — skid resistance** ← | A polishing machine |

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) each name a real and distinct aggregate test, so the option set requires the property to be matched to the method.**

> **The permissible values for the two related strength tests:**

| Test | Wearing course | Base course |
|---|---|---|
| **Aggregate CRUSHING value** | **30 %** | **45 %** |
| **Aggregate IMPACT value** | **30 %** | **45 %** ← |

> **The crushing and impact values are numerically similar and are broadly interchangeable, the impact test being quicker and needing simpler apparatus — which is why it is more often used on site.**

**THE POLISHED STONE VALUE deserves separate attention, because it is the test that concerns SAFETY rather than durability:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What happens** | **Traffic POLISHES the exposed aggregate over years, smoothing the microtexture** ← |
| **Consequence** | **SKID RESISTANCE falls, particularly in the wet** ← |
| **The aggregate may be perfectly hard and still polish** | **Hardness and polish resistance are DIFFERENT properties** ← |
| **Which rocks resist polishing** | **Those with hard and soft minerals together, so the surface renews itself as it wears — gritstone, some basalts** ← |
| **Which polish badly** | **Uniform, fine-grained rocks — LIMESTONE especially** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS CONTAIN THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE POINT: a very hard, uniform aggregate polishes to a glassy surface and becomes DANGEROUS in the wet, while a rock containing softer minerals wears differentially and keeps a rough microtexture.**

> **So the ideal wearing-course aggregate is NOT simply the hardest available — it is one that is hard enough to resist abrasion and heterogeneous enough to keep renewing its surface.**

> **That is why limestone, which performs adequately in the abrasion and crushing tests, is prohibited or restricted for wearing courses on high-speed roads in many specifications.**

**And the other aggregate properties that a specification controls:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **FLAKINESS index** | **Maximum 15 % (25 % for some layers) — flaky particles break under compaction and reduce interlock** ← |
| **ELONGATION index** | Maximum 15 % |
| **Combined flakiness and elongation** | Maximum 40 % |
| **Water absorption** | **Maximum 2 %; above that, durability is suspect** ← |
| **Soundness loss** | 12 % with sodium sulphate, 18 % with magnesium sulphate |
| **STRIPPING value** | **Maximum 25 % — resistance to the bitumen being displaced by water** ← |
| **Grading** | To the specified envelope |

> **FLAKINESS in the first row has a practical consequence beyond the numbers: flaky particles lie flat under the roller, so they form planes of weakness, they break under compaction and under traffic, and they interlock poorly.**

> **A flaky aggregate therefore produces a mix that is harder to compact, weaker once compacted, and prone to degrade further in service — and since flakiness arises from the crusher settings and the rock's cleavage, it is largely controllable at the quarry.**

> **Adjusting the crusher to produce cubical particles is cheaper than accepting a weaker pavement, which makes the flakiness index one of the more useful acceptance tests to enforce strictly.**

examTip.trick: **LA abrasion: tumbling with steel balls, measuring combined abrasion, attrition and impact. Max 30 % for a wearing course, 40 % base, 50 % sub-base.** Options (b), (c) and (d) name three other real tests.
examTip.trap: **A very hard, UNIFORM aggregate can polish to a glassy, dangerous surface** — hardness and polish resistance are different properties. Rocks with hard and soft minerals together renew their microtexture; limestone does not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Crushing value (gradual 400 kN), Impact value (dropped hammer), LA abrasion (tumbling balls), soundness (sulphate crystallisation), PSV (skid).** And FLAKY particles lie flat, break under the roller and interlock poorly — controllable at the crusher.

questions.stem: In bituminous road construction, a TACK COAT is applied:
options: To an absorbent granular surface, to bind the loose material and waterproof it before the bituminous layer
On an existing bituminous or concrete surface, to ensure bond between it and the new bituminous layer laid over it
As the final wearing surface of the road
Beneath the subgrade to prevent moisture rising
questions.solution:
**On an existing BITUMINOUS or cement concrete surface, to ensure BOND between it and the new bituminous layer laid over it.**

**Tack coat against prime coat — the distinction this question turns on:**

| | PRIME COAT | TACK COAT |
|---|---|---|
| **Applied to** | **An ABSORBENT, granular, non-bituminous surface — WBM, WMM, a stabilised base** ← (option a) | **A NON-absorbent surface — existing bituminous, or cement concrete** ← |
| **Purpose** | **PENETRATES and binds the loose surface particles, waterproofs it, and provides an adhesive base** ← | **Provides ADHESION between two bituminous layers** ← |
| **Material** | **LOW viscosity cutback or emulsion — it must soak in** ← | **Higher viscosity emulsion or cutback — it must stay on the surface** ← |
| **Rate of application** | **Heavier — 6 to 12 kg per 10 m²** ← | **LIGHTER — 2 to 3 kg per 10 m²** ← |
| **Curing** | **Must be left to CURE (24 hours or more) before the next layer** ← | **Applied shortly before the next layer, and must BREAK but not fully cure** ← |

> **THE KEY DISCRIMINATOR IS THE SURFACE BENEATH: absorbent surface takes a PRIME coat; non-absorbent takes a TACK coat.**

> **Option (a) describes the prime coat exactly, which makes it the designed distractor, and the two are constantly interchanged.**

**Why the tack coat matters — the consequence of omitting it:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The layers act as SEPARATE, UNBONDED slabs rather than as one composite** ← | **Each thin layer bends independently, so the tensile strains at its underside are far higher** ← |
| **SLIPPAGE cracking** | **Crescent-shaped cracks where the surfacing slides over the layer beneath, typically where vehicles brake or turn** ← |
| **Greatly reduced fatigue life** | **Analysis shows an unbonded overlay can lose most of its expected life** ← |
| **Delamination — the overlay peels off in sheets** | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW CONTAINS THE STRUCTURAL POINT AND IT IS A LARGE EFFECT: two bonded 50 mm layers behave as one 100 mm layer, whose bending stiffness is EIGHT TIMES that of a single 50 mm layer (stiffness going as the cube of the thickness).**

> **Two UNBONDED 50 mm layers behave as two separate 50 mm layers, with only TWICE the stiffness of one.**

> **So bonding the layers quadruples the effective stiffness of the pair, for the cost of a light spray of emulsion — which is among the best returns available anywhere in road construction.**

> **And the slippage cracking in the second row is the visible diagnostic: crescent-shaped cracks at bus stops, at junction approaches and on curves, exactly where horizontal forces are greatest, indicate that the tack coat was omitted or was contaminated by dust.**

**The bituminous surface treatments, as a complete set:**

| Treatment | Note |
|---|---|
| **PRIME coat** | **Onto an absorbent granular base, before the first bituminous layer** ← |
| **TACK coat** | **Between bituminous layers, for bond** ← |
| **SEAL coat** | **A thin final application to SEAL an open-textured surface and improve skid resistance** ← |
| **SURFACE DRESSING (chip seal)** | **A sprayed binder followed by chippings — a maintenance treatment that waterproofs and restores texture, adding NO structural strength** ← |
| **FOG seal** | A very light emulsion spray to rejuvenate an aged surface |
| **Slurry seal / micro-surfacing** | Emulsion, fine aggregate and filler; fills minor ruts |

> **SURFACE DRESSING deserves its emphasis because it is the most cost-effective maintenance treatment available and is chronically under-used:**

> **It costs a small fraction of an overlay, is applied quickly with simple plant, and it addresses the two things that actually destroy a pavement — WATER ENTRY and LOSS OF SKID RESISTANCE.**

> **Applied at the right moment, on a structurally sound pavement whose surface has begun to open up, it can add ten years to the life of the road.**

> **Applied too late, to a pavement already cracked and deforming structurally, it achieves nothing — it seals the surface without restoring the strength, and the underlying failure continues beneath it.**

> **THAT TIMING JUDGEMENT IS THE ESSENCE OF PAVEMENT MANAGEMENT, and the general rule is worth stating: preventive maintenance applied to a sound pavement is cheap and effective, while the same treatment applied to a failed one is wasted.**

> **The consequence for a road authority is uncomfortable but well established: money spent on roads that still LOOK acceptable buys far more than the same money spent on roads that are visibly failing — which is politically the harder case to make, and is the same incentive problem met in disaster mitigation.**

examTip.trick: **PRIME coat onto an ABSORBENT granular base (low viscosity, soaks in, 6-12 kg/10 m²); TACK coat onto a NON-absorbent bituminous or concrete surface (lighter, 2-3 kg/10 m²).** Option (a) is the prime coat.
examTip.trap: **Two BONDED 50 mm layers act as one 100 mm layer — EIGHT times the stiffness of one; unbonded, only twice.** So a light spray of emulsion quadruples the effective stiffness of the pair.
examTip.mnemonic: **Crescent-shaped SLIPPAGE cracks at bus stops and junctions mean the tack coat was omitted or dusty.** And SURFACE DRESSING is the best-value maintenance there is — but only on a structurally SOUND pavement; on a failed one it seals the surface and achieves nothing.

questions.stem: In traffic engineering, the PASSENGER CAR UNIT (PCU) is used to:
options: Convert a mixed traffic stream into an equivalent number of passenger cars
Count the number of passengers carried by each vehicle
Measure the fuel consumption of vehicles
Determine the maximum axle load permitted on a road
questions.solution:
**To convert a MIXED traffic stream into an EQUIVALENT number of passenger cars**, so that flows of different composition can be compared and capacity assessed.

**Why the conversion is necessary:**

> **A road carrying 1,000 cars an hour and one carrying 1,000 vehicles an hour of which half are trucks and bullock carts are not carrying comparable traffic at all.**

> **A slow, large vehicle occupies more road space, accelerates more slowly, and obstructs others — so it consumes far more of the road's capacity than one car.**

> **The PCU expresses that consumption in a common unit, so a mixed stream can be compared with a road's capacity, which is quoted in PCU per hour.**

**The IRC passenger car unit values:**

| Vehicle | PCU (mixed traffic, urban) |
|---|---|
| **PASSENGER CAR, tempo, auto-rickshaw, light commercial vehicle** | **1.0** ← |
| **MOTORCYCLE, scooter** | **0.5** ← |
| **Cycle** | **0.5** |
| **TRUCK, BUS, agricultural tractor** | **3.0** ← |
| **Cycle rickshaw** | **1.5** |
| **Horse-drawn vehicle** | **4.0** |
| **BULLOCK CART (small / large)** | **6.0 / 8.0** ← |

> **The BULLOCK CART's value of 6 to 8 is the striking one, and it is not merely about size: the cart is very SLOW, so it obstructs a long queue of faster vehicles behind it and consumes far more capacity than its length alone would suggest.**

> **THAT IS THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE: THE PCU REFLECTS SPEED DIFFERENCE AND MANOEUVRABILITY AS MUCH AS PHYSICAL SIZE.**

> **A slow vehicle in a fast stream is disproportionately disruptive, which is also why a heavily loaded truck on a steep hill gradient is assigned a much higher PCU than the same truck on the level.**

**A worked example:**

> **An hourly count on a road gives 400 cars, 600 motorcycles, 80 trucks and buses, and 10 bullock carts.**

| Vehicle | Number | PCU factor | PCU |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cars** | **400** | **1.0** | **400** |
| **Motorcycles** | **600** | **0.5** | **300** |
| **Trucks and buses** | **80** | **3.0** | **240** ← |
| **Bullock carts** | **10** | **8.0** | **80** ← |
| **TOTAL vehicles** | **1,090** | — | — |
| **TOTAL PCU** | — | — | **1,020 PCU/hour** ← |

> **Note that the 80 trucks (7 per cent of the vehicles) account for 240 PCU (24 per cent of the capacity used), and the 10 bullock carts (under 1 per cent of vehicles) account for 8 per cent.**

> **So the heavy and slow vehicles dominate the capacity consumed while being a small minority of the count — which is why a raw vehicle count is a poor measure of how loaded a road is.**

**DESIGN SERVICE VOLUME, which is what the PCU total is compared against:**

| Road | Design service volume (PCU/day) |
|---|---|
| **Single lane, 3.75 m** | **2,000** |
| **Intermediate lane, 5.5 m** | **6,000** ← |
| **TWO-LANE, 7.0 m, undivided** | **15,000** ← |
| **Four-lane divided** | **35,000** |

> **These are the thresholds at which a road should be widened, and comparing the PCU total with them is the standard capacity assessment.**

**And the associated traffic studies, since the PCU feeds all of them:**

| Study | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Traffic VOLUME count** | **Flow by type, direction and time — the basic input, converted to PCU** ← |
| **SPOT SPEED study** | **Speed limits (85th percentile) and design speed (98th)** ← |
| **Speed and delay study** | **Journey time, delays and their causes — the moving-observer method** ← |
| **ORIGIN-DESTINATION study** | **Where the traffic comes from and goes to — essential for planning bypasses and new links** ← |
| **PARKING study** | Demand, duration, turnover |
| **ACCIDENT study** | **Collision and condition diagrams; identifying black spots** ← |

> **THE ORIGIN-DESTINATION STUDY IS THE ONE THAT ANSWERS THE QUESTION A VOLUME COUNT CANNOT, and the distinction is important:**

> **A volume count tells you HOW MUCH traffic passes a point. It does not tell you whether that traffic has business in the town or is merely passing through.**

> **If most of it is through traffic, a BYPASS solves the problem. If most of it is local, a bypass will be empty and the congestion will remain.**

> **Bypasses have been built on the strength of volume counts alone and have carried very little traffic, because the flow turned out to be local — which is an expensive way to discover that the wrong study was done.**

> **The methods for an O-D study are roadside interviews, license-plate matching at the cordon, return postcards, and now automatic number plate recognition and mobile phone location data — the last of which has made the study far cheaper and more comprehensive than the interview methods it replaces.**

Flows of differing composition can be compared.

examTip.trick: **PCU converts a mixed stream to equivalent cars.** Car 1.0, motorcycle 0.5, TRUCK/BUS 3.0, bullock cart 6-8. Design service volume: 15,000 PCU/day for a two-lane 7.0 m road.
examTip.trap: **PCU reflects SPEED DIFFERENCE and manoeuvrability as much as size** — a bullock cart scores 6-8 because it obstructs a queue behind it, not because it is large. Heavy and slow vehicles dominate the capacity consumed while being a small minority of the count.
examTip.mnemonic: **A volume count says HOW MUCH; an ORIGIN-DESTINATION study says whether it is THROUGH or LOCAL traffic** — and only the latter tells you whether a bypass will work. Bypasses built on counts alone have stood empty.

questions.stem: A traffic ROTARY (roundabout) achieves its safety benefit principally because it:
options: Increases the speed at which vehicles can pass through the junction
Eliminates the need for any traffic signs
Converts crossing (right-angle) conflicts into merging and diverging movements
Allows vehicles to pass straight through without changing direction
questions.solution:
**It CONVERTS crossing conflicts into MERGING and DIVERGING movements**, greatly reducing both the number and the severity of the conflict points.

**The conflict points compared:**

| Junction | Conflict points (four-arm, two-way) |
|---|---|
| **UNCONTROLLED four-arm crossroads** | **32 — of which 16 are CROSSING conflicts** ← |
| **ROTARY (roundabout)** | **8 — 4 merging and 4 diverging, and NO crossing conflicts at all** ← |

> **THE ELIMINATION OF CROSSING CONFLICTS IS THE WHOLE SAFETY CASE, and the reason is about SEVERITY as much as number:**

| Conflict type | Collision angle | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **CROSSING (right-angle)** | **90° — the full relative speed is delivered as impact** ← | **SEVERE — and it strikes the vehicle's SIDE, where there is least protection** ← |
| **MERGING / DIVERGING** | **A shallow angle** ← | **Much less severe — a glancing or rear-end contact at low relative speed** ← |
| **HEAD-ON** | 180° | The most severe of all |

> **A right-angle collision is the most dangerous common type at a junction because the impact is delivered to the side of the vehicle — where there is no crumple zone, only a door — and because the relative speed is the full vector sum of the two.**

> **A roundabout makes such a collision geometrically impossible: every vehicle travels in the same rotational direction, so the only conflicts are shallow-angle merges and diverges at low relative speed.**

> **Add to that the REDUCED SPEED that the deflection round the island enforces, and the result is a large and well-documented reduction in serious injury accidents — commonly 40 to 60 per cent compared with a signalised junction, and more against an uncontrolled one.**

> **Option (a) inverts one of the mechanisms: a rotary REDUCES speed, and that reduction is part of why it is safe.**

**The design elements of a rotary:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **CENTRAL ISLAND** | **Deflects the traffic, enforcing a circulatory path and reducing speed** ← |
| **WEAVING LENGTH** | **The distance over which merging and diverging vehicles exchange positions — the capacity-determining element** ← |
| **Weaving ANGLE** | **Should be small (about 15°) for smooth merging** ← |
| **Entry and exit RADII** | Exit radius larger than entry, to encourage slow entry and free exit |
| **Entry WIDTH and flare** | Governs capacity at the entry |
| **Radius of the central island** | **At least 1.33 times the entry width** ← |
| **Design speed** | **30-40 km/h in rural areas, 25-30 km/h urban** ← |

> **THE WEAVING LENGTH IS THE CAPACITY CONTROL AND IS WHERE ROTARIES FAIL, and the reasoning is worth following:**

> **Every vehicle entering must merge into the circulating stream and every vehicle leaving must diverge from it, and both manoeuvres need road length in which to change lanes.**

> **If the weaving length is too short, vehicles cannot complete the exchange and the whole circulation locks up.**

> **Since the weaving length depends on the rotary's diameter, a rotary handling heavy traffic must be LARGE — and a large rotary consumes a great deal of land, which is exactly what is unavailable in a town centre.**

**When a rotary is NOT appropriate — which is the practical judgement:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **Traffic exceeding about 3,000 PCU/hour entering** | **Weaving capacity is exhausted; SIGNALS become superior** ← |
| **Very UNBALANCED flows** | **A dominant flow saturates the circulation and starves a minor arm entirely** ← |
| **Heavy PEDESTRIAN movement** | **Pedestrians must cross a continuously moving stream with no gaps and no signal to protect them** ← |
| **Insufficient LAND** | A rotary needs far more space than a signalised junction |
| **Steep gradients on the approaches** | Heavy vehicles cannot merge from a standstill on a slope |
| **More than about four arms, or awkward angles** | Weaving becomes impossible |

> **THE PEDESTRIAN OBJECTION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DECISIVE ONE IN A SOUTH ASIAN CITY CENTRE, and it deserves stating plainly: a rotary is designed to keep vehicles MOVING CONTINUOUSLY, which is precisely what denies pedestrians a gap to cross.**

> **A signalised junction stops the traffic periodically and can give pedestrians a protected phase; a rotary never stops, so pedestrians must find their own gaps in a circulating stream.**

> **Where pedestrian volumes are high — a bazaar, a bus park, a school — the rotary's vehicular efficiency is bought at the pedestrians' expense, and the correct answer is usually signals.**

> **That is why several prominent rotaries in Kathmandu and other South Asian cities have been converted to signalised junctions, and it reflects a broader shift in priority from vehicle throughput toward the safety of the people on foot who form the majority of road users.**

> **The UNBALANCED FLOW problem in the second row is the other common failure: where one approach carries most of the traffic, its stream circulates continuously and vehicles on the minor arms can never find a gap to enter — producing indefinite delay on the minor arm while the major arm flows freely.**

> **Signals allocate time explicitly and can be set to serve a minor arm adequately; a rotary allocates capacity by the ability to force a gap, which favours the strong flow entirely.**

Greatly reducing the number and severity of conflict points.

examTip.trick: **32 conflict points at an uncontrolled crossroads (16 of them CROSSING) against 8 at a rotary (4 merging, 4 diverging, none crossing).** A right-angle impact strikes the vehicle's SIDE at full relative speed.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) inverts a mechanism — a rotary REDUCES speed**, and that deflection is part of why it is safe.
examTip.mnemonic: **WEAVING LENGTH sets the capacity, and it needs DIAMETER — which is why rotaries fail above ~3,000 PCU/h and need land a town centre lacks.** And a rotary never stops, so PEDESTRIANS get no gap: where they are numerous, signals are correct.

questions.stem: In a rigid pavement, WARPING stresses arise because of:
options: The braking action of vehicles on the slab
A temperature difference between the top and the bottom of the slab
The friction between the slab and the sub-base during expansion
The impact of wheel loads at the joints
questions.solution:
**A TEMPERATURE DIFFERENCE between the top and the bottom of the slab**, which the slab's own weight and its restraints prevent it from accommodating freely.

**The mechanism:**

| Time | Temperature condition | Slab's tendency | Restrained by | Resulting stress |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DAY** | **Top HOTTER than the bottom** | **The top expands more, so the slab tries to curl DOWNWARD at the edges (convex up)** ← | **Its own WEIGHT holds the edges down** | **TENSION at the BOTTOM of the slab** ← |
| **NIGHT** | **Top COOLER than the bottom** | **The slab tries to curl UPWARD at the edges (concave up)** ← | **Its own weight holds the centre down** | **TENSION at the TOP of the slab** ← |

> **So the slab is stressed simply by the daily temperature cycle, with no traffic on it at all — and warping stresses can approach the magnitude of the load stresses.**

> **Option (c) describes FRICTIONAL stress, which is a different temperature effect — the resistance of the sub-base to the slab's UNIFORM expansion and contraction, rather than to its curling.**

> **Both are real and both arise from temperature, which is what makes that distractor work.**

**The three stresses in a rigid pavement, which must be kept apart:**

| Stress | Cause | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **WHEEL LOAD stress** | **Traffic** | **Westergaard's analysis: interior, edge and CORNER loading** ← |
| **WARPING (curling) stress** | **TEMPERATURE DIFFERENTIAL through the slab's depth** ← | **This question** |
| **FRICTIONAL stress** | **Resistance of the sub-base to UNIFORM expansion or contraction** ← | **Governs the spacing of contraction joints** ← |

> **The CRITICAL COMBINATIONS are worth knowing, because the stresses do not simply add at all times:**

| Season | Critical combination | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **SUMMER, mid-day** | **Load + warping + frictional** | **EDGE region** ← |
| **WINTER** | **Load + warping (both tension at the top at night)** | **CORNER region** ← |

> **THE CORNER IS THE MOST CRITICAL LOCATION IN A RIGID PAVEMENT, and the reason is that the corner is supported on only TWO sides while an interior point is supported all round.**

> **A corner load produces the greatest deflection, and at night the corner is also curling upward — so the load arrives on a corner that has lifted off its support and is cantilevering.**

> **That combination is why corner cracking is the characteristic rigid-pavement distress, and why dowel bars, thickened edges and a well-drained non-erodible sub-base are all directed at protecting the corners.**

**WESTERGAARD'S three load positions, since they define the analysis:**

| Position | Support | Relative severity |
|---|---|---|
| **INTERIOR** | **Supported on ALL sides** | **Least critical for stress** |
| **EDGE** | **Supported on THREE sides** | **Higher stress — often the critical case for stress** ← |
| **CORNER** | **Supported on TWO sides only** | **Greatest DEFLECTION; critical when combined with night-time curling** ← |

> **And the RADIUS OF RELATIVE STIFFNESS, which appears in all of Westergaard's expressions:**

> **l = [E h³ / (12 (1 − μ²) k)]^0.25**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **E, h, μ** | The slab's modulus, thickness and Poisson's ratio |
| **k** | **The MODULUS OF SUBGRADE REACTION — the subgrade's stiffness, from a plate load test** ← |
| **What l represents** | **The distance over which the slab distributes a load — a stiff slab on a soft subgrade spreads the load further** ← |

> **The h³ dependence means that slab THICKNESS dominates: increasing the thickness both reduces the stress directly and spreads the load over a larger area.**

> **And the FOURTH ROOT on the whole expression means that the subgrade's stiffness k has only a WEAK influence — a fourfold improvement in the subgrade changes l by only about 40 per cent.**

> **THAT IS THE FUNDAMENTAL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN RIGID AND FLEXIBLE PAVEMENT DESIGN, and it is worth stating explicitly:**

| Pavement | Sensitivity to the subgrade |
|---|---|
| **FLEXIBLE** | **HIGH — the subgrade carries the load, and the CBR strongly governs the thickness** ← |
| **RIGID** | **LOW — the slab bridges over weak spots, and k appears under a fourth root** ← |

> **So a rigid pavement is the better choice over a weak or variable subgrade, precisely because it does not depend on it — which is why concrete is often used over poor ground, on expansive soils and where drainage cannot be assured.**

> **The sub-base beneath a rigid pavement is provided mainly to prevent PUMPING and to give a uniform, non-erodible working surface, rather than to contribute structural strength — a different purpose from the sub-base of a flexible pavement, and a point that is routinely misunderstood.**

Which the slab's weight and its restraints prevent it from accommodating freely.

examTip.trick: **A temperature DIFFERENTIAL through the depth makes the slab try to curl, and its own weight restrains it.** Day: top hotter, tension at the BOTTOM. Night: top cooler, tension at the TOP. Option (c) is FRICTIONAL stress — uniform expansion, a different effect.
examTip.trap: **The CORNER is the critical location** — supported on only two sides, and at night it curls UP off its support, so the load arrives on a cantilever. Hence corner cracking, dowels and non-erodible sub-bases.
examTip.mnemonic: **l = [Eh³/(12(1−μ²)k)]^0.25 — k appears under a FOURTH ROOT**, so a rigid pavement is barely sensitive to the subgrade, while a flexible one depends on it entirely. That is why concrete suits weak or variable ground.

questions.stem: In flexible pavement design, the traffic is expressed in MILLION STANDARD AXLES (msa). The standard axle load used in India and Nepal is:
options: 6.0 tonnes
10.2 tonnes
8.16 tonnes
12.0 tonnes
questions.solution:
**8.16 tonnes** (80 kN).

**Why a "standard" axle is needed at all:**

> **Real traffic contains axles of every load, and their damaging effects are wildly unequal. A design method cannot handle every axle individually, so all of them are converted to an EQUIVALENT number of standard axles.**

> **The conversion uses the FOURTH POWER LAW:**

> **Equivalent standard axles = (axle load / 8.16)⁴**

| Axle load (tonnes) | Damage relative to one standard axle |
|---|---|
| **2 (a car's axle)** | **0.0036** |
| **4** | **0.058** |
| **6** | **0.29** |
| **8.16 (the STANDARD)** | **1.00** ← |
| **10** | **2.26** |
| **12** | **4.68** ← |
| **16 (a 2× overload)** | **14.8** ← |
| **20** | **36.1** ← |

> **THE CONSEQUENCES OF THIS TABLE ARE THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL FACTS IN PAVEMENT ENGINEERING:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A single axle at TWICE the legal load does the damage of about FIFTEEN legal axles** ← | ← |
| **A private car (about 1 tonne per axle) scores 0.0002** | **So roughly FIVE THOUSAND car passes equal ONE standard axle** ← |
| **Pavements are designed for TRUCKS; cars are structurally irrelevant** ← | ← |
| **OVERLOADING is the single greatest destroyer of pavements in South Asia** ← | ← |

> **The fourth power means that overloading CANNOT be designed for economically — a pavement built to withstand routine 100 per cent overloading would need to be built for fifteen times the traffic, which no road authority can afford.**

> **So overloading must be PREVENTED, not accommodated: axle load control at weighbridges is worth more to a road network than any amount of extra thickness, and it is the single highest-return intervention in road asset management.**

**Computing the design traffic in msa:**

> **N = 365 × A × [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]/r × D × F**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | **Commercial vehicles per day at the year of completion** ← |
| **r** | **Annual traffic growth rate — minimum 5 per cent per IRC** ← |
| **n** | **DESIGN LIFE in years — 15 for national and state highways, 10 to 15 for others** ← |
| **D** | **LANE DISTRIBUTION factor — the proportion of commercial vehicles in the design lane** ← |
| **F** | **VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR — the average standard axles per commercial vehicle** ← |

> **THE VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR IS THE MOST UNCERTAIN AND MOST INFLUENTIAL TERM, and it is where a design goes wrong:**

| Terrain and loading | Typical VDF |
|---|---|
| **Plain terrain, initial traffic under 150 CVPD** | **1.5** |
| **Plain, 150-1,500 CVPD** | **3.5** ← |
| **Plain, over 1,500 CVPD** | **4.5** ← |
| **Hilly terrain** | **Lower — 0.5 to 1.5, since vehicles carry less on steep grades** ← |

> **A VDF assumed at 3.5 where the real value is 7 (because of routine overloading) will halve the design traffic and produce a pavement that fails in half its intended life — and the error is invisible until the road begins to rut.**

> **So an AXLE LOAD SURVEY, weighing a sample of the actual commercial vehicles, is worth far more than any refinement of the design charts, and it is the measurement most often omitted.**

**And the DESIGN CRITERIA the msa figure is used against:**

| Criterion | Failure mode | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| **Vertical COMPRESSIVE strain on the SUBGRADE** | **RUTTING — permanent deformation in the wheel paths** ← | Controls the total thickness |
| **Horizontal TENSILE strain at the bottom of the bituminous layer** | **FATIGUE cracking — bottom-up alligator cracking** ← | Controls the bound layer thickness |

> **IRC:37 defines failure at 20 per cent of the pavement area cracked, or 20 mm of rutting, in the design lane — and it is worth noting that the design life is defined by a stated LEVEL OF DISTRESS rather than by collapse.**

> **A pavement at the end of its design life has not failed structurally; it has reached the condition at which rehabilitation becomes economic.**

> **That is a quite different concept of "design life" from the one used for a building or a bridge, and confusing the two leads to the mistaken belief that a fifteen-year pavement must be reconstructed after fifteen years — when in fact a timely overlay applied before that point extends it indefinitely, and is far cheaper than reconstruction.**

examTip.trick: **8.16 tonnes (80 kN), and ESA = (load/8.16)⁴.** A 16-tonne axle does the damage of nearly FIFTEEN standard axles; about 5,000 car passes equal one.
examTip.trap: **Overloading cannot be designed for economically** — the fourth power means routine 100 % overload needs fifteen times the traffic capacity. It must be PREVENTED at weighbridges.
examTip.mnemonic: **The VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR is the most influential and most uncertain term** — assume 3.5 where the truth is 7 and the pavement fails in half its life. An AXLE LOAD SURVEY is worth more than any refinement of the charts.

questions.stem: In the FIELD COMPACTION of a road embankment, the degree of compaction achieved is normally controlled by:
options: The number of passes of the roller alone
Visual inspection of the surface
The weight of the roller used
Measuring the field dry density and expressing it as a percentage of the laboratory maximum dry density
questions.solution:
**By measuring the FIELD DRY DENSITY and expressing it as a percentage of the laboratory MAXIMUM DRY DENSITY** obtained from the Proctor test.

**The control procedure:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1 — LABORATORY** | **Run a Proctor test on the fill material to establish its MAXIMUM DRY DENSITY (MDD) and OPTIMUM MOISTURE CONTENT (OMC)** ← |
| **2 — SITE** | **Place and compact the layer at a moisture content near the OMC** ← |
| **3 — MEASURE** | **Determine the FIELD dry density in place** ← |
| **4 — COMPARE** | **RELATIVE COMPACTION = (field dry density / MDD) × 100 per cent** ← |
| **5 — ACCEPT or re-roll** | Against the specified percentage |

| Layer | Typical requirement |
|---|---|
| **Embankment body** | **95 per cent of Standard Proctor MDD** ← |
| **SUBGRADE (top 500 mm)** | **97 per cent of Standard Proctor** ← |
| **Granular sub-base and base** | **98 per cent of MODIFIED Proctor** ← |

> **Options (a) and (c) describe the MEANS of compaction, not a measure of the RESULT — and that distinction is the point of the question.**

> **Specifying a number of passes by a roller of a given weight is a useful CONSTRUCTION instruction, and it is not an acceptance criterion: the same roller and the same passes will achieve quite different densities on different materials and at different moisture contents.**

> **What matters is the density achieved, and that must be measured.**

**The methods of measuring field density:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **SAND REPLACEMENT (sand cone)** | **The standard reference method; a hole is dug, the soil weighed, and the hole's volume found by filling with calibrated sand** ← |
| **CORE CUTTER** | **Quick, for fine-grained cohesive soils with no stones** ← |
| **Water/rubber balloon** | Volume by displacement |
| **NUCLEAR density gauge** | **Rapid, non-destructive, many readings in a shift — but requires a radiation license and trained handling** ← |
| **Electrical / electromagnetic gauges** | Non-nuclear alternatives |

> **The SAND REPLACEMENT method remains the reference because it measures the volume directly and needs no calibration against soil type — but it is slow, which is why the nuclear gauge dominates on large projects where many tests are needed.**

**THE MOISTURE CONTENT REQUIREMENT, which is where field compaction actually fails:**

| Moisture condition | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **DRIER than OMC** | **The soil is stiff; particles resist rearrangement; the target density cannot be reached however many passes are applied** ← |
| **AT the OMC** | **Maximum density for that compactive effort** ← |
| **WETTER than OMC** | **Water occupies volume the particles could fill; density falls; and the soil may become unstable and "pump" under the roller** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW CONTAINS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT: MORE ROLLING CANNOT COMPENSATE FOR THE WRONG MOISTURE CONTENT.**

> **A layer placed too dry will not reach the specified density no matter how many passes it receives, and continued rolling merely wastes plant hours and can break down the aggregate.**

> **The remedy is to add water and mix it in uniformly, or — for a soil too wet — to aerate it by harrowing and allow it to dry.**

> **The permitted range is usually OMC ± 2 per cent, and checking the moisture BEFORE rolling is far more productive than testing the density afterwards and re-rolling.**

**The choice of roller, since it must suit the material:**

| Roller | Suits | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **SMOOTH WHEELED (static)** | **Granular soils; finishing bituminous layers** ← | Static pressure |
| **PNEUMATIC TYRED** | **Most soils; excellent for bituminous layers — the KNEADING action seals the surface** ← | Kneading and pressure |
| **SHEEPSFOOT (tamping)** | **COHESIVE soils — CLAYS. The feet penetrate and compact from the BOTTOM of the layer upward** ← | Kneading and pressure at depth |
| **VIBRATORY** | **GRANULAR soils, sands and gravels — vibration rearranges the particles** ← | Vibration |
| **Impact / rammer, plate compactor** | Confined areas, trenches, around structures | Impact |

> **THE SHEEPSFOOT AND VIBRATORY ROWS EXPRESS THE GOVERNING PRINCIPLE, and it is worth stating: VIBRATION for GRANULAR soils, KNEADING for COHESIVE soils.**

> **A vibratory roller on clay achieves very little — the clay's cohesion resists particle rearrangement, and the vibration simply does not transmit.**

> **A sheepsfoot roller on sand is equally useless — the feet displace the sand sideways rather than compacting it, and they "walk out" without densifying anything.**

> **Using the wrong roller is therefore not merely inefficient but ineffective, and it is a common cause of a layer failing its density test repeatedly while the crew adds more passes.**

> **The sheepsfoot's distinctive behaviour is worth a closing note: as the layer densifies, the feet penetrate less and the roller gradually rises until it is "walking out" on the surface.**

> **That walking-out is itself a useful indicator that the layer has been compacted as far as that roller will take it — a rare case of the plant reporting its own completion.**

examTip.trick: **Relative compaction = field dry density ÷ laboratory MDD.** Embankment 95 %, subgrade 97 % (Standard Proctor), granular base 98 % (MODIFIED Proctor). Options (a) and (c) are the MEANS, not the result.
examTip.trap: **MORE ROLLING CANNOT FIX THE WRONG MOISTURE CONTENT** — a layer placed too dry will never reach the density however many passes it gets. Check moisture (OMC ± 2 %) BEFORE rolling.
examTip.mnemonic: **VIBRATION for GRANULAR soils, KNEADING (sheepsfoot, pneumatic) for COHESIVE ones.** The wrong roller is not merely slow but ineffective. And a sheepsfoot "walking out" tells you the layer is done.

questions.stem: In a SECTIONAL view of an assembly, which of the following is shown UNCUT (not hatched) even when the cutting plane passes through it?
options: A bolt, nut, rivet, shaft, key, web or rib
A hollow cylindrical body
A solid rectangular block
A flange plate
questions.solution:
**A BOLT, NUT, RIVET, SHAFT, KEY, WEB or RIB** — these are conventionally shown UNCUT even where the cutting plane passes through them.

**The full list of parts not sectioned:**

| Category | Items |
|---|---|
| **FASTENERS** | **Bolts, nuts, screws, studs, rivets, washers, pins, keys, cotters** ← |
| **SOLID rotational parts** | **Shafts, spindles, rods, balls and rollers of bearings** ← |
| **THIN reinforcing features** | **RIBS, WEBS, spokes of a wheel, gear teeth** ← |

**Why each is excepted:**

| Item | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Bolts, shafts, keys** | **Hatching them shows NOTHING useful — they are solid throughout, and their internal appearance is already known. Leaving them uncut makes the surrounding assembly far clearer** ← |
| **RIBS and WEBS** | **A DIFFERENT and more important reason — see below** ← |

> **THE RIB CONVENTION IS THE ONE WORTH UNDERSTANDING, because it is a deliberate departure from geometric truth:**

> **A rib is a thin stiffening plate. If the cutting plane passes ALONG its length and it is hatched, the section appears SOLID across the full width — giving a completely false impression of a massive body where in fact there is a thin fin.**

> **Leaving the rib unhatched shows it for what it is: a thin member, with open space each side of it.**

> **So the convention sacrifices literal accuracy for TRUTHFUL COMMUNICATION, which is what a drawing convention is for.**

> **Note the qualification: a rib is left unhatched when the plane passes ALONG it (longitudinally). If the plane cuts ACROSS a rib, it IS hatched — because then the section genuinely is the rib's small cross-section and hatching it is both true and informative.**

**The HATCHING (section lining) conventions:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Thin continuous lines at 45° to the principal outline** | **Spaced 1 to 3 mm apart, uniformly** ← |
| **ADJACENT parts hatched in OPPOSITE directions** | **So the boundary between two components is unmistakable** ← |
| **A THIRD adjacent part** | **Same direction as the first, but at a DIFFERENT SPACING** ← |
| **The SAME part in different views** | **Hatched identically in direction and spacing throughout the drawing** ← |
| **Very THIN sections (under about 2 mm)** | **Shown SOLID BLACK, with a small gap between adjacent thin parts** ← |
| **Large areas** | May be hatched only around the boundary |
| **Hatching must not cross a dimension or a note** | Break the hatching instead |

> **The ADJACENT-PARTS rule is the most useful in practice: on an assembly section, the change of hatching direction is what lets a reader see instantly where one component ends and the next begins, without reference to any label.**

**The types of section, since a full section is only one:**

| Section | Note |
|---|---|
| **FULL section** | **The plane passes right through the object** ← |
| **HALF section** | **A quarter removed — shows the EXTERNAL form on one half and the INTERNAL on the other. Ideal for SYMMETRICAL objects** ← |
| **OFFSET section** | **The cutting plane is STEPPED, so it passes through several features not in one plane** ← |
| **REVOLVED / removed section** | **The cross-section of a rib, arm or spoke, rotated into view or placed beside it** ← |
| **PARTIAL (broken-out) section** | **A small local area broken away to reveal one detail** ← |
| **Aligned section** | Angled features rotated into the plane |

> **The HALF SECTION is the most economical of these: one view does the work of two, showing outside and inside together — and it is available whenever the object is symmetrical, which mechanical and many civil components frequently are.**

> **And by convention, HIDDEN DETAIL is omitted from the sectioned half (it is now visible) and often from the unsectioned half too (it is shown in the section) — so the half section is also the cleanest to read.**

**And the CUTTING PLANE's own representation, which completes the set:**

| Element | Convention |
|---|---|
| **The cutting plane line** | **A chain thin line, THICKENED at its ends and at every change of direction** ← |
| **Arrows at the ends** | **Showing the DIRECTION OF SIGHT** ← |
| **Letters at the ends** | **A-A, B-B, and the view is titled "SECTION A-A"** ← |
| **Where the plane is obvious** | The line may be omitted on a simple symmetrical part |

> **The DIRECTION OF SIGHT arrows are the element most often drawn wrongly, and getting them backwards produces a section that is a mirror image of what was intended — the same class of error as reading a first-angle drawing as third-angle, and with the same consequence.**

examTip.trick: **Fasteners (bolts, nuts, rivets, keys), solid shafts, and RIBS/WEBS/spokes are never hatched** — hatching a solid shaft shows nothing, and hatching a rib along its length falsely suggests a massive body.
examTip.trap: **A rib is unhatched only when the plane passes ALONG it.** Cut ACROSS a rib and it IS hatched — there the section is genuinely the rib's cross-section.
examTip.mnemonic: **ADJACENT parts hatch in OPPOSITE directions; a third uses different SPACING** — that is what shows where one component ends. And a HALF SECTION gives outside and inside in one view, whenever the object is symmetrical.

questions.stem: An ISOMETRIC view differs from a PERSPECTIVE view in that in an isometric view:
options: Curved surfaces cannot be represented at all
Only two faces of the object can be shown
Parallel edges of the object remain parallel and are drawn to a common scale
The object must be drawn at full size
questions.solution:
**Parallel edges remain PARALLEL and are drawn to a common scale, whereas in a perspective view they CONVERGE to vanishing points.**

**The two compared:**

| | ISOMETRIC | PERSPECTIVE |
|---|---|---|
| **Parallel edges** | **Remain PARALLEL** ← | **CONVERGE to vanishing points** ← |
| **Scale along an axis** | **CONSTANT — the same everywhere** ← | **DIMINISHES with distance from the viewer** ← |
| **Measurable?** | **YES, along the three axes** ← | **NO — nothing can be scaled off it** ← |
| **Realism** | **Looks slightly "wrong" — distant parts appear too large** ← | **Matches how the eye actually sees** ← |
| **Ease of drawing** | **Straightforward, and easily constructed** | **More involved; needs vanishing points and a station point** |
| **Use** | **Technical illustration, assembly and erection drawings, pipework, manuals** ← | **ARCHITECTURAL presentation, client visualisation** ← |

> **THE MEASURABILITY IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE PRACTICAL DIVIDE: an isometric drawing preserves dimensions along its axes, so it can be dimensioned and worked from.**

> **A perspective view cannot be measured anywhere, so it is a picture rather than a drawing — excellent for showing a client what a building will look like, and useless for building it.**

**The ISOMETRIC construction:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The three axes are at 120° to one another** ← | **Two at 30° to the horizontal, one vertical** |
| **All three axes are equally foreshortened in a true projection** | **Hence "ISO-METRIC" — equal measure** ← |
| **ISOMETRIC SCALE (true projection)** | **0.816 of the true length on every axis** ← |
| **ISOMETRIC DRAWING (as normally made)** | **FULL true lengths used, giving a figure about 22.5 per cent larger and IDENTICAL in shape** ← |

> **The distinction in the last two rows is a classic examination point and is worth being precise about: because all three axes are foreshortened EQUALLY, using full lengths instead of 0.816 produces a figure of exactly the same SHAPE, merely larger.**

> **Since the shape is unaffected and full lengths are far easier to set off, virtually every practical "isometric" is an isometric DRAWING rather than a true isometric PROJECTION.**

> **Note also that CIRCLES appear as ELLIPSES in isometric — a circle on any isometric face becomes an ellipse whose major axis is perpendicular to the axis not in that plane. So curved surfaces are perfectly representable, which is why option (a) fails.**

**The family of pictorial projections, to place isometric among them:**

| Projection | Axes | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| **ISOMETRIC** | **Three axes equally inclined; 120° apart** ← | **Equal on all three** |
| **DIMETRIC** | **TWO axes equally inclined** | Two equal, one different |
| **TRIMETRIC** | **All three differently inclined** | All three different |
| **OBLIQUE — CAVALIER** | **One face TRUE and parallel to the paper; depth at 45°, FULL length** ← | **Looks too deep** |
| **OBLIQUE — CABINET** | **One face true; depth at 45° at HALF length** ← | **Looks more natural — the usual oblique** ← |
| **PERSPECTIVE — one, two or three point** | **Converging** | Diminishing |

> **THE OBLIQUE PROJECTIONS HAVE ONE ADVANTAGE THAT ISOMETRIC LACKS, and it is worth knowing: one face is drawn TRUE — undistorted and in its real shape.**

> **So an object whose interest lies mainly in one face — a control panel, a wall elevation, a component with a circular front — is far easier to draw obliquely, because that face keeps its true shape and any circles on it stay CIRCLES rather than becoming ellipses.**

> **The rule that follows: PUT THE MOST COMPLEX OR MOST CIRCULAR FACE PARALLEL TO THE PAPER in an oblique drawing, and the drawing becomes much simpler.**

> **And the CABINET variant halves the depth because a cavalier drawing at full depth looks unnaturally elongated — the eye expects some foreshortening, and halving it is a crude but effective approximation to what perspective would do.**

**And the PERSPECTIVE types, since architectural work uses them:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **ONE-POINT (parallel) perspective** | **The object's face is parallel to the picture plane; one vanishing point. Suits interiors and street views** ← |
| **TWO-POINT (angular) perspective** | **The object is at an angle; two vanishing points on the horizon. The commonest for buildings** ← |
| **THREE-POINT** | **A third vanishing point above or below, for looking up at a tall building or down from above** ← |

> **Two-point perspective is the architect's standard because it shows two faces of a building naturally and needs no special viewpoint, while three-point is reserved for dramatic views of tall structures where the vertical convergence is itself part of the effect.**

In perspective they CONVERGE to vanishing points.

examTip.trick: **Isometric: parallels stay PARALLEL, one scale throughout, MEASURABLE. Perspective: parallels CONVERGE, scale diminishes, nothing can be scaled off it.**
examTip.trap: **Isometric DRAWING uses full lengths; isometric PROJECTION foreshortens to 0.816** — identical in shape, 22.5 % different in size. And circles become ELLIPSES, so option (a) is false.
examTip.mnemonic: **In an OBLIQUE drawing one face stays TRUE — so put the most circular or complex face parallel to the paper** and its circles stay circles. CABINET halves the depth because full-depth cavalier looks elongated.

questions.stem: In the economic appraisal of a public project, the BENEFIT-COST RATIO is computed using:
options: The undiscounted totals of benefits and costs
The discounted (present) values of both benefits and costs
The benefits of the first year only
The ratio of the capital cost to the annual operating cost
questions.solution:
**The DISCOUNTED (present) values of both the benefits and the costs.**

> **BCR = (present worth of benefits) / (present worth of costs)**

| Result | Decision |
|---|---|
| **BCR > 1** | **The project is economically justified** ← |
| **BCR = 1** | The margin |
| **BCR < 1** | **Reject — the costs exceed the benefits in present-value terms** ← |

> **Discounting is essential because the costs occur EARLY (construction) and the benefits occur LATE and over many years — so comparing raw totals would systematically favour projects with distant benefits.**

> **Option (a) makes exactly that error, and it is not a trivial one: for an infrastructure project with a fifty-year benefit stream, the undiscounted ratio can be several times the discounted one.**

**A worked illustration:**

> **A project costs Rs 500 lakh now and yields Rs 60 lakh a year for 20 years. At a 12 per cent discount rate:**

| Quantity | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Present worth factor for 20 years at 12 %** | **(1 − 1.12⁻²⁰)/0.12** | **7.469** ← |
| **Present worth of benefits** | **60 × 7.469** | **Rs 448 lakh** ← |
| **Present worth of costs** | Already at present | **Rs 500 lakh** |
| **BCR** | **448/500** | **0.90 — REJECT** ← |
| **UNDISCOUNTED ratio, for comparison** | **(60 × 20)/500 = 1,200/500** | **2.40 — apparently excellent** ← |

> **The undiscounted ratio of 2.40 suggests a strongly worthwhile project; the correct discounted ratio of 0.90 says it should be rejected.**

> **THAT GAP IS THE WHOLE REASON DISCOUNTING IS INSISTED UPON, and it is large precisely because the benefits are spread over decades.**

**The definitional ambiguity in BCR, which is a genuine trap:**

| Treatment of operating and maintenance costs | Formula | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **O&M in the DENOMINATOR (with capital cost)** | **BCR = PW(benefits) / PW(capital + O&M)** ← | **The conventional public-sector definition** |
| **O&M SUBTRACTED from the benefits** | **BCR = PW(benefits − O&M) / PW(capital)** ← | **Gives a DIFFERENT number for the same project** ← |

> **Both are used, and they give different ratios — though they always agree on whether the ratio exceeds 1, since both reduce to the same NPV > 0 condition.**

> **So the BCR's MAGNITUDE is not comparable between projects unless the same definition was used, and any ranking by BCR must state the convention.**

> **That is one reason economists prefer NPV: it is unambiguous, whereas BCR depends on an arbitrary decision about which side of the line a cost falls.**

**BCR against the other appraisal measures:**

| Measure | Best for | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| **NPV** | **Choosing between MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE projects — it measures the VALUE CREATED** ← | Gives no sense of scale or efficiency |
| **BCR** | **RANKING projects under a BUDGET CONSTRAINT — it measures value per rupee spent** ← | **Definitionally ambiguous; can mislead on scale** ← |
| **IRR** | Screening; communicating a return | **Ranks badly between projects of different size; multiple roots possible** ← |
| **Payback** | A rough risk and liquidity check | **Ignores the time value of money AND everything after payback** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS BCR'S PROPER USE AND IT IS A REAL ONE: where a fixed budget must be allocated among many independent projects, ranking by BCR and funding downward maximises the total value obtained.**

> **NPV alone would favour large projects that consume the whole budget; BCR identifies which projects give the most value per rupee, which is exactly the question a constrained budget poses.**

**And the difference between FINANCIAL and ECONOMIC appraisal, which matters greatly for public works:**

| | FINANCIAL analysis | ECONOMIC analysis |
|---|---|---|
| **Viewpoint** | **The project entity — will it pay its way?** ← | **SOCIETY as a whole — is the nation better off?** ← |
| **Prices used** | **MARKET prices, including taxes and subsidies** | **SHADOW (economic) prices, with taxes and subsidies REMOVED** ← |
| **Transfers (taxes, duties, subsidies)** | **Included — they are real cash flows to the entity** | **EXCLUDED — they merely move money within society** ← |
| **EXTERNALITIES** | **Ignored** | **INCLUDED — pollution, time savings, accidents avoided, health effects** ← |
| **Discount rate** | Cost of capital | **Social discount rate** |

> **A ROAD PROJECT ILLUSTRATES THE DIFFERENCE STARKLY: financially it may earn nothing at all, since no toll is charged.**

> **Economically it may be highly beneficial — travel time saved, vehicle operating costs reduced, accidents avoided, market access improved, produce reaching market unspoilt.**

> **So a road that fails every financial test can be an excellent economic investment, and it is the ECONOMIC appraisal that justifies public expenditure on it.**

> **The converse also occurs: a project profitable to its owner because of a subsidy or a tax concession may be a net loss to the country, and only the economic analysis reveals it.**

examTip.trick: **BCR = PW(benefits)/PW(costs), both DISCOUNTED.** Costs come early and benefits late, so undiscounted totals systematically flatter a project — 2.40 against a true 0.90 in the worked example.
examTip.trap: **BCR is definitionally ambiguous** — O&M may sit in the denominator or be netted off the benefits, giving different numbers for the same project. They always agree on whether BCR > 1, but never rank by BCR without stating the convention.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use NPV for MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE choices, BCR for ranking under a BUDGET CONSTRAINT.** And distinguish FINANCIAL from ECONOMIC appraisal: a toll-free road earns nothing financially and may be an excellent economic investment.

questions.stem: The DISCOUNTED PAYBACK PERIOD of a project differs from the simple payback period in that the discounted version:
options: Ignores all cash flows after the payback date
Is always shorter than the simple payback period
Counts only the capital cost and not the operating cost
Accounts for the time value of money, and is therefore always longer than the simple payback period
questions.solution:
**It accounts for the TIME VALUE OF MONEY, and is therefore always LONGER than the simple payback period.**

**Why it must be longer:**

> **Discounting REDUCES the value of every future cash inflow, so the cumulative discounted inflow grows more slowly than the cumulative undiscounted inflow.**

> **It therefore takes LONGER to reach the initial investment — always, without exception.**

> **Option (b) inverts this, and the inversion is impossible: discounting can only make future receipts worth less, never more.**

**A worked comparison:**

> **A project costs Rs 100 lakh and returns Rs 30 lakh a year. Discount rate 10 per cent.**

| Year | Cash flow | Cumulative (simple) | Discount factor | Discounted flow | Cumulative (discounted) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **30** | **30** | **0.909** | **27.3** | **27.3** |
| **2** | **30** | **60** | **0.826** | **24.8** | **52.1** |
| **3** | **30** | **90** | **0.751** | **22.5** | **74.6** |
| **4** | **30** | **120 — recovered** ← | **0.683** | **20.5** | **95.1** |
| **5** | **30** | 150 | **0.621** | **18.6** | **113.7 — recovered** ← |

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE payback** | **Between years 3 and 4 — about 3.3 years** ← |
| **DISCOUNTED payback** | **Between years 4 and 5 — about 4.3 years** ← |

> **A full year longer, on a modest discount rate and a short project — and the gap widens sharply with the discount rate and with the length of the recovery period.**

**What the discounted payback fixes, and what it does NOT:**

| Defect of simple payback | Fixed by discounting? |
|---|---|
| **Ignores the TIME VALUE of money** | **YES — this is precisely what it corrects** ← |
| **IGNORES EVERYTHING AFTER THE PAYBACK DATE** | **NO — the defect remains entirely** ← (option a) |
| **Gives no measure of total value created** | **NO** ← |
| **Provides no ranking between projects of different scale** | NO |

> **OPTION (a) IS THEREFORE TRUE OF BOTH VERSIONS, which is what makes it the best-made distractor: it names a real defect that discounting does nothing to remedy.**

> **And that surviving defect is the serious one for infrastructure: a dam, a bridge or a water supply scheme delivers benefits for fifty years or more, and any payback measure stops counting at year four or five.**

> **A project with modest early returns and enormous later ones will be rejected by payback and accepted by NPV — and for long-lived public assets, NPV is right.**

**Why payback survives despite these defects:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is IMMEDIATELY understood** | **By managers, lenders and committees with no financial training** ← |
| **It is a rough measure of RISK** | **The sooner the money returns, the less exposure to things going wrong** ← |
| **It measures LIQUIDITY** | **How long the organisation's capital is tied up** ← |
| **It needs no forecast beyond the payback date** | **Which is genuinely useful where distant forecasts are worthless** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS PAYBACK'S BEST DEFENCE AND IS RARELY STATED: a cash flow forecast for years 15 to 50 is largely fiction, and NPV gives those fictional numbers real weight in the answer.**

> **Payback deliberately declines to rely on them. In a volatile environment — political instability, uncertain tariffs, rapid technological change — that refusal is a reasonable position rather than an oversight.**

> **The sound practice is to use payback as a SUPPLEMENTARY screen alongside NPV, not as the criterion: NPV to decide whether the project creates value, payback to check how long the organisation's capital is exposed.**

**And the ORDER of the appraisal measures, as a summary:**

| Measure | Accounts for time value? | Counts all cash flows? | Measures value created? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simple payback** | **NO** | **NO** | **NO** |
| **Discounted payback** | **YES** ← | **NO** | **NO** |
| **IRR** | **YES** | **YES** | **NO — a rate, not an amount** ← |
| **BCR** | **YES** | **YES** | **A ratio, not an amount** |
| **NPV** | **YES** | **YES** | **YES — an amount, in money** ← |

> **The table reads as a progression, and NPV is the only measure that answers all three questions — which is why it is the theoretically correct criterion and why every other measure is best understood as a partial view used for a particular purpose.**

examTip.trick: **Discounting shrinks every future inflow, so recovery takes LONGER — always.** Option (b) is impossible: discounting can only reduce the value of future receipts.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is true of BOTH versions** — discounting fixes the time value defect and does NOTHING about ignoring cash flows after the payback date. For a fifty-year asset that remaining defect is the serious one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Payback's best defence is that it refuses to rely on year 15-50 forecasts, which are largely fiction.** Use it as a SUPPLEMENTARY risk and liquidity screen alongside NPV — never as the criterion.

questions.stem: In PERT, an activity has an optimistic time of 4 days, a most likely time of 6 days and a pessimistic time of 14 days. Its EXPECTED time is:
options: 6 days
7 days
8 days
9 days
questions.solution:
**7 days.**

**The computation:**

> **t_e = (t_o + 4 t_m + t_p) / 6**

> **t_e = (4 + 4×6 + 14)/6 = (4 + 24 + 14)/6 = 42/6 = 7 days** ←

| Distractor | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **6 days** | **The MOST LIKELY time t_m taken by itself** ← |
| **8 days** | **The simple arithmetic mean (4 + 6 + 14)/3** ← |
| **9 days** | **The midpoint of the optimistic and pessimistic times, (4 + 14)/2** ← |

> **Each is a plausible way of "averaging" the three estimates, and only the weighted form is correct.**

**Why the weighting is 1 : 4 : 1:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The three estimates are taken to describe a BETA distribution** ← | **Which can be skewed, unlike a normal distribution** |
| **The MOST LIKELY time is weighted FOUR times** | **It is the mode, and by far the best-informed of the three estimates** ← |
| **The extremes carry weight 1 each** | **They pull the mean toward whichever tail is longer** ← |
| **Total weight 6** | Hence the divisor |

> **THE SKEW IS THE POINT OF THE WHOLE SCHEME, and this example shows it clearly: the pessimistic time is 8 days ABOVE the most likely, while the optimistic is only 2 days BELOW it.**

> **That asymmetry is realistic — an activity can go wrong in many ways and unexpectedly badly, but it can only go so right.**

> **So the expected time (7) exceeds the most likely time (6), pulled upward by the long pessimistic tail. A symmetric treatment would miss that entirely.**

> **The general lesson for programming: TASK DURATIONS ARE RIGHT-SKEWED, so the expected duration is always somewhat longer than the duration one first thinks of — which is a mathematical statement of why projects overrun more often than they underrun.**

**The VARIANCE, which is the other half of PERT:**

> **σ = (t_p − t_o)/6, so σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

> **Here σ = (14 − 4)/6 = 1.667 days, and σ² = 2.78 days².**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **The range t_p − t_o is taken to span SIX standard deviations** ← | **±3σ, which covers 99.7 per cent of a normal distribution** |
| **A WIDE range means a HIGH variance** | **The activity is uncertain** ← |
| **The PROJECT's variance is the SUM of the variances of the CRITICAL activities only** ← | **Because variances of independent events add** ← |
