| **The project's standard deviation is the SQUARE ROOT of that sum** | **NOT the sum of the standard deviations** ← |

> **The distinction in the last row is a standard error: VARIANCES add, standard deviations do not.**

> **So a critical path of nine activities each with σ = 1 has a project variance of 9 and a project standard deviation of 3 — not 9.**

**Using the variance — the probability of completion:**

> **Z = (target date − expected date) / σ_project, and the probability is read from the standard normal table.**

| Z | Probability of completing by the target |
|---|---|
| **−1.0** | **16 %** |
| **0** | **50 per cent — the EXPECTED date** ← |
| **+1.0** | **84 %** ← |
| **+1.64** | **95 %** ← |
| **+2.0** | **98 %** |

> **THE Z = 0 ROW IS THE RESULT WORTH CARRYING AWAY: the probability of finishing by the EXPECTED completion date is only 50 PER CENT.**

> **A programme quoted at its computed duration is therefore as likely to be late as early — which is not a promise but a coin toss.**

> **A contractual completion date should be set at a higher confidence: Z = +1.64 for 95 per cent certainty, which for the nine-activity example above means adding 1.64 × 3 = 4.9 days of float to the expected duration.**

> **A contractor who programmes to the mean and commits to it will be late on half of all projects, and will pay liquidated damages on those — which is a systematic and entirely avoidable commercial error.**

**And PERT's own limitations, stated fairly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **It considers the variance of the CRITICAL PATH only** | **A near-critical path with high variance can easily become critical, and PERT ignores it — so PERT is OPTIMISTIC** ← |
| **The three estimates are subjective** | Garbage in, garbage out |
| **Activities are assumed INDEPENDENT** | **In reality a delay in one often shares a cause with another** ← |
| **The beta distribution assumption is a convenience** | Not derived from data |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: because PERT ignores the other paths, and any of them might overrun enough to become critical, the true probability of completing on time is LOWER than PERT computes.**

> **The remedy in modern practice is MONTE CARLO SIMULATION, which samples every activity's duration many thousands of times and observes how often each path governs — capturing exactly the effect PERT's single-path treatment misses.**

examTip.trick: **t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6 = (4 + 24 + 14)/6 = 7 days.** The distractors are t_m alone (6), the simple mean (8), and the midpoint of the extremes (9).
examTip.trap: **VARIANCES add; standard deviations do NOT.** Nine critical activities each with σ = 1 give a project σ of 3, not 9. And σ = (t_p − t_o)/6, the range spanning ±3σ.
examTip.mnemonic: **The probability of finishing by the EXPECTED date is only 50 %** — set contractual dates at Z = +1.64 for 95 %. And PERT is OPTIMISTIC because it ignores near-critical paths, which is what Monte Carlo simulation fixes.

questions.stem: An activity has a normal duration of 10 days at a cost of Rs 40,000, and a crash duration of 7 days at a cost of Rs 52,000. Its COST SLOPE is:
options: Rs 1,714 per day
Rs 12,000 per day
Rs 5,200 per day
Rs 4,000 per day
questions.solution:
**Rs 4,000 per day.**

**The computation:**

> **Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) / (normal time − crash time)**

> **= (52,000 − 40,000) / (10 − 7) = 12,000 / 3 = Rs 4,000 per day** ←

| Distractor | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **Rs 12,000 per day** | **The TOTAL extra cost, not divided by the days saved** ← |
| **Rs 1,714 per day** | **12,000 divided by the CRASH TIME (7) instead of the time SAVED (3)** ← |
| **Rs 5,200 per day** | **52,000 ÷ 10 — the crash cost over the normal duration** ← |

> **The denominator is the TIME SAVED, not either duration — which is the point the distractors probe.**

**How the cost slope is used — the crashing procedure:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Find the critical path and the normal project duration** ← |
| **2** | **Compute the cost slope of every CRITICAL activity** ← |
| **3** | **Crash the critical activity with the LOWEST cost slope, by one time unit** ← |
| **4** | **RE-EXAMINE the network — a new path may have become critical** ← |
| **5** | **Repeat, and where two paths are critical, crash BOTH (or a shared activity)** ← |
| **6** | **STOP when the direct cost of crashing exceeds the indirect cost saved** ← |

> **TWO POINTS IN THIS PROCEDURE ARE WHERE MONEY IS WASTED IN PRACTICE:**

> **First, STEP 2 — crashing a NON-CRITICAL activity buys nothing at all. It shortens an activity that already has float, so the project finishes on exactly the same day and the money is simply spent.**

> **That is the commonest waste in project acceleration: the manager accelerates whatever is visibly behind, without checking whether it is on the critical path.**

> **Second, STEP 4 — as the critical path shortens, another path becomes critical, and from that point BOTH must be crashed together. The cost per day saved therefore JUMPS, and the crashing curve steepens at each such transition.**

**Why crashing is worth doing at all — the INDIRECT costs:**

| Cost type | Behaviour with project duration |
|---|---|
| **DIRECT costs (labour, material, plant for the activities)** | **RISE as the duration is shortened — overtime, extra shifts, more plant, less efficient working** ← |
| **INDIRECT costs (site establishment, supervision, plant hire, financing, overheads)** | **FALL as the duration is shortened — they accrue per DAY** ← |
| **PENALTY / liquidated damages avoided, or a BONUS earned** | **Falls, or is gained** ← |
| **TOTAL cost** | **Falls, reaches a MINIMUM, then rises — and that minimum is the OPTIMUM duration** ← |

> **So the object of crashing is not the shortest possible programme but the LEAST-COST programme, and the optimum is generally somewhat shorter than the normal duration and considerably longer than the fully crashed one.**

| Duration | Name |
|---|---|
| **NORMAL duration** | **Least DIRECT cost** ← |
| **OPTIMUM duration** | **Least TOTAL cost — the target** ← |
| **CRASH duration** | **The shortest technically achievable, at the greatest direct cost** ← |

**The practical limits on crashing, which the arithmetic does not show:**

| Limit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Some activities CANNOT be crashed at all** | **Concrete curing, a delivery lead time, a statutory approval period** ← |
| **Crashing reduces PRODUCTIVITY** | **Overtime working produces diminishing and eventually negative returns; a second shift is less efficient than the first** ← |
| **Crashing increases the ACCIDENT rate** | **Fatigue, congestion, rushed work — a real and documented effect** ← |
| **Crashing increases DEFECTS and rework** | Which may cost more time than was saved |
| **Site CONGESTION** | **Doubling the labour on a confined site does not double the output** ← |

> **THE SAFETY AND QUALITY CONSEQUENCES IN THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE NOT CAPTURED BY THE COST SLOPE AT ALL, and they deserve to be stated plainly because the arithmetic can otherwise appear to justify any degree of acceleration.**

> **Sustained overtime beyond about 50 hours a week produces measurably lower output per hour and a sharply higher accident rate, so the apparent gain is partly illusory and the cost includes a risk the cost slope does not price.**

> **An acceleration programme should therefore be assessed for its effect on safety and quality as well as on cost, and a proposal to crash a project by working the same crew longer — rather than by adding resources or changing method — deserves particular scepticism.**

examTip.trick: **Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost)/(normal time − crash time) = 12,000/3 = Rs 4,000 per day.** The denominator is the time SAVED, not either duration.
examTip.trap: **Crashing a NON-CRITICAL activity buys nothing** — it has float, so the project finishes on the same day. And when a second path becomes critical, both must be crashed and the cost per day JUMPS.
examTip.mnemonic: **Direct costs RISE and indirect costs FALL as the duration shortens — the total has a MINIMUM, and that is the optimum.** The cost slope does not price the higher ACCIDENT and DEFECT rates that acceleration brings.

questions.stem: In construction quality management, QUALITY ASSURANCE (QA) differs from QUALITY CONTROL (QC) in that QA is:
options: Process-oriented and preventive
The inspection and testing of the finished product
Carried out only by the client's representative
Applicable only to imported materials
questions.solution:
**PROCESS-oriented and PREVENTIVE** — it establishes the systems and procedures that ensure quality is built in, so that defects do not arise in the first place.

**The two compared:**

| | QUALITY ASSURANCE | QUALITY CONTROL |
|---|---|---|
| **Orientation** | **PROCESS — how the work is done** ← | **PRODUCT — what has been produced** ← (option b) |
| **Timing** | **BEFORE and DURING — preventive** ← | **AFTER the work — detective** ← |
| **Question asked** | **"Are we doing the right things, in the right way?"** ← | **"Did this item come out right?"** ← |
| **Activities** | **Procedures, method statements, training, approved suppliers, audits, calibration systems, document control** ← | **Sampling, TESTING, inspection, measurement, cube crushing, acceptance** ← |
| **Responsibility** | **MANAGEMENT — it is a system** ← | **Inspectors and testing staff** |
| **Finds defects?** | **PREVENTS them** ← | **FINDS them, after they exist** ← |

> **THE ESSENTIAL DISTINCTION IN ONE LINE: QA STOPS DEFECTS HAPPENING; QC CATCHES THEM AFTER THEY HAVE.**

> **Both are necessary — a system with QA alone has no verification, and a system with QC alone spends its time discovering defects it did nothing to prevent.**

**Why prevention is so much cheaper — the escalating cost of a defect:**

| When the defect is caught | Relative cost to correct |
|---|---|
| **At DESIGN stage** | **1** ← |
| **During procurement** | **10** |
| **During CONSTRUCTION, before the work is covered** | **100** ← |
| **After completion, in service** | **1,000 and more** ← |

> **The orders of magnitude vary between studies, and the PATTERN is entirely consistent and is the whole argument for QA: the earlier a defect is prevented or found, the less it costs, and the ratio is measured in powers of ten rather than percentages.**

> **A reinforcement error caught by an inspection before the pour costs an hour's delay. The same error discovered after the concrete has hardened may require demolition of the member, and after the building is occupied it may be uncorrectable at any reasonable price.**

> **THAT IS WHY THE HOLD POINT — a stage at which work may not proceed until it has been inspected and released — is the most valuable single device in construction quality management.**

**The COST OF QUALITY, which formalises the argument:**

| Category | Contents |
|---|---|
| **PREVENTION costs** | **Training, procedures, planning, supplier assessment — QA** ← |
| **APPRAISAL costs** | **Inspection, testing, calibration — QC** ← |
| **INTERNAL FAILURE costs** | **Rework, scrap, re-testing — defects found BEFORE handover** ← |
| **EXTERNAL FAILURE costs** | **Defects found AFTER handover: repairs, claims, liability, reputation** ← |

> **The total cost of quality typically runs at 5 to 15 per cent of a construction project's value, and the great majority of it falls in the two FAILURE categories.**

> **Increasing spend on PREVENTION reduces the failure costs by considerably more than it costs, which is why quality management is not an overhead but an investment — the same argument structure as disaster mitigation and preventive road maintenance.**

> **And it faces the same institutional obstacle: prevention's benefit is a defect that never occurred, which no one sees, while inspection and rework are visible activity.**

**The documents that constitute a QA system on a construction project:**

| Document | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **QUALITY PLAN (project quality plan)** | **The overarching document — what will be controlled, how, by whom** ← |
| **METHOD STATEMENTS** | **How each operation will be carried out safely and correctly** ← |
| **INSPECTION AND TEST PLAN (ITP)** | **Every check, its standard, its frequency, its acceptance criterion, and who signs** ← |
| **HOLD POINTS and witness points in the ITP** | **A HOLD point stops the work until released; a WITNESS point invites attendance but does not stop it** ← |
| **Checklists and pour cards** | The record at each stage |
| **Calibration records** | For every instrument used in testing |
| **NON-CONFORMANCE REPORTS (NCRs)** | **Recording a defect, its disposition and its corrective action** ← |
| **As-built records and the handover dossier** | The permanent evidence |

> **THE NON-CONFORMANCE REPORT DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE, because its purpose is widely misunderstood on site: an NCR is not a punishment and not an accusation.**

> **It is the record that a defect existed, what was decided about it (repair, rework, accept as-is with justification, or reject), and — most importantly — what CORRECTIVE ACTION was taken to stop it recurring.**

> **A project with NO non-conformance reports is not a project without defects; it is a project that is not recording them, which is a far more serious condition.**

> **The useful measure is not the number of NCRs raised but whether the same one keeps recurring — because a repeated NCR means the corrective action addressed the symptom and not the cause, which is precisely the failure QA exists to prevent.**

Establishing systems and procedures so that defects do not arise.

examTip.trick: **QA STOPS defects happening (process, preventive, management systems); QC CATCHES them after they exist (product, testing, inspection).** Option (b) defines QC.
examTip.trap: **The cost of a defect escalates by POWERS OF TEN** — 1 at design, 100 during construction, 1,000 in service. That ratio, not a percentage, is the argument for prevention.
examTip.mnemonic: **A HOLD POINT stops work until released; a WITNESS point does not** — the hold point is the most valuable device in site quality management. And a project with NO non-conformance reports is not defect-free, it is not recording them.

questions.stem: In a DESIGN AND BUILD (EPC) contract, compared with a traditional contract in which the employer provides the design:
options: The employer retains full responsibility for the design's adequacy
The contractor's price can be freely varied as the design develops
The contractor takes responsibility for both the design and the construction
No contract conditions or specifications are required
questions.solution:
**The CONTRACTOR takes responsibility for BOTH the design and the construction**, giving the employer a SINGLE POINT of responsibility.

**Traditional against design-and-build:**

| Aspect | TRADITIONAL (employer designs) | DESIGN AND BUILD / EPC |
|---|---|---|
| **Who designs** | **The employer's consultant** | **The CONTRACTOR** ← |
| **Responsibility for design adequacy** | **The EMPLOYER (through the consultant)** ← (option a) | **The CONTRACTOR** ← |
| **Points of responsibility for the employer** | **TWO — designer and builder, who may blame each other** ← | **ONE** ← |
| **Price certainty** | **Lower — variations arise from design development** | **HIGHER — usually a lump sum against a performance specification** ← |
| **Employer's control over detail** | **HIGH** ← | **LOWER — the contractor chooses how to meet the specification** ← |
| **Programme** | **Longer — design must largely finish before tendering** | **SHORTER — design and construction OVERLAP** ← |
| **Scope for the contractor's buildability input** | Limited | **Substantial — a real source of economy** ← |
| **Suits** | **Complex, bespoke or architecturally led projects** ← | **Well-defined, functional or repetitive projects; process plant; power stations** ← |

> **THE SINGLE POINT OF RESPONSIBILITY IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE PRINCIPAL ATTRACTION, and its value is best seen when something goes wrong:**

> **Under a traditional contract, a defect may be a design fault or a workmanship fault, and establishing which requires investigation and often litigation — with the designer and the contractor each blaming the other while the employer bears the delay.**

> **Under design and build there is no such gap: the contractor is responsible for the works, however the fault arose.**

> **That is a genuine and substantial benefit, and the employer pays for it in reduced control and, usually, in a risk premium built into the price.**

**The EMPLOYER'S REQUIREMENTS, which become the critical document:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **A PERFORMANCE specification — what the works must ACHIEVE, not how** ← |
| **Why it is critical** | **It is the ONLY definition of what the employer will get** ← |
| **A vague requirement** | **Will be met at the LOWEST standard the wording permits** ← |
| **An over-prescriptive requirement** | **Removes the contractor's design freedom, so the employer keeps the design risk after all** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE THE CENTRAL DIFFICULTY OF DESIGN AND BUILD, and it is a real tension:**

> **Specify too loosely, and the contractor — quite legitimately — delivers the cheapest thing that complies.**

> **Specify too tightly, and the contractor is merely building the employer's design while nominally carrying its risk, which is the worst of both arrangements: the employer has lost control of the detail and kept the design liability in substance.**

> **Drafting the Employer's Requirements well is therefore the single most important task in a design-and-build procurement, and it needs as much professional skill as designing the works would have done.**

> **This is why the arrangement suits FUNCTIONAL projects — a power station, a water treatment plant, a warehouse — whose output can be specified in performance terms, and suits an architecturally led building far less well, where the requirement is about appearance and quality that resist performance wording.**

**The broader family of procurement routes:**

| Route | Note |
|---|---|
| **TRADITIONAL (design-bid-build)** | **Sequential; the employer designs, then tenders** ← |
| **DESIGN AND BUILD / EPC (turnkey)** | **This question** ← |
| **MANAGEMENT CONTRACTING / construction management** | **A manager is engaged for a fee; the works are let in packages — fast, flexible, but the employer keeps most of the risk** ← |
| **BOT / PPP concession** | **The contractor also FINANCES and OPERATES, and is repaid from revenue** ← |
| **Framework and term contracts** | For repeated work over a period |
| **Partnering / alliancing** | **Collaborative, with shared risk and gain; suits long or uncertain programmes** ← |

> **The progression through this list is one of TRANSFERRING MORE RISK AND RESPONSIBILITY TO THE CONTRACTOR — from construction only, to design and construction, to finance and operation as well.**

> **And the governing principle is the one met under risk management: EACH RISK SHOULD BE ALLOCATED TO THE PARTY BEST ABLE TO CONTROL IT.**

> **A contractor can control workmanship, methods and — under design and build — the design. A contractor cannot control ground conditions, changes in law, or the demand for a toll road.**

> **Transferring uncontrollable risk simply produces a higher price, a weaker bidder, or a dispute when it materialises — which is why the most aggressive risk transfer is rarely the cheapest outcome for the employer, however attractive it appears at tender.**

examTip.trick: **One contractor for both design and construction, so the employer has a SINGLE point of responsibility** — no gap for designer and builder to blame each other across. Option (a) describes the traditional route.
examTip.trap: **The EMPLOYER'S REQUIREMENTS are the only definition of what will be delivered.** Too vague and the contractor legitimately builds the cheapest compliant thing; too prescriptive and the employer keeps the design risk in substance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Each procurement route transfers more risk to the contractor — but allocate each risk to the party best able to CONTROL it.** Ground conditions and demand are not controllable, so transferring them buys a higher price and a dispute, not safety.

questions.stem: An engineer engaged by a client to supervise construction is offered a share in the profits of the contractor executing that work. Under any engineering code of conduct, the engineer must:
options: Accept, provided the work is carried out to specification
Decline the offer outright and disclose it to the client
Accept, provided the amount is small
Accept, but disclose it only if a dispute later arises
questions.solution:
**DECLINE** — the arrangement creates a direct CONFLICT OF INTEREST between the engineer's duty to the client and their own financial interest.

**Why this particular arrangement is indefensible:**

> **The supervising engineer's function is to judge, impartially, whether the contractor's work complies — and to reject it where it does not.**

| The engineer's duty requires | The profit share creates an incentive to |
|---|---|
| **Reject defective work** | **Accept it, since rejection costs the contractor money — and now the engineer too** ← |
| **Certify only quantities properly executed** | **Certify generously** ← |
| **Value variations fairly** | **Value them favourably to the contractor** ← |
| **Enforce the programme and apply damages for delay** | **Not to** ← |

> **EVERY ONE OF THE ENGINEER'S PROFESSIONAL FUNCTIONS IS DIRECTLY OPPOSED BY THE FINANCIAL INTEREST, which is why this is not a matter of degree.**

> **Option (c)'s "provided the amount is small" fails on the point that matters: the test is not whether the engineer WOULD in fact be influenced, but whether a reasonable observer might REASONABLY BELIEVE their judgement could be affected.**

> **Professional impartiality must be evident, not merely felt — because the client and the public cannot see inside the engineer's mind and must be able to rely on the arrangement rather than on the individual's character.**

> **Option (d) fails on timing: disclosure after a dispute is worthless. The purpose of disclosure is to let the affected party decide, IN ADVANCE, whether to proceed.**

**The general treatment of conflicts of interest:**

| Step | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **1 — IDENTIFY** | **Recognise the conflict, including a POTENTIAL or PERCEIVED one** ← |
| **2 — DISCLOSE it FULLY and PROMPTLY** | **To all affected parties, in writing, BEFORE proceeding** ← |
| **3 — Where the conflict is manageable** | **Proceed only with the INFORMED WRITTEN CONSENT of all parties** ← |
| **4 — Where it is NOT manageable** | **WITHDRAW from one of the roles** ← |

> **Not every conflict requires withdrawal — many are manageable by disclosure and consent. But the case in this question is not among them: an interest in the profits of the party one is engaged to police cannot be cured by disclosure, because the impairment is total.**

**Other conflicts an engineer will meet:**

| Situation | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **Payment from more than one party for the same service** | **PROHIBITED without the knowledge and consent of all** ← |
| **A financial interest in a supplier or a product being specified** | **Must be DISCLOSED; usually the engineer should not specify it** ← |
| **Acting for two clients with competing interests** | **Disclose; usually decline one** ← |
| **A GIFT or hospitality from a contractor or supplier** | **Refuse anything that could reasonably appear to influence judgement** ← |
| **A relative employed by the contractor** | **Disclose; may require reassignment** ← |
| **Being both designer and independent checker** | **The check is not independent — a different person or firm is required** ← |
| **Moving to work for a contractor one has been supervising** | **Disclose; observe any restriction on handling matters one dealt with** ← |

> **THE GIFTS ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN RATIONALISED, and it is worth setting out the test rather than a monetary threshold:**

> **The question is not "would this influence me?" — to which the honest answer is almost always no — but "would a reasonable outside observer, knowing of this, doubt my impartiality?"**

> **A modest customary courtesy — a cup of tea, a calendar, a working lunch — passes that test. A paid trip, a substantial gift, repeated hospitality, or anything offered around the time of a decision does not.**

> **A useful practical rule is the publicity test: WOULD I BE COMFORTABLE IF THIS APPEARED IN A NEWSPAPER, or were known to the other tenderers? If not, decline it.**

**Why impartiality is structurally important, beyond the individual:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The supervising engineer often acts as CERTIFIER and as an impartial decider between the parties** ← | **A quasi-judicial function under most standard forms of contract** ← |
| **The employer relies on the certificate to pay** | And the contractor relies on it to be paid |
| **Neither party can verify the work independently** | **They rely on the engineer's judgement** ← |
| **If that judgement is bought, the whole contractual mechanism fails** | ← |

> **THE QUASI-JUDICIAL ROLE IN THE FIRST ROW IS WHY THE STANDARD IS SO STRICT: under the traditional forms of contract the engineer is paid by the employer and yet is required to act FAIRLY BETWEEN the employer and the contractor when certifying and deciding claims.**

> **That is already an uncomfortable position, sustainable only through a strong professional norm of impartiality — and any financial interest on either side destroys it entirely.**

> **It is also why modern contract forms increasingly separate the roles, appointing an independent adjudicator or dispute board for decisions rather than relying on the employer's own engineer — a structural recognition that the traditional arrangement asks a great deal of the individual, and that good systems should not depend on exceptional personal virtue.**

It creates a CONFLICT OF INTEREST between the engineer's duty to the client and their personal financial interest.

examTip.trick: **Every one of the supervising engineer's duties — rejecting defective work, certifying quantities, valuing variations, applying damages — is directly opposed by an interest in the contractor's profits.** It cannot be cured by disclosure.
examTip.trap: **The test is not whether you WOULD be influenced, but whether a reasonable observer might REASONABLY BELIEVE you could be.** So "the amount is small" (option c) misses the point, and disclosure after a dispute (option d) is worthless.
examTip.mnemonic: **IDENTIFY → DISCLOSE fully and in advance → proceed only with informed consent → otherwise WITHDRAW.** For gifts, apply the publicity test: would you be comfortable if the other tenderers knew?

questions.stem: Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, a person who practises as an engineer in Nepal WITHOUT being registered with the Council:
options: Is permitted to do so if supervised by a registered engineer
May practise freely, since registration is voluntary
Is permitted to do so for projects below a certain value
Commits an offence — registration is a legal precondition for practising and for using the title
questions.solution:
**COMMITS AN OFFENCE** — registration with the Nepal Engineering Council is a LEGAL PRECONDITION for practising engineering and for using the title of engineer.

**The central prohibition:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **No person may PRACTISE as an engineer without registration** ← | **The Act's core requirement** |
| **No person may USE THE TITLE of engineer without registration** ← | **The title is protected, not merely the activity** ← |
| **Registration requires a qualification RECOGNISED by the Council** | **From an institution the Council has recognised** ← |
| **The certificate must be RENEWED periodically** | **A lapsed registration is, legally, no registration** ← |
| **Practising while unregistered, or after removal, is an offence** | ← |

> **Option (b) states the opposite of the Act, and options (a) and (c) invent exemptions that do not exist — a value threshold or a supervision arrangement does not license an unregistered person to practise.**

> **(A registered engineer may of course EMPLOY unregistered staff and take professional responsibility for their work — that is quite different from an unregistered person practising in their own right and certifying their own designs.)**

**Where the requirement actually bites in daily work:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Signing or certifying DRAWINGS and DESIGNS** | **A municipality will not accept building drawings without a currently registered engineer's signature** ← |
| **Submitting a building permit application** | ← |
| **Being named as the engineer on a contract or a tender** | Prequalification requires registered staff |
| **Supervising and certifying construction** | ← |
| **Giving expert evidence, or acting as a consultant** | ← |

> **THE RENEWAL POINT DESERVES EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT CATCHES PRACTISING ENGINEERS OUT: an engineer whose registration has lapsed is in exactly the same legal position as one who never registered.**

> **Anything certified during a lapsed period is open to challenge, the engineer's professional indemnity insurance may not respond, and the client may have grounds for complaint.**

> **The practical discipline is to treat the renewal date as a fixed professional obligation of the same class as an insurance renewal — a diary entry, not a matter of memory.**

**Why the state grants and enforces such a monopoly:**

| Justification | Note |
|---|---|
| **The public CANNOT ASSESS an engineer's competence** | **Registration is the state's assurance that a minimum standard has been met** ← |
| **The consequences of incompetence fall on THIRD PARTIES** | **Not on the person who chose the engineer** ← |
| **Failures are CATASTROPHIC and IRREVERSIBLE** | **A collapsed building kills; the remedy arrives too late** ← |
| **There is a commercial incentive to cut corners** | Regulation supplies the counterweight |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DECISIVE ARGUMENT AND IT DISTINGUISHES ENGINEERING FROM MOST OCCUPATIONS: if a tailor makes a poor suit, the customer bears it and takes their business elsewhere.**

> **If an engineer designs a poor building, the people who live in it bear it — and they never chose the engineer, never saw the drawings, and could not have judged them.**

> **Markets protect the parties to a transaction; they do not protect those who are not party to it. Regulation exists to fill precisely that gap, and in a country as seismically exposed as Nepal the gap is a matter of life and death.**

**THE BARGAIN THIS REPRESENTS, which is the closing idea:**

| The state grants | The profession undertakes |
|---|---|
| **The EXCLUSIVE RIGHT to practise, which restricts competition and protects the members' livelihood** ← | **To maintain standards of competence and conduct** ← |
| **Self-regulation and the protected title** | **To DISCIPLINE its own members** ← |
| **Public standing and trust** | **To place the PUBLIC's safety above its members' commercial interests** ← |

> **A profession that fails to keep its side of that bargain forfeits the justification for its privileges — which is why the Council's disciplinary function is central rather than incidental, and why a license has force only because it can be TAKEN AWAY.**

> **And the practice that most directly hollows it out is one every Nepali engineer will encounter: being asked to SIGN drawings prepared by someone else, for a fee, without having designed or checked them.**

> **That is a plain breach — a certificate is a statement of personal professional judgement — and it is also the mechanism by which the whole regulatory system is defeated from within.**

> **A register whose members will sign anything offers no protection whatever. The buildings that fall in the next earthquake will all have been signed for, and the signatures will have meant nothing.**

> **That is the clearest possible statement of why registration and ethics are one subject rather than two, and it is a fitting note on which to close this set.**

examTip.trick: **Registration is a LEGAL PRECONDITION for both practising and using the TITLE.** Options (a) and (c) invent exemptions — a value threshold or supervision — that the Act does not contain.
examTip.trap: **A LAPSED registration is legally no registration** — anything certified in that period is open to challenge and the indemnity insurance may not respond. Treat renewal as a diary entry, not a memory test.
examTip.mnemonic: **Markets protect the parties to a transaction; regulation protects those who are NOT party to it** — the people who live in the building never chose the engineer. And signing drawings one has not designed or checked defeats the whole register from within.
